The arrangement for this purpose may be made by a roller, or pipe, sliding on the rope, and pushed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> so as to open the handles of the clip and tighten its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, when the person holds by the roller and draws it down (Plate CX. fig. 13); and, on the contrary, the clip may be opened by pressing on the handles with the other hand, or with the thighs; or any other simple mode of regulating the clip may be adopted, provided that it be not liable to be misunderstood, or misapplied in a moment of confusion. After all, a rope <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LADDER">ladder</a> would perhaps be preferable, as not being liable to be deranged; it is often kept ready made in the shops; and in the absence of any other rope, a common bed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CORD">cord</a> will generally be found strong enough to support the weight even of a stout <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>; for a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> inch rope may be safely trusted with two hundred weight, and ought, indeed, to support three times as much if new and good. Sect. II.—External Means of Escape from Fire.

NECKER

Pages 71-73

a well known statesman and financier of France. He was born, 30th September 1732, at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>, of a respectable family, originally from the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Germany. At the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of fifteen he quitted Geneva, and proceeded to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> with a view to push his fortune in that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. He entered first into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BANKING">banking</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Vernet, and afterwards into that of Thelluson, of which he became the cashier, and at length a partner. On the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Thelluson, he established a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> on his own account, by which he accumulated a very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> fortune. After twenty years of unremitting <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to business, he married a Protestant lady of respectable family, but in reduced circumstances, the patrimonial estate having been lost in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the revocation of the edict of Nantes. With this lady he appears to have enjoyed the highest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>. A short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, he was named minister of the republic of Geneva at Paris; and in accepting of this employment, he refused the emoluments which were attached to it,—a degree of forbearance not very usual in public men, but in which he resolutely persisted during the whole course of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Two works which he published, namely, *A Eulogium on Colbert*, and a treatise *On the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEGISLATION">Legislation</a> and Trade of Corn*, had greatly spread the reputation of his political talents; and he had fortunately succeeded in adjusting some differences between the East <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIA">India</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a> and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">Crown</a>, in such a manner as to receive the approbation of both parties,—a circumstance which added to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of his character. About this time the disorder in the state of the French finances had become so alarming, that it was found necessary to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> through the routine of official promotion, and to choose able men for the public <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> wherever they could be found. These inducements so far outweighed the objections to M. Necker, as a foreigner and a Protestant, that, after some private conversations with M. Maurepas, he was, in 1776, appointed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTOR">Director</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">Treasury</a>, and in the following year, Director-general of the Finances. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> object of M. Necker was to introduce order and economy in the public management. With this view, he found himself compelled either to suppress useless offices, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to diminish emoluments; and his retrenchments drew on him the enmity of all those who suffered by his economical reforms. A party was formed against him, chiefly composed of rapacious courtiers; and though the repeal of several oppressive imposts had conciliated the general goodwill of the people, he was daily the object of malicious libels. His severe <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> of economy had also excited the dislike of the minister M. Maurepas; though others ascribe his hostility to a different cause; namely, to his disappointment at not finding in Necker that subserviency which he expected from a person of his comparatively obscure origin, and a Protestant. Whatever was the reason, the minister was among the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of his enemies, and he is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> by his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, Madame de Stael, with secretly instigating those libellous attacks of which M. Necker was the object. To enable him, according to Madame de Stael, the better to struggle with his opponents, he requested some signal mark of royal favour, such as a seat in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">Council</a>, which was granted. This demand on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Necker gave rise to new and acrimonious discussions; in the course of which he tendered his resignation, after he had been in office five years. Others give a different account of this transaction. Under the influence, it is said, of that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> for popular applause, which was the torment of his life, he published, in 1781, the well-known piece on the state of the Finances entitled Le Compte Rendu au Roi, of which an immense number of copies were sold. Elated by this success, he made his demand for a seat in the Council, but was objected to on the ground of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. Being persuaded that this scruple would be abandoned, he persisted, and offered his resignation, which was accepted, and he became in this manner, as is alleged, the dupe of his presumption. The enemies of Necker reproached him with indulging, during his short administration, his passion for popularity at the expense of the public <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>. The great point which he laboured to establish in his Compte Rendu was, that there was no deficit in the public revenue, and that there was no <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> for additional taxes. In lieu of new impositions, he is charged with supplying the public necessities by the expedient of large loans,—postponing, in this manner, the evil <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, but accumulating under prosperity a progressive load of debt, which, sooner or later, must be provided for by adequate taxes,—and all this to procure a temporary popularity at the expense of his rivals. Notwithstanding these objections, he had numerous partizans, especially among the men of letters, who regarded his elevation to power as the triumph of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and liberal principles over aristocratical <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a>. After his resignation, he retired to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, where he purchased the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARONY">barony</a> of Copet. In 1784, he published an able <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, further illustrating his financial policy, entitled De l'Administration des Finances. This work, of which 80,000 copies were speedily sold, served to support the reputation of his plans, and also to keep together his adherents, whose numbers formed a counterpoise to the influence of his enemies at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>. In 1787, M. de Calonne convoked the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">Assembly</a> of the Notables, and in his opening speech to that body, he impeached the accuracy of the statements contained in the Compte Rendu. It was not to be supposed that M. Necker would quietly submit to this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>. He sent a memorial on the subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, with various other papers, for the purpose of proving the correctness of his calculations. His majesty having read these documents, requested that they might not be published; a proposition which by no means suited the views of M. Necker. His statements were accordingly printed, on which he was exiled, by a lettre de cachet, forty leagues from Paris. M. de Calonne did not, however, remain <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> in power; and the Archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOULOUSE">Toulouse</a>, by whom he was succeeded, was also obliged to resign, and to make way for M. Necker, the favourite of the people, who was reinstated in his former <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST">post</a> in August 1788. A new and remarkable era was now about to open in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> both of France and of the world. The writings of the French philosophers and men of letters had gradually given currency to notions of constitutional freedom. The people could no longer endure, like their forefathers, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONDAGE">bondage</a> of feudal privileges, by which the few acquired the power of oppressing the many. They had become jealous and discontented, and were deeply irritated at the insolence and oppression of the aristocratical body; and with those indignant feelings were mingled, in the minds of the popular leaders, the brilliant visions of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECULATIVE">speculative</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REFORM">reform</a>. But so long as the people wanted a legitimate organ through which their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> could be heard, it was clear that whatever might be their feelings, they could make little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> on the measures of the state. What was wanting in this respect was now about to be supplied; and the popular voice, hitherto so little considered, was, through the representative body, to become the predominant influence in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. At this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> the French Government was assailed by a complication of difficulties, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of which was the impracticability of raising the necessary supplies, and the danger of an immediate bankruptcy. A great scarcity also prevailed at Paris, which rendered the populace unusually discontented and tumultuous. In this emergency various expedients were suggested; and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONVOCATION">convocation</a> of the States General, which had been long talked of, was advised by M. Necker as likely to give general satisfaction to the people. In assenting to this proposition, it was the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of the court, that the different orders of the clergy, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, and commons, should vote in separate chambers, in or- der that the deputies of the commons might be controlled by the other two bodies. But the popular leaders were by far too penetrating to allow their influence to be annihilated by this device. They determined, from the beginning, that the three orders should sit and vote together; and, as is well known, after various fruitless efforts to bring about this union, the commons resolved to form themselves into an Assembly for the dispatch of business, without regard to the other two chambers. This decisive step proved effectual, and the three chambers at length all met and voted in one house, by which the whole power was thrown into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the commons. During these transactions, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> and his advisers pursued a weak and vacillating policy. They <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a>, when it was too late, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a> they committed, or supposed themselves to have committed, in putting into the hands of the people the powerful weapon of a representative body. But in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of yielding to the necessity of circumstances, and conciliating this new power, which they could now no longer resist, by conceding with a good <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> every <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> demand of constitutional <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, they endeavoured to recover the ground which they had for ever lost; vainly struggling against the power of the commons, and meditating even the most violent measures for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of their authority. It was in pursuance of these views that troops were drawn from the most distant parts and encamped around Paris—a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, the only <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> that could be put upon which was, that it was intended to overawe the deliberations of the Assembly, or, perhaps, to dissolve it at once at the point of the bayonet. These violent courses M. Necker opposed, and he was accordingly dismissed on the 11th <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1789, and ordered to quit the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> in twenty-four hours. This order he obeyed with equal secrecy and dispatch, and had arrived at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a> before it was generally known in Paris that he was out of office. It is impossible to describe the consternation which prevailed in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> when the dismissal and exile of this favourite minister was made known. The person who first communicated the intelligence was considered as a madman, and with difficulty escaped some harsh treatment; and the event was no sooner confirmed, than all the shops and places of amusement were shut up; and his bust, with that of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>, was paraded through the streets, dressed in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">mourning</a>. These proceedings were interrupted by a German regiment; the busts were broken in pieces; and in the course of the tumult one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> lost his life, while others were wounded. Fresh troops arriving, a serious conflict ensued; and an old man being cut <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in the Tuileries by an officer of distinction, the populace were enraged to the highest pitch, and being joined by the French Guards, who deserted their officers, they at last succeeded in overpowering the Germans. New outrages and tumults succeeded; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASTILLE">Bastille</a> was stormed; and the capital became the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of bloody massacres, while the people's minds were at the same time filled with dismay at the near approach of foreign troops, from whom they apprehended nothing less than the sack of the city. In the midst of these alarms, they besought the Assembly to intercede with the king for the recall of their favourite minister. The necessity of complying with this demand was at length seen by the king, and a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> was written to M. Necker, requesting him to return. M. Necker was at Basle when he received this letter, with the request contained in which he resolved immediately to comply. His progress to Paris was one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> triumph. He was cheered as he passed through the different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> by the acclamations of multitudes, who hailed him as their deliverer. This popularity, however, was not of long <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>. Alarmed by the excesses which had already taken place, M. Necker became desirous to support the authority of the sovereign; and, without conciliating the confidence of the king's friends, he lost that of the popular party. By the Royalists he was always hated; he now became an object of suspicion to the more violent patriots, and was reproached as an aristocrat. Seeing his popularity on the decline, he resolved to retire, and he accordingly wrote a letter to the Assembly, pleading the necessity of repose for the restoration of his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>. No notice was taken of this letter; and his personal safety being now in danger from the violence of the people, he quitted Paris, in a private manner, in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1790. After the loss of power and popularity, M. Necker seems to have sunk into the greatest dejection. "I could have wished," says Mr Gibbon, who passed some days with him about this period, "to have exhibited him as a warning to any aspiring youth possessed with the demon of ambition. With all the means of private happiness in his power, he is the most miserable of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> beings; the past, the present, and the future, are equally odious to him. When I suggested some domestic amusements, he answered with a deep tone of despair, 'In the state in which I am I can feel nothing but the blast which has overthrown me.'" His mind was soon diverted from the disappointments of ambition by domestic griefs of a more poignant <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; his wife, to whom he was deeply attached, dying after a long illness, in which he attended her with great affection. He had now recourse to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> to divert his melancholy, and several works, which he published, were the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of his labours. He died at Copet, on the 9th April 1804, after a short but painful illness. His public character is, of course, differently estimated, according to the political views of parties. In his private and domestic relations he was amiable and affectionate, and appears to have been greatly beloved. His writings, besides those already mentioned, are the following: An Answer to the Memorial of the Abbe Marelet, on the East India Company, 1769. Memorials on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCIAL">Provincial</a> Administrations, 1781. Answer to the Speech pronounced by M. de Calonne to the Assembly of Notables, 1787. New Explanations on the Compte Rendu, 1788. Of the Importance of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">Religious</a> Opinions, 1788. Observations on the Introduction to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> Book, 1790. On the Administration of M. Necker, by Himself, 1791. On the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EXECUTIVE_POWER">Executive Power</a> in Great States, 1791.

NEPAUL

Pages 73-74

a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> but narrow <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Northern Hindostan, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> range of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HIMALAYA_MOUNTAINS">Himalaya <a class=</a>"xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, on the south by the provinces of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAHAR">Bahar</a>, Oude, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DELHI">Delhi</a>, on the east it is limited by Bootan, and the territory of the rajah of Si-Kim; and previous to the late <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with the British, their conquests extended to the banks of the Suttelege, the eastern river of the Panjab. The kingdom was then divided into the following provinces, viz. Gorcrah, Kyrat, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORUNG">Morung</a>, Muckwany, Mockwanpore, Lamjung, 24 Rajahs, Kemoon, and Almora. The valley of Nepaul proper, from whence the kingdom takes its name, is nearly of an oval <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>; its greatest length from north to south being 12 miles, by 9 in the greatest breadth. On the north and south it is bounded by lofty mountains, but is more open to the east and west. This small tract is very populous, and, besides the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> Cata-madoo, is filled with villages. This valley, although situated between the 27th and 28th degrees of N. lat. is so elevated, that it enjoys an European <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, and the mountains, covered with snow, are in sight the whole year round. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is productive, and, in some places, yields two crops in the year. The mountains of Nepaul contain <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>; and, although <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> is not encouraged, it sends to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>, wax, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASTARD">bastard</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CINNAMON">cinnamon</a>, cardamums, walnuts, &c.; and takes in return, muslins and silks of Bengal, carpets, spices, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, and European goods. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> is despotic, and the rajah is considered as the proprietor of the soil. The natives are in general a hardy and courageous <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>; and during the late war gave the British much annoyance. This, however, partly arose from the seat of war being in a mountainous and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, to which the British <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEPOYS">sepoys</a> had not been accustomed. The prevailing <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> is the Hindoo, but many of the inhabitants are supposed to be descendants of Tartars, and reckoned impure. The tribe called Newars admit of poliantry, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather the women are at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to divorce their husbands, and take others as often as they choose. The Brahmins of Nepaul are very numerous, and deeply skilled in Sanscrit lore. One of the <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a> is said to contain 15,000 volumes in that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. There are five vernacular languages; but the Hindostany is pretty generally understood.—<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> Gazetteer, or Geographical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>, Vol. IV. For an account of the late war, see the Article <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, in this Supplement.

PANTOGRAPH

Pages 135-136

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> contrived for the purpose of copying drawings, so that the copy may either be of the same size, of a greater, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of a less size than the original. It consists of four moveable rulers fixed together by four pivots, and forming a parallelogram. At the extremity of one of these rulers prolonged is a point, which is drawn over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of the original <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a>, whilst a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a>, fixed at the end of another branch of the instrument, traces on <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> the lines of the copy. The pencil is placed in a hollow <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> is added on the top of the pencil; by this means, the point of the pencil is made to press on the paper with the force requisite for drawing the lines. The improvements in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of different parts of the pantograph described in the Memoires de l'Académie des Sciences, 1743, have been generally adopted. The pantograph, however, is not found convenient in practice; and, for the purpose of copying maps, plans, and other designs, artists most <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> employ the method of dividing the original <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> into a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of squares, and the paper on which the copy is to be made into the same number of squares. When this is done, they copy the lines contained within each <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> of the original, so as to form a similar <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> within the corresponding square of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RETICULA">reticula</a> which covers the copy. When the drawing consists of straight lines, a reduced copy is accurately made by means of an isosceles triangle, in which the base is to the side as any line of the copy is to the corresponding line in the original. By setting off with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPASSES">compasses</a> any line of the original drawing on the sides of the triangle, the base which completes the triangle is the length of the corresponding line to be laid <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> on the copy. The same operation is performed by the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECTOR">sector</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> a drawing is to be copied, of the same size as the original, without diminution or enlargement, engravers usually trace the copy on oiled paper laid over the original, or on the transparent papier de guimauve (marsh-mallow paper), made in France. A pantograph has been made, consisting of a rod, placed vertically, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> round a fixed point in its length, situated between its upper and lower extremity: the upper end of the rod being a point which is conducted by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> over the lines of the original drawing; the lower end of the rod being the pencil which traces the copy on paper. An instrument upon this principle is sometimes used for drawing the profile of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>, in order to form small portraits or silhouettes. The instrument called Micrograph and Prosopograph in Puissant's Geodesie, does not differ in principle from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> pantograph. A very ingenious instrument for copying drawings, either upon a reduced or enlarged <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>, has been lately invented by Mr Wallace, Professor of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">Mathematics</a> in the University of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>. Of this instrument, which may be fitly introduced under the present head, though differing in name, we have been favoured with the following <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>. It is a fact well known, that artists of various descriptions, who have frequent occasion to imitate original designs, have <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> felt the want of a convenient mathematical instrument, by which a copy may be made with neatness and expedition, that shall have any given proportion to the original. The Pantograph is the only instrument that has been hitherto employed; but although correct and plausible in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a>, in practice it is found to be so very imperfect, that the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> hardly ever thinks of making <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of it. A consideration of the essential <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> that would be rendered to the graphic art, by a copying instrument, which should be at once simple in its theory and easy in its application, induced Mr Wallace to turn his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the subject; and, in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> of 1821, he produced the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of a copying instrument, which he has denominated an Eido- graph (from ειδος and γραφειν). The instrument, and its application to the copying of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> variety of subjects, has been shown to engineers, engravers, and other competent judges in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> and in Edinburgh, and their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of its utility has been such as to leave no doubt of its completely fulfilling the views of the inventor. The instrument is represented in this figure: The beam, A B, which is made of mahogany, slides backward and forward in a socket, C; the socket turns on a vertical axis, supported by the fulcrum D, which stands on a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>. There is a slit in the beam, through which the axis of the socket passes, so that, when the beam slides in the socket, a portion of it passes on each side of the axis. There are two equal <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a>, E, E, below the beam, which turn on axes that <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> fixed at A, B, near its extremities; and a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> chain passes over the wheels as a band, by which a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROTATION">rotation</a> may be communicated from the one to the other. There are two arms, F, F, which slide in sockets along the lower face of the wheels, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> under their centres: at the extremity, G, of one arm, there is a metal tracer, with a handle attached to it, by which its point may be carried over the lines in any design; and at H, the extremity of the other arm, there is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK_LEAD"><a class="</a>xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> pencil fixed in a metal tube, which is ground to fit so exactly into a pipe, as just to slide up or down. In using the instrument, the pencil, in its tube, is raised by a thread which passes over a pulley, and it descends again by a weight with which it is loaded. From the perfect equality of the wheels, it is easy to see that, if the arms attached to them be placed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> in any one position, they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> retain their parallelism, although one of the wheels, and consequently both, be turned on their centres. Supposing, now, that BC and AC, the parts into which the axis is divided at the centre, have any proportion whatever to each other, if the distances of the tracing point G, and pencil point H, from the centres of their wheels have the very same proportion, then it follows, from the elements of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, that the tracing point G, the centre C, and the pencil point H, will be in a straight line; and further, that CG and CH, the distance of these <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> from the centre, will have to each other the constant proportion of CB to CA, or of EG to AH. Such being the geometrical <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of the Eidograph, if any subject to be copied be fixed to the table on which the instrument stands, and the tracing point be carried over every line of the design, the pencil point will trace a copy in all respects similar to the original. To facilitate the adjustment of the instrument, so that the copy may have any given ratio to the original, there are scales of equal parts on the beam and the two arms: By these and verniers, both halves of the beam, and equal lengths on the arms, are each divided into 1000 equal parts, and at certain intervals corresponding numbers are marked on them. By means of the scales, when any ratio is assigned, the adjustment is made without the least difficulty. To avoid any derangement by the chain slipping on the wheels, there are clamps at K and K, which hold it fast to the wheels at points where it never quits them. They are slackened when the instrument is adjusted. The inventor has committed its construction to Mr R. B. Bate, philosophical instrument-maker, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POULTRY">Poultry</a>, London, from whom it may be obtained.

PAUW

Pages 138-138

a moral <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> and historian, born at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> in 1739, is better known as the uncle of the revolutionist Anacharsis Clootz, than by the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> from whom he was descended: they are, however, reported by his nephew to have distinguished themselves in the revolutions of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> in the sixteenth century. It appears, upon the same authority, that his name was Cornelius, and not Nicolas, but that he was not related to Cornelius de Pauw, the critic, and the rival of Dorville; and that it was upon the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> of his sister to Clootz's father, that he obtained, through the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, a Catholic canonicate at Xanten, in the territory of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CLEVES">Cleves</a>. He was afterwards appointed reader to Frederic <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, perhaps as an advocate of the new doctrines and principles which that sovereign was disposed to patronise; but he is said to have declined the offer of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of an academician of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a>, and a bishopric at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRESLAU">Breslau</a>. His attacks on the Jesuits, whom he accused of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> misrepresentation and exaggeration in their historical and geographical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a>, made him unpopular with the Catholic clergy, though his learning and talents commanded a certain portion of their respect. He was simple in his manners, and somewhat negligent of his appearance; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> was embittered by a tedious and painful <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, and he died the 7th of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1799. 1. His <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> publications are his Recherches sur les Américains, 2 v. 8. Berl. 1770; ed. 2, 1772; a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> intended to show the "degraded state of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> Americans," and forming a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a> to the speculations of some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> writers of celebrity. 2. Défense des Recherches, 8. Berl. 1771. 3. Recherches sur les Egyptiens et les Chinois, 2 v. 8. Berl. 1773. Philosophical Dissertations on the Egyptians and Chinese, translated by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> J. Thomson, 2 v. 8. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, 1795. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> was undertaken, he observes, to show that "no two nations ever resembled each other less than the Egyptians and the Chinese;" and it must be admitted that he has sufficiently established his proposition. There is, indeed, one argument that he has employed, which appears to be founded on a mistake of the Greek historians of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, who have asserted that the Egyptians had <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> been in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of alphabetical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>; and the want of any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a> among the Chinese, is stated by M. de Pauw as affording a marked distinction from the Egyptians. There is, however, scarcely a shadow of resemblance in the particular hieroglyphical characters employed by the two nations, though the general system of beginning with a representation of a visible object, and departing, more and more, by degrees, from the fidelity of the delineation, must necessarily have been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to both. But it so happens, that out of about 70 Egyptian characters, which are compared by the Jesuits and Dr Morton with the Chinese in the Philosophical Transactions for 1769, there are about 20 of which the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> has been ascertained with tolerable accuracy in the Article Egypt of this Supplement; and of these there is only one that happens to have been rightly determined by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> with the Chinese, excepting two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> three which are obviously <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> pictures, as the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">Moon</a> and a Bow. There is also a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of a chain, among the old Chinese characters, which agrees remarkably in its form with the Egyptian hieroglyphic employed as a copulative conjunction; and there is a still more striking coincidence, which M. Jomard has noticed, between the Egyptian and Chinese characters for a thousand, both of which he derives from the seed vessel of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOTUS">lotus</a>, as containing a multitude of seeds; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the older Chinese characters be found to preserve this resemblance as perfectly as they ought to do, it must be confessed that the suspicion of a common origin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be much strengthened by the argument. Both the Egyptians and the Chinese were condemned, M. de Pauw observes, "to an eternal mediocrity;" and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of this observation is certainly not diminished by anything that has lately been inferred from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HIEROGLYPHICS">hieroglyphics</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROSETTA">Rosetta</a>. 4. There are several papers of M. de Pauw on antiquarian subjects in the Memoirs of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of Cassel, and one in particular On the Temple of Juno Lacinia, Vol. I. 1780. 5. Recherches sur les Grecs, 2 v. 8. Berl. 1787. Philosophical Dissertations on the Greeks, translated by Thomson, 2 v. 8. Lond. 1793. The work is principally devoted to the Athenians, among whom their boasted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> is shown to have been confined to a very small <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of citizens, who tyrannized over the rest of the inhabitants of their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The Lacedemonians, the Aetolians, the Thessalians, and the Arcadians, are separately discussed, but considered as comparatively contemptible; the Lacedemonians in particular, and their successors, the Mantineotes, are treated with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> severity, as a worthless <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of dishonourable vagabonds. The athletic <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of the Athenians is, however, highly applauded, from a visionary <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of the importance of the physical perfection of the body to the operations of the mind. An edition of the author's three principal works appeared at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> volumes octavo, 1795. [Dorsch, Chardon-la-Rochette, and Clootz, Magaz. Encycl. 1799. An. V. Vol. II. Widdigen, Westph. Nationalk. 1801, p. 215. N. Allg. T. Bibl. LXXIV. p. 77. Denina, Prusse Littéraire, III. N. Dict. Hist. IX. 8. Par. 1804. Chalmers's Biographical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>, XXIII. 8. Lond. 1815.]

PERTHSHIRE

Pages 165-166

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> in Scotland, having the shire of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERNESS">Inverness</a> and Aberdeen on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGUS">Angus</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Forfar, Fife, and Kinross, on the east; <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CLACKMANNAN">Clackmannan</a> and Stirling on the south; and Dunbarton and Argyle on the west; contains, according to the latest authorities, 2638 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles, of which 50 are occupied by <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>; or, in all, 1,688,320 English acres; being, next to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INVERNESS_SHIRE">Inverness-shire</a>, the largest county on the mainland of Scotland. It is situated between 56° 7' and 56° 35' north latitude, and between 3° 6' and 4° 47' west <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>, from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a>. Its greatest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, from east to west, is about 77 miles, and from north to south 68. It was anciently, and is still, popularly divided into eight districts: Atholl on the north, Stormont on the north-east, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PERTH">Perth</a> Proper and Gowrie on the east, Strathearn on the south, Monteith on the southwest, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BREADALBANE">Breadalbane</a> on the west, and Rannoch on the north-west. It is under the jurisdiction of one <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>, who has substitutes in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of Perth and Dunblane, and is divided into seventy-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> parishes. In a general view, this extensive county may be divided into Highlands and Lowlands; the former occupying a space so much greater than the latter, that not quite so much as a third <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the whole is fit for cultivation. This last portion is chiefly, though not without considerable exceptions, situated on the eastern and southern extremities, which contain some of the richest tracts in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> plain of Strathmore which has the Grampians on the north-west, and the Ochils and Sidlaw Hills on the east; varying in breadth from ten to fifteen miles, and extending through this and the contiguous counties, from <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> to sea, a distance of 100 miles. To the west, where the Grampians, at first rising gently, rear their rocky or heath-covered summits to the height of 4000 feet, and for almost the whole breadth of the county, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> grounds are penetrated by straths and glens, some of them of considerable extent, each traversed by its own mountain streams, and diversified by numerous lakes, many of which, having their wild and lofty banks covered with <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> wood, present scenes singularly romantic and beautiful. At least <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> of these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> are upwards of 3000 feet high: the three highest being Benlawers, on the west side of Loch Tay; Benmore, south-west; and Scheallion, north-east; the latter noted as the station chosen by Dr Maskelyne, Astronomer <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a>, to make observations on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTRACTION">attraction</a> of mountains. The most considerable lakes are—Loch Tay, almost in the centre of the Highland district, about fifteen miles <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, with a depth varying from fifteen to one hundred fathoms; Loch Erich, on the north-west, extending into Inverness-shire, still longer, but not so broad; Loch Rannoch, south-east of the former, twelve miles long; Loch Earn, south from Loch Tay; and Lochs Vennachar, Achray, and Katrine, on the south-west: the last of which, with the wild mountain scenery around it, called the Trosachs, has acquired deserved celebrity, from Sir Walter Scott's Lady of the Lake. Most of the streams either have their source in these lochs, or receive, as they flow through them, a great accession to their waters. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are the Tay, the Forth, the Earn, the Teath, and the Isla; of which the two first are by far the most considerable, though the Forth does not attain its full size till it has left this county. The Tay, the largest river in Scotland, and the Earn, belong exclusively to Perthshire. The Tay, under the name of the Dochart, has its source on the western confines, and soon after entering Loch Dochart, flows from thence north-east till it falls into Loch Tay. After leaving Loch Tay, from which it now takes its name, it pursues first a northerly and then a southerly course towards <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUNKELD">Dunkeld</a>, from which it proceeds eastward, and then south, through a very rich <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, till it falls into the Frith of that name, a little below the town of Perth; having been joined by the Almond and many other streams in its course, which, with all its windings, is not less than ninety miles. The salmon fishery on this river yields a rent of about L. 7000 a-year. South of Loch Tay is Loch Earn, where the river of that name has its source, and which, flowing east and south, through Strathearn and by the town of Crieff, after a course of twenty-four miles, falls into the Frith of Tay at Rhind. On the banks of this river, near its confluence with the Tay, is the village of Pitcaithly, long celebrated for its mineral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, which have lately found a rival at Dunblane, on the southern side of the county. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> of this extensive district, so different in elevation and exposure, varies considerably. In the central parts, the winters are stormy and very severe, the snow lying long, attended with keen <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FROST">frost</a>; and on the banks of the rivers in this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>, hearfrosts are frequent in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, and very injurious to the crops. On the east, the climate is mild and salubrious. At Longforgan, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARSE">Carse</a> of Gowrie, on the banks of the Frith of Tay, the thermometer, on an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> of twelve years, stood at 50°, and the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> annual <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> was 24.496 inches; and at Belmont, in Strathmore, for a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of ten years, the average height of the thermometer was 46.35, and the yearly quantity of rain during thirty years' observation 30.40 inches. Perthshire, as far as yet known, does not abound in useful minerals. There is no coal but at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CULROSS">Culross</a>, on a small detached tract lying on the Forth, south-east from the rest of the county; and, for want of coal, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a>, which is found in many parts, is of little value, though it is sometimes imperfectly calcined by means of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEAT">peat</a>. Some years ago, a machine was erected for pounding limestone, with the view of employing it in that state as a manure; but the experiment was not persisted in. In the higher grounds, the prevailing rock is <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANITE">granite</a>, and in the lower sandstone. Slates are found in many parts of the Highlands, but none in the low country. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">Copper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and ironstone, occur in some parts; and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of the two former were once worked, but are now abandoned. Shell <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARL">marl</a>, which has been long used as a manure, abounds in Stormont and Strathearn, on the east side of the county. On so great a variety of surface, every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> occurs that is found in Scotland. That which distinguishes this district, though it is not peculiar to it, is the alluvial soil on the banks of the rivers, which is of considerable extent, and in many parts of the richest <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>. The Carse of Gowrie, in particular, a tract of about 18,000 acres, lying along the north and north-west banks of the Frith of Tay, has been long celebrated for its fertility. Here there are upwards of twenty orchards, of all sizes, from one to twenty-four acres each. Perthshire has all the kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAME">game</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in other parts of the Highlands of Scotland, with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> and fallow deer, and roes, rabbits, pigeons, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a>. The territory of Perthshire was divided, in 1811, into 755 estates, of which 621 were under L. 500 Scots of valuation, and 95 above L. 2000; the valuation of the whole being L. 339,892, 6s. 9d. Scots, the highest of any of the Scottish counties excepting Fifehire. The real rent, as returned under the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">Property</a>-Tax <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">Act</a> in 1811, was, for the lands, L. 460,738, 13s. 11d. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">Sterling</a>, and for the houses, L. 36,697, 19s. 7d. This <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>-rent, which is more than that of any of the other counties by almost one-third, is equal to about a tenth part of the rent of all Scotland; yet it is only at the rate of about 5s. 6d. the English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACRE">acre</a>. In the same year, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of freeholders entitled to vote in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of a member for the county was 178. There are more oak-woods, and these of a greater value, here than in all the rest of Scotland, and very extensive plantations of all sorts of trees, particularly larch, have been made within the last 50 years; of which, those of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of Atholl are of great extent, and now of immense value. The county is much ornamented by the numerous seats of the proprietors, of whom 12 or 13 are noblemen. Among these are Blair Castle and Dunkeld <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">House</a>—Duke of Atholl; Taymouth—<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> of Breadalbane; Scone—Earl of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANSFIELD">Mansfield</a>; Dupplin Castle—Earl of Kinnoul; and Dunira—<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Melville. The general size of the farms in the Lowlands is from 100 to 300 acres. In the Highlands, the same system prevails that we have adverted to in describing the other Highland counties of Scotland; though here, as elsewhere, it is slowly giving way to one better adapted to the present times. In the crops, live stock, and general management of farms, we find nothing peculiar, except, perhaps, that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a> is cultivated to a greater extent than in the southern counties of Scotland. On the Carse of Gowrie, the highest rented land of the same extent in Britain, Perthshire, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we except the immediate neighbourhood of a few great towns, the order of cropping, after a plain fallow is—wheat, beans, and pease, barley with seeds, hay, and oats; and under this course, some of the best land yielded, so far back as 1795, a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>-rent of 31s. with three bushels of wheat, and about four and a half bushels of barley—altogether, at the prices during the late <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, equal to four guineas the Scots acre. This county has only two royal burghs, Perth the Towns-county town, and Culross. Perth is a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of great antiquity, formerly the usual residence of the Scottish sovereigns, who were crowned at Scone in its vicinity, and the seat of parliaments and courts of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>. Some of the most important events in Scottish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, both of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> description, occurred here. (See the article Perth in the Encyclopaedia.) It is now a well built thriving town, containing (in 1811) about 17,000 inhabitants. About 70 other towns and villages are scattered over the county, the most considerable of which have been already described in the Encyclopaedia. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of Perthshire are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, cotton, Manufacture-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, and a variety of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. It <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">Commerce</a>. has extensive bleachfields, printfields, and cotton-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>, with mills for extracting <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> from the seeds of flax and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RAPE">rape</a>, and for the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a> of flax and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>. Its exports are corn, linen and linen-yarn, cottons, boots and shoes, salmon, with coals from the ports of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINCARDINE">Kincardine</a> and Culross on the Frith of Forth; and it imports some of the materials of its manufactures, lime in great quantities, and articles required for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> consumption. In 1806, there belonged to the port of Perth 35 vessels, of 2635 tons in all, with 153 seamen. The county of Perth sends one member to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">Parliament</a>; and the towns of Perth and Culross have a share in the election of other two for the burghs; Perth being classed with St Andrews, Cupar Fife, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUNDEE">Dundee</a>, and Forfar; and Culross with Stirling, Dunfermline, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERKEITHING">Inverkeithing</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEENSFERRY">Queensferry</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a>, according to the census of 1801 and 1811, is exhibited in the following <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a>. See the general works quoted under the former Scottish counties, and Robertson's General View of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> of Perthshire. PHYSICAL GEOGRAPHY

Pages 198-208

As we approach the pole, in the northern hemisphere, generally the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> is greatest on the east side of both the old and new continents, and least on the west. Humboldt has generalised this fact, and inferred, that all continents and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> are warmer on the west side than the east. The following <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, extracted from Humboldt's admirable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a>, exhibits the different gradations of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> annual temperature in Western <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, continuing the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> to the equator. | Mean Annual Temperature. | |--------------------------| | Lat. | Old World. | New World. | Diff. | |-----|-----------|-----------|------| | 0 | 81°.5 | 81°.5 | 0 | | 20 | 77°.9 | 77°.9 | 0 | | 30 | 70°.7 | 67°.1 | 3.6 | | 40 | 63°.5 | 54°.5 | 9 | | 50 | 50°.9 | 38°.3 | 12.6 | | 60 | 41°.0 | 25°.0 | 16 | | 70 | 33°.0 | 0°.0 | 33 | We have few observations for the east <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>; but the following shows that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> of this region approaches to that of Eastern America rather than Western Europe. | Europe. | Asia. | America. | |---------|-------|----------| | <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, | Pekin, | <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILADELPHIA">Philadelphia</a>, | | Lat. 41° | Lat. 40° | Lat. 40° | | Temp. 63.3° | Temp. 54.8° | Temp. 53.4° | Thus the mean annual temperature of North America is 9° lower than that of Western Europe at the latitude of 40°, 16° lower at lat. 60°, and 33° lower at lat. 70°; a similar <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> obtains between the climates of Western Europe and Eastern Asia. By comparing places under the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a>, we find that this change is not sudden, but progressive. Petersburg, on the same parallel with Upsal, is 5° colder, and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOSCOW">Moscow</a> is 5° colder than <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COPENHAGEN">Copenhagen</a>. The annual temperature of West <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GREENLAND">Greenland</a> in lat. 70°, which is 17° <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 18°, according to Sir C. Giesecké, is very nearly the mean between that of the North <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> and Melville <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">Island</a>, as its intermediate situation would <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> us to expect.—(Edin. Phil. Jour. No. IX. 201.) These differences are rendered more sensible when we connect the places having the same annual temperature by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, which Humboldt has named isothermal lines. Thus the isothermal line of 59° (Fahrenheit) passes along the latitude of 43° in Europe, but descends to lat. 36° in America. The isothermal line of 41° passes from the latitude of 60° in Europe, to that of 48° in America, showing that the same annual temperature which is found at the 60th parallel on the eastern side of the Atlantic, is only found at 12° farther south on its western shores. The western coast of North America again is warmer than the east; and hence <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we were to trace the isothermal lines round the northern hemisphere, they would all have concave summits at the east sides of Asia and America, and convex summits at the west sides of America and Europe. The difference of mean temperature between <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> and winter (reckoning each to consist of three months) is nothing at the equator, and constantly increases as we approach the pole, as shown in the following table: | Mean Temperature. | |-------------------| | Latitude. | Of Winter. | Of Summer. | Difference. | | Algiers, | 37° | 61°.5 | 80°.2 | 18°.7 | | <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUDA">Buda</a>, | 47½ | 34°.0 | 70°.5 | 26°.5 | | Upsal, | 60 | 25°.0 | 60°.2 | 35°.2 | The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> difference of the seasons is smaller under the warm meridians of Western Europe than anywhere else, and seems to be greatest where the mean annual temperature is lowest,—near the east coasts of Asia and America. | Places on the Same Parallel. | |-----------------------------| | Latitude. | Winter. | Summer. | Difference. | | Copenhagen, | 55½° | 30°.7 | 62°.6 | 31°.9 | | Moscow, | 55½° | 10°.8 | 67°.1 | 56°.3 | | Rome, | 42 | 45°.8 | 75°.2 | 29°.4 | | Pekin, | 40 | 26°.4 | 82°.6 | 56°.2 | | <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEW_YORK">New <a c</a>lass="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, | 41 | 29°.8 | 79°.2 | 49°.4 | | Places having the Same Mean Annual Temperature. | |-----------------------------------------------| | Mean An. Temp. | Winter. | Summer. | Difference. | | St Malo, | 54° | 42°.3 | 66°.0 | 23°.7 | | New York, | 54° | 29°.8 | 79°.2 | 49°.4 | If we draw a line on the map in a north-east <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> from Bordeaux to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARSAW">Warsaw</a>, and continue it till it strike the Wolga in latitude 55°, all the places situated under this line, at the same elevation, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> have nearly the same summer temperature of 69° or 70° of Fahrenheit's scale. The lines of equal winter temperature decline in an opposite direction, and deviate much farther from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> of the parallels. Thus a straight line drawn from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, almost exactly at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> to the line of equal summer temperatures, would <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> over places, all of which, if equally elevated, would have nearly the same winter temperature of 37° or 38°. The other lines of equal summer and winter temperatures have a direction corresponding to these, but not exactly parallel. * Deduced by interpolation from the temperature of Natchez, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CINCINNATI">Cincinnati</a>, Churchill Fort, and Melville Island, reckoning that of Melville Island—2 Fahrenheit. On comparing the climate of the two hemispheres, we find that the southern is rather colder than the northern, but is more remarkably distinguished by the greater equality of its seasons. This last effect may obviously be referred to the influence of a greater surface of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> upon a smaller <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>. In the southern hemisphere also, the temperature seems more uniform under different meridians. At Port Jackson, Buenos Ayres, and the Cape, all nearly under one parallel, the annual mean temperature is almost exactly the same. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> general cause that affects the temperature of places is their elevation above the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the sea. The following table, by Humboldt, shows that the ratio of decreasing temperature, as we ascend in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>, is not the same at different latitudes, nor is it uniform at the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> for equal successive altitudes. | Height in English feet | Equatorial Zone from 0° to 10° | Temperate Zone from 45° to 47° | |-----------------------|---------------------------------|-------------------------------| | | Mean Temp. | Difference | Mean Temp. | Difference | | 0 | 81.5 | 0 | 53.6 | 0 | | 3195 | 71.2 | 10.3 | 41.0 | 12.6 | | 6392 | 65.1 | 6.1 | 31.6 | 9.4 | | 9587 | 57.7 | 7.4 | 23.4 | 8.2 | | 12792 | 44.6 | 13.1 | | | | 15965 | 34.7 | 9.9 | | | This table shows, that, at the equator, the thermometer sinks 10° in the first thousand yards of ascent, or 1° for 310 feet. In the next thousand yards it sinks no more than 6°, or 1° for 524 feet. In the third and fourth stages, there is a remarkable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ACCELERATION">acceleration</a>. In the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> to the limit of perpetual snow, at 15,965 feet of elevation, the decrease is 1° for 341 feet. Humboldt ascribes the smaller rate of decrease in the second and third stages to the large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> chiefly suspended in this region, which intercept the radiant <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. In the temperate zone the atmospheric cold increases more rapidly. The decrease of heat for the first thousand yards is at the rate of 1° for 253 feet, but to the limit of perpetual snow (at a temperature not of 32°, but of 23°.3) it is 1° for 317 feet, or, in round <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, 1° for 100 yards. Observations made, however, in the free regions of the air, may give different results from those which were made on the sides or summits of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. But generally in the temperate zone, of two adjacent places, if the one is 1000 yards higher than the other, it will have a climate 12° colder. For smaller heights the decrease is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a>. In the upper regions of the atmosphere, the difference between the heat of night and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, summer and winter, is smaller than at the surface of the earth. This <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> of decrease explains to us the extreme cold felt in the elevated plains of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>, and the mild temperature enjoyed in the torrid zone, on the table land of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>, the plateau of Pastos, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> lands. Humboldt calculates, that in the temperate zone, every hundred metres of ascent (110 yards) diminishes the heat as much as a change of 1° of latitude. The temperature of countries is affected by the local <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROXIMITY">proximity</a> of the sea, and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the adjacent land. The extremes of temperature are always comparatively little felt in small islands, remote from continents. In the United States intense cold is experienced as often as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> blows from the frozen plains round <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUDSON_S_BAY">Hudson's <a </a>class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">Bay</a>. (Warden's America, I. 154.) From high mountains, gusts of cold wind, called snow winds by mariners, rush <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> and cool the circumjacent plains. (Volney's Trav. in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, I. 340.) At Calabozzo, in Venezuela, the temperature, which was from 87° to 90° in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, rose to 104° or 105°, whenever the wind blew from the parched and dusty surface of the Llanos, or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> plains. (Humboldt, Pers. Nar. IV. 325.) The heat accumulates to an astonishing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, when the wind passes over extensive deserts of fine and almost impalpable sand, which rises in the air, and hangs over the surface like a fog, or mounts in whirling columns to a great height, mixing its <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> particles with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of the atmosphere, and communicating to it an intolerable heat. (Kinnear's Geog. Mem. of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, 216, 222.) In Europe, where the proximity of the sea cools every <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the surface by the agency of the winds, the accumulation of heat never proceeds so far as in Asia and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. Even in low plains, sheltered on the north, the temperature scarcely ever exceeds 100°; but at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAGDAD">Bagdad</a> and at <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol6.html#article-BUSHIRE">Bushire</a>, where the south wind arrives, heated by the burning sands of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, the thermometer sometimes stands at 120° or 125°; and on the west coast of Africa, where similar causes operate, it is said to rise to 130°.* Though the mean annual temperature is highest at the equator, the extreme summer heat, so far as it proceeds directly from the solar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, is greatest at the tropic, and is even rather greater at the latitude of 45° than at the equator. (Art. Climate, in this Supplement, p. 182, Table.) We may therefore conjecture that the hottest summer climate in the world is to be found in the western parts of the Sahara of Africa, under the northern tropic, where the winds blow over a zone of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> plains 4000 miles in breadth, unbroken by any considerable mountains, or by any surface of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> * Morier's Journey, II. 97. Edin. Phil. Jour. No. V. 197. Tuckey, II. 442. Humboldt repeatedly observed the temperature of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> in Equinoctial America at the hottest <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the day. It varied with the nature of the mineral substance. The highest he has recorded, we think, was that of a coarse granitic sand at Magpures, whose temperature at two P. M. was 140°.5. That of a fine granitic sand at the same place was 126°.5; of a granitic rock, 117°.6. We may hence conclude, that the air, though perfectly stagnant, could in no possible circumstances be heated above 140°, and this only within two or three feet of the ground. Humboldt's Pers. Nar. V. 165. except the narrow inlet of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> Sea. At the same time, it is possible that a much narrower surface than this may suffice to communicate the maximum effect of the solar heat to the atmosphere, and the actual heat <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> may depend more upon the nature of the surface and its low elevation, than upon its extent. It appears that within the tropics seas have very little effect in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEMPERING">tempering</a> the accumulating heat of the land, when situated to the westward of a continent, but a great effect when situated to the eastward. In the steppes of Caracass, which are open to the sea on the east, the heat rarely exceeds 99°, but even in the wooded regions of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENEGAMBIA">Senegambia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>, much nearer the coast, it rises to 130°.* In the temperate zones, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, it is clear that the sea exerts its influence in a direction precisely contrary. When the land lies to the eastward, the sea mitigates the extremes of heat and cold very much; when to the westward very little. This is abundantly proved by the difference of temperature already noticed between the east and west coasts of the two continents. Now, the sea can exert very little influence over the temperature of the land, except through the agency of the atmospheric currents; and the phenomena in both <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> seem to be accounted for by the prevailing direction of the winds. Within the tropics, these are almost constantly from the east; but from the tropics to the latitude of 60° north (and probably much farther), the prevailing winds are from the west.† Within the torrid zone, therefore, we should expect to find the extreme summer heat constantly accumulating from the east side of continents and islands to the west; but in the temperate zones, the extremes both of heat and cold will as regularly increase from the west to the east. This is found to be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, and whatever other causes may be conjoined with those now assigned, there can be no doubt that the latter have really a great influence. The temperature of each zone has such a correspondence with the amount of the solar impressions, as to lead to the inference, that the heat of the globe is entirely derived from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>; and Professor Leslie has calculated, that, upon this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>, the mean heat of the interior ought to be 66°.8.
