His appointment to the situation of Physician to the King was preceded by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> of letters of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, issued on occasion of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of the Dauphin from the small-pox. Louis, who was much struck with the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> and solidity of Quesnay's remarks, and who familiarly called him son penseur, gave him, in allusion to this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, three pansey <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> (in French pensées), for his arms, with the motto Propert cognitio nem mentis. The leisure Quesnay now enjoyed, enabled him to prosecute his studies with greater assiduity. In 1747, he republished an enlarged edition, in 3 tomes, 12mo, of his Essai Physique sur l'Economie Animale, originally published in 1736; in 1748, he published an Examen impartial des Contestations des Medecins et des Chirurgiens de Paris; in 1749, he published a Memoire sur la Sagesse de l'Ancienne <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEGISLATION">Legislation</a> de la Chirurgie en France, and two separate treatises, in 12mo, the one on Suppuration, and the other, De la Gangrene; in 1750, he republished his Traité des Effets et de l'Usage de la Saignée, written during his residence at Mantes, and originally published in 1730; and in 1753, he published his Traité des Fievres Continues, in 2 tomes 12mo. These works have been all held in very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> estimation; and an excellent judge has lately given it as his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that "the Traité de la Gangrene is by far the most valuable publication which we yet possess upon this subject." Every page of this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, he adds, "is distinguished by the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> for accurate observation, and perspicuous arrangement, which are so remarkable in all the other writings of Quesnay, this celebrated author." (Dr Thomson's Lectures on Inflammation, p. 502.) The Traité des Fievres was the last of Quesnay's professional works. He appears to have henceforth comparatively abandoned his medical studies. At no period, indeed, had he allowed them exclusively to occupy his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, and he now devoted himself, in preference, to other and, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> possible, still more interesting inquiries. He had always entertained a strong predilection for agricultural pursuits, the effect, perhaps, of his situation in early life; and this, combined with the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECULATIVE">speculative</a> and metaphysical <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> of his mind, seems to have led him to those peculiar notions respecting the paramount importance of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> as a source of wealth, and the constitution of society, which have rendered his name so justly celebrated in the history of economical science. The articles "Fermier" and "Grains" in the Encyclopédie, published in 1756 and 1757, contain the earliest development of his views on this subject. Both articles are written with great ability, and display an intimate acquaintance with the subject, considerable reading, and great powers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a>. In the article "Grains" the distinction between the produit total and the produit <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a>, between the productiveness of agriculture, and the unproductiveness of all other employments, the doctrine of the unrestricted freedom of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, and most of the other leading principles in the theory of the economists, are distinctly stated and illustrated with much ingenuity and talent. The Tableau Économique, and the Maximes Générales du Gouvernement Économique, annexed to it, under the title of Extraits des Économies Royales, de M. de Sully, were printed, by the express command of the King, at Versailles in 1758, with the following very remarkable epigraph for a work brought forth under such auspices, Pauvres paysans, pauvres royaume; pauvres royaume, pauvre Souverain! The maxims, which contain a short but comprehensive <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> of Quesnay's system, were reprinted, together with an analysis of the Tableau, and a selection from various articles contributed by Quesnay, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of his peculiar doctrines, to the Journal d'Agriculture, and the Ephemerides du Citoyen,* in the collection of Quesnay's economical works, entitled Physiocratie, ou Constitution Naturelle du Gouvernement le plus Avantageux au Genre Humain, edited by his friend and scholar, Dupont, in 1767. We have elsewhere entered at considerable length into an examination of the speculations of Quesnay and his followers, with respect to the constitution of po- --- * The Ephemerides du Citoyen was begun in 1767, and was, for a few months, conducted by the Abbé Baudeau, and then by Dupont. It was published monthly, and two numbers make a considerable duodecimo volume. The authors were all disciples of Quesnay, and zealous economists. Their discussions embraced only the moral and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> sciences; many branches of which they have treated with much ability and acuteness. There is a valuable Eloge of Quesnay in one of the numbers for 1775, written by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTE">Conte</a> d'Albon. The following extract from the approbation given by the Censeur to the third <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> for 1770 is curious: "J'exhorte," says he, "de nouveau les auteurs de ce Journal, à résister à la tentation de critiquer—Le bonheur du citoyen tient à sa confiance—On peut et l'on doit quelquefois avertir en secret ceux qui sont préposés à l'administration. Mais on ne doit prêcher aux particuliers que leur propre réforme, et non celle de l'état." VOL. VI. PART I. itical <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a>, and the sources of public wealth. (See the articles Economists and Political Economy.) That there is a good <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a> in them must be allowed; but this is far more than compensated by the many <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a>, discriminating, and original views, and important discoveries, which they contain. Perhaps, however, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> merit of Quesnay, and the sect of which he was the founder, does not consist so much in the discoveries they made, as in their having been the earliest philosophers who perceived that the institutions of society ought always to harmonize with the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> principles on which it is founded, or, as they termed it, with the *Ordre naturel et essentiel des Sociétés Politiques*. Economical science is defined by them to be, "L'étude et la démonstration des loix de la nature, relatives à la subsistance, et la multiplication du genre humain." L'observation universelle de ces loix est l'intérêt commun et général de tous les hommes. La connaissance universelle de ces loix est donc le préalable indispensable, et le moyen nécessaire du bonheur de tous." (*Éphemerides du Citoyen*, 1769, No. II. p. 13.) It is to be regretted that, in investigating these laws, they proceeded almost entirely on abstract and speculative principles, without sufficiently attending to the effects of particular institutions, and to the various phenomena manifested in the progress of society. But notwithstanding the defective <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> in which the economists conducted their researches, they succeeded in establishing and elucidating many important principles; and there is certainly much more reason to wonder at the general correctness of their conclusions, than to feel surprised at the errors into which they fell. Quesnay and his disciples established, that society was formed for the purpose of securing the greatest possible advantage to its members; that the security of property and the freedom of industry were its essential bases; and that the proper business of the politician was not to interfere to regulate the pursuits of individuals, but to protect the equal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> and liberties of all, and to secure the utmost freedom of competition in all the departments of industry. And though it is undoubtedly true, that most of these principles had been pointed out by previous writers, Quesnay and his school have the unquestionable merit of being the first who showed their dependence on each other, who presented them in a systematic and consistent form, and who were thus enabled to give a scientific demonstration of the injustice and impolicy of such institutions as <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> or mistaken views of national <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> had established in opposition to them. In our article on Political Economy we have shown the fallacy of Quesnay's opinion with respect to agriculture being the only source of wealth; and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> of all ages sufficiently proves that the *despotisme légal*, in the hands of an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> monarch, without *contrefores* of any kind, which he strangely supposed was the best of all possible governments, is about the very worst.* Notwithstanding his great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and the sufferings he experienced from the almost incessant attacks of the gout, the activity of Quesnay's mind <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> unimpaired. *Il a*, said one of his friends, *une tête de trente ans sur un corps de quatre-vingts.* He contributed, subsequently, to the publication of the *Physiocratie*, many acute and able articles to the *Éphemerides du Citoyen*; and continued wholly occupied with these studies and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, to which he had latterly begun to pay considerable attention, till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which took place at Versailles, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1774, in the 80th year of his age. Quesnay was a man of the most inflexible integrity; the nicest <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>; and the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>. Though highly esteemed by the King, and long resident at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">Court</a>, he never intermixed in the intrigues of which it was the constant <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>. No one ever scrupled to express himself freely in his presence, nor was the confidence placed in him ever betrayed. "*Il recevoit chez lui des personnes de tous les partis, mais en petit nombre, et qui toutes avoient une grande confiance en lui. On y parlait tres hardiment de tout; et ce qui fait leur éloge et le sien, jamais on ne rien repêche.*"† To the utmost frankness and sincerity, he added the easy address and polished manners of a courtier and the intelligence of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>. No man was ever less solicitous of distinguishing himself, or more careful to offend the self-esteem of others. His conversation was animated, without the least effort at brilliancy. So much, indeed, was he averse to every appearance of pretension, that he was in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of veiling the most profound remarks and observations, under the form of apologies, which generally referred to some subject connected with rural affairs, to which he was always particularly attached. He was most indulgent to the faults and errors of others, provided they were unalloyed by any taint of artifice or baseness, for which he never hesitated, whatever might be the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of the party, to express the utmost contempt. Quesnay was truly a patriot and a philosopher. And we doubt much whether another instance can be produced of one who had lived so long in a profligate and luxurious Court, unsullied by its vices, and aloof from its contentions; and who preserved, to an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> old age, all those generous and kindly feelings, with that unobtrusive but ardent zeal in the cause of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>, and that love of speculation and profound inquiry, which distinguished his earlier years. Quesnay, says Madame du Hausset, "*étoit un <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> génie, suivant l'opinion de tous ceux qui --- * We are at a loss to conjecture the grounds on which Mr Chalmers has presumed to affirm (*Biographical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>*, Vol. XXV. Art. Quesnay), that the "economists abused their influence by circulating democratic principles!" It would be quite as correct to say, that Locke and his followers had abused their influence, by circulating <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESPOTICAL">despotical</a> principles. † *Journal de Madame du Hausset* in the *Mélanges*, &c. p. 277. A striking instance of the confidence placed by the most opposite parties in Quesnay is given in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> volume of Marmontel's *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a>*. l'avoir connu et de plus un homme fort gai. Il aimait causer avec moi de la campagne; j'y avais été élevé, et il me faisait parler des herbages de Normandie et du Poitou, de la richesse des fermiers, et de la manière de cultiver. C'était le meilleur homme du monde, et la plus éloignée de la plus petite intrigue. Il était bien plus occupé à la cour de la meilleure manière de cultiver la terre que de tout ce que s'y passait." (Melanges, p. 313.) "Tandis," says Marmontel, "que les orages se formaient et se dissipent au-dessous de l'entresol de Quesnay, il griffonnait ses axiomes et ses calculs d'économie rustique, aussi tranquille, aussi indifférent à ces mouvements de la cour, que s'il en eût été à cent lieues de distance. Là-bas, on décidait de la paix, de la guerre, du choix des généraux, du renvoi des ministres; et nous, dans l'entresol, nous raisonnions d'agriculture; nous calculions le produit net, ou quelquefois nous divisons galement avec Diderot, d'Alembert, Duclos, Helvétius, Turgot, Buffon; et Mme de Pompadour, ne pouvant pas engager <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CETTE">cette</a> troupe de philosophes à descendre dans son salon, venait elle-même les voir à <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> et causer avec eux." Dr Smith was well acquainted with Quesnay. He frequently met with him during his residence at Paris in 1766; and while he bears the most <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> testimony to the "modesty and simplicity" of his character, he has pronounced his system to be, "with all its imperfections, the nearest approximation to the truth that has yet been published on the subject of Political Economy." (Wealth of Nations, Vol. III. p. 28.) So highly, indeed, was Dr Smith impressed with a sense of his merits, as a man and a philosopher, that it was his intention, had he not been prevented by Quesnay's death, to have <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> to him the Wealth of Nations. (Mr Stewart's Account of the Life and Writings of Dr Smith.) Quesnay had a son by his wife, to whom he was united when at Mantes. He gave him an excellent education; and exhibited a striking <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of his disinterestedness, by constantly refusing to solicit for him any place or situation under <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. This son ultimately settled in the country on an estate near Beauvoir. One of Quesnay's grandsons was appointed by Turgot to a place in the administration; and another entered the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, and acted as a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> of infantry at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Jemappes. No man was ever more esteemed by his friends than Quesnay, and none ever existed who was more ready to do all in his power to advance their interests. Mercier de la Riviere, the author of the work Sur l'ordre Naturel et Essentiel des Sociétés Politiques, and who had been Intendant at Martinique, seems to have occupied the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> place in his esteem, and was regarded by him as the only person in France who was qualified to conduct the administration of the Finances. He was also much attached to the Marquis de Mirabeau, Turgot, Dupont, the Abbé Baudeau, and the other leading economists, who willingly acknowledged him for their master, and enthusiastically exerted themselves to defend and propagate his doctrines. "The economists were in reality, and not merely in appearance, a sect of philosophers. Secta fuit servare modum, finemque tuiri Naturaeque sequi, ritumque imprenderi vero, Nec sibi sed tibi genitum se credere mundo. They acted from honest zeal for the truth, and not from fashion, eccentric tastes, or the love of singularity; their sole object was to enlighten and improve mankind; and to them, among political inquirers, belongs the rare praise of having first pointed out the natural order of things, or the observed course of nature in the conduct of the world, as the example and guide of human policy." (s. s.)

RAILWAY

Pages 460-467

a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> carriage-way, in which the track of the carriage-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a> being laid with bars, or rails, of wood, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, or metal, the carriage is more easily drawn along this smooth surface than over an ordinary road. Wooden <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RAILWAYS">railways</a> are said to have been introduced at the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a> coal-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a> so early as the year 1680, for transporting the coals from the mouth of the pits to the ships in the river Tyne. Even at that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, many of these mines employed each of them 400 or 500 carts in this traffic; it became, therefore, an object of manifest importance to reduce the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> expense thereby incurred in the keeping up of horses, drivers, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of wooden rails was the best, and, indeed, the only effectual method which could at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> have been devised for the purpose; for which also the situation was in other respects favourable, presenting in most <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> an easy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> towards the river. These railways then were very generally introduced, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> for a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> period in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. Slips of ground of the requisite breadth for the railway were marked out between the coal-pits and the river, and were either leased by the coal owners, or purchased of the different proprietors whose ground the proposed line of road intersected in its course. To obtain the most easy and regular descent, this line was varied in its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> to meet the inequalities of the ground; or, where these inequalities were inconsiderable, it was carried straight forward, and the regular slope made up by embankments and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a>. The ground being then smoothed and levelled as for an ordinary road, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> logs of wood, termed sleepers, cut in lengths equal to the breadth of the road, were laid across it, and firmly bedded into it at short distances, to sustain and hold fast the rails, or slips of wood, on which the waggon-wheels were intended to run. These rails were made of beech, and were laid end to end, so as to form two continued <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of rail or wooden ridges, running <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to each other, along each side of the road, crossing the large logs at each of their extremities, on which they rested as on so many foundations; and were also nailed, or otherwise secured, to keep each piece in its proper <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. The waggons were of the usual <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>, but of a large size, so as to contain several tons of coals, and set upon low wheels; the smoothness of the way rendering wheels of the ordinary size unnecessary. On these rails a single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> could readily draw three tons of coals from the pits to the river. Where any steep declivity occurred on the road, this was termed a run, or an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-INCLINED_PLANE">inclined <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANE">plane</a>; and on it the descent of the waggons was retarded, and regulated by a species of brake, or crooked <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEVER">lever</a>, termed a convey, attached to the waggon and managed by the driver. The banks of the Tyne, near Newcastle, are remarkably steep on each side; but instead of forming inclined planes on them, the railway was here continued on a wooden stage, raised to the same height as the top <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the river, and carried forward until it came perpendicularly over the river side, where a wooden <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATFORM">platform</a>, termed a staith, was erected for the convenience of delivering the coals; the waggons being emptied into a trough, or spout, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> which the coals descended either directly into the ships, or into the store below. Such was the construction of the original railways, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> railways in which we evidently perceive all the parts and members of the railway as it is formed at the present <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; viz. the regular-formed road, the rails, the sleepers, the low waggons, and the inclined plane. Their only defect consisted in the soft and decaying <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the wood, the wear and tear of which caused such expense for repairs, as greatly limited their application; so that it was only the shortness of the distance, and the great <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of the traffic, which rendered their application at all beneficial. It was only about the year 1738 that they were attempted in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COLLIERIES">collieries</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITEHAVEN">Whitehaven</a>; and it does not appear that they were adopted in any other part of the kingdom. The use of iron, therefore, in place of wood, was an essential improvement in the construction of railways, and caused, indeed, a complete change in this, as it has done in every other branch of practical <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a> into which it has been introduced. Flat bars of iron were at first fastened on the top of the wooden rails; but after various unsuccessful attempts, the rails themselves were at last wholly composed of iron, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> in short bars, united at their extremities, and resting on sleepers, or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> blocks of stone, disposed at short distances along each side of the road; and this construction having been once fairly reduced to practice, was not only adopted universally in place of wood, but soon led to new and more extensive applications. Iron railways were quickly introduced into all the coal and mining districts of the kingdom. They were employed on <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a>, in place of locks, to raise the barges on an inclined plane from a lower to a higher <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>; in some instances they were adopted in preference to the canal itself; and, on the whole, they now form an important auxiliary to inland <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, pushing the channels of trade and intercourse into districts otherwise inaccessible, and even into the interior of the mines. The railways in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> are so numerous, that Railways in England and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WALES">Wales</a> would exceed our limits to specify the particular lines. In the Newcastle coal district, on the river Wear, in the coal and mining districts of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a>, as well as of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DERBYSHIRE">Derbyshire</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFFORDSHIRE">Staffordshire</a>, there are numerous railways branching off from the navigable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> and canals to the different mines. In <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHROPSHIRE">Shropshire</a> also, and in the great mining districts along the vale of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a>, the use of railways is very general, and it was here that the inclined plane was first brought in aid of inland navigation. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURREY">Surrey</a>, there is a railway of a considerable extent, termed the Surrey Railway, and this presents one of the few attempts that have been made to form public railways for general use. In the great mining districts on the west of the Severn, including South Wales, the rail or tram roads are very numerous; and here, owing to the steepness and impracticable nature of the ground, they have been of essential utility in supplying the place of canals. In the year 1791, there was scarcely a single railway in all South Wales, and in 1811, the completed railroads connected with canals, collieries, iron, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>-works in the counties of Monmouth, Glamorgan, and Caer- Railway, marthen, amounted to nearly 150 miles in length, exclusive of a great extent within the mines themselves; of which one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> in Merthyr-Tydvil possessed 30 miles under ground. In <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-MONMOUTHSHIRE">Monmouthshire</a>, the Sirhoway railway forms one of the first in point of magnitude which has hitherto been constructed. It extends from Pilgelly, near Newport, to the Sirhoway and Tredagar lime-works, distant 23 miles, whence it is continued five miles farther to the Trevil lime-works, in Brecknockshire, along with a branch to the west, to the Rumney and Union Iron-works. This railway was made by the Monmouthshire Canal Company, under the authority of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">Parliament</a>. From Sirhoway, a branch proceeds eastwards to the Ebbwy works, and from thence down the course of the Ebbwy to Crumlin <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">Bridge</a>, whence it joins the canal from Newport; and from Sirhoway again, the Brinare railway is continued over the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> Mountain to the vale of the Uske at Brecon, and from thence to Hay on the river <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WYE">Wye</a>. In Glamorganshire, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> railways are the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARDIFF">Cardiff</a> and Merthyr-Tydvil, the Aberdare, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-SWANSEA">Swansea</a> railways. In <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-CAERNARVONSHIRE">Caernarvonshire</a>, the principal railway is that which extends from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-CAERNARVON">Caernarvon</a> to the lime-works near Llandebie, a distance of 15 miles. From this account of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> railways in England and Wales, it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> appear that this species of inland carriage is principally applicable where trade is considerable and the length of conveyance short; and is chiefly useful, therefore, in transporting the mineral produce of the kingdom from the mines to the nearest <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a>, whether <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, river, or canal. Attempts have been made to bring it into more general use, but without success; and it is only in particular circumstances that navigation, with the aid either of locks or inclined planes to surmount the elevations, will not present a more convenient medium for an extended trade. South Wales, however, presents an example, where the trade being great, and also chiefly descending, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> rugged, and the supply of water scanty, railways have been adopted with complete success; and have been found in some cases at least equal to canals in point of economy and dispatch. The Surrey railway, not having these advantages, has scarcely answered the expectations of its projectors, more especially the southern line from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROYDON">Croydon</a> to Gadstone. It was at one time proposed to continue this railway to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTSMOUTH">Portsmouth</a>, but the plan was abandoned. In Scotland there are various railways proceeding from the different mines throughout the kingdom. The principal one in point of magnitude is the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of Portland's railway, extending from the town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KILMARNOCK">Kilmarnock</a> to the harbour of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TROON">Troon</a>, a distance of nearly ten miles. Its chief object is the export of coal and lime, in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> a great trade is carried on by means of the railway. In the coal and mining districts round Glasgow, there are numerous smaller railways, and also in the coal fields of Mid <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOTHIAN">Lothian</a> and Fife. Plans have been proposed for a public railway from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> to the different coal-works in the neighbourhood. An extensive railway was also at one time projected from Glasgow to Berwick-upon-Tweed, but none of those schemes have been carried into effect. The original wooden railways already mentioned are the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> on which all the succeeding ones have been formed, and of which we shall now describe shortly the construction. In regard to the road itself, this should, in the first place, be formed in such a direction, and with such a declivity as may best <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> the nature of the ground through which it passes, and of the trade to be carried upon it. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the trade, for example, be all or chiefly in one direction, the road should obviously decline that way, so that the waggons, with their contents, may descend on this inclined plane as much as possible by their own gravity. The inclination should also be proportioned to the extent of the trade up the railway, so that the draught each way may be equal. If the exports and imports, therefore, be equal, the road should be on a level; and where the ground will not permit that declivity or level best suited to the trade, the line should be varied, and the inequalities made up, if it can be done at a moderate expense, so as to bring it as near as possible to the proper standard. If the inequalities are such as to render this impracticable, the only resource lies in inclined planes. Where the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of level, for example, between the two extremities of the road is such as would render an equal declivity too steep, the road must then be carried, either on a level or with the due <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of slope, as far as practicable, and then lowered by an inclined plane; on which the waggons are let gently down by means of a brake, are dragged up by means of an additional power to that which draws them along the road, or at once let down and drawn up by means of a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROLLER">roller</a> or pulley, the heavier preponderating over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a>. In laying out a line of railway, therefore, as every situation presents peculiar circumstances, no general rule can be laid down, and the plan must be left to the skill and judgment of the engineer. The line of railway being fixed on, the road is then properly formed, and of such a width as will be sufficient for containing the opposite rails, and for forming a foot-path on one side. The distance between the opposite rails varies from three feet to four and one half feet; some preferring a long and narrow waggon, and others a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> short one. Hence a breadth of from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> to twelve feet will be sufficient for a single road, and from fifteen to twenty for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> one. The next operation is the setting and firm bedding of the stone sleepers. These consist of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> blocks of stone, each of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of one or two cwt. Their shape is immaterial, provided their base be broad, and their upper surface present an even and solid basis for the rail. They are placed along each side of the road, about three feet distant from each other from centre to centre; the opposite ones being separated by the width between the opposite rails. The ground under them is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> down to form a firm foundation, or, if it be of a soft nature, is first laid with a coat of gravel or small metal, and this beaten under the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>; the situation of each stone being properly gauged both as to its distance from the adjoining ones, and as to the level or declivity of its upper surface, on which the rails are in- tended to rest. The space between the sleepers is then filled up with gravel, metal, or other road materials, such as may consolidate into a hard and firm <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>. The next object is the construction of the iron rails; and on this point two very different plans have been adopted, each of which has its <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a>, and is practised to a great extent. The one is termed the flat rail, or tram plate; the rails being laid on their side, and the waggon-wheels travelling over their broad and flat surface. The other is termed the edge rail; the rails being laid edgewise, and the wheels rolling on their upper surfaces. The flat rail, or tram plate, consists of a plate of cast-iron, about three feet long, from three to five inches broad, and from half an inch to an inch thick; extending from sleeper to sleeper, and having a flanache turn up or crest on the inside, from two and a half to four inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. This rail bears on the sleepers at each end at least three inches, where the rails are cast about half an inch thicker than in the middle. As there is no intermediate <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> for the rail between the sleepers, except the surface of the road, the use of the flanache is not merely to prevent the waggon from being drawn off the road; it resists the transverse strain arising from the weight of the waggon; on this account it is often, and with great propriety, raised higher in the middle than at the sides, forming an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> of a circle; and, to strengthen the rail still farther, a similar flanache, arched inversely, is added below, as represented in Plate CXV., figs. 1, 2, 3. The weight of each rail is from forty to fifty pounds. To unite these rails into one continued line, they are merely laid to each other, end to end, all along each side of the road; being kept in their places, and at the same time made fast to the sleepers, by an iron spike driven through the extremity of each rail into a plug of oak fitted into a hole in the centre of each sleeper. This spike is about six inches long; it has no head, but the upper end of it forms an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> square, about one inch broad, half an inch thick; and the hole in the rails, through which it passes, is formed by a rectangular notch, half an inch square, in the middle of the extremity of each rail; the opposite notches of each rail forming, when laid together, the complete oblong square of one inch by half an inch, and slightly dovetailed from top to bottom, so as to fit exactly the tapering head of the spike, which is driven clear below the upper surface of the rail. Plate CXV., fig. 4, represents a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECTION">section</a> of a rail, with its sleeper and fastening. Wherever the rails <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> any road, the space between them and on each side must be paved or causewayed to the level of the top of the flanaches, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a> on the road may be enabled to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> clear over the rails. In single railways it is necessary to have places at certain intervals where the empty waggons, in returning, may get off the road to allow the loaded ones to pass. A place of this kind is termed a turn-out; and the waggons are directed into it by a moveable rail termed a pointer, fixed at the intersection between the principal rail and the turn-out, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> on its extremity, so as to open the way into the turn-out, and shut that along the road. This contrivance is also used whenever one line of railway crosses another. It is represented at Plate CXV., fig. 5, where, also, fig. 6 is a plan of the railway and of the turn-out. The tram roads have been universally adopted in Wales, where they are preferred to any other species. They are also used in most parts of England. The Surrey railway is of this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, and was designed by Mr Jessop. In Scotland the Duke of Portland's railway, which, we believe, was planned by the same engineer, is of the same kind, and the rails nearly of the same dimensions. These flat railways have one advantage, in admitting waggons or carts of the ordinary construction, and this is particularly exemplified in the Troon railway. According to an account with which we have been favoured by Mr Wilson of Troon, "there are several kinds of waggons used upon the railway under certain restrictions; such as four-wheeled waggons with flat bottom and low shelmets for carrying stone, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a>, grain, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, slates, &c. from the harbour to Kilmarnock, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>," &c. "The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> make of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CART">cart</a> is allowed to use the railway if the wheels are cylindrical, and there be no greater load on each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> than 28 cwt. A great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> is done with these carts in carrying timber, barks, grain, &c., as, with the same cart, they can carry these articles into and through the streets of the town." The other railways in Scotland, however, are chiefly of the edge kind. In the principal collieries of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of England, also, the flat rail has been almost entirely superseded by the edge rails, and the latter are now generally admitted to be decidedly superior in the ease of draught which they occasion; the edge of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> presenting less friction, and being less liable to clog up with dust and mud, or to be obstructed with stones driven off the road upon the surface of the rails. The edge rail consists merely of a rectangular bar of cast-iron, three feet long, three or four inches broad, and from one-half inch to one inch thick; set in its edge between sleeper and sleeper, and bearing on the sleepers at its extremities. The upper side of the rail is flanached out to present a broader bearing surface for the wheels, and the under side is also cast thicker than the middle, for the sake of strength. But the greatest strength is evidently attained by casting the rail not rectangular, but deeper in the middle than at the ends, to resist better the transverse strain. The ends may be safely reduced nearly to one-third of the depth in the middle, and still be equally strong. To unite the rails together, and at the same time preserve them in their places, and in their upright position, and to bind them also to the sleepers, they are set in a cast-iron socket or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, which is attached firmly to the sleeper. This socket embracing the extremities of the adjacent rails, which are here made to overlap a little; a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PIN">pin</a> is driven at once through the rails and through the socket, and binds the whole together. This is the general method of uniting the edge rails, but the shape and dimensions of the metal chair and of the overlap of the rails are varied according to the judgment and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of the engineer. Plate CXV., fig. 7, represents a section of an edge railway with the sleepers and waggons, &c.; and figs. 8, 9, 10, is an enlarged section of a rail and sleepers with a plan. Since edge railways have come into more general use, an essential improvement has been made in their construction by the use of malleable iron, in place of cast-iron, in forming the rails. The advantage of malleable iron rails is, that they are less subject to breakage than cast-iron; a circumstance of importance in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, where it is not easy to avoid those jolts and sudden shocks which cast-iron is least of all capable of withstanding; and though they should happen to give way, they are easily repaired. They can also be laid in greater lengths, and requiring therefore fewer <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a>; they can be bent with ease to the curvature of the road; when worn out they are of greater value; and lastly, their first cost is very little, if at all, greater than that of cast-iron rails. Malleable iron is, no doubt, less able to withstand exposure, decaying more readily under the influence of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> and moisture; but hitherto this inconvenience has not been felt, and, on the whole, the malleable iron is now decidedly preferred. These rails are laid and joined in the same manner as the cast-iron, only in greater lengths. Malleable iron, we believe, was first introduced in railways by Mr George Grieve, at Sir John Hope's collieries, near Edinburgh, where it was first tried on the lighter <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> which is done underground. The rails consisted of square bars one inch or one and one-fourth inch square, nine feet long, resting on one or two sleepers in the middle, and resting and made fast to sleepers at the extremities; a simple knee being formed on each end of the bar, and the two <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a> of each two adjacent rails jammed into one socket in the sleeper. The use of these rails was found so beneficial, that they have since entirely superseded the flat cast-iron rail in general use at the time of their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>. For heavier loads the rails are made deeper. We have been favoured with the following account of their construction by an engineer (Mr Neilson of Glasgow) who has formed several of the kind. "One of them is on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> of Glasgow, commencing at the Hurlet extensive coal and lime-works, and extending to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAISLEY">Paisley</a> canal, a distance of about two miles. It is formed of flat bar iron two and one-fourth inches deep, by nearly three-fourths of an inch thick, and the rail in lengths of nine feet, each rail being supported at every three feet by a sleeper and cast-iron chair. The joinings are formed by a cast-iron dovetailed socket suited to receive the jointed ends of the bar, and a dovetailed glut or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEY">key</a>, by which means the several rails are joined as if into one continued bar." An improvement has lately been made in the construction of malleable iron rails, which promises to be of essential utility. It consists in the use of bars, not rectangular, but of a wedge form, or swelled out on the upper edge. In the rectangular bar there is evidently a waste of metal on the under surface, which, not requiring to be of the same thickness as where the waggon-wheel is to roll, may be evidently reduced with advantage, if it can be done easily. The bar may then be made deeper, and broader at the top than before, so as with the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of metal to be equally strong, and present a much broader bearing surface for the wheel. This has been accomplished by Mr Birkinshaw of the Bedlington Iron-works, who has obtained a patent for these broad topped rails. The peculiar shape is given them in the rolling of the metal, by means of grooves cut in the rollers, corresponding with the requisite breadth, and depth, and curvature of the proposed rail. Mr B. recommends his rails to be of 18 feet in length. We have seen one of these patent rails at Sir John Hope's colliery; and it certainly forms the most perfect iron rail which has hitherto been contrived; combining very simply and ingeniously its form the qualities of lightness, strength, and durability. It is twelve feet long, two inches broad along the top, about half an inch along the bottom, and still thinner between. It rests on sleepers at every three feet, and at those places the rail is two inches deep, while in the middle point between the sleepers it is three inches deep. Fig. 11 is a longitudinal section of this rail, and figs. 12 and 13 are transverse sections at the sleepers, and at the middle point between each sleeper. All these inequalities, we believe, are produced on the metal by means of the rollers; and this circumstance is well deserving of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, as it may obviously be applied not merely to the formation of railways, but to a variety of other purposes in the arts. The moulding and shaping of the metal in this manner is quite a new attempt in the iron manufacture, and it is not easy to say how far such an invention may yet be carried by the skill of British artists. The waggons used on railways are of various sizes, but of nearly the same general shape, and all set on four wheels from two to three feet diameter. They are made to carry from 20 to 50 cwt. exclusive of the waggon itself, which weighs from 12 to 15 cwt. The axles of the fore and hind wheels are fixed three feet asunder or more, so that the rail is never loaded with more than one-fourth of the waggon at once. According to Mr Wilson, "The size of the coal waggons of Kilmarnock colliery are, on an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> length 80 inches, mean breadth 45 inches, and depth 30 inches. Each contains 40 bushels, equal to 32 cwt. of fine coal, and 35 cwt. of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALLING">malling</a> coal. The weight of the waggon, exclusive of the coal, is 13 cwt. Each waggon, including two pair of wheels and axles, costs from about L.13 to L.15, and are mostly lined with sheet iron." In Sir John Hope's railway the waggons are also nearly of the above dimensions. In the Sirhoway railway each waggon carries two and one-half tons. In regard to the expense of constructing a railway, this will depend greatly on the ease or difficulties to be met with in forming the road; and making up the inequalities to the required slope. The above railway described by Mr Neilson cost only L.660 per <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a>; but where there are considerable embankments to form, bridges to build, and deep <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTINGS">cuttings</a>, the expense may rise to L.4000 and L.5000 per mile. The usual rate of tonnage on coals, &c. conveyed on railways is 2d. per ton per mile. An important consideration regards the work done, or capable of being performed on a railway. On this point, however, the accounts from different railways are various; the performance depending on many circumstances little attended to in the general estimate of work; such as the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the horses, the state of the road, the greater or less declivity of the rails, and various other circumstances. More exact observations or experiments are therefore wanting to form correct notions on this subject; but in the mean time, we shall state such facts as have been noticed by different observers. The most exact experiments were made by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Wilkes, Esq. of Measham in Derbyshire. The result is, that one horse, value L20, on a railway declining at the rate of one foot perpendicular to 115 in the length of the road, "drew 21 carriages or waggons, laden with coals and timber, amounting in the whole to 35 tons, overcoming the vis inertiae repeatedly with great ease." This performance appears, no doubt, enormous; but was evidently owing not so much to the diminution of friction by the railway as to the great declivity; circumstances whose effect must be distinguished in order to obtain any general rule for future works. It is well known that, on any inclined road or plane, every carriage has a tendency to descend of itself, and with a force in proportion to its own weight, exactly as the height of the plane is to its length. In the above example, therefore, the carriages, independent of any <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> force of traction, would have been urged by their own gravity with a force of 115th of their weight, and equal, therefore, to 680 lbs. But as it will not be too low an estimate to assume 150 lbs. as the working draught of a horse, hence the waggons would descend by their <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> weight as if they had been dragged on a level way by at least four horses. If, then, to this 680 lbs. we add 150 for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the horse, the sum, or 830 lbs. will be equal to the power necessary to overcome the friction and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INERTIA">inertia</a> of these waggons, and which appears by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> to amount to 3/4th of their whole weight; so that, if the railway had been level, the horse would only have drawn 61/4th tons. Carriages on an ordinary road require 1/3th or 1/5th of their actual weight to draw them along; so that, on a railway, the ease of draught is six times greater than on a common road. The same horse, Mr Wilkes observes, drew up the acclivity five tons with ease. Here the weight of the waggons, or its 115th part, would act against the horse, which would not only have to overcome their friction and inertia, but to drag also this additional load upwards. But 1/4 + 1/15 of 5 tons = 216 lbs., the force of traction, which was evidently a strained effort. The same horse drew three tons up an acclivity of 1 in 20. Here 1/4 + 1/15 of 3 tons = 407 lbs., a power of traction which few horses could exert, and none could sustain for any length of time. The other experiments of Mr Wilkes agree nearly with the above. Mr Outram, Engineer, observes, that, with a declivity of 1 in 108, the waggons will almost descend of themselves, so that the horse has only to pull a little at his load. This would make the friction and inertia nearly 1/105th of the weight, and the draught of a horse nearly 6/5th tons. Mr Telford observes, that in a railway, with a declivity of 1 in 98, a horse will readily take down waggons containing from 12 to 15 tons, and bring back the same with four tons in them. The total load, in the first case, would be about 18 tons, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> 8 tons. Here the waggons being urged with 1/5th of their weight; this makes the friction and inertia equal to 1/70th of the weight, and the draught of a horse on a level way only 4/7th tons. In the Troon railway, the declivity is about 1 in 660; and, according to Mr Wilson's account, some horses take down two and some three waggons each, containing 33 cwt. of coal, and weighing itself 13 cwt., travelling at the rate of three miles an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>. The total load here may be averaged at 115 cwt.; and, the waggons being used with 1/60th of their weight, this makes the friction and inertia 1/3th of the weight, very nearly equal to the last. We have been favoured by Mr Grieve with the following particulars regarding Sir John Hope's railway, which is of the edge kind. It is on a level; and one horse draws five loaded waggons, each containing 30 cwt. of coals, and weighing, unloaded, 12 cwt. equal in all to 210 cwt. or 10½ tons; travelling at the rate of four miles an hour, deducting stoppages. This makes the friction 1/50th of the load. This performance is beyond any that we have yet stated, and shows decidedly the ease of draught of the edge rail. Previous to the formation of this railway, it required eight horses for the work which is now done with one. On the whole, then, it may be concluded, that on a level tram road, making allowance for the weight of the waggons, one horse will be required for every four tons of coals, or other articles conveyed; and on an edge railway, one horse will be required for every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> tons. On an ordinary canal, one horse, with a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a>, will be sufficient for every 30 tons. But the first cost of a canal is three or four times greater than that of a railway; so that, in some cases, it may become a question, whether a railway might not be adopted with advantage. On some of the railways near Newcastle, the waggons are drawn by means of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEAM_ENGINE"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol19.html#article-STEAM">steam</a>-engine working in a waggons by itself, the wheels of which are driven by the engine, and acting on a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACK">rack</a> laid along the railway, impel forward both the engine and the attached waggons: in some cases the wheels of the waggons operate without rail work, by the mere friction between them and the railway. The steam-engines employed for this purpose are of the high pressure kind; these requiring no condensing <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a>. But this application of steam has not yet arrived at such perfection as to have brought it into general use. REFRACTION (Double). See Addendum to this Volume.

RENNIE

Pages 469-473

Mechanist, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARCHITECT">Architect</a>, and Civil Engineer, was born on the 7th <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1761, at Phantassie, in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of Prestonkirk, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of East <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOTHIAN">Lothian</a>. His father, a highly respectable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a>, died in 1766, leaving a widow and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> children, of whom John was the youngest. The first <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> were acquired at the village school; and as it frequently happens, that some trifling circumstance in early <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> gives a bent to the pursuits, and fixes the destinies, of the future <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, so it fared with young Rennie. The school was situated on the opposite side of a brook, over which it was necessary to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> by means of a rustic <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> of stepping-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>; but when the freshes were out, the only alternative of crossing the stream was by means of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a>, which was kept at the workshop of Mr. Andrew Meikle, an ingenious mechanic, well known in Scotland as the inventor of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THRESHING">threshing</a>-machine, and many improvements in agricultural implements. In passing through this workshop, which stood on his family <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, young Rennie's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> was forcibly drawn to the various operations that were in progress; and a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his leisure and holiday-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> was passed therein. The sons of Mr Meikle, and the workmen, seeing the delight which he appeared to take in examining their labours, were in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of indulging him with their tools, and showing him their various uses. His evenings were chiefly employed in imitating those models which had particularly attracted his attention in the workshop; and it is known in the family, that, at little more than ten years of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, he had constructed the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of a windmill, a pile-engine, and a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEAM_ENGINE"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol19.html#article-STEAM">steam</a>-engine. That of the pile-engine is still in existence, and is said to be remarkably well made. Having <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> at Preston school till twelve years of age, he had a quarrel about that time with his schoolmaster, whom he deemed incompetent to give him further instruction, and therefore entreated that he might be permitted to leave the school. But his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> mind became restless; for the first time he felt the hours hang heavily on his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>; and having expressed a wish to be placed under his friend Mr Meikle, he employed himself with this ingenious mechanic for about two years: but his mind expanding with his growth, he began to feel that the progress of his intellectual faculties was likely to be retarded by a constant application to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANUAL">manual</a> labour. He therefore at length determined to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> himself under the tuition of Mr. Gibson, an able teacher of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUNBAR">Dunbar</a>; where he soon distinguished himself in so particular a manner, that Mr <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> Loch, General Inspector of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">Fisheries</a> in Scotland, in describing a visit which he paid to the school at Dunbar in 1778, notices the great proficiency displayed by young Rennie; prophesying that at no distant <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> he would prove an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>.* From this school, in less than two years, he returned to Mr Meikle, with a mind well stored with every branch of mathematical and physical science which Mr Gibson could teach him. About this time, Mr Gibson being appointed <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> to the public academy of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PERTH">Perth</a>, he earnestly recommended young Rennie to succeed him at Dunbar. But his views were of a more aspiring <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a>. As a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of favour, he undertook the management of the school for about six weeks, when he returned to his family, occasionally visiting and assisting his friend Mr Meikle, but mostly improving himself in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> and making models of machinery. His first <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">essay</a> in practical <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a> was the repairing of a corn-mill in his native village; and he erected two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> three others, before he was eighteen years of age. Resolved, however, that these <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> occupations should not interfere with his studies, he laid his plans so that he should be able to proceed occasionally to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, with a view of improving himself in physical science. He there attended the lectures of Professors Robison and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a>, and formed that acquaintance with the former of these gentlemen, which was gradually raised into friendship, and which, perhaps, may be said to have laid the foundation of his future fortune; for by him he was introduced to Messrs Bolton and Watt of Soho near <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRMINGHAM">Birmingham</a>. With these gentlemen he remained but a few months, for the purpose of receiving explanations respecting the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ALBION">Albion</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">Mills</a>, then erecting, the machinery of which he superintended. This exactly suited his views, for, conscious of his own powers, he deemed the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">Capital</a> the proper <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> to try their strength, and in this he was not mistaken. In proceeding from Edinburgh to Soho, he had taken the route by Carlisle, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANCASTER">Lancaster</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LIVERPOOL">Liverpool</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANCHESTER">Manchester</a>, for the purpose of visiting the different mills and public works in those great commercial and manufacturing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>; and the remarks which he made on the bridge then <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> over the Lune at Lancaster, on the docks at Liverpool, and more particularly on the Bridgewater canal, are distinguished by great sagacity, and were of essential <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to him afterwards. On leaving Soho, he again made a tour through the manufacturing districts of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEEDS">Leeds</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHEFFIELD">Sheffield</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROTHERHAM">Rotherham</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a>. For some time after he was settled in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, the Albion Mills, of which Bolton and Watt and Mr Wyatt were the projectors and leading proprietors, and who engaged him to superintend the execution of the mill-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, occupied a great share of his attention. Mr Watt, in his Notes to Professor Robison's Account of the Steam-Engine, says, That, "in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of the mill-work and machinery, they derived most valuable assistance from that able mechanician and engineer Mr John Rennie, then <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> entering into * Loch's Essays on the Trade, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">Commerce</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">Manufactures</a>, and Fisheries of Scotland, Vol. III. p. 211. business, who assisted in placing them, and under whose <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> they were executed." He also says, that the machinery, which used to be made of wood, was here made of cast-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, in improved forms, and thinks that this was the commencement of that system of mill-work which has proved so beneficial to this country. In fact, Rennie's mills are the most perfect <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of mechanism in that way that exist, distinguished by a precision of movement, and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> and proportion of parts that now serve as models throughout the empire. His <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-mills are so accurately calculated, that every particle of water is effectively employed, and none of it lost, as in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of constructing water-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a>. There is reason to believe that the difficulties which occurred at the Albion Mills with regard to the ebb and flow of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-TIDES">tides</a>, and which required all the ingenuity of that extraordinary genius Mr Watt, first led Mr Rennie to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of that branch of civil engineering connected with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HYDRAULICS">hydraulics</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HYDRODYNAMICS">hydrodynamics</a>, and in which he soon became so celebrated, as to have no rival after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Smeaton, in whose steps, he always used to say, he was proud to follow. Our limited space <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> not permit us to enter upon even an enumeration of all his great works, much less to give any detailed account of them; we must therefore content ourselves by mentioning some of the most important designs and undertakings in his threefold capacity of mechanist, architect, and civil engineer; three branches of art so intimately blended, as scarcely to admit of a separation. First, as a Mechanist.—Immediately after the completion of the Albion Mills, in 1786 or 1787, Mr Rennie's reputation was so firmly established in every thing connected with mill-work, that he found himself in a very extensive line of business. To him the planters of Jamaica and of the other West <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIA">India</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> applied for their <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-mills, which he constructed in a manner so superior to the old ones, that he soon obtained almost a monopoly of these expensive works. The powder-mill at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUNBRIDGE">Tunbridge</a>, the great flour-mill at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WANDSWORTH">Wandsworth</a>, several <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a>-mills, the machinery for various breweries and distilleries, were mostly of his manufacture; and wherever his machinery was required to be impelled by steam, the incomparable engines of his friends Messrs Bolton and Watt supplied the moving power; but, contrary to what has been stated in some of the public journals, he never had the least concern in directing, contriving, or advising any one part or movement of the steam-engine. He also constructed those beautiful specimens of machinery, the rolling and triturating mills at the Mint on Tower-Hill, to which Bolton and Watt's engines give <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>; and, at the time of his death, he was engaged in the construction of a rolling-mill, and similar machinery, for the intended mint at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-CALCUTTA">Calcutta</a>. As a bold and ingenious piece of mechanism, which may be considered as distinct from positive <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, there is nothing in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> that can bear a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> with the Southwark Bridge. The three immense <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, the centre one of 240, and each side <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> of 210 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAN">span</a>, consist entirely of masses of cast-iron, of various forms and dimensions, put together, on the same principle as a similar fabric of hewn <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; a method of employing iron, which may be considered to form a new epoch in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of bridge building. Various sinister predictions were entertained against this <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and beautiful bridge, which was to be rent in pieces by the expansive power of the first <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, or, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it escaped that, by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a> of the first winter's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>; but it has stood the test of many winters and summers, and appears not to feel either. Mr Rennie was applied to by the East India <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of a cast-iron bridge to be thrown over the river <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol10.html#article-GOOMTY">Goomty</a> at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUCKNOW">Lucknow</a>, at the desire of the Nabob Vizier of Oude. It consisted of three arches of cast-iron, the centre arch ninety, and each of the other arches eighty feet span. The arches were cast, and a superintending engineer sent out with them, but on their arrival the Nabob, in one of those moments of caprice to which eastern despots, even in their impotency, are so liable, changed his mind, and would not allow it to be put up. Secondly, as an Architect.—As there are few parts of civil engineering that do not occasionally require the aid of architecture, Rennie, at a very early stage of his progress, was called upon for a display of his skill in this line. Among his first undertakings in either line was that of the Lancaster Canal, which presented many difficulties, and, among others, that of carrying it by an aqueduct over the Lune, so as not to interrupt the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> of the river. Being one of the largest fabrics of its kind in Europe, and of a pleasing design, it is an object that arrests the attention of strangers, and is very generally admired. The bridges of Leeds, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MUSSELBURGH">Musselburgh</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KELSO">Kelso</a>, Newton-Stewart, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOSTON">Boston</a>, New Gallo-way, and a multitude of others, attest the architectural skill, the solidity, and, we may add, the good <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of Rennie; whilst a thousand smaller ones, with the various locks, wharf-walls, quays, embankments appertaining to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, and harbours in every part of the United <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">Kingdom</a>, are so many proofs of his diversified <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a>, and his skill in adapting the means to the end. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAKWATER">Breakwater</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLYMOUTH">Plymouth</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">Sound</a> can scarcely be called an architectural work, but it is constructed on true hydrodynamic principles, and so gigantic in its dimensions, and cyclopean in its structure, as equally to defy the force of the waves and the ravages of time. To Mr Whidby, who has zealously superintended the execution of this immortal work, now near its completion, the highest praise is also due; nor was the plan finally determined on without his advice and assistance. But the architectural work which, above all others, will immortalize the name of Rennie, is the Waterloo Bridge, a structure which even foreigners admit has no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> in Europe (and if not in Europe, certainly not in the whole world) for its magnitude, its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, and its solidity. That a fabric of this immensity, presenting a straight <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> line, stretching over nine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> arches, should not have altered more than a few inches, not five, in any one part, from that straight line, is an instance of firmness and solidity utterly unknown, and almost incredible; but all Rennie's works have been constructed for posterity; he made nothing slight; nor would he engage in any undertaking where, from an ill-judging economy, a sufficiency of funds was not forthcoming to meet his views. Another work, from a design of his, is now likely to be carried into execution, to which for some years past he had given his attention. It is that of a new stone bridge over the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, to replace that disgrace to the present age, the existing London Bridge. His design, which has been selected by a Committee of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">House</a> of Commons out of at least thirty that were offered, consists of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANITE">granite</a> bridge of five arches, the centre one of 150 feet span, which will be the largest stone arch in the world constructed in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times.
