This last is now by far the most extensive manufacture in the county; and is conducted in all its various branches, from the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a> of the yarn to the finishing of the finest fancy goods. In 1810, the cotton yarn sold was said to amount to £630,000; and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> employed in the buildings and machinery of the mills was estimated at £300,000. About 7000 looms were then employed in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEAVING">weaving</a> of muslins, besides 500 which were wrought by <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEAM">steam</a>, and produced coarse cottons to the value of £125,000 yearly. Paisley was long distinguished for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> manufacture, which is now inconsiderable; and that of thread, though still extensive, is said to be on the decline. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOAP">Soap</a>-making, tanneries, distilleries, breweries, and foundries, with a great many bleachfields and print-fields, furnish employment to a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> portion of the inhabitants. The principal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> are Paisley, Greenock, and Port-Glasgow. (See these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">Articles</a> in the Encyclopaedia.) It is at these towns, or rather at the two last, that the foreign and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COASTING">coasting</a> trade of the country, and the principal foreign trade of Scotland, is carried on. Greenock and Port-Glasgow have an extensive trade with <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> and the West Indies, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, and the west of England; and coastwise, and, by means of the Forth and Clyde Canal, with every part of Scotland. The canal proposed to be carried from Glasgow to Ardrossan, through Paisley and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JOHNSTONE">Johnstone</a>, has been executed as far as Johnstone, eleven miles from Glasgow; and passing through several populous parts of Renfrewshire, affords great accommodation to the trade between Paisley and Glasgow. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERRING">herring</a> and whale <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">fisheries</a> were once prosecuted to a greater extent than at present, though the former is still considerable; and the merchants of Greenock are extensively engaged in the Newfoundland and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOVA_SCOTIA">Nova Scotia</a> fisheries. As Renfrewshire does not raise enough of grain for its consumption, a good deal of corn is usually imported from Ireland and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CANADA">Canada</a>, as well as coastwise. The other imports are the raw materials of its manufactures, and the commodities required for the consumption of its inhabitants; and its exports, the produce of its manufactures, mines, and fisheries, and of its import trade from America and the West Indies. Notwithstanding the extensive manufactures of this county, the great fluctuation in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a> of labour, and its dense <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a>, which, in 1811, was at the rate of 384 per square <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a>, there are regular assessments for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> only in two or three parishes. In the rest of the county, the poor are supplied by voluntary contributions, aided by assessments imposed when circumstances require them. The county sends one member to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">Parliament</a>; and represents its only <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> burgh, Renfrew, a place containing about 1600 inhabitants, joins with Glasgow, Rutherglen, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUMBARTON">Dumbarton</a>, in the election of another for the Scottish burghs. Paisley and Greenock, notwithstanding their wealth and population, have no vote. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">Sheriff</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">Court</a> is now held at Paisley; yet Renfrew is still considered the county town, where the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> sessions are held, the head courts, and the meetings of the freeholders for the election of members of Parliament. The population in 1754 was only 26,645; in 1801 it amounted to 78,056; in 1811 it was 92,596; to which, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there be added the number of registered seamen, about 5000, and of men serving in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a> at the latter period, it would appear that it had quadrupled within 57 years, a rate of increase unexampled in any other county of Scotland. In 1821 it was 119,175; of which 51,178 were males, and 60,997 were females. The families employed in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> were 2725; in trade and manufactures, 15,780; in other occupations of various kinds, 5172. The increase of the population from 1811 to 1821 was 19,579. See the general works quoted under the former Scottish counties, and Wilson's General View of the Agriculture, &c. of Renfrewshire.

ROBISON

Pages 480-485

a distinguished Professor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>, born, in 1739, at Boghall, in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of Bal dernock, and in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Stirling, was a younger son of John Robison, Esq. who- * Derrien, Notice Historique et Descriptive sur la Route de Montcenis. had formerly been a merchant at Glasgow, and had retired to live in considerable affluence on his estate at Boghall, not far from that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. He was of a family sufficiently respectable to enable his son at a subsequent <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> to prove himself, to the satisfaction of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">Court</a> of St Petersburg, a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> born. As a younger <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, that son was originally intended for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and went at an early <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of Scotland, in 1750, to enter as a student of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> in the University of Glasgow; so that he was initiated almost in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of Latin and Greek literature under the able instruction of Dr Moore, the well known professor of Greek; and he acquired such a knowledge of these languages as served to constitute him a correct classical scholar through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. He pursued his studies with so much <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, as to obtain the approbation of his teachers, and the admiration of his contemporaries, who were delighted with the originality and ingenuity of his conversation, though he did not himself reflect with perfect satisfaction upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of application which he had exerted in his academical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>. He took a degree of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">Master</a> of Arts in 1756, having studied <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> under Dr Robert Simson, and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORAL_PHILOSOPHY">moral philosophy</a> under Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a> Smith. The example of so correct and rigid a follower of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> methods of demonstration, as Dr Simson, must unquestionably have exercised considerable influence on his yet unformed <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> in mathematics; but he seems to have had a natural preference, either from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of his mind, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> from some previously acquired habits of thinking, for the geometrical method; for we are informed that "he first attracted the regard of Dr Simson by owning his dislike of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALGEBRA">algebra</a>, and by returning a neat geometrical solution of a problem which had been given out to the class in an algebraical form; with this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of solution the professor was delighted, though the pupil candidly acknowledged that it had been adopted only because he could not solve the problem in the manner required of the class." He had imbibed, in the course of his studies, an insuperable aversion to the pursuit of his original objects in the church; not certainly from any want of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> feeling, or from a dislike to the kind of life that was intended for him, but probably from some difficulties that had occurred to him respecting particular <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of doctrine or of practice. He was therefore compelled to provide himself with some other occupation; and he readily accepted the offers of some of his friends in 1758, to recommend him to Dr Blair, a prebendary of Westminster, who had formed a scheme for sending <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Edward, the young <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, to complete his professional education at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> with a son of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">Admiral</a> Knowles; and Mr Robison was to have instructed his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Highness in mathematics and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>. He was much disappointed, on his arrival in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, to find that the expedition had never been seriously intended; and he readily accepted an engagement to attend young Knowles as a private <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a>, when he went as a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MIDSHIPMAN">midshipman</a> on board of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a> of 90 guns, with Admiral Saunders, who had the command of a force intended to co-operate with General Wolfe in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of Quebec; and upon the appointment of his friend as a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> on board of the Royal William, Robison was himself rated as a midshipman in that ship. The fleet arrived on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> in April 1759; in May they got up the river, and Mr Robison was one of a party of 100 seamen draughted from the Royal William into the Admiral's ship, under the command of Lieutenant Knowles: in this capacity he had an opportunity of seeing considerable <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, and of making some surveys of the river and of the neighbouring <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, an employment for which he was perfectly qualified, both as a geometrician and as a draughtsman. He also remarked the effect of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AURORA_BOREALIS"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol3.html#article-AURORA">Aurora</a> Borealis on the compass, which had been noticed by Mairan and Wargentin some years before, but which was then not <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> known. After the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, which was signalised by the victory and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the gallant Wolfe, the Royal William sailed with his body to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and arrived at Spithead in November. The next year she was sent to cruise off <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINISTERRE">Finisterre</a>, but in six months she was obliged to return home, from having the greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the men disabled by the scurvy. He used to consider the two years that he spent on board of the Royal William as the happiest of his life; and no inconsiderable part of his gratification was derived from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEAMANSHIP">seamanship</a> as he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> it practised under the auspices of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Hugh Pigot. He did not, however, acquire any firm <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the mode of life which he had temporarily adopted; he was rather disposed to resume his academical pursuits, and he had overcome his earlier objections to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> profession. He could not, however, refuse the friendly invitation of Admiral Knowles to come and live with him in the country, and to assist him in some important experiments which he was making upon <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> and nautical subjects. In the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of February 1762, Lieutenant Knowles was appointed to the Peregrine sloop, of 20 guns, and Mr Robison accompanied him with the hope of becoming a purser. He visited <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a> and several other parts of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>; but he found a cruise in a small ship much less convenient and agreeable than in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> one, and, fortunately for himself and for mankind, he finally quitted the Peregrine and the naval service in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, and returned to live with Admiral Knowles; who soon after recommended him as a proper person to take <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of Harrison's timekeeper, which had been completed by the labour of 35 years, after many unsuccessful experiments, and which was now sent out by desire of the Board of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">Longitude</a> to the West Indies, under the care of young Harrison and of Mr Robison. The rate of the chronometer was ascertained at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTSMOUTH">Portsmouth</a> the 6th November 1762, and it indicated, at Port Royal in Jamaica, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> amounting to $5^\circ 2^\prime 47''$, which is only four seconds less than the true longitude. After a few days, the observers had a prompt opportunity of returning home by the Merlin sloop, which was sent to Europe with despatches. The voyage was most disastrous with respect to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, and at last the ship took fire; but she arrived safe at Portsmouth in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, and on the 2d of April the watch gave 11° 58' 6" instead of 12°, for the time of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> noon, so that the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a>, after six months, was only 1° 53', amounting to no more than about 20 miles of distance. Mr Robison received, upon his return, the afflicting intelligence of the total loss of the Peregrine, which had foundered at sea with her commander and the whole of the ship's company. He was also greatly disappointed in the failure of some hopes which had been held out to him from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">Admiralty</a> and the Board of Longitude; though in fact there is little reason for the public to regret that he was not gratified with the pursership, which he claimed as the reward of his services. He was indeed afterwards actually made a pursuer by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDWICH">Sandwich</a>, in 1763; but he then declined accepting the appointment. His biographers very naturally complain of the neglect of those Boards which ought to have recompensed him; but certainly the Board of Longitude had no power whatever, and probably not much influence, in the appointment of a pursuer; and after all, the delay of a year or two was nothing very uncommon in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>. He had now no other resource than to return to Glasgow, and to resume his academical pursuits with renewed energy. It was from this time that he dated his serious application to his studies; he became extremely intimate with Dr Reid and Dr Alexander Wilson, and he had the advantage of being a witness of two of the greatest steps in the improvement of physical science that have been made in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times, Dr <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a>'s experimental <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and Mr Watt's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of a new <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEAM_ENGINE"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol19.html#article-STEAM">steam</a>-engine. Dr Black was the first that determined the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of heat required for the conversion of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a> into <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; Mr Watt, who was settled as a mathematical <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>-maker at Glasgow, had been employed in repairing a working <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of Newcomen's engine for one of the professors of the university, and it was the difficulty of supplying this model with steam that suggested to Mr Watt the eligibility of having a separate condenser, and that led him, in conjunction with Dr Black, to a knowledge of the quantity of heat consumed in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a>. Amid the enthusiasm which is always inspired by the progress of scientific discovery, and of practical improvement, Mr Robison found every encouragement and every facility for the pursuit of his favourite objects. He was recommended by Dr Black, upon his removal to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> in 1766, as his successor in the lectureship of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, though without the appointment of a professor. He took charge, also, of the education of Mr Macdowal of Garthland, and of Mr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Knowles, afterwards Sir Charles. Admiral Knowles was soon after recommended by the British <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> to the Empress of Russia, in order to effect a reformation in her navy, having been employed on a similar service in Portugal almost fifty years before; he had always been a firm friend to Mr Robison, and now engaged him on this mission, with a salary of L.250 a year; and they proceeded together to St Petersburg in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1770. Being hospitably entertained on their way by the Prince Bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIEGE">Liege</a>, whom they found to constitute, with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> and all his servants, a lodge of freemasons, Mr Robison was easily persuaded to become one of that fraternity; in a few days he was made an apprentice, and by degrees attained the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of Scotch master, as he has himself related in his publication upon the subject. He <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> nearly two years at St Petersburg, still acting in the capacity of private secretary to Sir Charles, who was appointed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the Board of Admiralty, much to the advantage of the Russian navy, though his improvements were frequently retarded by the prejudices of the native officers. Mr Robison was then appointed inspector general of the corps of marine cadets at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRONSTADT">Cronstadt</a>, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> salary, and with the rank of Lieutenant <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a>. His duty was to receive the report of about forty teachers and professors, respecting the studies of 400 young noblemen, who were their pupils, and to class them according to his judgment of their merits; but he had himself nothing to teach, nor could he have had much occasion for "lecturing fluently in the Russian <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>," though he was introduced by his friend Kutussoff to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> Duke Paul as a proficient in that language; but to the Empress he was not personally known. At Petersburg he could have lived without regretting his country, in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of such men as Euler and Alpinus, admired by the Russians, and beloved by the British; but Cronstadt in winter was deplorably melancholy; and he was induced, without much difficulty, in 1773, to make some little pecuniary sacrifice in accepting the professorship of Natural Philosophy at Edinburgh, which had become vacant by the death of Dr Russell, and to which he had been recommended by Dr Robertson, then <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">Principal</a> of the University. His determination was not disapproved by the Russian government, who granted him a pension of about L.80 a year for life; but it was only paid as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> as three or four young men, who had accompanied him as pupils, continued to reside at Edinburgh; some discontent having been expressed because he did not keep up a correspondence with the Academy on the improvement of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> education. He arrived at Edinburgh in September 1774; he married soon after, and continued to reside in that city for the remaining thirty years of his life, paying only an annual visit to his native <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, where he possessed a part of his paternal estate; not being solicitous to extend it, although "he did not diminish it otherwise than as it had been diminished before," that is, in making provision for younger children. His predecessor had been very judicious and successful as a lecturer, though not a mathematician of the highest order; he had himself more practical knowledge and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>, and was better acquainted with the foreign mathematicians, who had naturally fallen under his notice during his residence on the Continent. His lectures were considered by most of his pupils as somewhat too difficult to be followed; a complaint which, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it did not depend on their own want of preparatory information, arose perhaps rather more from the hasty manner of his enunciation, than from the abstruseness of his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. "The singular facility of his own <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a>," says Professor Playfair, "made him judge too favourably of the same power in others." To understand his lectures completely was, on account of the rapidity, and the uniform flow of his discourse, not a very easy task, even for men tolerably familiar with the subject. On this account, his lectures were less popular than might have been expected from such a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of talents as the author of them possessed." This inconvenience was increased "by the small <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of experiments he introduced, and a view that he took of Natural Philosophy, which left but a very subordinate place for them to occupy. An experiment, he would very truly observe, does not establish a general proposition, and never can do more than prove a particular fact:" but he seems to have carried this principle to some little excess: it is, in fact, the illustration, and not the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>, of general principles that is the object of a public <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXHIBITION">exhibition</a> of experiments; and it is very doubtful whether <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHIMEDES">Archimedes</a>, or Newton, or Leibnitz, or Euler, would have been very successful as shownmen. With respect, however, to "accuracy of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a>, to clearness, brevity, and elegance of demonstration, and even to neatness and precision in experiments," Professor Robison was very successful; his course extended "to every branch of physics and of mixed mathematics," and entered so fully into the detail of each particular <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the subjects, that "a more perfect system of academical instruction is not easily to be imagined:" nothing, in short, was wanting, but so much previous knowledge of mathematics in his pupils as he thought he had a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to expect, though his expectations were too rarely fulfilled. The Philosophical Society of Edinburgh had been almost suffered to sink into oblivion after the publication of the third volume of its Essays, in 1756. Professor Robison became a member of it soon after his return from Russia, and was chosen Secretary of the new Society upon its formation by Royal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a>, in 1783, when it incorporated with itself the whole of the surviving members of the former Society. In 1798, he received the compliment of a degree of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a> of Laws from the University of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEW_JERSEY">New <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERSEY">Jersey</a>; and a similar <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> was paid him at Glasgow the year after. In 1800 he was elected, as successor to Dr Black, on the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> of the Foreign Members of the Royal Academy of Sciences of St Petersburg. He was attacked, in 1785, by a severe disorder, from which he was never afterwards wholly free, though it produced little inconvenience besides pain, with some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEPRESSION">depression</a> of spirits, which was, however, attributed rather to the closeness of his application than to the immediate effect of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, which was a glandular induration. For many years he was obliged to obtain the assistance of substitutes in the delivery of his lectures; but towards the end of his life he was able again to perform the duties of the professorship in person. He continued his literary labours with little intermission, and was most happy in the care and attention of his wife and children, whose virtues he found the best alleviation of his sufferings. He took a slight <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, after giving a lecture, on the 28th of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1805, and died on the 30th. 1. It was comparatively late in life that Professor Robison assumed the character of an author, having communicated to the Royal Society of Edinburgh, in 1785, a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> on the Determination of the Orbit and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">Motion</a> of the Georgium Sidus, which was published in the Edinburgh Transactions, Vol. I. He had observed the opposition of the planet, in 1786, with an equatorial <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TELESCOPE">telescope</a> only, and he had computed the elements of its orbit with greater accuracy than any other astronomer had then done; although his suspicion of the effect of such a planet on the motions of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a> has not been confirmed by later investigations, the irregularities of these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>, on the contrary, having been otherwise explained. 2. A <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> paper, published in the same collection, Vol. II. p. 82, relates to The Motion of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">Light</a>, as affected by refracting or reflecting substances which are themselves in motion: the author corrects some errors of Boscovich, who had miscalculated the effect of a water telescope; but he seems to agree with Dr Wilson in the suggestion of another experiment of a similar <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, which, to say the least, is wholly superfluous. 3. The most important, beyond all <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a>, of Professor Robison's scientific publications, are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> which he communicated from time to time to the third edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica, and to its Supplement. It was under the care of Mr Colin Macfarquhar that the twelve first volumes of that edition of this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> were published;* and upon his death, in 1793, the task of continuing it was committed to Dr Gleig, to whom Professor Robison became a most essential co-operator, and from that time "the work ceased to be a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> compilation." The first of his contributions, according to Professor Playfair, was the Article <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">Optics</a>, but he probably only revised and enlarged that article; it was followed by Philosophy, which he wrote jointly with Dr Gleig; by Physics, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PNEUMATICS">Pneumatics</a>, Precession, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROJECTILES">Projectiles</a>, Pumps, Resistance, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">Rivers</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">Roof</a>, Rope-making, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROTATION">Rotation</a>, Seamanship, Signal, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">Sound</a>, Specific Gravity, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STATICS">Statics</a>, Steam, Steam Engine, Steelyard, Strength, Telescope, Tide, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRUMPET">Trumpet</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">Variation</a>, and Waterworks; and in the Supplement, by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">Arch</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, Boscovich, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARPENTRY">Carpentry</a>, Centre, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYNAMICS">Dynamics</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">Electricity</a>, Impulsion, Involution, Machinery, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGNETISM">Magnetism</a>, Mechanics, Percussion, Pianoforte, Position, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEMPERAMENT">Temperament</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">Thunder</a>, Trumpet, Tschirnhaus, and Watchwork. Notwithstanding some degree of prolixity and want of arrangement, which could scarcely be avoided in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of original articles for such a mode of publication, the whole of them, taken together, undeniably exhibit a more complete view of the modern improvements of physical science than had ever before --- * The third edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica consisted of eighteen volumes; the Supplement to it of two volumes. been in the possession of the British public; and display such a combination of acquired knowledge with original power of reasoning, as has fallen to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> of a few only of the most favoured of mankind. 4. It is not altogether with so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> approbation that his friends and his biographers have mentioned a work, of a nature rather <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> than philosophical, entitled *Proofs of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSPIRACY">Conspiracy</a> against all the Religious and Governments of Europe*, 8vo. Ed. 1797; though it went through several editions. The principal part of the book consists of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ILLUMINATI">Illuminati</a> and the German Union, whom he considers as having become the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> agents in a plot first formed by the Freemasons, at the suggestion of some ex-jesuit, who proposed for their model the internal economy of the order which he had quitted; and whatever fagadation this outline may have had in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, there is no doubt that the manner, in which Professor Robison has filled it up, betrays a degree of credulity, extremely remarkable in a person used to calm reasoning and philosophical demonstration. For example, in the admission of a story told by an anonymous German author, that the minister Turgot was the protector of a society that met at Baron d'Holbach's, for the purpose of examining the brains of living children, in order to discover the principle of vitality. He does not accuse the English Freemasons of having participated in the conspiracy; but he considers the Continental lodges as having been universally implicated in it. 5. After the death of Dr Black in 1799, he undertook to superintend the publication of his *Lectures on Chemistry*, which appeared in 1803. 2 vols. 4. And he executed this task, which was rather laborious than difficult, with equal zeal and ability. He endeavoured to reduce to their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> estimate the comparative pretensions of the French and British chemists, though he is somewhat puritanically severe in criticizing the literal meaning of the compliments paid to Black by Lavoisier, on which he founds a charge of insincerity. 6. His last publication was the first volume of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> which was to form a complete system, entitled *Elements of Mechanical Philosophy*, 8. Ed. 1804. It comprehended only Dynamics and Astronomy; and it never became very popular: it was too difficult for the many, who wished for general and philosophical notions only, and not sufficiently precise and demonstrative for the few, who wanted practical and numerical results. In attempting to combine the separate merits of the *Exposition du Systeme du Monde*, and of the *Mécanique Céleste*, the author sacrificed both the popular simplicity of the former, and the mathematical perfection of the latter. A few inaccuracies, which ought not to escape the attention of the reader of the work, have been pointed out in the *Imperial Review* for March 1805; a journal long since discontinued. 7. The contents of the volume last mentioned, together with some <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> intended to have formed part of a second, and the greater part of the articles furnished by Professor Robison to the *Encyclopædia*, were collected into a *System of Mechanical Philosophy*, with Notes, by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> Brewster, LL.D. 4 vols. 8. Ed. 1822; a spirited book-seller in London having undertaken the risk of the publication. 1. The first volume begins with the articles *Dynamics, Projectiles, Corpucular Forces, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CAPILLARY">Capillary</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTRACTION">Attraction</a>, Bosovich's Theory*, and Rotation, all as remodelled for the *Elements*: then follow *<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STRENGTH_OF_MATERIALS">Strength of Materials</a>, Carpentry, Roof, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">Construction</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">Arches</a>, Construction of Centres*. 2. The article *Steam-Engine* is enriched with notes and an appendix, by the late Mr Watt; the next is Machinery; then <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESISTANCE_OF_FLUIDS">Resistance of <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">Fluids</a>, Rivers, Waterworks, Pumps. 3. Astronomy, Telescopc, Pneumatics. 4. Electricity, Magnetism, Variation, Temperament, Trumpet, Watchwork, and Seamanship. The notes are not numerous, and the editor's principal labour has been to retrench some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> that appeared to him superfluous, when the papers were to stand as parts of such a collection. "Although Dr Robison's name," says Dr Brewster in his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a>, "cannot be associated with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> discoveries of the century which he adorned, yet the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of his talents and his virtues <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be long cherished by his country. Imbued with the genuine spirit of the philosophy which he taught, he was one of the warmest patrons of genius wherever it was found. His mind was nobly elevated above the mean jealousies of rival ambition, and his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of science and of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> was too ardent to allow him either to depreciate the labours of others, or to transfer them to himself. To these great qualities as a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, Dr Robison added all the more estimable endowments of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> and of social life. His friendship was at all times generous and sincere. His piety was ardent and unostentatious. His <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRIOTISM">patriotism</a> was of the most pure and exalted character; and, like the immortal Newton, whose memory he cherished with a peculiar reverence, he was pre-eminently entitled to the high distinction of a Christian, patriot, and philosopher." His person was handsome, and his physiognomy prepossessing; and he appears to have been endowed with an extraordinary combination of talents, even exclusively of those which were called into immediate <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> in his professional pursuits; for he was a good linguist, an excellent draughtsman, and an accomplished musician: his conversation was always energetic and interesting, and sometimes even poetical; and his liberality of sentiment was only limited by his regard for what he considered as the best interests of mankind. A short account of his life was published in 1802, by a contributor to the *Philosophical <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGAZINE">Magazine</a>*, who, among other inaccuracies, thought himself at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to assert that he was an admirer of the algebraical form of representation, in preference to the geometrical. His friend, Dr Gleig, stepped forwards soon after to correct these mistakes, in the *Antijacobin Review* for 1802, and his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> was copied into the *Philosophical Magazine*. He asserts, from his own knowledge, that even yet Professor Robison "delights much more in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a> than in any of the modes of algebra, assigning, as the reason of his preference, that in the longest demonstration, the geometrician has al- ways clear and adequate <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>, which the most expert algebraist can very seldom have." It may perhaps be asserted, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, that the same reasoning would <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> us always to employ actual multiplication or division, in preference to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOGARITHMS">logarithms</a> or of a sliding rule; and that the whole of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGIC">magic</a> of calculation depends on the abstraction of the results from the numerous and separately unimportant steps by which they are obtained: but the having once seen those steps clearly is certainly of great importance to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of reasoning, even when the memory no longer retains them; and no mathematician of correct taste can study the ancient geometricians without admiring the elegance and precision of their method, even amidst the pedantry which too frequently envelopes their expressions, and without being grateful for their punctuality in collecting their results into the very convenient form of distinct <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a>, and in making such references from each proposition to the foundations on which it depends, as to enable him readily to trace back their steps to the most elementary principles; which is scarcely possible in any of the works of the most modern school of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a>. Professor Robison, however, seems rarely to have cultivated the higher mathematics for their own sake only, or any further than as they could be applied to the study of the phenomena of nature, or to the practice of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a> of art; in fact, without some such limitation, there would be no track to guide us in the pathless regions of quantity and number, and their endless relations and functions. But besides the utility of the pure mathematics, as a branch of early education, in exercising and fortifying the powers of the mind, it is impossible to foresee with certainty how much of mathematics may be wanted by the natural philosopher in any given <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a>; and Professor Robison, as well as many others of his countrymen, would certainly have been the better for the possession of a little more, as the author of the criticisms in the Imperial Review has already had occasion to remark. [Phil. Mag. XIII. Dr Gleig, in Antijacobin Mag. XI. 1802. Stark's Biographia Scotica. Aikin's General Biography, VIII. 4. Lond. 1813. Playfair, in Ed. Trans. VII. 1815, p. 495. Chalmers's Biographical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>, XXV. Svo. Lond. 1816.]

ROSS-SHIRE

Pages 506-508

one of the northern counties of Scotland, situated between 57° 8' and 57° 59' <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>. latitude, and between 4° and 5° 46' west <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a>. Including the small <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Cromarty, which consists for the most <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of detached tracts surrounded by Ross-shire, the boundaries are the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> on the east and west, the county of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUTHERLAND">Sutherland</a> on the north, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INVERNESS_SHIRE"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol11.html#article-INVERNESS">Inverness</a>-shire on the south. On the east are the Firths of Dornoch, Cromarty, and Moray, arms of the sea which run up into the interior; the latter, the most considerable, washing its south-eastern extremity. The west <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> is still more indented with similar, though smaller, inlets, here called lochs; of which the largest are the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> and Little Loch <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROOM">Broom</a>, Loch Groinard, Loch Ewe, Garloch, where there has <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> been a regularly productive cod-fishery, Loch Terridon, Lochs Kisserne and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARRON">Carron</a>, and Loch Duich. From north to south Ross-shire extends about 56 miles, and from east to west somewhat more than 70; having an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a>, according to the latest authorities, of 2129 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 1,362,560 English acres, without including the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a>, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBRIDES">Hebrides</a> belonging to this county, or the space occupied by the county of Cromarty. In the Agricultural Survey by Sir George Mackenzie, its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> is computed to be greater by about half a million of acres. Ross and Cromarty contain 33 parishes, of which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> are on the west coast, and four in the island of Lewis. One <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> lies within the bounds of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNOD">synod</a> of Glenelg, and all the rest in that of Ross. Many of these parishes are very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, but the ministers are assisted in their duties by missionaries maintained by the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> bounty, and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> for Propagating Christian Knowledge. In the Encyclopaedia <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be found a pretty full <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of this extensive district, to which we must refer, and shall notice here only such circumstances as may be necessary to give a general view of its present condition. Excepting a narrow tract on the sea-coast on the east, where the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> are not unfavourable to cultivation, the general character of Ross-shire is that of a rugged mountainous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, interspersed with narrow glens, fresh <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, and mountain streams, with here and there fringes of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> wood, and plantations of some extent, and a few gentlemen's seats; but, upon the whole, it is a wild and desolate region, upon which a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> falls in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, and snow in winter, the latter lying among the recesses of some of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> all the year. Including the woodlands, only about 9 acres in 100 are supposed to be susceptible of cultivation. The landed <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of Ross-shire, valued in the cess-books at L75,043, 10s. 3d. Scots, consisted, in 1811, of 85 estates, of which 50 were under the valuation of L500 Scots each, 25 above L500, and below L2000, and 10 above L2000; from which it would appear that they are generally of great extent; the medium size being upwards of 16,000 English acres. But their value is far from being in proportion; the real rent of the lands in that year having been L91,089, 18s. 8d., and of the houses L2798, 1s. 4d. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">Sterling</a>; the former affording a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> rental for each estate of not quite L1072, or about 1s. 4d. per <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACRE">acre</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> seats are Brahan Castle, Stewart Mackenzie; Tulloch Castle, Davidson; Fowlis Castle, Monro, Bart.; Coul, Mackenzie, Bart.; Novar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">House</a>, Munro, Bart.; Invergordon Castle, Macleod; Balnagowan, Ross, Bart.; Tarbat House, Hay Mackenzie; Geanies House, Macleod; Conan House, Hector Mackenzie, Bart.; Rosehaugh, Roderick Mackenzie, Bart.; Cromarty House, Ross; and Lochalsh, Innes, Bart. The occupation of this district in an agricultural Rural Review, and the system of management which prevails among the tenantry, do not differ materially from what we have already described under Inverness-shire and the other Highland counties of Scotland. The native farmers hold a few acres of arable <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, with grazings <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> contiguous, but in some <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> at a distance—raise oats, bear or big, and potatoes; and keep a great many cattle and horses, which are always stunted in their growth for want of food, and in severe winters many of them perish. Except in seed-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a>, and while they are preparing <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEAT">peat</a> for their winter's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, the tenants spend much of their time in idleness, or in the practice of illicit <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a> among their hills, though in some parts, particularly on the west coast, also in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>; and their labour, and that of their cattle, is, generally speaking, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> and unproductive. Several of the proprietors, however, and some farmers brought hither from other counties, conduct their farming operations upon the most approved system; and upon the east coast all the crops grown in Scotland may be seen under excellent cultivation. Sheep-farming, too, notwithstanding the opposition of the small tenants, has been introduced into this as well as most of the other Highland counties. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-LEASES">Leases</a> for nineteen years have become <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> here as in other parts of Scotland. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> are <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DINGWALL">Dingwall</a>, at the bottom of the Frith Towns of Cromarty, Fortrose, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAIN">Tain</a>, on the south coast of Dornoch Frith; all royal burghs, but very small places, and situated on the east side of the county. On the west, the only <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of any consideration is the village of Ullapool, on the banks of Loch Broom, built within these thirty years by the British Society for extending the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">Fisheries</a>, &c. at an expense of upwards of L20,000. But the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERRING">herring</a>-fishery on this coast, always precarious, having failed for several years in succession, the inhabitants have been often reduced to great distress, and notwithstanding every encouragement, many have abandoned it. It remains to be seen whether the recent repeal of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> duties may not <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> to a more spirited and successful prosecution of the fisheries, so much to be desired for the employment and subsistence of the people of this and other parts of the Highlands, who are by far too numerous to be employed beneficially in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>. Even the loch-fishings, hitherto much neglected, might be rendered a valuable resource in this respect. There is scarcely any thing in Ross-shire that deserves the name of a manufacture, except one of a somewhat peculiar description, and which may be worth notice for that reason. We allude to the practice of obtaining tar, so necessary for the sheep-stocks of the county, and other purposes, from the roots and trunks of the fir-trees found in the mosses. These mosses, which are of great extent here, as Ross-shire, which has about 90 freeholders, sends one member to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">Parliament</a>; and in the elections for the Scottish burghs, Dingwall and Tain are associated with Dornoch, Wick, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KIRKWALL">Kirkwall</a>, and Fortrose with Forres, Nairn, and Inverness. The jurisdiction of one <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> extends over this and the shire of Cromarty; and his substitutes hold their courts at Tain, Dingwall, and Fortrose, for the mainland of the county, and at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STORNOWAY">Stornoway</a>, in Lewis, for the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> politically attached to it. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of the two counties of Ross and Cromarty, according to the census of 1801, was 52,291; in 1811 it amounted to 60,853; and in 1821 to 68,828, of which 32,324 were males, and 36,504 were females. The families employed in agriculture were 7947; in trade and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> 3356; in other occupations of various kinds 3203. The increase of population from 1811 to 1821 was 13,485. See the general works quoted under the former Scottish counties, and Sir George Mackenzie's General View of the Agriculture of the Counties of Ross and Cromarty. Also the article Cromarty in this Supplement.

ROXBURGHSHIRE

Pages 508-510

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> in Scotland, on its south-eastern extremity, where it meets with England, situated between 55° 6' and 55° 43' <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude, and between 2° 12' and 3° 7' west <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a>. It is sometimes called Teviotdale, from its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> river the Teviot, but improperly, as it also includes a tract called Liddesdale on the south-west, which is unconnected with the Teviot. Its boundaries are <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol4.html#article-BERWICKSHIRE">Berwickshire</a>, from which it is separated in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> by the river Tweed, on the north; <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SELKIRKSHIRE">Selkirkshire</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUMFRIES">Dumfries</a>-shire on the west, and south-west; and the English counties of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a> on the south-east and east. Between Berwickshire and Selkirkshire, a small tract touches the county of Mid-<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOTHIAN">Lothian</a>; on the south, between Dumfries-shire and Cumberland, the county terminates almost in a point; on the west it surrounds small portions of Selkirkshire in some places, and in others projects into that county; and it has the Cheviot hills on the east; the outline being exceedingly <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> on all sides. According to the latest authorities, its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> is 715 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 457,600 English acres; containing 30 entire parishes, and part of other four, which properly belong to the counties adjoining. For the purposes of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-POLICE">police</a>, it is divided into the four districts of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KELSO">Kelso</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JEDBURGH">Jedburgh</a> on the east, and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELROSE">Melrose</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAWICK">Hawick</a> on the west. In an agricultural view, it may be considered as divided into arable <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> and hilly pasture; the pasture land, estimated at about 3/4ths of the whole, occupying the eastern, southern, and western <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, and surrounding, in a circular form, the arable, which lies on the north and north-east sides of the county. Except upon the banks of the streams, which are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> of no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> width, there is very little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> or flat land in this district; and, compared with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> grounds in other parts of Scotland, hardly any part of it can be said to be mountainous. The cultivated districts are beautifully diversified with narrow valleys, each traversed by its own rivulet, often fringed with wood, and bounded by gentle acclivities; and the hills in pasture are, with few exceptions, clothed in verdure to their very summits. On the confines of Northumberland, the most elevated <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>, the hills seldom reach the height of 2000 feet, but there are many from that height <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to 800 or 1000 feet. The most considerable are Minto and the Eildon hills, both in the arable <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>; and Dunion, Ruberslaw, Wisp, Hownam <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, Milwood-Fell, Carter-Fell, and Chilhill, in the pastoral districts. Most of them having a conical form, insulated at their base by streamlets, and not rising in a continuous range, present very conspicuous objects, and at a distance seem higher than they are found to be when approached. The beauties of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> scenery have, over all the lower grounds, been heightened and improved by the wealth and industry of its inhabitants; all this division abounding in gentlemen's seats, comfortable, and sometimes elegant <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">farm</a>-houses; the fields inclosed with hedges of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THORN">thorn</a>, and belts of wood, and many spots covered with young trees. On the skirts of the hills, too, cultivation has made considerable progress of late, as much, perhaps, as could be expected in the natural circumstances of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; but the interior of the pastoral district is in general naked, without trees or fences, and very thinly inhabited. The prevailing <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> of the arable land, and over most of the hills, is what is called a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> loam, though of different qualities, excellently adapted to the turnip culture. Tracts of a clayey or more heavy soil, however, occupy a considerable space, especially on the north-west. Clay is also found on the north, near the Tweed, where it is rich and fertile. Moss, marsh, and heath, occur in the southwest, and occasionally in other quarters; but altogether they cover but a small proportion of the surface. No district in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> is better supplied with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> and streams, though it has only two that deserve the name of rivers, the Tweed and the Teviot. The Tweed, which crosses the north part of the county, and for part of its course forms the boundary with Berwickshire, enters it from Selkirkshire, on the north-west, and leaves it below Redden on the north-east; carrying with it nearly all the waters that <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through, or have their source in, this district. Its banks, especially near Kelso, where it is crossed by an elegant <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, built about 20 years ago, are perhaps equal in richness and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> to those of any river of the same <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> in Britain. The Teviot more properly belongs to this county; rising and terminating within its bounds. It has its source in the southwest extremity, near the confines of Dumfries-shire, and flowing north-east almost through the middle of the district, joins the Tweed, in which its name is lost, a little above the town of Kelso. From Hawick downwards it is a considerable stream, and, like the Tweed, flows through a very fertile and well cultivated country. The principal rivulets that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into the Teviot from the south are Allen, Slitrick, Rule, Jed, Oxnam, and Kale; and from the north and west, Borthwick and Ale. The Liddel and Hermitage, which run on the south-west, and whose united streams retain the name of Liddel, from which this tract is called Liddesdale, soon leave Roxburghshire; and after forming the boundary between Dumfriesshire and Cumberland, fall into the Esk above Longtown. The other streams are the Etterick, which joins the Tweed from the south-west as it enters this county; another Allen and the Leader, which fall into the same river from the north; and the Eden, which, after an easterly course, partly on the boundary with Berwickshire, enters the Tweed on the north-east, a little before it leaves the county. The Beaumont also rises here among the Cheviot hills on the east, but after a short course, passes by Kirkbyetholm, and enters Northumberland. Of the smaller streams, the Ale, Jed, Rule, and Hermitage, are distinguished for their natural scenery; to which we may add the Liddel, celebrated by the late Dr Armstrong, a native of Liddesdale. Tweed is the only river frequented by salmon, except at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of spawning, when they are found in most of the other streams. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TROUT">Trout</a> abounds in the Ale, Rule, Jed, and Kale, and there are a few small <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> which contain perch and pike. Roxburghshire is not rich in minerals. Coal has been found on the Carter Hill, near the borders of Northumberland, and in the southern extremity of Liddesdale. It is worked at the latter <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, but this is too remote to render it of much value to the inhabitants of this county, who are chiefly supplied with coal from Northumberland. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">Limestone</a>, which abounds in various parts, is not wrought to any extent, owing to the want of coal. There are excellent sandstone quarries at Sprouston on the Tweed, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARL">marl</a> in several parishes, particularly at Eckford, on the Teviot, and Ednam, near the Tweed. But the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of marl as a manure is confined to a narrow circle around the places where it is found; lime, of which a much smaller <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> answers the purpose, being most in request; and the lime is almost all like the coal brought from Northumberland, from 20 to 30 miles distant from many parts of the arable district. The valued rent of Roxburghshire is £314,663, 6s. 4d. Scots, being next to Fife and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PERTH">Perth</a>, the highest in Scotland; and the real rent of the lands, in 1811, was £230,663, 9s. 9d. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">Sterling</a>, and of the houses £11,508, 6s. 3d. It is one of the few counties where the rent in Sterling falls below the valuation in Scots <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>; a circumstance which is certainly not owing to the want of improvements to sustain rent, nor to the present rents being too low; but to the mistaken vanity of its land owners, whose rent rolls at the time of the valuation are understood to have been stated too high. Of this valuation, which in 1811 was divided among 349 estates, about one-third belongs to lands held under entail, and more than two-thirds to families of the name of Kerr, Scott, Elliot, and Douglas. The principal proprietors are the Dukes of Roxburgh and Buccleuch, and the Marquises of Lothian and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TWEEDDALE">Tweeddale</a>; but there are 33 estates in all that have a valued rent of upwards of £2,000 Scots each; and 55 more are from £500 to £2,000. Yet moderate and small properties are very numerous; the remaining 261 estates being under £500 Scots. Several of these exceeding a valuation of £400 Scots, and held of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">Crown</a>, have been acquired by professional farmers, who have thus become freeholders, and enjoy a share of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> influence. Among the seats in the county, which are too numerous to be mentioned here, the most splendid is Fleurs, the mansion of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of Roxburgh, beautifully seated at the confluence of the Tweed and Teviot, near Kelso. Roxburghshire is divided, for the most part, into larger farms, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we except a few sheep farms in the Highlands, than any other county in Scotland; many of them, consisting of land partly arable and partly pasture, being from 1000 to 3000 acres; and several of these, in some instances, are in the occupation of one tenant. Farms altogether arable, containing from 500 to 1000 acres, are not uncommon. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> and knowledge required for conducting concerns so extensive entitle such men to suitable accommodations in their houses and farm-offices, many of which are accordingly laid out and constructed in a superior style. Most of the farm servants are married and live in houses apart, set down together in some convenient quarter of the farm, each having a small garden attached. It is the practice here, as in other parts of the lowlands of Scotland, to pay most of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a> in the produce of the farm, and not in money; every married ploughman, or hind, getting a certain quantity of corn, a cow kept, and some land allowed for potatoes, and often also for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>: he is also commonly allowed to keep a pig and a few hens. Whatever may be the fluctuation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a>, these labourers are thus always provided with the necessaries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a> made from their cow, with its calf, and the eggs of their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a>, and, if the family be not <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, a part of their corn, supplies them with the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> they need; while they fatten their pigs, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> up the flax for the use of their families. No class of men of their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> are to be compared with these hinds for propriety of conduct and frugality; and few of the labouring classes anywhere are so comfortable and contented with their condition. The practice of paying wages in kind is not, it must be admitted, free from objections; a little pilfering is sometimes detected on the one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and a hard <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, on the other, may be willing to pay in produce of an inferior <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>; but after all, the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> that has been had of this system over five or six of the principal agricultural counties of Scotland, and the north of England, warrants us in asserting that it works well for both parties, and might have some effect in keeping down <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RATES">rates</a> if it prevailed more generally among our southern neighbours. On the best soils, the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROTATION">rotation</a> of crops is very simple, corn being taken every <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> year with a green crop intervening; but, in general, the land does not admit of such constant tillage, and two-fifths, or a half, is commonly in pasture from seeds. Un- der a six years' course, the most profitable on rather weak soils, and in a district where there are no large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> to furnish manure, the rotation from pasture is oats, turnips, barley or wheat, clover and rye-grass, partly cut for hay the first year, but chiefly pastured with sheep, and then <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in pasture two years longer. Under this system the crops are almost always good, and the land, instead of being exhausted, is kept in a state of progressive improvement. Though little of the soil be naturally adapted to wheat, yet this grain is now raised to a great extent on all the better descriptions of sandy loam; generally after turnips eaten on the ground by sheep, which, by their treading, give consistency to the soil, as well as leave it greatly enriched by their manure. Only a small part is under beans, somewhat more under peas; barley has in many instances been superseded by wheat; so that wheat and oats are the principal crops of grain; while, whatever be the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of acres in corn, nearly half the quantity is allotted to turnips, and the other half to clover and rye-grass. Potatoes occupy but a very small part of every farm; and flax, where raised at all, is only in small patches for the use of the farm servants. The turnip crop, however, has been lately attacked with a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> which has already begun to make some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> in the system, leading to the more extensive culture of potatoes, and also of cabbages. This disease, which has been long known in England, but which was a stranger in this and other parts of Scotland 10 or 12 years ago, popularly known by the name of fingers and toes, converts the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BULB">bulb</a> of the turnip, when one has been allowed to form, into a shapeless and morbid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> which no animal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> eat, and becomes putrid, and disappears altogether on the first approach of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FROST">frost</a>. It often prevails over extensive fields, while others adjoining escape; and it seems to make no <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> whether the land be fresh from pasture or has been long in tillage. The pastoral district of this county is occupied with an excellent breed of sheep called the Cheviot, from the general name of the hills on which they feed; for an account of which breed we must refer to the Article <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">AGRICULTURE</a> in this Supplement. On the arable farms, the short-horned cattle and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEICESTER">Leicester</a> sheep, neither of them, however, always in a pure state, form the principal stock; and, as so large a proportion of even the arable land is always in grass, the number of both is very great. By means of turnips, most of the disposable stock, whether of cattle or sheep, are carried forward till they are ready for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUTCHER">butcher</a>; when the far greater part is sent to the weekly market of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORPETH">Morpeth</a> in Northumberland, for the consumption of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a> and other towns in the north of England. The progress which agriculture has made in this district has not been favoured by its situation in respect to markets. It has no large towns, and comparatively a small <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a>. Most of the corn, as well as live stock, must, therefore, be carried out of the county; and Berwick-upon-Tweed, the nearest seaport, is upwards of 30 miles from much of its corn lands. The towns are Kelso, Jedburgh, Hawick, and Melrose; and of the villages the most considerable are Roxburghshire, Yetholm and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KIRKCUDBRIGHT">Kirkcudbright</a>, near its eastern boundary. Kelso, pleasantly situated on the north <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the Tweed, is a well built, cleanly, and cheerful place, containing near 5000 inhabitants, the capital of this and the adjoining county of Berwick. Some branches of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> and woollen manufacture, and that of thread, have been long carried on here, with a considerable brewery. Jedburgh, the county town, situated on the rivulet Jed, in the interior, though a place of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> formerly, has been long <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STATIONARY">stationary</a>, if not declining. Hawick, which stands on the Teviot, at the point where it is joined by the Slitrick, is a more thriving place, and has <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of carpeting, stockings, and other sorts of woollen goods. Melrose, near the south bank of the Tweed, about 10 miles west from Kelso, is no otherwise distinguished than for its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>. (See MELROSE in the Encyclopaedia.) The two Yetholms are worthy of notice for their <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>, at which a great part of the cattle, sheep, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, of the county are sold; and Kirkcudbright for being the residence of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GYPSIES">gypsies</a>, and their principal colony in Scotland. Roxburgh, which gives its name to the county, and whose castle was of such importance in the wars between England and Scotland, has long since ceased to exist, and has left no trace of its former <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>. At Jedburgh, Kelso, Melrose, and the village of Gattonside, there are some valuable orchards, particularly at Jedburgh and Melrose, where some very old trees which belonged to their abbeys are still remarkably prolific. This county, placed on the borders of the two Antiquities kingdoms, the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of frequent warfare and depredation, presents the ruins of a great many castles and towers, and other remains of an early <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>.
