It was also distinguished for its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> buildings, of which there are still magnificent remains at Kelso and Jedburgh, as well as at Melrose. Roxburghshire, which has about 140 freeholders, represents one member to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">Parliament</a>; and Jedburgh, its only <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> burgh, joins with Lauder, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HADDINGTON">Haddington</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUNBAR">Dunbar</a>, and North Berwick, in electing another for the Scottish burghs. This is one of the few Scottish counties in which there are regular assessments for the poor; and, not many years ago, it presented the still greater anomaly of a Scottish clergyman <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITHES">tithes</a> in kind. Among the eminent men to whom this district has given birth are Thomson, Armstrong, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Kames, Elliot, the brave defender of Gibraltar, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARK">Park</a>, the African traveller, and William Dawson, the father of the improved agriculture of Scotland. The population, according to the census of 1801, was 33,682; in 1811 it amounted to 37,230; and in 1821 to 40,892, of which 19,408 were males, and 21,484 were females. The families employed in agriculture were 3613; in trade and manufactures 2822; in all other occupations 2204. The increase of population from 1811 to 1821 was 7210. See the general works quoted under the former Scottish counties, and Douglas' General View of the Agriculture of Roxburghshire. RUMFORD (<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNT">Count</a>). See THOMPSON (Sir Benjamin).

RUSH

Pages 510-512

a celebrated American physician, born, 5th <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1745, near <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PENNSYLVANIA">Pennsylvania</a>, was descended from a family who were originally <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUAKERS">Quakers</a>, and who had accompanied Penn, in 1683, to his infant colony. He lost his father at an early <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and having been first placed by his mother at a school kept by the Rev. S. Finley, he proceeded to finish his classical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a> of Princeton, and there took a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of Bachelor of Arts before he was sixteen. He then determined to make the profession of physic the pursuit of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and went to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> it, first under the care of Dr Redman of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILADELPHIA">Philadelphia</a>, and then at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, where he was created a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a> of Physic in 1768. At the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his return from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, a new school of medicine was about to be founded in Philadelphia, and he became Professor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a> immediately upon his arrival. In 1776, he began to take an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, with the rest of his countrymen, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> struggle of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, and he was chosen a member of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONGRESS">Congress</a> for the state of Pennsylvania; in 1777 he was appointed Surgeon General to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, and not <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> after became Physician General: he also contributed his best efforts to the improvement of the internal <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the state which he represented. But he soon withdrew his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> from political affairs, in order to devote it exclusively to medical and literary subjects, and he <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to be actively engaged in the practice of physic for the remainder of his life. In 1776 he married Miss Julia <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STOCKTON">Stockton</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEW_JERSEY">New <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERSEY">Jersey</a>. He had by her thirteen children, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> of whom survived him in respectability and prosperity. In 1791, when the two medical colleges of Philadelphia were incorporated into a single university, he was appointed Professor of the Institutes of Medicine, and of Clinical Practice. In 1793, he greatly distinguished himself by the new and apparently successful modes of practice that he introduced in the epidemic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> fever, which was then causing <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> mortality throughout the United States; and which, shortly before his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, he was induced to believe not contagious, but derived from some general causes independent of the previous existence of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>. He died on the 13th of April 1813, after an illness of five days, of a typhous fever, with some pulmonary symptoms. He had for a considerable part of his life been threatened with consumption, but had combated its attacks with unusual success. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of his writings is considerable in proportion to their bulk; the times and the state of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> in which he lived being such as to produce rather hasty and spirited than highly finished compositions. 1. His inaugural dissertation was entitled De Concoctione ciborum in ventriculo, and contained an explanation of the opinions relating to digestion, which he had learned from Dr <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CULLEN">Cullen</a>. Edin. 1768. 2. Account of the Effects of the Stramonium. Amer. Phil. Trans. I. 1770. 3. On the Utility of Wort in ill-conditioned Ulcers. Med. Obs. Inq. IV. 1770; addressed to Dr Huck. 4. Inquiry into the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Medicine among the Indians of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, an anniversary <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORATION">oration</a> delivered in 1774. 5. Remarks on Bilious Fevers, addressed to Dr Huck. Med. Obs. Inq. V. 6. Account of the Influence of the Revolution on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">Human</a> Body: with Observations on the Diseases of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">Military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">Hospitals</a>. 7. Inquiry into the Cause of the Increase of Bilious and Intermittent Fevers in Pennsylvania. Am. Trans. II. 8. Observations on Tetanus. 9. Inquiry into the Influence of Physical Causes upon the Moral <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">Faculty</a>. 10. Remarks on the Effects of Ardent Spirits upon the Body and Mind. 11. Inquiry into the Causes and Cure of Pulmonary Consumption, in his Medical Inquiries and Observations, I. Phil. 1788. His <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> object, in the cure of consumption, is to recommend <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, and every thing which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> enable the patient to take exercise; anticipating a practice which has become somewhat fashionable in England of late years, from its frequent success as a temporary palliative. The subject is continued in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> volume of the Inquiries, published in 1793; and bleeding is very strongly recommended in the earlier and only curable stages. Consumption, he observes, is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in America, though scrofula scarcely ever occurs; and it has sometimes been known to be clearly communicated by infection to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a> belonging to a family, who had, of course, no <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSANGUINITY">consanguinity</a> that could account for a similarity of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>. Five volumes, in the whole, of this collection appeared from 1788 to 1798; a second edition was published, in four volumes 8vo, 1804; a third in 1803, revised and enlarged, with a continuation of the Histories of the Yellow Fever from 1793 to 1809; a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">Defence</a> of Bloodletting, as a Remedy for certain Diseases; A View of the State of Medicine in Philadelphia; An Inquiry into the Sources of the usual Forms of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">Summer</a> and Autumnal Diseases in the United States; and the recantation of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the contagious <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the yellow fever already mentioned. 12. Information to Europeans disposed to Emigrate to the United States, in a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">Letter</a> to a Friend. 13. Observations on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">Population</a> of Pennsylvania. 14. Observations on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">Tobacco</a>. 15. A New <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">Mode</a> of Inoculating Small-Pox, a Lecture. Reprinted. 8. Phil. 1792. 16. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on the Study of the Latin and Greek Languages, American <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">Museum</a>; condemning it as a waste of time, oppressive to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> dunces who are tortured into their parts of speech, to the great scandal of a humane and republican <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and subversive of a proper respect for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of boys and, consequently, for the rights of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. 17. Essays, Literary, Moral, and Philosophical, 8vo. 1798: containing a republication of the last article, together with the author's Eulogiums on Dr Cullen and on Professor Rittenhouse, delivered in 1790 and 1796, and with some other miscellaneous papers of less moment. Ed. II. 1806. 18. Lectures on the Cause of Animal Life, 1791. 19. Account of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">Sugar</a> Maple Tree. Am. Tr. III. 1791. 20. Observations on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">Colour</a> of the Negro. Am. Tr. IV. 1792; attributing the blackness to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEPROSY">leprosy</a>. 21. History of the Yellow Fever. 1794. This celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> has been translated into French and Spanish; at the time of its publication, an almost superstitious dread was entertained by medical men of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANCET">lancet</a> in idiopathic fever; and few books have ever had so powerful and extensive an effect in altering the general treatment of a disease as this history had produced in every part of the world; probably, indeed, it may have carried a number of the younger and bolder practitioners into an opposite <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a>; but, with respect to the author's claims to merit on the occasion, it must be allowed that the innovation showed an uncommon <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of courage, with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> and good <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>; and the accurate <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the disease, that he has given us, fully establishes his claim to the character of an accurate nosologist. 22. On the Symptoms and Cure of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DROPSY">Dropsy</a>, and especially of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">Water</a> in the Head. 1793. 23. An Account of the Influenza of Philadelphia in 1789, 1790, 1791. 24. Observations on the State of the Body and Mind in Old Age. 1794. 25. Observations on the Nature and Cure of Gout and Hydrophobia. 1797. 26. Inquiry into the Cause and Cure of the Cholera Infantum. 1797. 27. Observations on Cynanche Trachealis. 1797. 28. Introductory Lectures. 1801. Ed. 2. 1811; with ten new introductory lectures, and two lectures on the Pleasures of the Senses and of the Mind. 29. In 1809, he published the works of Sydenham and of Cleghorn, with Notes, and in 1810 those of Pringle and Hilary. 30. On Diseases of the Mind. 8. 1812; an elaborate work, which had long been impatiently expected. 31. A Letter on Hydrophobia. 1813; addressed to Dr Hosack, and containing additional reasons for believing the seat of the disease to be chiefly in the blood vessels; an opinion which, in all <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, has at least tended to shorten the sufferings of several individuals on whom the experiment of profuse depletion has been tried. Dr Rush's numerous publications obtained him many marks of respect from his contemporaries, and procured him admission, as an honorary member, into the most distinguished literary and philosophical <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> of Europe. His name was familiar to the medical world as the Sydenham of America; his accurate observations and correct discrimination of epidemic diseases well entitled him to this distinction; while, in the original energy of his reasoning, he far excelled his prototype. His literary and professional character, indeed, appears to have been greatly influenced by the moral and political sentiments which were prevalent in his day. A <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of innovation led him to that proud defiance of established authority which is <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> as likely to be pernicious as to be salutary. The study of the learned languages he deprecated, in one of his early essays, as unfit for a republican education; and this was the first step to the true Jacobin doctrine, that it was unrepulican and aristocratical to have received any education whatever. In physic, his rejection of the prejudices of antiquity was somewhat more consistent with moderation, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> that he attempted was occasionally more successful than his literary speculations; nor can it be denied that there are a multitude of original suggestions in his works, which may very probably be found capable of affording valuable hints to the lovers of medical experiments. Hosack and Francis in the Amer. Med. Philos. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">Register</a>. Chalmers's Biographical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>, XXV. 8. Lond. 1816. (A. L.)

RUSSIAN EMPIRE

Pages 512-524

The Article Russia in the Encyclopaedia appears to have been drawn up with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, and, as far as it was founded on the documents collected by Mr Tooke, with accuracy; but the changes that have taken <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and the additional information that has been communicated, render it necessary to give some account, in this place, of the present state of the empire. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> changes in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> have arisen from the possession of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINLAND">Finland</a>, and the erection of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a> into a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> under the control of Russia. In <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, some additions of territory have been gained from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, settlements have been established on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of that continent, and claims have been made to some extensive tracts of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> which are supposed to conflict with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, of the United States of America, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. General View of the Russian Empire. The Russian dominions, including Poland, form a connected territory, extending from the frontiers of Germany and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a> eastward to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> which divides America from Asia, and beyond that, on the continent of America, to an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> hitherto undefined, and which is likely to become the subject of discussion with the other powers established in that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the globe. Its most western point is in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> 18° 6', and its most eastern in 202° 26' east from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. Its northern and southern boundaries have deep indentations; the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of the former are in 78° north latitude, and of the latter 39° 50'. The extent of this empire has been calculated by different writers with considerable variations. Some have included the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAUCASUS">Caucasus</a>, others the whole of the Caspian Sea; whilst some, again, have omitted the one and not the other. The comparative results of the several calculations, and the modes by which they have been conducted, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> to the conclusion, that an extent of 7,350,000 English <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles, or 4,704,000,000 acres, is the nearest approximation to accuracy. The whole of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a> is not equal to two-thirds of Russia; and the Roman Empire, at the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of its greatest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a>, did not comprehend more than one-fourth of the territory now subject to that power.* The extent of the European portion of her dominions is only calculated at about one-fifth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the whole. The increase of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> in Russia appears to have been equal to that of any other European country. The accounts were very imperfectly kept before the year 1796, as neither the females nor the privileged classes were noticed. By estimates, founded upon the return of taxable males, the inhabitants were calculated to have been, in 1723, 11,736,676; in 1743, 13,653,191; in 1763, 17,886,139; and in 1783, 25,482,214. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of the Academy of Petersburg give the population of the following years till 1805, thus: | Year | Population | |------|------------| | 1800 | 33,159,860 | | 1801 | 34,043,357 | | 1802 | 34,802,828 | | 1803 | 35,134,177 | | 1804 | 36,043,483 | In these accounts, the inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOSCOW">Moscow</a> and Petersburg, the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> and their families, and the wandering tribes, amounting to 2,900,000 persons, were not included. With the addition of these classes, the result of the calculation gave, as the whole <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inhabitants, 41,253,483. The following <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">Table</a> is formed from the reports published by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNOD">Synod</a> (which, however, includes only the members of the Orthodox Greek <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>), and shows the rate of the progressive increase of the population, as far as relates to that most numerous proportion of the people. | | 1806 | 1810 | 1816 | 1820 | |-------|--------|--------|--------|--------| | Marriages | 299,057 | 320,389 | 329,683 | 317,805 | | Births | 1,361,286 | 1,374,926 | 1,457,606 | 1,570,399 | | Deaths | 818,585 | 903,380 | 820,383 | 917,680 | | Deaths of Persons above 100 years old | 293 | 350 | 689 | 807 | Taking the account of the population, as stated before, to have been in the year 1806 - 41,253,483 And inferring an annual increase by excess of births over deaths at 500,000 from 1806 to 1822, being 16 years, or And for acquired territory, viz. | Year | Population | |------|------------| | 1807, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BIALYSTOCK">Bialystock</a> | 219,050 | | 1809, Finland | 1,101,898 | | 1812, Caucasus provinces | 120,000 | | Moldaw and Bessarabia | 310,000 | | 1815, The portion of Poland | 3,472,500 | We estimate the inhabitants of this empire This vast population consists of several distinct races, which have been classed and calculated by several different writers under the following heads: 1st, Slavonians. These, comprehending the inhabitants of Russia, Poland, Lithuania, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURLAND">Courland</a>, are estimated at 44,930,000. 2d, Finns. These consist of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> residents of Finland, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVONIA">Livonia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAPLAND">Lapland</a>, and some other tribes, which together amount to about 2,360,000. 3d, Tartars. They comprehend several tribes, and a great number of subdivisions of tribes. The Tartars proper are divided into fourteen different branches; the Noggers into six; besides which are the Kirgusiens, the Aralians, the Chewensens, the Bucharens, the Bashirs, the Teleutes, and the Jakutes, who are taken together at 1,800,000. 4th, The Caucasians, which comprehend the Ischerekessens, the Awcheses, the Lesghies, the Ossetts, and Kistesses, estimated at 1,300,000. 5th, Monguls. Under this head are comprehended the Monguls proper, the Calmucks, the Buritens, and the Kuriles, supposed to amount to 350,000 only. 6th. The Mandshurs, in two branches, viz. Tungusens and Lamutes, whose numbers do not exceed 80,000. 7th, Polar People, comprehending Samoiedes, Korjacks, Ostjacks, Kamschats, and some smaller tribes, whose whole numbers are not more than 300,000. 8th. The Colonists. These include the various foreigners established in the empire with peculiar rights. The Jews amount to about 500,000; the Germans to 250,000; and the other Europeans and Asiatics to about 750,000; making together, under this head, 1,500,000. The comparative <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> classes in the Russian dominions have been recently stated as follow: * See Kraft, Sur la Surface Geometrique de la Russie. Novis <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">Act</a>. Petersb. T. I. p. 389—400. † It appears that the marriages in 1820 were fewer by 22,470 than in the year 1819. ‡ The births of 1820 exceeded those of 1819 by 48,265. § The deaths of 1820 were fewer than those of 1819 by 1,429. || J. B. Georgi Beschreibung aller Nationen des Russischen Reichs. Hempel's and Geisler's Abbildung und Beschreibung der Völker unter Alexander. Le Peuples de la Russie, par le Comte Ch. de Rechberg. The people of Great and Little Russia, the Cossacks, the Greeks, Arnauts, Walachians, Moldavians, and Bulgarians, adhere to the Greek church. The Catholics are chiefly in Poland and Lithuania, and among the colonists. The Lutherans are to be found mostly in Finland, Courland, and Esthonia, and among the German colonists. The Armenians are mostly in the southern part of the Asiatic division of Russia, in the vicinity of Astrachan. The Calvinists, Hermuthers, Mennonites, are all colonists, except a few in Poland. Tartary contains chiefly Mahomedans. Schamanism or idolatry is practised by the Samoiedes and other Polar tribes. All religious sects, whether <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> or others, enjoy equal civil rights; and the same protection in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of their various modes of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>. The predominant party, the Greek church, possess about 70,000 places of worship, which are served by about 160,000 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> clergy. There are 480 monasteries, and 156 nunneries, under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the regular clergy. The whole are governed by a Consistory, of which the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">Emperor</a> is perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>, and which is divided into three departments; and these again into thirty-six sections or dioceses. The learning of the inferior clergy is very considerable; many of them can merely repeat by rote a few established prayers, can scarcely read, and much less write. They are allowed to marry once, but not after becoming widowers. Their sons must all be devoted to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> profession. They are generally paid small stipends by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>; but some few of them enjoy landed <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> attached to their benefices. A few men of learning are to be found among the higher ranks of the clergy; but their number and acquirements have never been very distinguished. The Catholic church, governed by a Consistory, comprehends one archbishopric, six bishoprics, and about forty religious establishments belonging to the several orders of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENEDICTINES">Benedictines</a>, Franciscans, Carmelites, Bernardines, and Trinitarians. The Lutherans, established in Finland, in Courland, and Livonia, are under the superintendence of their respective Consistories, each of which has a bishop as their president. The other religious Christian denominations are rather voluntary associations, recognized by the state, than, properly speaking, established ecclesiastical communities. Few of the Mahomedans are very rigid in their adherence to the regulations of their prophet. They have colleges for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>; several mullahs, and two muftis. The mufti of Ufa enjoys a stipend of 1500 roubles from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, and has two mullahs in Casan. The mufti of Taurus has joined with him a cadi, an effendi, and five ulemas, who regulate religious affairs, and administer the laws in that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. The worshippers of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAMA">Lama</a> have their principal religious establishment at Darsan, in the province of Udinsk. Their priests are numerous, and, in the province of Irkurtz alone, are said to be near 300, where they are very successful in making converts among the wandering tribes. The inhabitants of Russia are divided into the following classes or ranks; for though all offices are equally open to every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of subjects, yet exclusive privileges are enjoyed by some numerous bodies. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBLES">Nobles</a> in Russia, though distinguished by the several titles of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNT">count</a>, or baron, are all upon an equal footing, and enjoy equal privileges. Their persons and lands are freed from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-TAXATION">taxation</a>; they are exempted from the recruiting ballot; and are not subject to bodily penalties. These exemptions are, however, more apparent than real; for though their lands and persons are not taxable, yet a capitation tax, at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> of the government, may be imposed on their slaves, who form the most valuable part of their possessions. Though not in person compelled to serve in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, yet they are bound to furnish from their slaves a number of recruits in proportion to the demands of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. In some of the more recently acquired provinces, such as Livonia, Esthonia, and in Poland, the nobles have, or rather exercise other privileges, extending even to the power of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, over their vassals; but these powers arise from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> and general acquiescence much more than from the existing <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>. The Clergy are exempt from taxation, and from corporal <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>; which privileges are extended to each eldest son, who must, however, though his father is excused, take the risk of being called upon for military service. The Citizens are divided into three guilds or classes, according to the amount of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> they possess; and have some most whimsical privileges proportioned to their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>. Those of the first rank, with a capital of from 10,000 to 50,000 roubles, may carry on home or foreign trade; may be owners of ships; may drive a carriage with two horses; and are exempt from corporal punishment. The members of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> guild, possessing a capital of from 5000 to 10,000 roubles, can only carry on home trade, but enjoy all the other rights of the first guild. The members of the third guild must enjoy a capital between 1000 and 5000 roubles; they may carry on retail trades, be proprietors of barges and boats, keep taverns, and drive one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, though not in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COACH">coach</a>; but are not exempt from corporal punishments. Besides these there are the foreign and designated citizens. In this class is comprehended each person who has twice served any civic office; learned men and artists who can produce academic testimonials; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BANKERS">bankers</a> who possess capitals from 100,000 to 200,000 roubles; wholesale dealers, that keep no shops, and shipowners, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the sea. These may harness two or four horses to a coach; may possess country houses and gardens; may own ships; and are exempt from bodily penalties. None of the trading classes are exempt from the military conscription; but they are allowed to procure substitutes. The next class is that of the Peasants or free inhabitants of the country. In this rank are included, 1st, The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of proprietors who cultivate their own lands, but do not enjoy the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of possessing slaves. The males of this description amount to about 1,150,000. 2d, The Tartars, the Bashirs, and several other races, less numerous, to the south of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>, who are all proprietors of the lands they cultivate. 3d, The peasants of Finland. Since the acquisition of New Finland, the privileges enjoyed by the peasants of that country, under the Swedish government, have been <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> and confirmed to them; and the same rights granted to those of Old Finland, where all are now either proprietors or renters. 4th, The colonists, consisting of foreign families of agriculturists, who are proprietors of the lands they cultivate, and whose number is about 65,000. 5th, The military colonists. These are <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> who, after having served a prescribed period, have had <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> given to them, and a capital sufficient to cultivate it, in the southern provinces. And lastly, The free cultivators, a new class, founded by the present Emperor in 1803. They comprehend several villages, which have been liberated as an experiment. The number of individuals in 1810 was 19,757, since which period they have rapidly increased, and are said now to be near 20,000. The class next below these is that of the Serfs. They are chiefly peasants on the Crown lands, or of the province of Livonia. The first of these, the Crown peasants, amount to near 12,000,000, some of whom labour in the fields, the others in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a> and manufactories. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> of this class seems to be placed on the confines betwixt <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>. They may rise to the rank of citizens, they may acquire property, they enjoy the protection of the laws; and, under some restrictions, may quit their residences to obtain employment for a limited <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; but they are liable to be hired to the service of the mines, or to be sold. Although the Empress Catherine rarely gave these peasants away as presents to favourites, and the present Emperor has never done so, yet there is no legal security against the practice; and consequently their condition is scarcely less precarious than it was formerly. The peasants of Livonia, amounting to about 560,000, were slaves until the year 1804, when they first obtained the rights of serfs. They are now subject to some peculiar claims, but those claims are fixed, and they cannot be removed from the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> without their own consent. The last and most numerous class is that of the Slaves. Slaves. These amounted, in 1782, to 6,678,000 males, and at present are estimated to include 23,000,000 persons. They are in law considered as things, not as persons; may be bought, sold, or exchanged, with no more restrictions than are enacted in dealing for cattle; and have no other protection against their masters than what is created by a regard to their pecuniary <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>. They belong to the nobles, or to such civil or military officers as have acquired the right of possessing them. They are divided into agricultural, mining, manufacturing, or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> slaves, and have their condition only improved when drawn for military service. The accounts of the agricultural and manufacturing productions of Russia are fully detailed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">Commerce</a> article of the Encyclopaedia already mentioned. They &c. have undergone very few alterations in their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> since that article was written; and, consequently, only that their amount has increased with the increase of population and the extension of territory, no other notice seems here to be required beyond the value of the imports and exports at different periods. The following Table exhibits a view of the Imports into, and Exports from, the whole of the Russian dominions, by sea and by land, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> assignation roubles, estimated at four francs each, at several periods: | Year | Imports | Exports | Together | Value in Pounds <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">Sterling</a> | |------|---------|---------|----------|-------------------------| | 1797 | 36,980,111 | 54,601,368 | 91,581,479 | 15,263,570 | | 1802 | 56,330,094 | 63,277,759 | 119,607,853 | 19,934,642 | | 1803 | 55,557,075 | 67,148,643 | 122,706,318 | 20,451,053 | | 1805 | 55,529,118 | 72,434,095 | 127,968,213 | 21,277,152 | | 1819 | 167,599,003 | 219,589,310 | 378,188,310 | 66,531,235 | The chief exports are corn, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, tallow, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, flax-seed, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, furs, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> goods, live cattle, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POTASH">potash</a>. The principal imports are cotton and woollen goods, wines, dyers' drugs, raw <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, cotton <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEA">tea</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, coffee, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, silk goods, fruit, and foreign silver <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-COIN">coin</a>. The Government of Russia is an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>, in which the Emperor is the sole framer of the laws; but, as in other absolute monarchies, the exercise of power is tempered and somewhat moderated by the rights and privileges to which many bodies in different provinces have, by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> established usage, such claims as would be dangerous to the monarch to infringe. In the administration of the government, there is an uniformity preserved throughout all the several provinces, and in the different branches into which the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EXECUTIVE_POWER">executive power</a> is divided. The Emperor, through the directing <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, issues his ukases or laws to the Governors of the several provinces; which laws are executed by a Board, divided into sections, of which they are presidents. Besides the civil, there is a military governor in each department, to whom alone the affairs of the army are intrusted. There are deviations from this regularity of system among some tribes of Cossacks, who are ruled by their hereditary chiefs, and among the ruder classes. The ministers are appointed to different branches, denominated Foreign Affairs, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">War</a>, Marine, Interior, Instruction, Finance, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">Justice</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-POLICE">Police</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a>, and Ecclesiastical. The Civil and Criminal codes of Russia are very imperfect, notwithstanding the efforts directed towards its improvement by the Empress Catherine, and the more practical, but unfinished attempt of the present Emperor. In the cities, two burgomasters and four counsellors; and in the country, one justice, with two noble and two plebeian proprietors, form tribunals of the first instance. From these, appeals may be made to higher courts in the several provinces; and from them again to the supreme tribunals at St Petersburg or Moscow. Among the less civilized people, great deviations from this system are still indulged; and their chiefs exercise an hereditary power in civil as well as in criminal matters, over their several tribes. A kind of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">Court</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONSCIENCE">Conscience</a> exists in most places, which hears verbal complaints; acts as arbiters in differences about smaller matters; and exercises power in behalf of minors and imbeciles. The Finances of the Russian empire are not submitted to general inspection with the same freedom, nor with the same accuracy, as is now practised by most other governments. The great depreciation experienced in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> currency creates some difficulty in ascertaining the amount of the income, expenditure, and national debt. Besides the payments in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, so many personal services and other benefits are derived to the crown, that the bare produce of the taxes falls considerably short of the effective revenue which is extracted by the government. The chief taxes are the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPITULATION">capitulation</a>-tax of two roubles from each <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEASANT">peasant</a>, and five from each burgher; the property-tax of $\frac{1}{2}$ per cent. on the capital of the traders; and the duties on the importation of foreign goods. The other material sources of revenue are, the monopoly of distilled corn spirits; the profits of the coining, of postage, and of stamped paper; and the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of wood from the annual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTINGS">cuttings</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> forests. These several branches have been estimated to have afforded, in the year 1820, about thirteen or fourteen millions Sterling, including the kingdom of Poland. The expenses of the state, for many years, exceeded the income; and thus the public debt has been constantly increasing; but, it is said, the revenue now equals, or rather exceeds the expenditure. The national debt is supposed to amount to 1,000,000,000 roubles, or about L.160,000,000 Sterling. One-half of this is believed to consist in the government paper roubles, which have been issued at a gradually increasing depreciation. The other half, or funded debt, is principally owing to foreigners, and the interest is paid to them in silver money. This state of debt, for so extensive and so numerously peopled a country, may not appear very heavy; but in Russia, there is only paper money in circulation, and the constant drain to pay the interest of the debt in the precious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, makes the difficulty of returning to a metallic currency almost insurmountable. The project of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SINKING_FUND">sinking <a c</a>lass="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUND">fund</a> was adopted in 1817; but it has hitherto made but a slight progress in redeeming the debt, or in diminishing the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of circulating paper; which is not at the present period worth one-fourth of its nominal value. The increase of the Russian army has far exceeded what has been experienced in either the territory, the population, or the revenue of the empire. | Period | Troops | |-------------------------|--------| | <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CZAR">Czar</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> I. in 1687 | 10,000 | | Emperor Peter I. in 1724 | 108,350| | Empress <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> in 1747| 162,750| | Empress Catherine in 1771| 198,107| | in 1786 | 263,662| | Emperor Paul in 1800 | 368,715| | Emperor Alexander in 1805| 428,287| | in 1820 | 989,117| At the last of these periods the land force was composed of the following descriptions of troops: - 189 regiments and 565 battalions infantry: 618,722 - 76 regiments and 563 squadrons cavalry: 118,141 - 30 battalions <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>: 47,088 - Extra corps: 27,632 - <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">Irregular</a> troops (horse and foot): 105,534 - Garrison troops: 77,000 Besides this prodigious force, a national <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a>, is organised in all parts of the empire, except in Siberia and the two northern European provinces. The expense of this vast force is very small; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> for their equipment, provisioning, and arming, being of the cheapest and coarsest kind; and as the recruits are procured by ballot, and the pay of officers and men is low, the whole expense of the establishment is only 20,000,000 roubles, or about L.3,000,000 Sterling. The institutions for military education are fully commensurate to the extent of the force. In the Cadets-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> at Petersburg are 1000 youths; and the whole number in the empire, under appropriate instruction for the military profession, amount to nearly 3000. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a> of Russia has been neglected; and although the present force is equal to what existed in 1813, yet its character is much inferior, as many of the ships are become old. Very little timber of the best <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> is to be found in the Russian territory; but every other article, required for a navy, is abundantly and cheaply supplied from domestic sources. The fleet consists of 32 ships of the line, 18 frigates, 6 cutters, 7 brigs, 25 floating batteries, 121 <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUN">gun</a>-boats, and numerous armed small craft. This force is divided between the Baltic, the Caspian, and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> Seas. The whole number of officers, seamen, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARINES">marines</a>, with which the fleet is manned, is about 32,000, who are obtained by ballot from the seafaring people of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> provinces. The naval ports are at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRONSTADT">Cronstadt</a>, Revel, Sweaborg, and Rotschensalm, on the Baltic; at Archangel, on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">White</a> Sea; at Nikolajew, Sewastopol, Taganrog, and Cherson, on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BLACK_SEA">Black Sea</a>; and at Astrachan, on the Caspian. Having thus given a view of the general condition and circumstances of the Russian empire, in those respects in which alterations have taken place since the article in the Encyclopaedia was written; we may now proceed to a more particular description of its members and divisions. **European Russia, including the Dependent Kingdom of Poland.** The grand division of European Russia is into six provinces, viz. | Names | Extent in Square Miles | Population | |---------------------|------------------------|------------| | East Sea Province | 192,064 | 3,857,107 | | Great Russia | 938,929 | 21,330,279 | | Little Russia | 88,256 | 6,124,585 | | South or New Russia | 192,862 | 2,550,700 | | West Russia | 139,712 | 8,480,022 | | Poland | 46,741 | 2,732,524 | It thus appears, that in the whole of European Russia, the density of the population is somewhat less than 2½ persons to each square <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a>, or nearly one person to 282 English statute acres. The East Sea province is divided into the following governments, viz. | Names | Extent in Square Miles | Population | |----------|------------------------|------------| | Petersburg | 18,090 | 808,512 | | Finland | 134,444 | 1,346,139 | | Esthonia | 6,890 | 396,032 | | Livonia | 20,110 | 737,734 | | Courland | 9,544 | 568,690 | The inhabitants in this province are nearly one to twenty acres of land. The principal cities in the government of Petersburg are, Petersburg, one of the capitals of the empire, with 300,000 inhabitants; Kronstadt, with 35,000; <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NARVA">Narva</a>, with 3800. In Finland are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELSINGFORS">Helsingfors</a>, with 8000 inhabitants; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABO">Abo</a>, with 11,300; Uleaborg, with 3350; and Wiborg, with 3200. The chief <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Esthonia is Revel, with 15,000 inhabitants. The cities of Livonia are <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGA">Riga</a>, with 30,000; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DORPAT">Dorpat</a>, with 6000; and Pernau, with 2500. The only city of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, in Courland, is Mittau, containing 12,000 inhabitants. No other places than those here noticed, in the East Sea province, contain so many as 2000 inhabitants. The province of Great Russia is divided into 19 governments, whose names, extent, and population, are as follows: | Names | Extent in Square Miles | Population | |-----------|------------------------|------------| | Moscow | 10,500 | 1,289,823 | | Smolensko | 22,088 | 1,207,055 | | Pskow, or Pleskow | 22,293 | 783,945 | | Novgorod | 54,997 | 960,000 | | Olonez | 80,759 | 352,904 | | Archangel | 346,133 | 162,666 | | Wologda | 163,712 | 802,178 | | Kostroma | 38,570 | 1,422,700 | | <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NISHEGOROD">Nishegorod</a>| 20,501 | 1,349,508 | | Wolodimir | 18,669 | 1,306,046 | | <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TULA">Tula</a> | 11,904 | 1,093,721 | | <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KALUGA">Kaluga</a> | 12,736 | 1,159,600 | | Twer | 24,213 | 1,233,358 | | Jaroslav | 14,528 | 1,022,991 | | Kurst | 14,954 | 1,611,109 | | Orel | 16,779 | 1,270,085 | | Riissan | 14,553 | 1,270,291 | | Tambow | 22,869 | 1,391,400 | | <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WORONESH">Woronesh</a> | 32,487 | 1,436,357 | The inhabitants in this province are nearly one to twenty-four acres of land. The chief cities in the government of Moscow are, first, Moscow, one of the capitals of the empire, nearly the whole of which was destroyed by the fire in 1812, when the French troops were in possession of it. It has been since rebuilt in a great part, as far as regards the dwellings of individuals, but many of the public edifices are yet unfinished. There are now rebuilt upwards of 200 churches, more than 9000 houses, and between 6000 and 7000 booths. The number of inhabitants in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> of 1820 was about 200,000; and in the following winter, when the nobles, with their numerous establishments of domestics and slaves, took up their residence in the city, they are said to have been increased to about 50,000. The city of Kolomna contains 5809 inhabitants, Serpuchov 5540, Vereja 5941, and Moshaish 3944; all the others have less than 3000 inhabitants. In the government of Smolensko, the city of that name contains about 12,000 persons, Weasma 1150. Pleskow contains 10,000, and Toropez 12,000 inhabitants. Novgorod has 10,000, and Storaja Russa 5250 persons. In the government of Olonez the city of Petrossawodsh has 3285, and Kargapol 3032. The only city in the government of Archangel is of that name, and contains 8000 souls. The population of the city of Wologda amounts to 10,529, and of Oustjug to 12,000. Kostroma contains 8000, Galitzkaja 3300, and Galitsch 6000 inhabitants. Nishegorod has 12,000, and Arsamas 8000 persons. No place in the government of Wolodimir contains 2000 persons; the capital of the same name has only 1500. Tula or Toola, the chief city of the government of that name, has 30,000 inhabitants, Bjeleu 7000, and Obajew 3200. The city of Kaluga contains 25,000 souls, Borowsk 6000, and Koselsk 3500. In the government of Twer, the city of that name contains about 20,000 people, Stariza 3500, Ostaschkow 6207, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TORSHOK">Torshok</a> 15,000, Wolotschok 3500, Kalasin 3521, Kashin 3513, and Beshezk 3120. In Jaroslav, the city of the name has a po- The government of Kurst contains the city of that name, with 20,000 inhabitants, Rylsk with 6000, Sudsha with 7000, Bielgorod with 8000, Krotsha with 4000, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-OBOJAN">Obojan</a> with 5500. The city of Orel has 20,000 inhabitants, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINSK">Minsk</a> 6000, Bolchow 14,000, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BRIANSK">Briansk</a> 5000, Trubochwsk 3500, Siawsk 5,000 Liwny 6000, and Jelez 8000. The city of Riassn, in the government of that name, contains 5000 souls, Soraisk 4500, and Kasimow 10,000. The government of Tombow contains Tombow, with 15,000 souls, Hoslow with 8000, Lebedjan with 3500, Lipesk with 6400, Kirsanow with 4500, Morshansk with 5500, Shazh with 6500, Temnikow with 4500, and Jelatuna with 5800. Woronesh has no city of more than 3000 souls, except the capital of the same name, which contains about 15,000. The city of Kiev, or Kiow, contains about 40,000 inhabitants; the population of no other place in the government reaches beyond 5000. Charkow contains 15,000, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUMY">Sumy</a> 15,000, Bielopolje 9000, Lebidjan 8970, Achtirya 12,788, Bogoduchow 6749, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALKJ">Walkj</a> 9286, Smijew 5000, and Isjun 4248 inhabitants. The smaller <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> in Slobodsk Ukraine are numerous. In the government of Tschernigow, the city of that name contains 10,000, Neskin 16,000, Gluchow 9000, Nowgorod 8000, Starodub 4000, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MGLIN">Mglin</a> 5077 inhabitants. Pultowa has 10,000, <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol15.html#article-MIRGOROD">Mirgorod</a> 7437, Lubui 6000, Pereslavl 6000, Solotonscha 5500, and Kremenschuk 8000 inhabitants; besides which, the smaller towns and villages in the government of Pultowa are well peopled. The province of South Russia, a great part of which has been added to the empire in the course of the eighteenth, and the first ten years of the nineteenth century, is divided into five governments, viz. | Names | Extent in Square Miles | Population | |---------------------|------------------------|------------| | Catherineoslaw | 29,757 | 944,994 | | Cherson | 25,728 | 523,600 | | Taurida | 43,562 | 437,428 | | Bessarabia | 18,711 | 310,000 | | Land of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DON">Don</a> Cossacks | 77,034 | 398,103 | The inhabitants are about one to forty-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> acres of land. The city of Catherineoslaw contains about 5000 inhabitants; none of the other places more than 2000; and only two reach to that number. The towns in the government of Cherson are almost wholly of very recent foundation. The capital of that name contains 5000 inhabitants, Nicolajew (founded in 1789) 9000, and Jelisawetgrad 12,000. The greater part of the inhabitants of Taurida are of the Tartar race, and of the Mahomedan <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. The population of the cities has been very fluctuating since this district first came under the Russian government. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KAFFA">Kaffa</a> or Feodosia, formerly the seat of the Genoese trade, with the countries around the Black Sea, and then stated to have had a population of 40,000, when visited by Dr Clarke, had only 50 families; but in 1820 had increased to more than 4000 persons. Simferopol, a frontier garrison city, has 20,000 inhabitants, of various nations and religions. Baktschisarai contains 5777 persons, mostly Tartars, and Koslow 4410 of the same description. Bessarabia was formerly a part of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOLDAVIA">Moldavia</a>. Akerman, a strongly fortified place, has a population of about 10,000. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISMAIL">Ismail</a>, celebrated for its siege, and once containing 40,000 people, is still in ruins, and nearly without inhabitants. The only city among the Don Cossacks is Ischerkask, in a very unhealthy situation, but containing a population of 15,000. West Russia comprehends those provinces of Poland and Lithuania which have been formed into a component part of the Russian empire. The cities of Wolhynia are Berdychev with 10,000, Zaslow with 4500, Staro Constantino with 4200, Ostrog with 4500, Rowno with 3270, Waldiner with 3126, and Dubno with 5635 inhabitants. In Podolia are the cities of Kamenetz, with 5650 inhabitants, and Mohileu with 7000. The city of Bialystock contains 3350 inhabitants; and no other place of that government 2000. The ancient kingdom of Poland has, by successive divisions, been reduced to a small territory, when compared with its former extent. A description of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">Duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POSEN">Posen</a>, a part of it, is to be found in this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, under the head of Prussia. Galititia is united to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>; part is included in the present province of West Russia; and a very small portion, con- taining the city of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRACOW">Cracow</a>, and the surrounding district, is formed into an independent republic. The part now called the kingdom of Poland is, properly speaking, a Russian viceroyalty. It has, indeed, been permitted to retain some of its ancient forms and institutions; but it is effectively, at present, a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> province of the Russian empire, and in that view we must now consider it. The grand divisions are into eight Waywodeships, and these are again subdivided into Obwodeships. | Name of Waywodeship | Extent in Square Miles | Population in 1819 | Capitals and their Inhabitants | |---------------------|-----------------------|-------------------|-------------------------------| | Massovia | 6858 | 481,000 | <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARSAW">Warsaw</a> 98,000 | | Kalitch | 6862 | 512,000 | Kalitch 7,310 | | Cracow | 4500 | 445,000 | Kielce 5,000 | | Sandomir | 5982 | 432,000 | Radom 1,500 | | <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUBLIN">Lublin</a> | 6657 | 490,000 | Lublin 10,300 | | Polachia | 4864 | 286,000 | Siedlec 2,145 | | Augustow | 6870 | 335,000 | Suwalki 3,000 | | <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLOCK">Plock</a> | 6635 | 364,000 | Plock 6,000 | The inhabitants are one to about nine acres of land. Poland is generally a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> country, but towards the south is more undulating, and some of the hills rise to the height of 2000 feet above the level of the sea. It is well supplied with running streams. To the north of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VISTULA">Vistula</a> and the Bug, the soil is for the most part <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a>, but generally fertile. In the south, the soil is a rich vegetable mould, intermixed with marshes and morasses. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> is colder in the winter than in the same latitude in Germany and France. The productions are, corn of all kinds, hemp, flax, hops, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, wood, fruit, cattle, abundance of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAME">game</a>, river fish, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, and wax. The minerals are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, lead, iron, and calamine. There is much marble, alabaster, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a>; and in some parts salt, sulphur, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a>, and coal. The manufacturing labour is chiefly destined to provide clothing, and the most homely articles for domestic use. The Jews are the chief traders, manufacturers, and innkeepers; and their dwellings, in the towns and villages, are far better than those of the clergy, or even the lower <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>. The inhabitants have increased at an extraordinary rate since the return of tranquillity. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the year 1815 and 1819 appears to be 708,400 individuals, many of whom are German colonists. The number of Jews in 1819 was 212,944. All religious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROFESSIONS">professions</a> enjoy equal rights. The Roman Catholic is the predominant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>; their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HIERARCHY">hierarchy</a> consists of an archbishop and five <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>. There is a Unitarian bishop of the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RITUAL">ritual</a>, who presides over 200 churches. The Lutherans are about 150,000, who have a consistory and superintendent. The Calvinists are about 6000. Besides these are several smaller Christian sects, and more than 100 families of Mahomedans. The nobility are very numerous, comprehending more than 60,000 families. They are distinguished by different titles, but have none of the privileges of rank, unless they possess property. Many of them are very <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, but about 100 enjoy very extensive estates. Some restrictions in the use of titles have been recently introduced, which prevent those from assuming them who do not possess a graduated specific amount of income according to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>. Professors of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> of ten years standing, civil and military officers of the same length of service, and such burghers as make useful discoveries, may be now admitted into the ranks of nobility. The burghers have some civil rights granted in addition to those formerly enjoyed. The peasants have, however, been most benefited by the divisions that have been made of Poland. Under the ancient system, this numerous class of persons had neither property nor rights; and their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> proverb, "We have nothing but what we drink," is sufficiently descriptive of their low condition, and their habitual intemperance. They have now acquired personal freedom, and the right of holding landed property. To this extension of freedom may, in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, be attributed the recent increase of inhabitants; as many of the German emigrants would not have availed themselves of the greater fertility of the Polish soil, whilst the old slavish <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGRADATION">degradation</a> of the peasants was continued. The present <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of Poland is a limited monarchy. The Emperor nominates the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a>, who has the sole executive power. The legislature is divided into two chambers. The upper, or senate, consists of thirty members, nominated for life by the king; of whom ten are bishops, or clergy (approved by the Pope), ten are Waywodes, and the other ten Castellans, or Magnates. The lower house consists of sixty members, who must have attained 40 years. They are chosen for nine years, but every third year the retirement of one-third of them is determined by lot. They are elected by the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> assemblies of the nobles, where there are at least 600 qualified electors. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a> is appointed for civil affairs, another for criminal matters, and a third for finances. These three persons, with the ministers who sit in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>, not by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a>, but of right, are the only members permitted to speak, and all the others give their votes in silence. The assemblies are convened every other year, and sit only fourteen days to dispatch such business as is laid before them. They have no power to initiate a law, nor the right to exercise any inquisitorial functions. The assent of the upper chamber is not indispensable for promulgating a new law, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it be approved by the lower chamber, on the recommendation of the king. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POLES">Poles</a> had formerly few or no written laws; but in the year 1257, Boleslau the Fifth introduced the use of the law-book of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGDEBURG">Magdeburg</a>, which has been continued ever since as the compendium of civil and criminal law. The local courts consist of the landowners; the next higher court extends over each Waywodeship, and from them there is a court of general <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a>. A new code of laws has been drawn up, but is not yet in practice. The income of Poland is about L.850,000 Sterling, derived from a hearth and capitation-tax; from stamps, customs, lotteries, and posting. The civil <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> is about L.170,000; one-half of which arises from the national domains, the other is taken from the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>. The debts of the state, including old and new, amount to 200,000 Polish gulden. The expenses are not accurately known, as no budget has yet been made public since the introduction of the new constitution, and the accession of the Russian Imperial family. The army consists of 30,000 infantry and 20,000 cavalry, of whom the royal guards form a body of 12,000; but the military organization is not yet completed. Every Pole, without exception of rank or religion, is, by the law, a soldier from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of twenty to thirty; but, in practice, numerous exceptions to the general rule are allowed. The muskets are supplied from a manufactory at Kouskie, but the cannon, as well as cloths for uniforms, must be drawn from other countries. There is a scarcity of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>, although saltpetre is abundant. **Asiatic Russia.** The dominion of Russia comprehends the whole of Northern Asia, and extends from longitude 37° 14' to 190° 22' east from London; and from latitude 38° 58' to 78° 2' north. This vast dominion is calculated to be spread over 2/6ths of the land of the globe, and to be rather more than one-third of the surface of the whole of the continental portions of it. The eastern division of the Asiatic Russian territory, from the river Jenisy, or Yenesii, has, on its southern and eastern parts, vast mountain ranges; and on its interior there are several chains that run to the Arctic Ocean in vast masses. It is covered with woods, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, or extensive elevated plains, and terminates towards the shores of the Frozen Ocean, in vast fields of eternal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a>. The division to the westward has, indeed, some ranges of mountains, especially the Altai chain on the south, the Ural range on the west, and the ridge of Caucasus on the south-west, with their various projecting branches; but taken as a whole, it may be described as a vast level plain, partially watered, but by its climate and soil, ill adapted for the increase or the comfort of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> beings. The soil to the westward of the Ural mountains is generally very fertile, and produces abundant returns of corn, but to the eastward it is barren, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, and scarcely exhibits any symptoms of vegetation. Although Russia in Asia is in part surrounded by, and in some parts covered with mountains, yet there are several barren plains of great extent, usually denominated Steppes. The most remarkable of these are, the Kirgissch Steppe, between the Irtish and the Orenburg boundary line. It is a very dry and barren district, with some lakes, whose <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> is saline. The few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> have copious streams in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> from the melted snows, but in summer become dried up. The Wolgau Kalmuck Steppe, between the Ural and the Wolga, extending from the Caspian Sea to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMARA">Samara</a>, is of the same description. The Kuman Steppe, extending from the Caspian Sea to the Don and the Wolga, resembles a lake recently dried up; being formed of a mixture of sand and clay with an undulating surface, intermixed with salt lakes, and utterly destitute of vegetation. The other steppes, with slight varieties of character, are that of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TEREK">Terek</a>, between the rivers Terek and Kuma, touching on the Caspian Sea; of Kuban, extending from Kuban to the Manitsch and the lake of Bolschei; of Jettish to the eastward of the Ural; of Ischim on both sides the river of that name, between Tobol and the Irtish; and the Baraba, between the Irtish and the Ob. To these may be added the Arctic plain, between the 67th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of latitude and the Frozen Ocean, whose whole surface is little more than morasses, mixed with rocks, and bound up by <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FROST">frost</a> betwixt ten and eleven months in the year. These extensive plains are sometimes passed by the wandering tribes, who find subsistence on the less sterile spots which are to be met with on the banks of the rivers that bound them. The rivers of Asiatic Russia that empty themselves into the Arctic Sea, are among the most considerable of the ancient world. The most remarkable of these are, 1st, The Ob, whose course is 2800 miles in length, during which it receives the great rivers, the Tom, the Kek, the Irtish (which, before the junction, runs 2500 miles, and takes into its stream the waters of the Ischim, the Tobal, and many other rivers), the Tyda, and all their tributary streams. 2d, The Yenesii, or Jenisy, which has a course of 2000 miles, with fewer sinuosities than are usually observed in other great rivers. It receives the waters of fourteen large streams and all their tributary collections. 3d, The Piasana, whose course is 300 miles. 4th, The Taimurskoe, a short stream issuing from a lake of the same name, in latitude 70°. 5th, The Khatanga, which empties itself into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of Khatangaskoi, on the Frozen Ocean. 6th, The Anabara, an Arctic stream. 7th, The Olenk, whose waters only become considerable after entering the Arctic circle. 8th, The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LENA">Lena</a>, one of the largest of the Asiatic Russian rivers. It rises in the Backal mountains to the north of China, in latitude 52° 30', and empties itself into the ocean in latitude 70° 40', and longitude 164° 26', after receiving the waters of fourteen large rivers and their numerous tributary streams. 9th, The Omoloi. 10th, The Jana. 11th, The Indigirka. 12th, The Alazeja. 13th, Kolyma. 14th, The Tchauna; and, 15th, The Amgonia. The streams whose courses have been traced to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into the sea of Kauntschatka, between Asia and America, are the Anadyr, the Katirka, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KAMTSCHATKA">Kamtschatka</a>, the Penshena, the Tilcha, the Ischiga, the Tauna, the Okhota, the Uda, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARGUN">Argun</a>, and the Shilka. The Black Sea receives from Russian Asia the great rivers Kooban and Rioni, with their tributary waters, and several smaller streams which arise on the western sides of the mountains of Caucasus. The rivers which discharge themselves into the Caspian Sea are, 1st, The Wolga, which comes --- * The best recent works on Poland are, Guide du Voyageur en Pologne, Varsovie, 1820; Polen Staatsveränderungen und Letztere Verwaltung, von F. Jäkel, Wien, 1819. out of the centre of European Russia, and forms the principal means of internal water <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> between the European and Asiatic portions of the empire. Its course is upwards of 2500 miles in length, during the progress of which it receives the streams of fourteen large, and of a vast number of smaller rivers. 2d, The Kuma, rising in the northern Caucasus. 3d, The Teret, a mountain <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TORRENT">torrent</a>, nearly dry in summer. 4th, The Akharaan. 5th, The Sulach, both rivers only abundant in the spring, and nearly dry in summer. 6th, The Kur, a stream formed by a union of several others in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEORGIA">Georgia</a>, and navigable from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEFLIS">Teflis</a>. 7th, The Ural, rising in the Uralian range of mountains, and forming a course of nearly 1400 miles, during which it receives the waters of six large, and numerous smaller rivers. 8th, The Jemba, a river coming from the north, and running about 450 miles. The lakes in Russian Asia are very numerous, and some of them very extensive. One of the largest is the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAIKAL">Baikal</a> in Siberia, between latitude 52° and 55°, and longitude 104° 26', and 109° 56', extending over 11,180 square miles. Its water is clear and bright, the depth varies from 18 to 480 feet. It is covered with ice from the middle of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> till April. The river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGARA">Angara</a>, which runs to the Jenisy, issues from it. It receives the waters of several streams which come either from the Chinese territory or its vicinity. The lakes next in extent are the Tchani and the Piasenskoe, both in the government of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TOMSK">Tomsk</a>. Almost every province has one or more lakes, several of which are of salt water, on whose banks a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRYSTALLIZATION">crystallization</a> prepares culinary salt for the use of the inhabitants. The agriculture necessarily varies both in its practices and its productions in countries so extensive as those we are sketching. By an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a> table before us, it appears that the winter corn (wheat and rye) does not yield, on an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a>, more than three and a half for one grain that is sowed; and the summer corn (barley and oats) not much more than two and a half for one. The increase of production seems to be about as progressive as the increase of population. By a return of the whole produce of the harvest of 1808, it appears that the whole quantity raised was 43,424,966 tschewerts on 29,854,622 <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>; from which, if two-sevenths be allowed for seed, there will remain for subsistence 21,324,760 quarters. Taking the whole population at 10,164,000, and allowing for 1,164,000 who eat no <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, there will have been about 18 bushels of corn for each individual. In many parts the goats and sheep, and in some the oxen, furnish food for the inhabitants; whilst aid for the subsistence of others is afforded from the fish of the seas, lakes, and rivers. The mines of Russian Asia are by far more productive than those of any other portion of the empire; as from them is extracted the whole of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, and lead, nine-tenths of the copper, and eleven-twelfths of the iron which is brought into use. By the latest returns the whole produce was as follows: | Product | Quantity | |-------------|---------------| | Gold | 17,940 ounces | | Silver | 540,000 ounces| | Copper | 3,360 tons | | Lead | 900 tons | | <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">Bar</a>-iron | 1,680,000 tons| | Vitriol | 5,184 tons | | Rock Salt | 14,675 quintals| According to the work from which these statements are taken,† the culinary salt, annually prepared in Asiatic Russia, is 830,000 quintals.
