The idea of propelling vessels by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> paddles, instead of oars, seems to have occurred at a remote <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of carrying the project into execution is clearly, though concisely, described in a very curious and learned treatise, De Re Militari, by Valturius of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIMINI">Rimini</a>. This remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> is justly deemed one of the finest and earliest specimens of typography and wood-engraving. It was first printed by John of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERONA">Verona</a> in 1472, and from the same press an Italian translation of it by Paul Ramusio issued in 1483. It was afterwards reprinted at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1532, in the original Latin, by the celebrated Printer, Christian Wechelius. Of the numerous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> described and delineated in that rare volume, several have been frequently reproduced as new inventions during the course of the last century. Such waste of ingenuity, is really a serious evil, arising from inattention to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> arts, and the want of a public repository to exhibit their successive improvements. Mr Dibdin has given, in his Bibliotheca Spenceriana, fac-similes of several warlike engines from Valturius; but we have copied the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of a flat-bottomed <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> for crossing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> by the circumvolution of paddles or vanes. (See Plate CXVI.) These vanes consisted of pitched sail-cloth; and it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be seen, that the impulsion was communicated by means of cranks. The action of each axle is said to have been <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to that of twelve oars. (Valturius, De Re Militari, p. 314.) We must not, however, suppose that the power thus applied was really augmented by such machinery. It has been ascertained that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> force is advantageously exerted in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of rowing; but this operation requires skill, and not more than one person can work conveniently at the same oar. Where paddles are substituted, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> strength is sufficient; and a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of men may combine their labour in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> a crank. Animal power will, indeed, effect the same purpose. Accordingly, some of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> ferry-boats in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> are fitted with paddles driven by gin-horses. It is clear, therefore, that, three or four centuries ago, boats, propelled by the action of paddle-wheels, were used on some of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> rivers in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and, most probably, in other parts of the Continent, for the transporting of troops. Valturius even speaks of pontoons, composed of three parts, like drums, which could be conjoined at any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and again separated, to facilitate their carriage over <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>. The method of changing a reciprocating into a rotatory <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, by the help of a crank, though not applied to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEAM_ENGINE"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol19.html#article-STEAM">steam</a>-engine till 50 or 60 years after its <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>, had been understood and practised at the very dawn of the mechanical arts. The atmospherical steam-engine, which had been invented by Newcomen and improved by Beighton, began to be pretty generally adopted in the coal-works about the year 1720; and it does not seem to have required any <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> stretch of imagination to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> such an efficient power to other purposes besides the raising of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. Mr J. Hulls. The first attempt, however, on record to apply steam to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> was made by a person of the name of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JONATHAN">Jonathan</a> Hulls, who, on the 21st of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1736, obtained a Patent, to endure for 14 years, for what may, without any impropriety, be called a Steam-Boat. The Letters Patent, and a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of this boat, illustrated with a plate, are contained in a very rare Tract, published by Hulls in 1737, under the following <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>: A Description and Draught of a new invented Machine for carrying Vessels or Ships out of or into any Harbour, Port, or River, against <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">Wind</a> and Tide, or in a Calm. As the origin of the invention has been much disputed, we shall subjoin some extracts from this pamphlet, which lay totally forgotten till within these few years, and is even yet, on account of its great rarity, but very little known.* He introduces his description by a concise view of the principles of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIMENTAL_PHILOSOPHY">experimental <a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>; in which he observes (p. 39), "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> a person were to descend to the bottom of a well full of water, his body would be pressed the same as if he descended the same depth into the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; for there is the same pressure against a pool-head as there is against the sea-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> at the same depth, as hath before been demonstrated. "Thus I have endeavoured to explain the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the pressure of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> on other bodies, by comparing it with other <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a> that are visible to our eye, as <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>, water, &c. and, since the pressure is so very great, it is the more fit to be applied to a purpose wherein all sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANUAL">manual</a> operations are insufficient. For this present undertaking cannot be supposed to be done by strength of men or horses, or any machine driven by either. "The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> being of a great <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, and striving to get in where there is a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VACUUM">vacuum</a>, I shall endeavour to show how this vacuum is made, and in what manner this force is applied to drive the machine. "In some convenient <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Tow-Boat there is placed a vessel about two-thirds full of water, with the top <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> shut; this vessel being kept <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a>, rarifies into a steam. This steam being conveyed through a large pipe into a cylindrical vessel, and there condensed, makes a vacuum, which causes the weight of the atmosphere to press on this vessel, and so presses <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> a piston that is fitted into this cylindrical vessel, in the same manner as in Mr Newcomen's engine, with which he raises water by fire. (See Plate CXVI.) "It hath been already demonstrated, that a vessel of thirty inches diameter, which is but two feet and an half, when the air is driven out, the atmosphere will press on it to the weight of four tons, sixteen hundred weight, and upwards; when proper instruments for this work are applied to it, it must drive a vessel with a great force." <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">Note</a>.—The bigness of the machines may be proportioned to the work that is to be performed by them; but, if such a force as is applied in this first <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">essay</a> be not sufficient for any purpose that may be required, there is room to make such addition as will move an immense weight with tolerable swiftness. "It is my <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> it will not be found practicable to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the machine here recommended in the vessel itself; that is to be taken in or out of the port, &c. but rather in a separate vessel, for these reasons: "1st. This machine may be thought cumbersome, and to take up too much room in a vessel laden with goods, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, &c. "2d. If this machine is put in a separate vessel, this vessel may <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> at any port, &c. to be ready on all occasions. "3d. A vessel of a small burthen will be sufficient to carry the machine to take out a large one. "4th. A vessel will serve for this purpose for many years, after she is thrown off, and not safe to be taken abroad." The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> above quoted are followed by the * It consists of forty-eight <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAGES">pages</a>, in duodecimo; was "printed for the author, and sold, price sixpence, at the Pamphlet Shops in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> and Westminster." Explanation of the Machine. The Figure to which this Explanation refers is copied, from that given by Hulls, in Plate CXVI. "A represents the chimney coming from the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a>. "B, The tow-boat. "CC, Two pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, framed together, to carry the machine. "Da, D, and Db, are three wheels on one axis, to receive the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> Fa, Fa, and Fb. "Note.—F is the same rope that goes into the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a>. "Ha and Hb are two wheels on the same axis with the fans II IIII, and move alternately in such a manner, that when the wheels Da, D, and Db, move backward or forward, they keep the fans II IIII in a direct motion. "Fb is a rope going from Hb to Db, that when the wheels Da, D, and Db, move forward, moves the wheel Hb forwards, which brings the fans forward with it. "Fa is a rope going from the wheel Ha to the wheel Da, that when the wheels Da, D, and Db, move forward, the wheel Ha draws the rope F, and raises the weight G, at the same time as the wheel Hb brings the fans forward. "When the weight G is so raised, while the wheels Da, D, and Db, are moving backward, the rope Fa gives way, and the power of the weight G brings the wheel Ha forward, and the fans with it, so that the fans always keep going forward, notwithstanding the wheels Da, D, and Db, move backwards and forwards, as the piston moves up and down in the cylinder. "LL are <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> for a catch to drop in from the axis, and are so contrived, that they catch in an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> manner, to cause the fans to move always forward, for the wheel Ha, by the power of the weight G, is performing his office, while the other wheel Hb goes back in order to fetch another stroke. "Note.—The weight G must contain but half the weight of the pillar of air pressing on the piston, because the weight G is raised at the same time as the wheel Hb performs its office, so that it is, in effect, two machines acting alternately by the weight of one pillar of air of such a diameter as the diameter of the cylinder is. "If it should be said that this is not a new invention, because I make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the same power to drive my machine that others have made use of to drive theirs for other purposes; I answer, The application of this power is no more than the application of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> and known <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> used in mechanism for new invented purposes." P. 43. This Explanation is followed with the annexed "Answers to some Queries that have been made concerning the possibility and usefulness of this undertaking." "Query I. "Is it possible to fix instruments of sufficient strength to move so prodigious a weight as may be contained in a very large vessel? "Answer. All <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a> will allow it is possible to make a machine to move an immense weight, if there is force enough to drive the same; for every member must be made in a proportionable strength to the intended work, and properly braced with laces of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, &c. so that no part can give way or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a>, if the braces, &c. necessary for this work had been put in the draught, it would have been so much crowded with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, that the main instruments could not be so well perceived. "Query II. "Will not the force of the waves break any instrument to pieces that is placed to move in the water? "Answer. First, It cannot be supposed that this machine will be used in a storm or tempest at sea, when the waves are raging; for, if a merchant lyeth in a harbour, &c. he would not choose to put out to sea in a storm, if it were possible to get out; but rather stay until it is abated. "Secondly. When the wind comes a-head of the tow-boat, the fans will be protected by it from the violence of the waves; and when the wind comes side-ways, the wind will come edge-ways of the fans, and therefore strike them with the less force. "Thirdly. There may be pieces of timber laid to swim on the surface of the water on each side of the fans, and so contrived as they shall not touch them, which will protect them from the force of the waves. Up inland rivers, where the bottom can possibly be reached, the fans may be taken out, and cranks placed at the hindmost axis, to strike a shaft to the bottom of the river, which will drive the vessel forward with the greater force. "Query III. "It being a continual expense to keep this machine at work, will the expense be answered? "Answer. The work to be done by this machine will be upon particular occasions, when all other means yet found out are wholly insufficient. How often does a merchant wish that his ship were on the ocean, when, if he were there, the wind would serve tolerably well to carry him on his intended voyage, but does not serve, at the same time, to carry him out of the river, &c. he happens to be in, which a few hours work of this machine would do. Besides, I know engines that are driven by the same power as this is, where materials for the purpose are dearer than in any navigable river in England; therefore, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> demonstrates, that the expense will be but a trifle to the value of the work performed by those sort of machines, which any person that knows the nature of those things may easily calculate." P. 45—48. Thus, Jonathan Hulls appears to have been the first person who suggested the propulsion of vessels by paddle-wheels moved by steam. His mode of converting the rectilineal into a rotatory motion was ingenious, though not so simple as the crank. It is most probable, however, that he possessed not the means, and did not receive at the time sufficient encouragement to carry his scheme into execution. A <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> elapsed before a similar project was attempted. About the year 1772 the celebrated Mr. Watt had completely remodelled the steam-engine; and before 1779 it was, by various improvements, reduced to a compendious form, and adapted to almost every purpose where great power was required. The idea of employing it to propel vessels then naturally suggested itself. One of the first to whom it occurred was the Marquis De Jouffroy, who, in 1781, constructed a steam-boat on the Saone at Lyons; it was 10 feet long, and he made several experiments with it. In the year 1785 two keen competitors for the invention of steam-navigation appeared in America; namely, James Rumsey of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a>, and John Fitch of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILADELPHIA">Philadelphia</a>. The following extracts from a Pamphlet, very little known in this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, published by the latter in 1788, are curious: "I confess the thought of a steam-boat, which first struck me by mere accident, about the middle of April 1785, has hitherto been very unfortunate to me; the perplexities and embarrassments through which it has caused me to wade far exceed anything that the common course of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> ever presented to my view."—In <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> I formed models, and in August laid them before <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONGRESS">Congress</a>, as will appear on their files. In September I presented them to the Philosophical <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, as per certificates." "Philadelphia, Sept. 27, 1785. At a special meeting of the American Philosophical Society, a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a>, accompanied with a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> and description of a machine for working a boat against the stream, by means of a steam-engine, was laid before the Society by John Fitch." "At a meeting of the American Philosophical Society on December 2, 1785, a copy of the drawing and description of a machine for working a boat against the current, which some time ago was laid before the Society by Mr John Fitch, he this evening presented to them. Extract from the Minutes, "Samuel Magaw, "one of the Secretaries." "In October I called on the ingenious Mr Henry of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANCASTER">Lancaster</a>, to take his opinion on my drafts, who informed me that I was not the first person who had thought of applying steam to vessels; that he had conversed with Mr Andrew Ellicot as early as 1775, and that Mr Paine, author of Common <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">Sense</a>, had suggested the same thing to him in the winter of 1778." "In Virginia I waited on his Excellency General <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WASHINGTON">Washington</a>, who, in the course of conversation, informed me, that the thought of applying steam was not original; that Mr Rumsey had mentioned steam to him: but nothing that passed in the conversation with General Washington had the least tendency to convey the idea of Mr Rumsey's relying on steam; and General Washington's <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, p. 10 of Mr Rumsey's pamphlet, clears up the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>—for the General himself did not conceive any such thing. Knowing that the thought of applying steam to boats had been suggested by other gentlemen long before; I left his Excellency, with all the elated prospects that an aspiring projector could entertain, not doubting but I should reap the full benefit of the project: for although I found that some had conceived the thought before, yet I was the first that ever exhibited a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> to the public; and was fully convinced that I could not interfere with Mr Rumsey, otherwise the known candour of General Washington must have pointed out to me such interference. I immediately applied to the Legislature of Virginia for assistance to execute my plan, who signified their wish to encourage my designs, but that the state of their finances prevented it." "Finding that undoubtedly I was the first person in America that could be termed the inventor of a steam-boat, either agreeably to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a>, I thought it prudent to apply to the different states for the exclusive privileges for the emoluments of such invention, which were granted by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEW_JERSEY">New <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERSEY">Jersey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1785, by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DELAWARE">Delaware</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEW_YORK">New <a c</a>lass="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PENNSYLVANIA">Pennsylvania</a>, in the winter and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> following, and by Virginia in October 1787. "I have from the time of my first thought pursued my scheme with unremitting application, without a suspicion of an interruption, until the circulation of Mr Rumsey's invidious pamphlet, the contents of which I now find it necessary next to take under consideration, not doubting but that the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> and tendency of that production will be a sufficient apology for the plainness with which I shall treat it." "Mr Rumsey says, in page 2, that 'in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of September 1784, he exhibited the model of a boat to his Excellency General Washington, at Bath, in Berkeley <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, calculated for stemming the current of rapid rivers only, constructed on principles very different from his present one. Satisfied,' says he, 'of the experiment of her making way against a rapid stream, by the force of the stream, the General was pleased to give me a most ample certificate of her efficacy.' Here it is to be observed, that no mention was made to General Washington of steam at the time of such <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXHIBITION">exhibition</a>: the principles upon which the boat was propelled were entirely unconnected with, and distinct from steam; being simply a model, propelled by water wheels, cranks, and setting <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>: a mode which was many years ago tried on the river Schuylkill by a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a> near <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">Reading</a>, but without success. From an exhibition of this plan it was that Mr Rumsey procured the certificate from General Washington, and on that certificate were Mr Rumsey's laws founded. In his petitions to the several legislatures, he prayed for no exclusive <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> for the use of steam-boats; neither did he make mention of steam to their committees, or even suggest an idea of the kind." Patrick Miller, Esq. of Dalswinton, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUMFRIES">Dumfries</a>-shire, made many experiments on the best mode of impelling single, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a>, and triple vessels with paddle- --- *The Original Steam-Boat supported; or a Reply to Mr James Rumsey's Pamphlet, showing the true priority of John Fitch.* Philadelphia, 1788. wheels, by the power of men and horses; and printed and circulated extensively an account of a Triple Vessel and wheels, in February 1787. In this Tract, he states,—"I have also reason to believe that the power of the Steam-Engine may be applied to work the wheels, so as to give them a quicker motion, and, consequently, to increase that of the ship. In the course of this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> (1787), I intend to make the experiment." As the power of men produced only the slow motion of five miles per <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, Mr James Taylor, then residing in Mr Miller's family, and now at Cumnock, suggested the application of a steam-engine as the moving power; and he carried Mr Miller to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Gilbert Meason, Esq. St Andrew's <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">Square</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, to see the model of a steam-carriage invented by Mr William Symington of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FALKIRK">Falkirk</a>. Mr Miller was much pleased with the model, and desired Mr Symington to make him a small steam-engine, to work a twin or double boat on Dalswinton Loch. The engine having been accordingly executed and put on board the boat, the experiment was made at Dalswinton in autumn 1788; and it succeeded so well, that Mr Miller commissioned Mr Symington to purchase a gabert, or large boat, at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARRON">Carron</a>, and to fit up a steam-engine on board of her, to make a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> on a larger <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>. Every thing being completed, the trial was made on the Forth and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLYDE">Clyde</a> Canal, in summer 1789, Messrs Miller, Stainton, Taylor, &c. being on board, and the result answered their most sanguine expectations. From a manuscript Memorial on Steam-Navigation, drawn up by Mr Symington, with the perusal of which we have been favoured, we make the following extract: "Mr Miller being then very much engaged improving his newly purchased estate in Dumfries-shire, and I also employed to construct large machinery for the use of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a> at Wanlockhead, the idea of carrying the experiments, at that time, any farther, was entirely given up, till meeting with the late Thomas <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Dundas of Kerse, who wished that I would construct a steam-boat for dragging vessels on the Forth and Clyde Canal, in place of horses. Agreeably to his Lordship's request, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of experiments, which cost nearly L. 3000, were set on foot in the year 1801, and ending in 1802, upon a larger scale, and more improved plan, having a steam cylinder 22 inches diameter, and four feet stroke; a complete model of which, with a set of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAKERS">breakers</a> attached, may be seen (if not in Lord Dundas's house, Arlington Street) in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">Institution</a>, London, which proved itself very much adapted for the intended purposes, as will appear from the following simple yet authentic narrative. Having previously made various experiments, in March 1802, at Lock No. 20, Lord Dundas, the great <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> and steam-boat promoter, along with Archibald Speirs, Esq. of Elderslie, and several gentlemen of their acquaintance being on board, the steam-boat took in two loaded vessels, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">Active</a> and Euphemia of Grangemouth, Gow and Esplne masters, each upwards of 70 tons burthen, and with great ease carried them through the long reach of the Forth and Clyde Canal, to Port-Dundas, a distance of 19½ miles, in six hours, although the whole time it blew a very strong breeze right <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AHEAD">ahead</a> of us; so much so, that no other vessels could move to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WINDWARD">windward</a>, in the canal, that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, but those we had in tow; which put beyond the possibility of doubt the utility of the scheme in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> or rivers, and ultimately on open seas; though in this state of forwardness it was opposed by some narrow-minded proprietors of the navigation, under a very mistaken idea, that the undulation of the water occasioned by the motion of the wheel would wash and injure its banks: in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> the boat was, with great reluctance, laid up in a creek of the canal, near Bainsford Draw-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, exposed for years to public view; where Henry <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELL">Bell</a> from Glasgow, who frequently inspected the steam-boat at Carron in 1789, did also particularly examine this; and afterwards, in conjunction with other gentlemen, in the year 1811, constructed the first steam-boat, Comet, to ply on the river Clyde, which was soon followed there by many more, and its use is now rapidly extending to different regions of the globe." It is indisputable, therefore, that Mr Symington was the first person who had the merit of successfully applying the power of the steam-engine to the propulsion of vessels. The boat which he constructed was, like that proposed by Hulls, really a Tug. It is much to be regretted, that there existed not enterprise enough at that time in Scotland to encourage the ingenious artizan to repeat his experiments on the Clyde. All the subsequent improvements, however, in steam-navigation may be fairly traced to Mr Symington's attempt, and we cannot help thinking that he has a strong claim on the national <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a>. He is still alive, and we fear not in the most flourishing circumstances. Should the state decline rewarding such meritorious services, the opulent proprietors of steam-boats might well evince their liberality and discernment, by bestowing on him some recompence. Considering the importance to America of navigating her mighty rivers, it is not surprising that the application of the power of steam to the propulsion of boats should, by persevering efforts, have been first carried into successful practice in that continent. This was achieved by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> and zeal of Mr Fulton, who appears evidently, however, to have derived all his primary knowledge of the subject from Scotland. Mr Symington's Memorial, above referred to, gives the following remarkable statement: "When engaged in these last experiments in 1802, I was called upon by Mr Fulton, who very politely made himself known, and candidly told me that he was lately from North America, and intended to return thither in a few months, but having heard of our steam-boat operations, could not think of leaving this country without first waiting upon me in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> of seeing the boat, and procuring such information regarding it as I might be pleased to communicate; he at same time mentioned, however advantageous such invention might be to Great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, it would certainly become more so in North America, on account of the many extensive navigable rivers in that country; and as timber of the first <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, both for..." <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> the vessels, and also for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a> to the engine, could be purchased there for a small expense; he was decidedly of opinion it could hardly fail, in a few years, to become very beneficial to trade in that part of the world; and that his carrying the plan to North America could not turn out otherwise than to my advantage; as, if I inclined it, both the making and superintendence of such vessels would naturally <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> upon me, provided my engagements with steam-boats at home did not occupy so much of my time as to prevent me from paying any <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to those which might afterwards be constructed abroad. "Mr Fulton having thus spoken, in compliance with his most <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> request, I caused the engine fire to be lighted up, and in a short time thereafter, put the steam-boat in motion, and carried him from Lock No. 16, where the boat then lay, four miles west the canal, and returned to the place of starting, in one hour and twenty minutes, to the great astonishment of Mr Fulton, and several gentlemen, who, at our outset, chanced to come on board. "During the above trip, Mr Fulton asked if I had any objections to his taking notes respecting the steam-boat, to which question I said, none; as I considered the more publicity that was given to any discovery intended for general good, so much the better; and having the privilege secured by letters-patent, I was not afraid of his making any encroachment upon my right in the British dominions; though in the United States, I was well aware, I had no power of control. In consequence, he pulled out a memorandum-book, and, after putting several pointed questions respecting the general <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> and effect of the machine, which I answered in a most explicit manner, he jotted down particularly everything then described, with his own remarks upon the boat, while moving with him on board, along the canal; but he seems to have been altogether forgetful of this, as, notwithstanding his fair promises, I never heard any thing more of him, till reading in a newspaper an account of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. "From the above incontrovertible facts, which can be corroborated by a number of people of respectability living at this day, it is very evident that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> is not indebted to North America for the invention of steam-packets, it being hereby established beyond the possibility of doubt, to be truly British, both in idea and practice, and that Mr Fulton's steam-vessel did not make its first appearance in the Hudson River earlier than 1806 or 1807, four years at least <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POSTERIOR">posterior</a> to his having been on board the Charlotte Dundas steam-boat, and minutely examined it, when at work upon the Forth and Clyde Canal, and 18 years later than the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> of the first experiments made by me upon steam-boats, on the lake at Dalswinton, Dumfries-shire, in Great Britain." The following statement upon the same point, by Mr Henry Bell of Glasgow, was addressed by him to the Editor of the Caledonian Mercury, and published in that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> in October 1816:—"Sir, I observed in your paper lately a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAGRAPH">paragraph</a> respecting steam-boats, in which the Americans claimed the right to the discovery, which is become of so much utility to the public. On this account I propose to give you a full statement of what I conceive to be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. Mr Miller of Dalswinton first wrote upon the method of moving vessels or rafts through water by paddles, wrought by a capstan, or by the wind, in the manner of a wind-mill, which idea he afterwards gave to all the different Courts in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. It will be recollected by most people in this country, that the French proposed to erect rafts for conveying troops to invade this country by means of Mr Miller's wind-mill or capstan plan; for it may be stated that this <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> built two vessels at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEITH">Leith</a>, and put them in motion upon his new improvement, and even sent one of them to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, as a present. After this, he thought that an engine could be so constructed as to be applied to work his machinery for the moving of his paddles; and accordingly he employed an engineer to put his plans in execution; but they failed for want of being properly executed.—But to give you a more correct account of the manner Mr Fulton, the American engineer, came to the knowledge of steam-boats, that gentleman had occasion to write me about the plans of some machinery in this country, and begged the favour of me to call on Mr Miller of Dalswinton, and see how he had succeeded in his steam-boat plan; and if it answered the end, I was to send him a full drawing and description of it, along with my machinery. This led me to have a conversation with the late Mr Miller, and he gave me every information I could wish for at the time; I told him where, in my opinion, he had erred, or was misled by his engineer; and, at the same time, I told him that I intended to give Mr Fulton my opinion on steam-boats: the friends of Mr Miller must have amongst their papers Mr Fulton's letter to me, for I left it with Mr Miller. Two years thereafter I had a letter from Mr Fulton, letting me know that he had constructed a steam-boat from the different drawings of machinery I had sent him out, which was likely to answer the end, but required some improvement on it. This letter I sent to Mr Miller, for his information, which must also be among his papers. This letter led me to think of the absurdity of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> my opinion to other countries, and not putting it in practice myself in my own country; and, from these considerations, I was roused to set on foot a steam-boat, for which I made a number of different models, before I was satisfied. When I was convinced that they would answer the end, I contracted with Messrs John Wood and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a>, ship-builders in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PORT_GLASGOW">Port-Glasgow</a>, to build me a steam-vessel, according to my plans, 40 feet <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEEL">keel</a>, and 10 feet 6 inches beam, which I fitted up with an engine and paddles, and called her the Comet, because she was built and finished the same year that a comet appeared in the north-west part of Scotland. This vessel is the first steam-boat built in Europe that answered the end, and is at this present time upon the best and simplest method of any of them; for a person sitting in the cabin will hardly hear the engine at work. She plies on the Frith of Forth, betwixt the east end of the Great Canal and Newhaven, near Leith. The distance by water is 27 miles, which she performs, in ordinary <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, in 3½ hours up, and the same down. There were many attempts to make steam-boats in this country... before this one, but none of them ever answered the end; and even three years after the Comet was set a sailing, there was a number of our first rate engineers joined together, and obtained a patent for what they conceived a new discovery on the paddles for impelling the vessel forward. They were disappointed in their plan, and had to return to the mode of the Comet. The first American steam-boat which completely succeeded was launched at New York on the 3d October 1807 (five years before the construction of the Comet at Port-Glasgow), and soon after pried between that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALBANY">Albany</a>, a distance of 160 miles. In Britain, steam-vessels were first brought into use in 1812 upon the Clyde. They were built at Port-Glasgow, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GREENOCK">Greenock</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUMBARTON">Dumbarton</a>, where the art of ship-building had for many years been conducted by carpenters eminent in their profession. When launched, they were towed at a very trifling expense up the Clyde to Glasgow, situated in the midst of inexhaustible mines of coal and iron, and where the number of skilful practical engineers and artificers rendered the construction of the engines and machinery easy, and the prices moderate. The early experiments were, of course, made upon a small scale. The first steam-boat actually put to use there was the Comet (40 feet keel, 10½ feet beam, 4 wheels, 4 shovel-shaped paddles on each, with a cistern of fresh water to feed the boiler), built, as already mentioned, by Mr Henry Bell. She had an engine of only three horses' power, being intended merely for passengers; who, till then, had no other means of conveyance on the river than small row boats, either quite open, or supplied with only an awning to secure them from the weather. Small as this engine was, it rendered the passage certain in one tide; the vessel being able to make head-way even against the wind, and in rough weather. The success of the first experiment soon excited competition; and a larger vessel, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> (58 feet on deck, 11 feet beam, with an engine of 8 horses power), was completed in March 1813, and for a time proved very profitable to the proprietors. The third boat, the Clyde, which began plying in July of the same year, was still larger in her dimensions; being 70 feet keel, 75 feet on deck, 13 feet beam, with an engine of 14 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> power. At present there are about thirty-five steam-vessels on the Frith of Clyde, some of which sail from Glasgow almost every hour, or half-hour, during daylight, to the various ports on the river, and the lochs communicating with it; as Dumbarton, Helensburgh, Loch-Long, Rothsay, Loch-Fine, and Campbellton, on the right bank, and Port-Glasgow, Greenock, Gourock, Innerkip, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGS">Largs</a>, Milport, Ardrossan, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AYR">Ayr</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRVINE">Irvine</a>, Girvan, Stranraer, &c., on the left bank. Many of them occasionally visit Islay, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULL">Mull</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAFFA">Staffa</a>, Icolmkill, and adjacent <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, during the summer months; and also <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDONDERRY">Londonderry</a>, Coleraine, and other ports of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. Several vessels of larger dimensions, are employed as regular packets to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELFAST">Belfast</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">Man</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LIVERPOOL">Liverpool</a>, &c., and thus a constant <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> between the united kingdoms is maintained. Since 1821, two steam-vessels have regularly sailed from Leith to Aberdeen, calling at several of the intermediate ports. Five or six steam luggage-boats are constantly employed as lighters and draggers of other boats, for the speedy conveyance of goods from Glasgow to the ports of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a>, and occasionally towing large vessels in or out of harbour. The annual voyages of each of these 35 vessels may be averaged at 10,000 English miles; consequently, the whole sail 350,000 miles yearly, or nearly 14 times the circumference of our globe. The success of steam-vessels at Glasgow soon excited attention in other <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, and several of the Clyde vessels were purchased as models. It is worthy of mention, that shortly after the time of their appearance on the Clyde, Mr Lawrence of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a> established a steam-boat on the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a>, and having carried her to ply on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, the Company of Watermen made such opposition to this innovation, that he was obliged to take her back. Now, however, not only are all the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> navigable rivers in Britain thus navigated, but steam-vessels ply regularly from London to Aberdeen, sometimes passing the Pentland Frith. On the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLYHEAD">Holyhead</a> station, to carry mails between England and Ireland, there are three steam-vessels employed, viz. the Royal Sovereign, 210 tons; two 40-horse engines; the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METEOR">Meteor</a>, 190 tons, two 30-horse engines; and the Ivanhoe, 165 tons, one 56-horse engine. They have answered the purpose much better than sailing vessels; as a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of which, during the last year the latter were employed, exactly 100 Irish mails arrived in London late; while, during the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> months after the steam-boats were first established, only 22 arrived late; and that winter happened to be extremely boisterous. These boats use sails occasionally, and go to sea when sailing vessels dare not leave port. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> passage of the Royal Sovereign, from Houth to Holyhead, is six hours, fifty-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> minutes; from Holyhead to Houth seven hours, thirty-six minutes. Of the Meteor, from Houth to Holyhead, seven hours, four minutes, and back, eight hours, thirteen minutes. The average passage is half the time, in which the average passage of sailing vessels used to perform the voyage. The shortest passage was from Houth to Holyhead, five hours, thirty minutes; which, the distance being about 73 miles, is nearly 12 miles an hour. It is difficult to say what is the maximum speed of steam-vessels. Several of those between London and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARGATE">Margate</a> make the voyage in seven hours and a half, a distance of 84 miles. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">Hero</a> made the voyage, wind and tide in her favour, in six hours, sixteen minutes. The Eclipse, from Belfast to Greenock, 120 or 130 miles, has been known to come in nine hours; and, on one occasion, having about 3000 square feet of canvas set, besides the engine at work, she came from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AILSA">Ailsa</a> to Greenock at the rate of 9 miles. The Henry Bell, a new steam-trader between Glasgow and Liverpool, has delivered goods at various warehouses in Glasgow, several hours before the invoices, or advice of the shipment, had arrived in course of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST">post</a>. The New York steam-vessels run up Steam-boats frequently ply between London and Dieppe, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROUEN">Rouen</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAVRE">Havre</a> de <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">Grace</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CADIZ">Cadiz</a>, Corunna, Alicante, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIGO">Vigo</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a>, and other ports of France, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>. One was lately established between <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEGHORN">Leghorn</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>; but soon abandoned, owing to the oppression of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-QUARANTINE">quarantine</a> laws, and the rapacity of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the Two Sicilies. Another steam-vessel was launched by an American gentleman on the Lake of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>; but, being a very bad sailer, it is about to be replaced by another. Every season they are becoming more numerous, and adventurous in sailing to greater distances and through heavier seas; such as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">Bay</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISCAY">Biscay</a>, the Mediterranean, the Baltic, the Gulfs of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINLAND">Finland</a>, Bothnia, &c. A steam-packet, carrying the mail, now sails between <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KIEL">Kiel</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLSTEIN">Holstein</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COPENHAGEN">Copenhagen</a>. In the Adriatic, the Carolina goes every <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> day from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRIESTE">Trieste</a>, and the Bridano to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PAVIA">Pavia</a>; the latter voyage being usually accomplished in 37 hours. The Royal George steam-packet makes her passage from <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTSMOUTH">Portsmouth</a> to Corunna in from 60 to 64 hours; a distance of between 400 and 500 miles. Having thus endeavoured to give a sketch of the origin and progress of steam-navigation, we shall now proceed to describe the form and parts of a steam-boat (suppose of 100 tons), and to some other details, calculated to furnish a more particular view of the present state of steam-navigation in Britain and other countries. Fig. 1, Plate CXVII., is an elevation; fig. 2, a longitudinal <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECTION">section</a>; fig. 3, a ground plan; fig. 4, a transverse section. The same letters refer alike to the respective parts of each figure: A, the two boilers, with their two manhole doors, one to each; B, the chimney; C, the steam <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a>; DD, the cylinders of the two engines; EE, the two air pumps; F, the side <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEVER">lever</a>; one on each side of each engine; GG, the crank of the paddle-wheel shaft; H, the rod that works the steam valves or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> gear, moved backward and forward by an eccentric wheel on the shaft; I, the nozzles; K, pillars of the framing; LL, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> where the fireman stands to put coals into the furnace; MM, place where the coals are stowed away; NN, the paddle-wheels and covers; O, ladies' parlour; P, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> cabin; Q, second cabin; having each a raised <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANTERN">lantern</a> or sky-<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, besides the lateral windows of P and Q; R, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a>'s room; S, breakfasting-room; TT, refreshment rooms for the second cabin passengers; U, small boat ready to be let down on an emergency; V, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDDER">rudder</a>; WW, seamen's beds; XX, space for lumber or spare fuel. The fireman stands in the space LL; an iron trap-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LADDER">ladder</a> leads down to it from the deck, flush with which are two <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> gratings for the admission of fresh air to himself and the fire; his coals are built up behind him, and he brings down only a few lumps at a time, which he breaks into small pieces as required. The chimney B is a series of sheet-iron cylinders rivetted at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a>, and slipt the one over the other. Each boiler has a flue within, making various convolutions under the surface of the water; through which the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>, until they enter the chimney. These wheels being ponderous, acquire sufficient momentum to turn the crank, and supersede the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of a fly. The air-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PUMP">pump</a>, feed-pump, and occasional <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> water-pump, are wrought by rods from FF, the side horizontal levers. To prevent the waste steam of the boilers from annoying the passengers, a pipe conveys it into the chimney. Besides this, a waste steam <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VALVE">valve</a> is within reach of the engine-man, who loads and unloads it as he finds necessary. It is a curious fact, that a great flow of steam into the chimney prevents <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> smoke from issuing from it, which otherwise would. The paddle-wheels are firmly wedged on their shaft, and whatever pressure they exert against the water causes an equal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REACTION">reaction</a> on the vessel, which is thus impelled either forwards or backwards according to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of circumvolution. The principal cabin is painted, and otherwise tastefully fitted up, and furnished with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STOVE">stove</a>, the chimney of which rises up through the deck. The second cabin occupies the fore-end of the vessel, and is also completely furnished, less elegantly. Small steam-boats from 30 tons upwards are generally laid out much in the same way, only varying according to the nature of their employment. When intended for sea voyages, a great part of the internal space is allotted for sleeping births. Plate CXVI. exhibits a sketch of one of the Clyde vessels, the City of Glasgow, of 300 tons. | 2 | 80 | | 1822 | Towart Castle | 120 | 2 | 50 | | 1818 | Trusty | 88 | 1 | 10 | The Soho, the largest vessel in this list, indeed the largest steam-boat yet built in Europe, was launched in July 1823, intended to ply between Leith and London, a distance of about 460 miles. She is impelled by two engines of 60 horse power each; her length of deck is 163 feet; breadth 27; depth of hold 16 feet, 10 inches; burden 510 tons. Her accommodations are extensive, having space for 112 beds. The ladies' cabin is eight feet high. The Soho is, however, of somewhat smaller dimensions than the American steam-boat, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">Chancellor</a> Livingston, plying on the Hudson river between New York and Albany, constructed by Mr Fulton. The following are some particulars respecting this vessel. Her keel is 154 feet long; deck 165; broad; burden 320 tons; draft of water about seven feet three inches; principal cabin 54 feet long, 7 high; ladies' cabin, above the other, 36 long, with closets; forward cabin 30 long, 7 high. Permanent sleeping-births, in principal cabin, 38; in ladies' cabin, 24; in fore cabin, 56; in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>'s cabin on deck, 2; engineers' and pilots', 2; forecastle, 6; fire-men, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COOKS">cooks</a>, &c., 6; total, 135. Her engine is of 75 horse power; diameter of cylinder 40 inches, length five feet; piston rod, 8½ feet; stroke, five feet; boiler, 28 feet long, 12 broad, with two funnels; paddle-wheels, 17 feet diameter; paddle-boards five feet, ten inches long, with two fly-wheels, each 14 feet diameter, connected by pinions to the crank wheel. The machinery rises 4½ feet above the deck. Average rate of sailing eight and one-half to eight and three-fourths miles an hour. With a strong wind and tide in her favour, she has made twelve; but with a strong wind and tide against her, not more than six miles per hour. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> employed on board are—13 mariners, 11 cooks, waiters, stewards, &c.;—in all 24. This vessel, however, is still much surpassed in size by the Lady Sherbrooke, of 787 tons, and 60 horse power; being the largest of eight which ply on the river St Lawrence. This gives 13 tons for each horse power, whereas in the Soho, the same burthen has three times as much action applied to it. The American steam-vessels, though fast sailers, are thus impelled by comparatively smaller engines than those built in this country. It appears from the Report of the Select Committee of the House of Representatives, for session 1817, that there were then 17 large steam-boats in constant employment on the American rivers, besides ferry-boats. But since that time they have increased so rapidly, that there are now (1823) about 300. The following are the names of 35 vessels, and their tonnage, plying on the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MISSISSIPPI">Mississippi</a> and its tributary rivers alone, viz. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALABAMA">Alabama</a>, 200 tons; Buffalo, 300; <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CEDAR">Cedar</a> Branch, 250; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CINCINNATI">Cincinnati</a>, 120; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">Constitution</a>, 75; Eagle, 70; Etna, 390; <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">Exchange</a>, 200; Experiment, 40; Frankfort, 320; General Jackson, 200; General Pike, 250; Governor Shelby, 120; Harnot, 40; Hecla, 70; Henderson, 85; Independence, 300; James Monroe, 90; James Ross, 320; Johnston, 80; <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KENTUCKY">Kentucky</a>, 80; <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUISIANA">Louisiana</a>, 54; Madison, 200; Maysville, 150; <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol15.html#article-NAPOLEON">Napoleon</a>, 332; Ohio, 443; Paragon, 400; Rifleman, 250; Rising States, 150; St <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a>, 220; <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TAMERLANE">Tamerlane</a>, 320; Vesta, 100; <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VESUVIUS">Vesuvius</a>, 390; Volcano, 250; Washington, 400;—in all 7259 tons. Belonging to some of the States, there are steam frigates and ships of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> carrying guns, some of them 100-pounders. These vessels are 13 feet thick in the sides, of alternate layers of oak and cork; are so constructed, that they can eject boiling water on their enemies; and there are <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of cutlasses and pikes which project from their sides, and draw back again every fifteen seconds. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVANNAH">Savannah</a>, of 350 tons, was the first steam-vessel that crossed the Atlantic. She arrived at Liverpool 20th June 1819, in 21 days from land to land; 18 of which her engine was going; her daily consumption of coal was about 10 tons, so that she must have had at least 200 on board, leaving 150 for the weight of engine and cargo. Her paddles were occasionally taken off, when she sailed by wind and the whole of the paddle-wheels were capable of being taken to pieces and shipped, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of bad weather. As the distance is not much short of 4000 miles, she must have averaged nearly 200 per day. By far the greatest number of steam-vessels use low pressure engines. A larger proportion of American vessels have high pressure engines than in this country. High pressure engines are wrought with steam of a great variety of strengths, from 30 to 160 lbs. per square inch. Some engineers assert, that it is capable of being used at 1000 lbs. The steam is not condensed, but, after having acted on the piston, is allowed to blow off into the air. The diameter of their steam cylinders may be made of any size proportioned to the strength of the steam used. Thus, when it is 160 lbs., the area of the cylinder may be only a sixteenth part of the area of one using steam of 10 lbs.; consequently, a five inch cylinder wrought with such strong steam will be equal in power to a 20 inch cylinder wrought with such weak steam. High pressure engines require neither air-pump, conductor, nor the parts therewith connected; and as the volume of steam used is in proportion, their boilers may consequently be much smaller. Hence these engines occupy less room and tonnage, and require somewhat less fuel; but the risk of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXPLOSION">explosion</a> is considerable. Were it otherwise, they would be very valuable at sea, because their power can be increased on emergencies, by merely increasing the fire, whereas the power of condensing engines is much more circumscribed, and confined to their original construction. The free effective power of large

STONE-MASONRY

Pages 617-623

\[ \frac{\sqrt{2R(f-hw)}}{h^3w^2} + \left( \frac{3\<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAN">tan</a> c}{2} \<a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>)^2 \] and as \( c = 10^\circ \), tan. \[ c = 18^\circ \text{ hence } \frac{3\tan c}{2} = 27^\circ \text{ and its <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> } = 0.729. \] Also \( f = 5000 \) and \( w = 100 \), consequently, \[ d = \frac{h^2}{50-h} \left( -27 + \sqrt{4.8 - 0.0131} \right); \text{ and making } h \text{ successively } 10, 20, \text{ &c. feet, the numbers obtained <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be the same within one-tenth of a foot, as those in the following <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">Table</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> 5.} \] **Table V.—A Table of the Thicknesses for Retaining Walls, Revetments, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOCK">Dock</a>-walls, &c.** | Height of Wall | Thickness of Rectangular Walls to support. | |---------------|------------------------------------------| | | <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">Water</a> | Dry Sand | Moist Sand | | 10 feet | 4.0 feet | 2.7 feet | 3.1 feet | | 20 feet | 12.9 feet | 8.6 feet | 9.8 feet | | 30 feet | 29.2 feet | 19.4 feet | 22.2 feet | | 40 feet | 62.5 feet | 41.7 feet | 47.5 feet | Our <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> informs us that the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> walls must be of a superior strength; indeed, we know that when its consolidation takes <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, under considerable pressure, it is of much greater strength. According to what <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a> of the pressure the strength increases, we have not experiments to determine, and we therefore point out the circumstance to the notice of experimental inquirers. 57. The preceding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a> being confined to the conditions under which the equilibrium could not be disturbed by the pressure, it would be quite unnecessary to consider the phenomena of actual fracture, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it were not for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> which even these phenomena afford of the defects of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of constructing these walls. The back of the wall is generally formed of inferior materials, hence the technical <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> *<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> mortar* and *backing mortar*; but, even with inferior mortar, the workmanship is so carelessly done, towards the back of the wall, that when it fractures a portion is left behind. A moment's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the pressure (see fig. 9) must show the importance of using good mortar, and making good bond at the back of the wall; if any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> be neglected it ought to be the middle, which is of least importance, provided the wall be well bound together by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> bond <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. The strength of a wall to sustain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> will always be greatly increased by any roughness <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> irregularity in the back of the wall, such as projecting stones or bricks; in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> it is easy to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> much stability by this means. The friction against a smooth wall must add much to its strength; we have not thought it necessary to include its effect in our calculations; but intend that, with counterforts, it should be considered as a set-off against accidental pressures, &c.* Counterforts are usually placed at about three times the thickness of the wall apart, and are made of the same width as the thickness of the wall. In fig. 11 is shown a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> a wall to sustain the pressure of earth according to the form proposed by Vitruvius, Lib. VI. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAP">Cap</a>. IX. And fig. 12 is a plan from Perrault's Notes.* Various other plans have been proposed, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of which <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> Pasley has collected in his Course of Fortification; but most of them have little to recommend them. It seems desirable that every kind of curved work should be avoided; and perhaps that plan which unites the most economy with the greatest stability is shown by figs. 13 and 14, Plate CXIX. The spaces A, A, A, are proposed to be filled with gravel or fragments of stone; the whole of the stone-work to be well bonded; and the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> and back wall of that thickness which is best suited for bond, in the kind of material to be employed. **Bond of Walls and Cramps.** 58. It is not sufficient to depend entirely upon the cementing power of mortar in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of walls; the stones themselves should also be bound together by their disposition. The art of disposing stones for this purpose is called bonding. Part of the longest stones should be employed to bind the wall in length, and the other part to bind it crossways; the former are called stretchers, the latter headers. Figs. 15, 16, 17, 18, and 19, show various methods of bonding walls; these are selected from Greek and Roman examples. The courses of stone are often <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>, as in fig. 17; and in some works we find both irregular courses and broken ones; that is, such as are intercepted by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> blocks of stone. Broken courses should be avoided, because they occasion irregular settlements. The bond of walls requires to be most carefully attended to in the construction of piers, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>, and, in general, every part exposed to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> strain. On this subject it also may be remarked, that crossing the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> properly is a more effectual means of bonding a wall than that of employing very <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> stones, unless they be very strong ones. For if a stone exceed about three times its thickness in --- * See Philosophical <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGAZINE">Magazine</a>, Vol. LI. p. 401, where the effect of such friction is considered. length, it cannot be so equally bedded but that it is liable to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> from unequal pressure; and the fracture <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> takes place opposite to a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a>, and therefore destroys the bond of the wall. This defective mode of construction we have often had occasion to notice. In works of hewn stone destined to support great pressure, or to bear the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of a heavy <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, it is necessary that the stones should be of great bulk, and connected in the firmest manner. Sometimes this is effected by forming the stones so as to lock them together. The Eddystone and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELL">Bell</a>-Rock <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">Light</a>-Houses are bound together at the base on this principle. (See Bell-Rock in this Supplement.) Where less strength is required, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> cramps are used, and sometimes pieces of hard stone are dovetailed into the adjoining blocks. We think cramps of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a>-iron might be employed with much advantage in all these <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>. 59. The proper <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of mortar to be employed in stone-work is another point to which it will be useful to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> the mason's attention. A stone cannot be very firmly bedded upon a very thin layer of mortar; and if the stone be of an absorbent <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, the mortar will dry too rapidly to acquire any tolerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> (Vitruvius, Lib. II. Cap. VIII.), however well it may have been prepared. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, if the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> of mortar be thicker than is necessary to bed the stone firmly, the work will be a long <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in settling, and will never be perfectly stable. When the internal part of a wall is built with fragments of stone, they should be closely packed together, so as to require as little mortar as possible. Walls are often bulged by the hydrostatic pressure of mortar, when it is too plentifully thrown into the interior, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> the labour of filling the spaces with stones. The walls of houses are frequently built with hewn stone on the outside, and rubble stone on the inside. The settlement of these two kinds of stone-work during the setting of the mortar are so different, that the walls often separate; or where this separation is prevented by bond stones, the wall bulges outwards, and bears unequally on its base. These evils are best prevented by using as little mortar as possible in the joints of the interior part of the wall, and not raising the wall to a great height at one time. Foundations. 60. The nature of the materials employed in masonry having been considered, and also the methods of uniting them, we have, in the next place, to turn our attention to the nature of those foundations on which it is commonly required to raise permanent structures of such heavy <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. In founding on dry ground, the nature of the foundation is ascertained without much difficulty. When it is found to be of firm hard rock, that will bear the action of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, no particular precautions are necessary; but in all other cases it is desirable to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> the trenches to such a depth as will prevent them from being affected by the change of seasons. <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FROST">Frost</a>, we believe, seldom penetrates so low as two feet below the surface (see <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">Climate</a> in this Supplement, Vol. III. p. 179); but in clayey ground, the effect of shrinkage, by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, is often sensible at four feet below the surface; for to that depth the cracks in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> often extend. Consequently, in clay, the depth of the foundations should never be less than four feet, and in heavy buildings, deeper in proportion to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> they are to support. In large works it is also necessary to examine the matter, inclination, and thickness of the under <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STRATA">strata</a>, particularly when the upper stratum is of inconsiderable thickness. For this purpose, the older writers on <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, with much propriety, recommend that a well should be dug near the place, to ascertain these <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a>. A knowledge of the inclination and nature of the strata will also be of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in planning <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAINS">drains</a>, a subject of no small importance to the durability and comfort of a mansion. In soft ground the base of the wall should be made wide, and it may be reduced to the proper thickness by small off-sets or steps, as in fig. 20. On clay or dry sand the breadth at the bottom may be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the thickness of the wall. On <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> gravel or chalk the breadth may be to the thickness as 3 is to 2. If the ground be soft and wet, with a firm bottom within the reach of piles, then piles may be employed with advantage; but they are very likely to rot, in a few years, where the ground is not wet; and, therefore, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of soft ground, not sufficiently wet to preserve piles from decay, we should recommend, in preference, a very wide base or footing, well bonded together, with bars of cast-iron, disposed so that one part could not <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> without causing the adjoining ones to go <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> at the same time; and the whole of the base should, for greater strength, be built in the best water cement. It is a practice with some architects to employ <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> beams and planking in such cases, and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of its decay, in many instances it has been necessary to replace the timber with stone and brick at an enormous expense. It should be a maxim in construction, never to employ timber in a permanent structure where it is not either absolutely wet or perfectly dry. When ground is very soft and wet, and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> stratum is beyond the reach of piles, a solid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> may be formed to erect the superstructure upon; by means of a grating of timber, planked over. The brick or stone work which is built upon the planking should be joined with a water cement. When such ground is not absolutely wet, instead of planking we would employ a connected grating of cast-iron, with stone or brick work built in water mortar. In all these cases the greatest difficulty consists in preventing irregular settlements; and hence the advantage of employing wood or iron to bind the base together, and render it, as far as possible, an inflexible and solid mass. In all edifices which press perpendicularly on their foundations, the centre of pressure should coincide, as nearly as may be, with the centre of gravity of the surface which sustains it. In wharf walls, ter- <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> walls, abutments and piers of bridges, and the like, the resultant of the pressures should <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> in the centre of gravity of the surface which supports it. Foundations are most difficult to manage where the ground is irregular, particularly for highly finished buildings, which are so much disfigured by a small settlement. In such cases we would endeavour to procure an inflexible base by means of cast-iron beams. It is a good plan to form <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTER">counter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> under the openings, provided these arches be carefully built; but where they are not well built, they yield so much as to be no better than common walling. Excavating and removing the earth from foundations is frequently a considerable part of the expense of large works; hence the peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of management which will economize this branch of labour, has become an interesting subject of investigation.
