The others were made by Rondelet. (Traité de l'Art de Bâtir, Tome I. and Tome III.) We have selected those which will be most useful, with others of a more interesting and curious nature; such are Rondelet's experiments on the effect of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> mortar, the strength and density of ancient mortar, and the resistance of stones used in ancient and modern structures. 46. It was observed by Rondelet, in the course of his very numerous experiments, that it was not the heaviest stones which offered the greatest degree of resistance to compression, but those of a fine even grain and close texture, with a deep colour; that of granites, the most compact and perfectly crystallized are the strongest (L'Art de Bâtir, I. 213, 215); and when all other qualities were the same, it appears that the strength was in proportion to some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a> of the specific gravity. The writers who have contributed to our experimental knowledge of the strength of stones are not numerous; the chief are Emerson, in his Mechanics, 4th Ed. p. 115; Gauthey, in his Memoire sur la <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> que peuvent porter les Pierres en Rozier's Journal de Physique, Tome IV. 1774, and in his Construction des Ponts, Tome I. p. 267; Coulob, Mémoires présentés à l'Académie, 1773; Rondelet, in his Traité de l'Art de Bâtir, Tome I. et III. The latter volume contains the experiments made by Perronet and Soufflot. Rennie, Philosophical Transactions for 1818, or Philosophical <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGAZINE">Magazine</a>, Vol. LIII.; Tredgold, Philosophical Magazine, Vol. LVI., p. 290. 47. The last column in each of the three tables of stone experiments shows the greatest load that we suppose should be borne by a superficial foot of the different kinds of stone contained in those tables; we now propose to give the results of some calculations respecting the extent to which stone has been loaded in practice. The foreign ones are reduced to our own weights and measures, and the whole stated in round numbers. The pillars of the Gothic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Allsaints at Angers, of the stone, No. 24, Table III. support on each superficial foot a pressure of 86,000 lbs.* The pillars of the dome of the Pantheon at Paris, the lower part of which are of Bagneux stone (No. 25, Table III.), support on each superficial foot 60,000 lbs.† The pillar in the centre of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">Chapter</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELGIN">Elgin</a>, which is of red sandstone, supports on each superficial foot 40,000 lbs.‡ The piers which support the dome of St Paul's, in London, sustain a pressure on each superficial foot of 39,000 lbs.† The piers which support the dome of St <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>'s at Rome, sustain a pressure on each superficial foot of 33,000 lbs.† The pressure on the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEY">key</a>-stone (No. 23, Table III.) of the Bridge of Neuilly has been estimated for each superficial foot at 18,000 lbs.§ On these examples we have to remark, that the calculators of them have considered the pressures to be uniformly distributed over the pressed surface; this can only be true when the direction of the resultant of the straining force coincides with the axis of the pier or pillar; besides, stones cannot be wrought absolutely level, nor bedded in perfect contact. From these circumstances, the strength of piers, columns, pillars, and arch-stones, should be estimated by equation (12), and when the line of direction falls within the pier, always making \( y = \frac{1}{2} \) half the least <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIMENSION">dimension</a> of the section, an allowance which will include the effect of the greatest possible inequality of action. We shall, in that case, have \( \frac{fbd^2}{d + 6d} = \frac{fbd}{4} = W. \) (17.) If the pressure on the Bagneux stone in the piers of the dome of the Pantheon at Paris be estimated by this formula, it will be found that it is sufficient to split the stones, and this has actually happened. 48. The chief elements of the theory of arches Principles of have already been given in the Article BRIDGE Arches, Domes, &c. (Sect. II.) in this Supplement, to which we refer the reader, at the same time expressing a hope that the excellent article referred to will be useful in correcting some absurd notions respecting catenarian and other curves, which are too <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> entertained. The conical support of the lanterna of St Paul's is a fine example of an appropriate form, while the catenarian dome of the French Pantheon exemplifies a scientific blunder of the first magnitude. The principles of domes, of groins, and of vaulting of every kind, are the same as those of arches, excepting that each kind has its peculiar manner of distributing the load on the different parts. See Prop. M and N, Art. BRIDGE. Of the Pressure of Earth, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">Fluids</a>, &c. against Walls. 49. When a high <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of earth, or a fluid, is to be sustained by a wall, as it is often necessary to do in forming bridges, locks, quays, reservoirs, docks, and Walls. --- * Gauthey, Rozier's Journal de Physique, Tom. Traité l'Art de Bâtir, II. 308. military works, the construction is very expensive; however economical the means employed may be; hence it is desirable to devote some space to an object of which the importance is manifest. Let EC, Plate CXVIII., fig. 8, be the line according to which the earth would separate, if the wall were to yield in a small degree; then AEC will represent the section of the prism of earth, the pressure of which causes the wall to yield. Put W = the weight of the prism AEC, when its length is unity. R = the resistance of the wall, when its length is unity. a = the angle ECA, which the plane of fracture makes with a vertical line. c = the angle ACA, which the back of the wall makes with a vertical line. F = the friction of the earth when the pressure is unity. h = the vertical height of the wall AC in feet. and S = the weight of a cubic foot of earth, water, or other matter to be supported. If g be the centre of gravity of the prism of earth, the triangles rpg, CgE, being similar, the effort of the prism to slide, in the direction EC, reduced for the friction, will be \[ \frac{W(1-F\<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAN">tan</a> a)}{\sec a} \] (18.) This effort is to be opposed by the resistance of the wall, which let us suppose to be collected at c, the centre of pressure, and, reducing it to the direction CE, the effect of friction being allowed for, it becomes \[ \frac{R(F+\tan a)}{\sec a} \] (19.) Hence, in the case of equilibrium, \[ \frac{W(1-F\tan a)}{\sec a} = \frac{R(F+\tan a)}{\sec a}; \] Or, \( R = W\left(\frac{1-F\tan a}{F+\tan a}\right) \) (20.) 50. But, in the case now considered, the radius being unity, \( W = \frac{h^2S}{2}(\tan a - \tan c) \). Therefore, \[ R = \frac{h^2S}{2}\left[\frac{(\tan a - \tan c)(1-F\tan a)}{F+\tan a}\right]. \] (21.) 52. (25) when c=10°. | |--------------------|-----------------|----------------------------|-----------------------------|-------------------------------------| | Water | 0° | 62.5 lbs. | R=314/2 | R=314/2 | | Fine dry sand | 33° | 92 | R=138/4 | R=138/4 | | Do. moist | | 119 | R=1785/4 | R=64/2 | | <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTZ">Quartz</a> sand (dry) | 35° | 102 | R=1377/4 | R=464/2 | In sand, clay, and earthy bodies, the natural slopes should be taken when the material is dry, and the clay and earth pulverised. When any of these bodies are in a moist state, the parts cohere, and the angle of repose is greater, though the friction be actually less. The preceding Table shows that the pressure of water is greater than that of any of the other kinds of matter, and from the nature of fluids it is evident, that if water be suffered to collect behind a retaining wall, calculated to sustain common earth only, it will most likely be overturned. Such accidents may be prevented by making proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAINS">drains</a>. 53. The preceding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a> will apply, without sensible <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a>, to the curved walls which have lately become fashionable. Fig. 10 is a section of one of these walls, as executed from a design by Rennie. The vertical height, AB, 21 feet; the wall of uniform thickness, with counterforts 15 feet apart; and the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of the walls described by a 69 feet radius, with the centre in the horizontal line DA produced. The wall is built of brick, and the uniform part is 4½ feet thick. The radius is usually thrice the vertical height of the wall; when this proportion is adhered to, the angle c will be ten degrees, for which the value of R is calculated in the Table. Resistance of Walls. 54. In the first place, we propose to investigate the resistance a wall offers to being overturned; and, in so doing, it appears desirable that the resistance of the mortar in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> should be considered one of the elements of the strength of the wall. Good mortar adds much to the firmness of walls, and still more to their durability; and, all things considered, its first cost is less than that of bad; besides, the resistance of mortar to compression must be considered, for, in practice, we have no perfectly hard arrises to fulfil the conditions of common mechanical hypotheses. Put A = the area of the wall. w = the weight of a cubic foot of masonry. y = the horizontal distance, ga, between the vertical passing through the centre of gravity of the wall, and the point where the axis cuts the plane of fracture, the same notation being applied to the other quantities as in the foregoing equations. Let G, fig. 9, be the centre of gravity of the wall; and on the vertical GG set off gL, the height of the centre of pressure: also, let IK represent A × w = the weight of the wall, and HI the force R of the earth. Then, completing the parallelogram, EI will represent the direction and intensity of the straining force; consequently, \( \frac{R}{Aw} = \tan a \) (28.) Which determines its direction, and its intensity is \[ W = \frac{Aw}{\cos a} \] (29.) But, we have found, equa. (10), \[ W = \frac{fbd^2}{d \cos a + 6l \sin a + 6y \cos a} \]; and as W = \[ Aw \left( \text{Equa. (29.)} \right) \tan a = \frac{R}{Aw}; \text{Equa. (28)}; l = \frac{h}{2}, \text{art. 51;} \text{and } b = \text{unity; the equation reduces to} \] \[ f'd^2 - Adz = 6Aw = 2Rh. \] (30.) If the section of the wall be a parallelogram, then A = hd, and \( \frac{h}{2} \tan c = y \); these values of A and y being substituted in Equa. (30), it becomes \( -whd^2 + f'd^2 + 3h^2wd \tan c = 2Rh. \) (31.) Or, \( d = \frac{h^2w}{f-hw} \left( \frac{-3 \tan c}{2} + \sqrt{\frac{2R(f-hw)}{h^2w}} \right) \) \[ + \frac{9 \tan c}{4}. \] (32.) When the section of the wall is a rectangle y = 0, therefore Equa. (31) reduces to \[ d = \sqrt{\frac{2Rh}{f-hw}} \] (33.) This last Equation is also correct for a wall of which the back is vertical, and the front sloping. We suppress the investigation, to afford the young student an opportunity of proving that the diminution of weight is exactly counterbalanced by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> of the distance of the centre of gravity from the axis. The tendency of a wall to slide forward may be easily prevented, by giving an inclination to the joints. 55. To illustrate these rules we shall give two examples, and in these show the construction of a table, which the reader may enlarge at his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. Example I. Let it be required to determine the thickness of a rectangular wall for supporting the front of a wharf 10 feet in height, the earth being a loose sand, and the wall to be built of brick. The weight of a cubic foot of brick-work may be estimated at 100 lbs., and the resistance of mortar being valued at 5000 lbs. per superficial foot, the experimental value being 7900 lbs., Table III. Experiment 42, and the difference an allowance for any irregularity in building, consequently, \( f = 5000; w = 100 \); and by Table IV. \( R = 13-8h^2 \); hence, Equa. (33), \( d = \sqrt{\frac{2Rh}{f-hw}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 13-8 \times h^2}{5000 - 100h}} \) \[ = \sqrt{\frac{h^2}{181 - 3-62h}}. \] When h = 10 feet, then the thickness of the wall \( d = 2-644 \) feet. If h be made successively 10, 20, 30, 40, &c. feet, the numbers under the head of dry sand in the following Table will be obtained, observing that they are only calculated to the nearest tenth of a foot. The proper thickness being found for supporting one kind of material, that for any other may be easily determined; as the thickness varies as the square root of R, Equa. (33). Let the thickness for dry sand be \( d \), then \( \sqrt{13-8}: \sqrt{31-25}: d: 1-5d \) the thickness for supporting water. \( \sqrt{13-8}: \sqrt{17-85}: d: 1-14d \) the thickness for supporting moist sand. In this manner, by means of Table IV. the thicknesses for other kinds are easily calculated. Example II. If a retaining wall be intended to support a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> and loose kind of earth, to be constructed of brick, and to be inclined 10 degrees from the vertical, the thickness being uniform; it is required to determine that thickness for any given height. By Equa. (32), \( d = \frac{h^2w}{f-hw} \left( \frac{-3 \tan c}{2} + \right. \)

TENNANT

Pages 711-714

a distinguished Chemist, born at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SELBY">Selby</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, 30th November 1761; was the only child of the Rev. Calvert Tennant, younger son of a respectable family in Wensley Dale, near <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHMOND">Richmond</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a> of Selby; his mother was <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> Daunt, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of a surgeon of that town. His father had been a fellow of St John’s <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, and began to teach his son Greek when he was only five years old. He had the misfortune to lose him four years after; and before he grew up, his mother also, while he was riding with her, was thrown from her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> and killed on the spot. He was sent, after his father’s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, to different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, at Scerton, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TADCASTER">Tadcaster</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEVERLEY">Beverley</a>; in these he was remembered as a boy retired in his manners, and somewhat melancholy, and indolent with respect to puerile amusements. He learned but little at school, and may be considered as in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> self-educated; having been fond, almost as a child, of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> books of science, and of amusing himself with little experiments which he found described in them; and while he was at school at Tadcaster, he took great delight in attending a course of Walker’s lectures on <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIMENTAL_PHILOSOPHY">experimental <a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> which were given there. At Beverley he was under the care of Dr G. Croft, who had made himself known to the public by some controversial writings; here he never entered much into the pursuits of his contemporaries, but profited by a good library belonging to the school; and among other books which he read with avidity was Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton’s Treatise on <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">Optics</a>. He had entertained a great desire to complete his chemical studies under the immediate instruction of Dr Priestley, who was then enjoying deserved reputation for his recent experimental discoveries; but Dr Priestley’s occupations did not permit him to undertake the task of directing his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, however agreeable it might have been to him to have assisted such a pupil. In the meantime he had not neglected his classics, but had acquired a sufficient knowledge of the learned languages to appreciate with correct <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> the beauties of the great writers of antiquity. Notwithstanding his admiration for Dr Priestley, he was an early convert to the antiphlogistic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>; which, with all its errors, was still a material step in the advancement of science. In 1781 he went to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, with the view of qualifying himself for the profession of physic, and he had the advantage of attending Dr <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a>'s lectures, which were then in great reputation. In October 1782, he entered as a pensioner of Christ's College, Cambridge, where he became intimately acquainted with the late Professor Harwood, who had been first a surgeon in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, but having lost, by the misconduct of an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGENT">agent</a>, the fortune that he had there acquired, submitted cheerfully to the toil of recommencing his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CAREER">career</a> as a physician, though already past the middle <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>: his talents for conversation were such as were extremely likely to captivate a young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of superior discernment; and he formed a friendship with Tennant which <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> uninterrupted throughout their lives. At Cambridge he studied a little of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, in the works of Newton, but much more of chemistry and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>: he already began to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> his inventive powers in an attempt to economize the consumption of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a>, which he did not make public until 20 years after, though he mentioned it at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to some of his friends. He also occupied himself incessantly in general, and especially in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> reading, though he was far from having the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of a student: but his rooms were always in confusion from the mixture of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HETEROGENEOUS">heterogeneous</a> materials that were accumulated in them. His residence at Cambridge was perhaps the happiest time of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; his spirits unrestrained, his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> unbroken, his feelings acute, and his conversation brilliant, though simple and unaffected. In the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> of 1784 he paid a visit to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, and to Scheele, whose acquaintance extremely delighted him, and most of all from the simplicity of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> that he employed in his researches. A year <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> two afterwards he went to France, and being taken ill at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, he was joined there by his friend Harwood, with whom he returned through <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>; at the time that the bigotted people of the Low Countries were in insurrection against a philosophical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESPOT">despot</a>, while Holland remained free and prosperous. He was particularly intimate with Dr Milner, the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">Master</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a>'s College, and was recommended by his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIGNATURE">signature</a>, together with those of Waring, Maskelyne, Jebb, and Watson, as a Fellow of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, into which he was admitted in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1785. He removed, together with his friend Harwood, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1786, from Christ's College to Emmanuel, and in 1788 he took a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of Bachelor of Physic. In 1791 he communicated to the Royal Society his very interesting discovery of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of obtaining carbon from the carbonic acid. Having observed that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a> did not decompose the phosphate of lime, he concluded that phosphorus ought to decompose the carbonate of lime, and the result fully justified his manner of reasoning. He paid a third visit to the Continent in 1792, intending to go on through France into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and arrived at Paris not <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> before the 10th of August; but he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> some indications of an impending convulsion, and was fortunate enough to quit Paris on the 9th. He visited Gibbon at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAUSANNE">Lausanne</a>, and was much interested in the sagacity that this eminent writer displayed in his conversation. He went on to Rome and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, where he was fully impressed with all the admiration that he had been taught to anticipate for the treasures of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> art possessed by those cities; and in his return through Germany, he was greatly amused by the mixture of knowledge and credulity that he observed among the studious of that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. At Paris he found everything enveloped in gloom and overwhelmed with terror, in 1793; his friend Lametherie was alarmed by the visit which he paid him, but he had the integrity to preserve for him entire some <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of considerable value, with which he had entrusted him. Upon his arrival in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, Mr Tennant took chambers in the Temple, and was in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of living much with some of his early acquaintance, who had adopted the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> as their profession; to his own he was in great measure indifferent, neither seeking to practise it, nor being well calculated to succeed greatly in it with the public, though he studied it with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, and took pains to make himself master of its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and its philosophy, being a particular admirer of Sydenham, when considered in relation to the age in which he lived. He took his degree of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a> of Physic in 1796, and in the same year he gave the Royal Society a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of carbonic acid afforded by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a>, which he measured by heating it with nitre, and obtaining a precipitate by the addition of muriate of lime; and he found that the diamond afforded no more carbonic acid than an equal <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of charcoal. A subsequent <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> contained the result of his observations on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of heated nitre on <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and platinum. The <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of travelling appeared to be his predominant <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>; he studied in his travels, not only the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and political history of the countries that he saw, but also their languages, and the philosophy of their etymologies. He observed, too, the peculiarities of their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>; and, in 1797, he determined, after visiting an agricultural friend in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a>, to devote his attention to practical farming as a serious pursuit. He purchased some allotments of unenclosed <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> in that neighbourhood, but he left the management of them chiefly to his friend, and made afterwards considerable additions to the property by further purchases. In 1798 or 1799, he bought a tract of newly enclosed land on the Mendip hills, near Cheddar, where he built a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and resided for some months every summer through the remainder of his life. These speculations, though their results were at first doubtful, yet succeeded remarkably well on the whole; more especially considering the benefit that his health derived from the travelling and the exercise that they rendered necessary: but they occupied too much of his attention, and of that time which might have been employed so much more to the advantage of the public, and to his own ultimate satisfaction. In 1799 he gave the Royal Society a paper on the magnesian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a>, or dolomite, which he considers as rather a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> than an accidental mixture; and the forms of the crystals, as they have been determined by later observers, together with the laws of definite proportions, have tended to confirm this conjecture: he found that grain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> scarcely germinate, and soon perishes, when sown in the neutral carbonate of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGNESIA">magnesia</a>. In 1802 he published his paper on <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMERY">emery</a>, which he showed to be a substance similar to the corundum or adamantine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAR">spar</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, and not an ore of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, as had been <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> supposed. In the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> he was making some experiments on crude <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLATINA">platina</a>, when he discovered in it a singular dark powder, which was left undissolved by the nitromuriatic acid, and which was also observed the next year by Messrs Descottis and Vauquelin. In 1804 Mr Tennant showed that the powder contained two new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, which he named <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRIDIUM">Iridium</a> and Osmium; and he received the Copleian medal from the Royal Society in November, as an acknowledgment of the merit of his various chemical discoveries. In 1805 and 1806 he paid two successive visits to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, by way of Scotland, one of them in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> with Browne the traveller, for whom he had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> esteem, and to whom he suggested the observation of the temperature of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> as a mode of determining the heights of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>; a method, however, which had been long before recommended by Achard and others. He became latterly more fond of general society than he had been in his earlier years, and he used to receive miscellaneous parties at his chambers, and to show them <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a>, and minerals, and novelties of various kinds. In 1812 he was persuaded to convert these mixed exhibitions into a more regular course of lectures, principally upon <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERALOGY">mineralogy</a>, calculated especially for the ladies of his acquaintance, and which highly delighted all his audience: "Their attention was perpetually kept alive by the spirit and variety with which every topic was discussed, by anecdotes and quotations happily introduced, by the ornaments of a powerful but chastised imagination, and, above all, by a peculiar vein of pleasantry, at once original and delicate, with which he could animate and embellish the most unpromising subjects;"—a circumstance which, though not of much immediate importance to the public, yet probably led him the more readily to accept the Professorship at Cambridge, and would thus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he had survived longer, have greatly extended the sphere of his utility. He delivered, in 1813, a lecture on mineralogy to the Geological Society, and gave them also an account of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a> of a volcanic substance from the <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIPARI_ISLANDS">Lipari <a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">Islands</a> containing the boracic acid, which has since been examined on the spot by Dr Holland. In the month of May he was elected Professor of Chemistry in the University of Cambridge, all opposition having been withdrawn before the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a>. The following <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> he gave his first and last course of lectures there. His introductory lecture still exists in manuscript, and is said to contain a masterly sketch of the history of the science. He communicated to the Royal Society, in 1814, a paper on the easiest mode of procuring potassium, and another on the economy of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> in distillation, proposing to heat a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> boiler by the condensation of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEAM">steam</a> of the first. In the spring and summer of this year he was occupied in searching for the origin of iodine, and he succeeded in detecting this substance in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-water, by the test of its tarnishing the surface of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> silver. One of the last services, that he rendered the Royal Society, was in the capacity of a member of a committee which was formed in order to investigate, at the request of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, the degree of danger that might attend the general introduction of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAS">gas</a> lights into the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>; he undertook, together with his friend Dr Wollaston, to make some experiments upon the inflammation of the gas, and they discovered conjointly the very important fact, that the gas contained in a small tube will not communicate the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>: a fact which, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of Sir Humphry Davy, has been rendered productive of consequences so important to the public safety; although Sir Humphry having been abroad at the time of this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a>, and the report of the committee not having been then published, he had to rediscover this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, and many more, in his most ingenious and successful researches. It was early in the month of September that Mr Tennant went for the last time to France, being impatient to observe the changes that an eventful <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> of twenty years had produced in that highly interesting country. He was greatly delighted with Lyons and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARSEILLES">Marseilles</a>, and, returning to Paris in November, he lingered there till February 1815; on the 15th of that month he arrived at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-CALAIS">Calais</a>; the 20th he went to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOULOGNE">Boulogne</a> with Baron Bulow, in order to embark there; they did embark on the 22d, but were forced back by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, and meant to try again in the evening; in the meantime, they took horses and went to see Bonaparte's Pillar, about a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> off, and going off the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> on their return, to look at a small fort, of which the drawbridge wanted a bolt, they were both thrown, with their horses, into the ditch. Bulow was only stunned, but Tennant's skull was so severely fractured, that he died an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> after. His papers published in the Philosophical Transactions were eight in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. 1. On the Decomposition of Fixed Air, 1791, p. 182. 2. On the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> of the Diamond, 1797, p. 123. 3. On the Action of Nitre upon Gold and Platina, p. 219. 4. On the different sorts of Lime used in Agriculture, 1799, p. 305. 5. On the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">Composition</a> of Emery, 1802, p. 398. 6. On two Metals found in the Black Powder remaining after the Solution of Platina, 1804, p. 411. 7. On an easier Mode of procuring Potassium than that which is now adopted, 1814, p. 578. 8. On the Means of producing a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> Distillation by the same Heat, p. 587. 9. The analysis of A Volcanic Substance containing the Boracic Acid appeared in the Transactions of the Geological Society, Vol. I. 1811. Mr Tennant was tall and slight in his person; his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> was thin, and his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>; he resembled a little the portraits of Locke; he was general- ly negligent in his dress, but, on the whole, agreeable in his appearance. He was distinguished for good <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, for quickness of perception, and for penetration; but, as his friend and biographer Mr Whishaw observes, in the admirably energetic sketch that he has given of his character, he was one of those who, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the words of Dr Johnson, "without much labour, have obtained a high reputation, and are mentioned with reverence rather for the possession than the exertion of uncommon abilities." "His curiosity and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> were incessant; he had a vigilance of observation which suffered nothing to escape him, and was continually gaining new information from a variety of interesting sources. But although the knowledge thus acquired was remarkable for its correctness, and complete for the purposes of its possessor, yet the industry and perseverance, by which it ought to have been embodied and made permanent for the benefit of others, were too often altogether wanting. The ardour and energy of Mr Tennant's mind co-operated unfortunately, in this respect, with his want of method and of systematic habits of application; since he was constantly pressing on to new discoveries, instead of arranging and bringing to perfection those which he had already made. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> was a great storehouse of discoveries, and hints for discovery, of ascertained facts, probable conjectures, and ingenious trains of reasoning relative to the various important subjects upon which he had at any time been engaged. These he was continually treasuring up, with the intention of reducing them to order, and preparing them for use at a more convenient season. But that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> rarely arrived. In the carelessness of intellectual wealth, he neglected those stores of knowledge which he had accumulated, and suffered them to remain useless and unproductive, till his attention was recalled to them, perhaps after a long course of years, by some new fact or discovery, some remark in conversation, or other accidental occurrence." The effect of his peculiar <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> of humour was heightened by a perfect gravity of countenance, a quiet familiar manner, and a characteristic simplicity of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. He was firmly attached to the general principles of freedom, being fully convinced "of their influence in promoting the wealth and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of nations; a due regard to these principles, he considered as the only <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> foundation of the most important blessings of social life, and as the peculiar cause of that distinguished superiority, which our own country so happily enjoys among the nations of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>." "The cheerful activity of a populous town, the improvements in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEAM_ENGINE">steam-engine</a>, the great galvanic experiments, and above all the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of the prospects afforded by that revolution in chemical science which has illustrated our own age and country; these magnificent objects, when presented to Mr Tennant's mind, excited in him the liveliest emotions, and called for the most animated expressions of admiration and delight." "He thought himself passionate and irascible; and certainly his feelings were quick; but they were transitory." He possessed a strong sense of high <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, as well as of duty; and his liberality and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> were evinced by some practical occurrences in which he had occasion to exercise them: his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a> had defrauded him, and when the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of reckoning came, had destroyed himself: he not only forgave the debt, but provided also for the widow and her family. "His amiable temper and unaffected desire of giving <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, no less than his superior knowledge and talents, had rendered him highly acceptable to a numerous and distinguished circle of society, by whom he was justly valued, and by whom his premature death was sincerely lamented. But the real extent of his private worth, the genuine simplicity and virtuous independence of his character, and the sincerity, warmth, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTANCY">constancy</a> of his friendship, can only be felt and estimated by those to whom he was long and intimately known, and to whom the recollection of his talents and virtues must always remain a pleasing though melancholy bond of union." [Whishaw in] Thomson's Annals, Vol. VI. 1815. p. 1, 80.

THIS SIMPLE MACHINE MIGHT BE MADE THE

Pages 58-71

s simple machine might be made the means of intelligible <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> in all the languages of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and its utility thus become universal. For instance, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a French <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Spaniard should see an English ship, their wants and wishes may easily be interchanged, although the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the one should be totally ignorant of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of the other; that is to say, provided the established <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TELEGRAPH">telegraph</a> book was translated into their respective languages: for example, Position of the Arms. 3. 6 represents, in English—<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. French—vaisseau de guerre. German—kreig’s schiff. Italian—nave de guerra. Position of the Arms. 4. 5 represents, in English—leak. French—voie d’eau. German—leck. Italian—crepatura. The encouragement afforded by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">Government</a> to improve every branch of science connected with the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, and men in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> in general, has been carried much farther by England than any other European <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>; and has produced the happiest results for commercial enterprise—by determining with accuracy the precise position of ships—by shortening <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> voyages—and by the discovery of new lands and unexplored regions. From the commencement of the eighteenth century, when a national reward was first offered to the man of science, or the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> who should discover a method sufficiently exact to determine the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> of a ship’s <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, to the present <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, the improvements in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of all kinds of instruments for measuring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>, in the calculations of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> and other tables, and above all, in the manufacture and adjustments of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHRONOMETERS">chronometers</a>, have <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in gradual progression; and may now be considered to have arrived at such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of perfection, more especially the chronometers, that the discovery of the longitude can scarcely be said to remain a desideratum. We may form an idea what the progress in the improvement of chronometers has been, when a public reward was offered by <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">Parliament</a> in the year 1814 to the first who should determine the longitude at sea within a degree, and in 1820, three chronometers, after remaining in the Arctic regions for eighteen months, returned to England without altering their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RATES">rates</a> more than a few seconds of time. The officers of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Navy are much more generally versed in the sciences of late years than heretofore. In fact, it is now necessary for a young man to be well acquainted with a certain portion of mathematical and astronomical knowledge, to enable him to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>, without which he cannot be qualified for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>. The Royal Naval <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTSMOUTH">Portsmouth</a>, for the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of a certain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of youths, has been the means of introducing a better system of naval education into his Majesty’s ships of war. The examinations also of the several warrant officers and their qualifications for their respective stations, are more strictly attended to than heretofore; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> is, that a much better system of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> without rigour, is established throughout the fleet, and more comfort in every respect to every class of officers and men employed. The encouragement given to the navy from its Pay and first regular establishment, has marked it as a favourite <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in the minds of the public. The sea-pay, the half-pay, and other emoluments, have gene- **NAVY** Navy rally been superior to those enjoyed by the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, but subject to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> fluctuations in every reign, and to frequent changes in the same reign. Thus <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> William, in 1693, gave to an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a>, L. 4 a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>—a vice-admiral, L. 3—and a rear-admiral, L. 2—which, with the compensation for servants, amounted to more than their present pay; yet their allowances were still further increased in 1700, till a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> took place, in consequence of an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> from the Commons. From this time to the year 1806, very little <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> took place, when a small addition was made to the pay of each class. But the first regular establishment of half-pay for all flag-officers, captains, first-lieutenants, and masters, was, by King William, in the year 1693, provided they had served a year in their respective qualities, or had been in a general engagement with the enemy. A regular established half-pay was further sanctioned by Order in Council of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> in 1700; the conditions of which were, that no officer should enjoy the benefit thereof who shall absent himself without permission of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">High</a> Admiral or Lords Commissioners of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">Admiralty</a>, or who shall be dismissed for any misdemeanour, or by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>-martial, or who shall not behave himself to the Navy. satisfaction of the Lord High Admiral, or who shall have leave to go out of his Majesty's dominions, if employed in the merchant service or otherwise, or if he enjoys the benefit of any public employment. Since the above <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> the rate of half-pay to the several officers of the navy has undergone various modifications.
