point of half-pay and other pecuniary emoluments, the navy has much the advantage over the army, more particularly in the chance of prize-money, which but seldom falls to the share of the army, except on some conjoint expedition. On the commencement of a war a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a> is issued by the King, directing that the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a> produce of all prizes taken by any of his ships of war, shall be for the entire benefit and encouragement of the flag-officers, captains, commanders, and other commissioned officers, and of the seamen, marines, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> on board at the time of the capture; and directing also in what manner the distribution shall be made. Many very handsome and, in some instances, very splendid fortunes have been made by captures of the enemy's ships. Another great encouragement for young men to enter the naval service arises from the honours bestowed by the Sovereign for any brilliant exploit. Thus, in consequence of the skill and bravery which were exhibited in the great and glorious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the 1st of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1794, his Majesty was graciously pleased to confer on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> Howe the Order of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARTER">Garter</a>; Vice-Admirals Graves and Sir Alexander Hood were made Barons of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">Kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>; and Rear-Admirals Bowyer, Gardner, and Pasley, together with Sir Roger Curtis, Captain of the Queen Charlotte, were created Baronets. <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a> medals and... chains were also distributed to such admirals, and gold medals to such captains, as were particularized in Lord Howe's dispatches. The first lieutenants of each ship were promoted to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of commanders; and pensions of L.1000 per annum were granted to Rear-Admirals Bowyer and Pasley. For the action of 14th February 1797, Lord St Vincent was advanced to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of an Earl, and a pension granted to him of L.3000 a-year; Vice-Admirals Thompson and Parker were created Baronets; Commodore Nelson received the Order of the Bath, and Captain Calder of the Victory, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">Knighthood</a>; and gold medals were distributed to the admirals and captains. For the action of the 11th October 1797, Admiral Duncan was created a Viscount, with a pension of L.2000 a-year; Vice-Admiral Onslow made a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARONET">Baronet</a>, and Captain Fairfax had the honour of Knighthood. Gold medals were also distributed to the admirals and captains. For the action of the 1st August 1798, his Majesty was pleased to testify his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of the importance of this brilliant achievement, by raising Sir Horatio Nelson to the dignity of the Peerage, by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Baron Nelson of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>; and by directing medals to be distributed to the captains. The first lieutenant of the Majestic was made a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST">post</a>-captain, and the first lieutenants of the other ships were promoted to the rank of commanders. And for the attack of the Danish fleet at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COPENHAGEN">Copenhagen</a>, Lord Nelson was raised to the dignity of a Viscount, and on Admiral Graves was conferred the Order of the Bath. For the ever memorable action of Trafalgar, in which Lord Nelson fell in the arms of victory, his Majesty was pleased to confer on his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> the rank of an Earl, with a pension of L.5000 a-year; and the sum of L.120,000 was voted by Parliament for the purchase of an estate to be annexed to the title. Admiral Collingwood was raised to the dignity of a Baron; Lord Northesk was honoured with the Order of the Bath, and Captain Hardy was created a Baronet. The captains had medals; five lieutenants were made post-captains; 24 lieutenants, commanders; 22 midshipmen were made lieutenants; and the senior captain of marines made brevet-major. By this last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of Lord Nelson's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> was annihilated the last remaining hope of the combined navies of France and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and a blow given to the naval power of the enemies of Great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, which they never recovered during the remainder of the war. In the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> victories of Sir John Warren, Sir John Duckworth, Sir Robert Calder, Sir Richard Strachan, Lord Gambier, and Lord <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXMOUTH">Exmouth</a>, and even for brilliant actions of single ships, appropriate distinctions have never been withheld. Exclusive of peerages and baronetcies, the honours bestowed for gallant conduct in the naval service consist of 25 <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> Crosses of the Bath, 70 Knights Commanders, and 130 Companions of the Bath. The provision which is made for officers, in the event of losing a limb, or being so severely wounded in the service, as to be of equal <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of body with the loss of a limb, is another encouragement for entering the naval service. For an admiral, from L.300 to L.700 per annum. A post-captain, wounds, L.250, loss of a limb, L.300. Commander, do. L.150, do. L.200. Lieutenant, do. L.91, 5s. do. L.91, 5s. Marine officers the same as in the army. A provision is likewise made for the widows of the widows' commission and warrant officers of his Majesty's navy, under the title of the "Widow's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHARITY">Charity</a>," the management of which is vested in a Court of Assistants annually chosen, consisting chiefly of the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty (the First Lord being <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">President</a>), and the flag-officers of the navy, making in the whole eighteen. The funds arise from, 1. A deduction of three-pence in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> from the pay, half-pay, and pensions of the commission and warrant officers of the navy. 2. The amount of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a> and value of the victuals of one fictitious man in every 100, borne on the books of ships in sea-pay. And, 3. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">Interest</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> vested in the funds. During the late war, the amount of the revenue from these sources was from L.90,000 to L.100,000; and the amount of pensions were about L.70,000 a-year. The pensions are allowed according to the following scale, being similar in most <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> to the widows of officers in the army of corresponding ranks: the latter are provided for by an annual vote of Parliament. **Scale of Pensions.** | Officer Title | Pension | |---------------|---------| | Flag-Officer | L.120 | | Captain | | | Rear-Admiral | 100 | | Post-Captain | 90 | | Post-Captain | 80 | | Commander | 70 | | Lieutenant | 60 | | Commander | 50 | | Master | 40 | | Surgeon | 40 | | Purser | 30 | | Boatswain | 25 | | Gunner | 25 | | Carpenter | 25 | | Second Master | 25 | And the widows of officers of the Royal Marines are entitled to the following pensions: | Officer Title | Pension | |---------------|---------| | General Officer | L.120 | | <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> | 90 | | Lieutenant-Colonel | 80 | | Major | 70 | | Captain | 50 | | First Lieutenant and Surgeon | 40 | | Second Lieutenant and Assistant Surgeon | 30 | In addition to these pensions, there has recently been a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUND">Fund</a>. been established a *Compassionate Fund*, for the relief of such widows and orphan children as may appear to be objects of compassion. The sums annually required are voted by Parliament, and at present do not exceed from L6,000 to L7,000 a-year. No provision, however, had been made for the brave seamen who fought the battles of their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, excepting for such as had been wounded in fight with the enemy. In the year 1588, after the memorable defeat of the Spanish Armada, the wounded seamen petitioned <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> for relief, upon which, with the advice of the Lord High Admiral and the Commissioners of the Navy, and with the consent of the inferior officers and seamen, the sum of sixpence a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> was deducted out of the wages of warrant officers and seamen, for the relief and maintenance of such as were hurt or maimed in the service. The money so raised was deposited at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHATHAM">Chatham</a> in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHEST">chest</a>, under the superintendence of the Yard Officers and the Warrant Officers of the Navy. As the funds increased, the management of them was transferred to certain Commissioners and Governors; and in order to do away in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> the inconvenience of compelling seamen from the western ports to go to Chatham for their pensions, the chest was removed, by the 43rd Geo. III., to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a> Hospital; and the power and authorities of the former <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TRUSTEES">trustees</a> were vested in the First Lord of the Admiralty, the Comptroller of the Navy, the Governor of Greenwich Hospital, and the Auditor of the same hospital, all for the time being, who, by this act, are created a body politic and corporate, by the name of the *Supervisors of the Chest of Greenwich*; the said supervisors to appoint five *Directors* from the officers of Greenwich Hospital, to have the immediate management of the business. In the course of the late war the funded <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> amounted to nearly L1,000,000 in the 3 per cents. the monthly sixpences, medals, &c. to nearly L70,000 per annum; and the § of 5 per cent. on the net proceeds of prizes to about L40,000; making a net annual income of about L130,000. The annual allowances made to pensioners were regulated according to the following scale: | Condition | Allowance | |------------------------------------------------|-----------| | Total <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol2.html#article-BLINDNESS">blindness</a> | L20 | | Loss of sight of one eye, the other impaired, according to the degree of blindness | L8 to L18 | | Loss of sight of one eye; the other not impaired | 6 | | Loss of arm, taken out of the socket, each | 20 | | Loss of arm above the elbow, each | 16 | | Loss of arm below the elbow, each | 14 | | Loss of leg above the knee, each | 14 | | Loss of leg below the knee, each | 12 | | <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">Double</a> rupture | 12 | | Single ditto, retainable by a truss | 4 | | Single rupture, not retainable, or very bad, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the injury, from | L6 to L10 | | Loss of thumb, or fore finger, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> | 6 | | Loss of thumb, or fore finger, first <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> remaining | 4 | In all cases of wounds, fractures, &c. for which no positive scale could be affixed, an allowance was made from the examining surgeon's report of the injury sustained, and a pension was granted for life, or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> of years, according to circumstances. When the wound or hurt was not thought of sufficient consequence to entitle the party to a pension, a sum of money was given as a full compensation. Every man, at time of entry on the list, was paid the amount of half a year's pension, as present relief, which money was not deducted from growing pension. Since the conclusion of the late war, the funds of the chest of Greenwich have been amalgamated with those of Greenwich Hospital, both of which are now under one and the same management. The establishment of Greenwich Hospital embraced more extensive objects. The first idea of this noble <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> and ornament of this kingdom, has been ascribed, with every appearance of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, the consort of William III. Being desirous that our gallant seamen, worn <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> or infirmities, as well as suffering from wounds, should not be left destitute, she made a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a>, jointly with King William, of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">Palace</a> of Greenwich, and certain lands adjoining, to be appropriated to this purpose, in order, as stated in the King's commission, to "the making some competent provision that seamen, who, by age, wounds, or other accidents, shall become disabled for further service at sea, and shall not be in a condition to maintain themselves comfortably, may not <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> under hardships and miseries, but may be supported at the public <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>; and that the children of such disabled seamen, and also the widows and children of such seamen as shall happen to be slain in sea service, may, in some reasonable manner, be provided for, and educated." In 1695 the committee appointed to examine and report on the premises, recommended an additional wing to King Charles's <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, which being approved by the King, Sir Christopher Wren undertook the conduct of the new erections without any pay or reward. Since that time various additions and improvements have been made to this magnificent pile of building, which was completed very nearly as it now appears, in the year 1778. The King granted L2,000 a-year towards the carrying on, perfecting, and endowing this hospital. The great Officers of State and wealthy individuals also subscribed liberally to the undertaking. It was at the same time enacted by Parliament, that a deduction of sixpence per man per month should be made out of the wages of all mariners for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the hospital; and power was given to the Lord High Admiral to appoint commissioners for receiving the said duty, whose office is situated on Tower Hill. In 1699 his Majesty contributed the sum of L19,500, being fines laid by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">House</a> of Lords on certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> convicted of smuggling. In 1705 Queen Anne assigned to the use of the hospital the effects of Kid the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIRATE">pirate</a>, amounting to upwards of L6,000. In 1707 Robert Osboldiston, Esq. devised by will half of his estate, which was valued at L20,000. In the same year Anthony Bowyer gave the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVERSION">reversion</a> of a considerable estate for the use of the hospital. By several statutes, the forfeited and unclaimed shares of prize-money were given to the hospital, and various grants, from time to time, continued to be made by Parliament. But the most substantial grant was that made by the Commons of the rents and profits of the forfeited estates of the Earl of Derwentwater, amounting at that time to about L. 6000 a-year, and at present to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> rental of L. 60,000, of which, after payment of all expenses for improvements, repairs, collections, and incumbrances, the annual receipt may be estimated from L. 30,000 to L. 40,000. At present the permanent revenues of the hospital consist of the following heads: 1. Sixpence per man per month for all seamen and marines belonging to his Majesty's naval service, and sixpence which was formerly paid to the chest at Chatham. 2. The same from all seamen employed in the merchants' service. 3. The duties arising from the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> and South Foreland <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>-houses. 4. The rents and profits of the Derwentwater estates, including the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a>. 5. Rents of the market of Greenwich, and of certain houses there and in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. 6. Interest of money invested in the public funds. 7. Forfeited and unclaimed shares of prize-money. 8. Fines for various offences. It is evident that the funds of the establishment must vary considerably in times of war and peace; being lowest in the latter period, when the demands are heaviest upon it, especially for a certain number of years after the closing of a war. The rental of the estates belonging to the hospital in the counties of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURHAM">Durham</a>, have risen from L. 23,000 in 1805, to L. 43,000 in 1816. The present gross rental of these estates and the lead mines, as above stated, amounts to about L. 60,000. The merchant seamen's sixpences amount to about L. 20,000 a-year; the naval seamen and marines to L. 15,000; the North and South Foreland lights to L. 7000; the interest of funded property to L. 50,000, making, with other contingencies, an annual revenue of about L. 150,000; the whole of which is expended on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> establishment, the clothing, maintenance, and allowances to pensioners and other attendants, repairs, taxes, and contingencies. During the war, and for a few years after the war, the funds of the hospital were adequate to the payment of the out-pensioners, which, taken at 35,000, the greatest number they ever reached, and allowing to each, on an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a>, L. 11 a-year, must have amounted to the sum of L. 385,000. Their numbers may now have decreased to 30,000, and the amount of their pensions to L. 330,000, to be voted by Parliament; the funds of the hospital no longer affording a surplus beyond its own support, from which only, by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, the out-pensioners had any claim. The establishment of this noble institution consists of a governor, who is a flag-officer in the navy, lieutenant-governor, four captains, eight lieutenants, all resident within the hospital. A <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>, auditor, paymaster of pensions, secretary, clerk of the check, two chaplains, two physicians, three surgeons, two dispensers, steward, clerk of the works, and several clerks. The number of in-pensioners is about 3000, and the number of nurses 180, all of whom must be the widows of naval seamen, and under the age of 45 years at the time of admission. Under the naval administration of Earl Grey, the following officers were added to the out-pensions of Greenwich Hospital, to be selected by the Admiralty according to their respective claims on the service: | Officer | Per Year | |--------------------------|----------| | Post-Captains | L. 80 | | Commanders | | | Lieutenants | | in addition to their half-pay. The out-pensions to seamen were first established in 1763, by act of 3d Geo. III. ch. 16, in consequence of which 1400 out-pensioners were appointed, at L. 7 per annum each, after undergoing an examination at the Admiralty as to their claims. At the close of the long revolutionary war, the applications became so numerous, and the claims of the seamen who had been wounded, or worn out in the service, so strongly grounded in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> and justice, that it became necessary to adopt a scale of pensions, and to establish certain rules and regulations, by which seamen of his Majesty's fleet and royal marines should be remunerated for wounds or hurts, debility, and length of service. The following are the regulations: **For Wounds, Hurts, or Debility.** Every seaman, landman, boy, or royal marine, wounded or hurt in his Majesty's service, is to receive a sum of money from the Chest of Chatham in the nature of smart money, as heretofore; and also be entitled to a pension proportioned to his wounds or hurts, of not less than sixpence a day, and not more than one <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHILLING">shilling</a> and sixpence a day. For sickness or debility, after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years' service (and under special circumstances before that period), of not less than fivepence a day, nor more than threepence, according as he may appear capable of assisting himself. Beyond fourteen, and less than twenty-one years' service, not less than eightpence, nor more than one shilling and threepence. After twenty-one years' service, one shilling and sixpence a day. **For Length of Service.** Every able seaman, discharged on the reduction of the fleet, who has served faithfully fourteen years, and less than twenty-one, is entitled to a pension of one halfpenny a day for every year of such service. Twenty-one years' service entitles him to a free discharge, and a pension of one shilling a day; and if he may choose to continue in the service, one halfpenny a day in addition for every additional year of service. Ordinary seamen and landmen, entitled to four-fifths and three-fifths of able seamen's pensions. The privates of royal marines are considered as ordinary seamen. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> petty officers, in addition to the above rates of pension, are entitled to one half-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENNY">penny</a> a day for the number of years' service; the inferior petty officers to one farthing. All the above mentioned pensions may be forfeited by misconduct, by desertion, and by <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> of a Court-Martial. Also, by neglecting, or omitting, to attend at such port, or place, and at such time as shall, in time of war, or in prospect of a war, be appointed for the assembling of the pensioners, by the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty. To this noble institution is appended an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a>, for the maintenance and education of the children of officers and seamen of his Majesty's naval service. The Naval Asylum was originally instituted by the Patriotic Fund and private subscriptions, and afterwards established at Greenwich, by warrant under the King's sign-<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANUAL">manual</a>, dated <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1818, appointing the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty to be commissioners and governors, who, with twenty-four directors, were to superintend and manage the same. The object was, the maintenance and education of a certain number of orphans and other children of the non-commissioned officers, seamen, and marines of the royal navy. As it was manifest, however, that this establishment, so contiguous to the hospital of Greenwich, could be managed without inconvenience by the commissioners and directors of that hospital, under a more effective and economical system, his Majesty was pleased, by his warrant of January 1821, to annul the former warrant, and to vest the superintendence and internal management of the said asylum in the commissioners and governors of Greenwich Hospital. The two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> of Greenwich Hospital, and the Naval Asylum, and the funds thereof, are now therefore incorporated. The internal management is confided to the Board of Directors, and one of the captains of the hospital is intrusted with the general superintendence. A chaplain, and proper schoolmasters, schoolmistresses, matron, with inferior assistants, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a>, with moderate salaries, reside in the building. The number of children maintained and educated in the Institution are: | In the Boys' Upper School | 200 | |---------------------------|----| | Ditto, Lower School | 600 | | Girls | 200 | In the whole, 1000 To the upper school no boys are admitted but the sons of seamen and marines, slain, drowned, or dead; of pensioners in the hospital; of seamen disabled, past their labour, or otherwise objects of charity; of officers in the navy and marines, on the production of a required certificate of poverty. The age of admission from eleven to twelve; the continuance in the school three years, when they are bound apprentices to the merchant service. Presentations by the directors in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROTATION">rotation</a>. The boys and girls of the lower school are the children of seamen and marines of the naval service, admitted by the Board of Directors, giving a preference to orphans. The age of admission from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> to twelve years inclusive; but none to be retained beyond the age of fourteen. The boys to be sent into the navy, or merchant service, or put apprentices to some trade. The girls, at the age of fourteen, to be apprenticed to trades, or sent to service. Thus are all the classes of officers, seamen, and marines, who have faithfully served in the navy, provided for by the state; and the children of such as may be in indigent circumstances receive an education at the public expence, suited to their condition in life. The total expence of the whole navy, including every branch of the service, civil and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a>, for one whole year, in the middle of the late war, may be estimated at about L. 18,000,000 In the year 1822, according to the estimates laid before Parliament, at about 5,000,000

THOMPSON

Pages 714-718

a well-known <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">Philosopher</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">Political</a> Economist, was born in 1753, at a village in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEW_HAMPSHIRE">New <a class=</a>"xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAMPSHIRE">Hampshire</a>, then called Rumford, and now Concord. His father died while he was very young, and his mother married another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, who banished him from her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> almost in his infancy: he inherited only a small pittance from an uncle, who died soon after his father. A clergyman named Bernard showed him <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> kindness, and taught him some of the higher <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> at an early <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, so that at fourteen he was able to calculate and delineate an eclipse of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. He had been intended for some commercial employment; but he preferred the pursuit of literature in any form: he attended the lectures of Dr Williams, and afterwards those of Dr Winthrop, the astronomer, at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a> of "Harvard;" and while he was still a stripling, he was established in the temporary occupation of a village schoolmaster; hoping, however, for an early opportunity to engage in some more agreeable employment: and at nineteen, he was fortunate enough to obtain the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of Mrs Rolfe, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Mr Walker, a clergyman, who had been employed with considerable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> in conducting some public business. For a year <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> two he lived retired and happy: but having obtained a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITIA">Militia</a> from the Governor of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, together with some other distinctions, of a civil <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, he was consequently led to adhere to the party of the Royalists, and he was soon obliged, by the success of the Independent forces, to take refuge at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOSTON">Boston</a>, then occupied by the English troops. It was in November 1779 that he secretly quitted his residence, leaving his wife, whom he never <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> again, and his infant daughter, who joined him twenty years after in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. He was employed to raise a regiment for the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>; but when Boston was evacuated, in 1776, he was sent with some important dispatches to England. Here he soon acquired the confidence of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> George Germaine, then Colonial Secretary of State, and was appointed Secretary of the province. Thompson of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEORGIA">Georgia</a>, though he never exercised the office; but he remained attached to that department of the public service. In 1777 he commenced his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CAREER">career</a> as an experimental philosopher, by employing his leisure hours, during a visit to Bath, in making some experiments on the cohesive strength of different substances: and upon his return to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, he communicated them to Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Banks, with whom he formed an intimate acquaintance, which he kept up throughout the remainder of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. In 1778 he was admitted a Fellow of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, and he made in that year his first experiments on <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>. In order to pursue these experiments, he went, in 1779, on board of the Victory of 110 guns, commanded by his friend Sir <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Hardy. He passed the whole of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> on board of the fleet; and the results of the observations, that he then made, furnished the materials of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> which he contributed to Stalkart's Treatise on Naval <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>. He added to it a code of signals for the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">Navy</a>, which was not published. In 1780 he was appointed Under Secretary of State, and he was constantly employed, for some little <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, in the office on the business of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. He succeeded, by means of his American friends and agents, in raising a regiment of cavalry, called the King's American Dragoons, of which he was appointed <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIEUTENANT">Lieutenant</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> Commandant; and this success induced him to go to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> to serve with it. At <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARLESTOWN">Charlestown</a> he was entrusted with the command of the remains of the cavalry of the British <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>;—he speedily restored the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> of the corps, and gained its confidence and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a>: he often led it on against the enemy, and frequently with considerable success. He proceeded, in 1782, to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEW_YORK">New <a c</a>lass="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, where he assumed the command of his own regiment, having received the colours from the hand of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> William Henry, now <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of Clarence. In the autumn, General Clinton was succeeded by Sir Guy Carleton, whose friendship and confidence he speedily obtained: his regiment was recruited from the fragments of several others, and he was sent for the winter to Huntingdon in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">Island</a>. He was chosen, in 1783, to conduct the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of Jamaica, which was then threatened by the enemy: but the general peace superseded the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of the intended expedition. After his return to England, he made great efforts in the cause of the loyalist officers, and he was successful in persuading the Ministry to make a proper provision for them: he was himself made a full Colonel, upon the recommendation of General Carleton, only two years after his appointment as Lieutenant-Colonel. He had acquired a strong predilection for a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> life, and was desirous of being sent with his regiment to the East Indies: and when the regiment was reduced, he wished to serve with the Austrians in a war which was then meditated against the Turks. With this view he left England in September 1783, and on his passage to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOULOGNE">Boulogne</a>, he had an agreeable ship-mate in the person of Gibbon, the historian, who did <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> to his merits as a "soldier, philosopher, and statesman." At Strasburg, his appearance on the parade in his uniform excited the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of the present King of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>, then Prince Maximilian of Deux Ponts, who invited him to his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, and being delighted with the accuracy and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of his military knowledge, gave him a strong recommendation to his uncle, then <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTOR">Elector</a>: and instead of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> or two, as he had intended, he staid a fortnight at Munich. He was also very cordially received at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a>, and passed a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the winter there; but the war against the Turks not taking <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, he went by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> and the Tyrol again to Munich, where he arrived in the winter of 1784; and being formally invited by the Elector to enter his service, he went to London to ask leave to accept the proposal; and it was granted him, together with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">Knighthood</a>. On his return to Bavaria, he was made a Colonel of cavalry, and Aide-de-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMP">Camp</a>-General to the Elector. The first four years of his residence at Munich were principally employed in acquiring information, and in preparing his plans of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REFORM">reform</a>: and in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time he <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> his physical researches. He made his first experiments on <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> in 1786, during a journey to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MANNHEIM">Mannheim</a>. In 1785 he was made Chamberlain to the Elector, and member of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">Academies</a> of Munich and of Mannheim: in 1786 he received from the King of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a> the Order of St Stanislaus; in 1787 he took a journey to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a>, and was made a member of the Academy of Sciences of that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>: in 1788 he was appointed Major-General of the Bavarian cavalry, and Privy Counsellor of State; and he was placed at the head of the War Department, in order to pursue his plans for the improvement of the army. It was in 1789 that he established the House of Industry at Mannheim: he founded also the Military Academy of Munich; he improved the military <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-POLICE">Police</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; he formed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">Schools</a> of Industry for the wives and children of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>; and he embellished the city by a new arrangement of the public gardens. The House of Industry at Munich, which he has described at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> in his Essays, was founded in 1790: and from this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> may be dated the total abolition of mendicity in Bavaria. His exertions were rewarded by the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of Lieutenant-General of the Bavarian armies, and by a regiment of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>. In 1791 he was created a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> of the Holy Roman Empire, and obtained the Order of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">White</a> Eagle. His <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> having suffered from constant application, he obtained permission to take a journey into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and he returned to Bavaria in 1794. He had a severe illness at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, and he was not sufficiently recovered, upon his return, to resume his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> duties; but he employed himself in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> the first five of his Essays. In 1795, he came to England in order to publish the Essays, and in hopes of exciting the public attention to the importance of attempting a similar reform among the lowest orders in Great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. He went to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a> in 1796, to pay a visit to Lord Pelham, now <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHICHESTER">Chichester</a>, then Secretary of State for <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>; and he was of essential service in the arrangement of several of the public institutions of that country. He was made a Member of the Royal Irish Academy, and of the Society for the Encouragement of Arts; and he received, after having left the country, the public thanks of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JURY">Jury</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Dublin, and of the Lord Mayor of that city, as well as of the Lord Lieutenant at the head of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">Government</a>. Upon his return to London, he superintended some improvements at the Foundling <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">Hospital</a>, and presented several models of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> and implements to the Board of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a>: and he established two prizes, for discoveries relating to Heat and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">Light</a>, by placing two sums of L.1000 in the British and in the American funds, to be adjudged biennially, for Europe by the Royal Society of London, and for America by the American Academy of Sciences. He was recalled to Bavaria by the exigencies of the moment, which were such as to cause the Elector to take refuge in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>; General Moreau having advanced with his army to the confines of Bavaria. After the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Friedberg, Count Rumford was left in command of the Bavarian army, with instructions to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> according to his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a> under the circumstances that might occur; and his firmness was such, as to prevent either the Austrians or the French from entering Munich. On the Elector's return, he was placed at the head of the department of the general police of Bavaria. His exertions in this office were such, as to impair the state of his health, and by way of an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> retirement, he was sent to England in the capacity of Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary: but being a subject of the King of England, he was judged incapable of being received as the diplomatic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGENT">agent</a> of a foreign <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>, and he, therefore, continued to live in England as a private individual. He was very active about this time in projecting and superintending the establishment of the Royal <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">Institution</a> of Great Britain, which was more particularly intended for the application of science to the conveniences and comforts of civil and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> life, but which has been no less successful in giving opportunity and facility to some of the most refined researches in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY">natural <a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> that have distinguished the age, than in serving as a medium for making the treasures of science accessible to the less studious part of the public, and as a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> for a variety of other similar undertakings in different parts of the world. Count Rumford was soon afterwards officially invited to America by the government of the United States, with an offer of an honourable establishment in a public situation; but he considered it as inconsistent with his engagements in Europe to accept the proposal. In the autumn of 1800, when he went to Scotland, a visit of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> was paid him by the magistrates of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>: he was consulted respecting the abolition of mendicity, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> that he recommended were speedily executed with complete success. He was made an honorary member of the Royal Society, and of the Royal College of Physicians of Edinburgh; and he received a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> snuff box as a compliment for his assistance in reforming the culinary establishment of Heriot's Hospital. After so active and diversified a career, it was not to be expected that he would be satisfied with the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONOTONY">monotony</a> of a permanent residence in London: he was so accustomed to labour for the attainment of some object, that when the object itself was completely within his reach, and the labour was ended, the prospect, which ought to have been uniformly bright, became spontaneously clouded, or even the serenity became unenjoyable for want of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> to afford a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a>. He had fitted up a small house at Brompton, with every contrivance for comfort and convenience that could render it fit for the abode of hospitality and of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a>; and the arrangements are fully described in the Bibliothèque Britannique of his friend, Professor Pictet; but after all he never was known to give a single entertainment in it. The enthusiasm excited by the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a> of some of his inventions had subsided, and he was even mortified by becoming, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> with the most elevated personages of the country, the object of the impertinent attacks of a popular satirist. It was partly, however, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not entirely, the superiority of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> of France, that determined him to remove to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of 1802: he went in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> to Munich, and the following year he made a tour in Switzerland and in Bavaria, accompanied by Mr. Lavoisier, whom he married soon after their return: but their habits were incompatible with matrimonial comfort, and they separated soon after; Count Rumford retiring to Auteuil, about four miles from Paris, where he occupied a house which had formerly belonged to Helvetius and to Cabanis, while his lady continued to live in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>. His latter years were passed almost wholly in solitude; he saw only his neighbour Mr Caneleux, Mr Underwood, and a Mr Parker, an American: he did not even attend the sittings of the Institute, though he had been made one of its eight foreign associates some time before, and always retained a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> esteem for its secretary Cuvier, and for some others of its members. His income was abundantly sufficient for his own expenses, having obtained from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> of the King of Bavaria a pension of L.1200 a year; and he was allowed by Bonaparte to remain unmolested, though a British subject, when it was found that he had no intercourse with society, amusing himself principally in walking about his garden, and in a solitary <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAME">game</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILLIARDS">billiards</a>. He had so completely persuaded himself, in the latter part of his life, of the great superiority of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a> above narrow ones, that he drove about the streets of Paris in a broad wheel-ed chariot; and having rediscovered, after Professor Leslie, that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> bodies radiate more heat than others, he wore, in the winter, a white hat and a white coat, in order to economize the heat of his person. "These peculiarities, and a peremptory unyielding disposition," says one of his biographers, "were the causes that set him apart from social intercourse, and in all his connexions in life, seem to have rendered him less the object of personal attachment than of esteem for his talents and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>." He was about to return to England when he died, the 21st August 1814, leaving only one daughter, who still resides in his house at Brompton. 1. Count Rumford's first publication appears to have been the chapter on Marine Artillery that he furnished to Stalkart's Treatise on Naval Architecture, 1780. 2. New Experiments on Gunpowder, with the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">Description</a> of an Epronvette. Phil. Trans. 1781. P. 230. The effect of the powder on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> was measured by the recoil of the piece, with a correction deduced from the recoil when the piece was empty. It was observed to be sooner heated when fired without ball than with it. The force of the powder is made at least 1300 atmospheres, upon Robins's principles. 3. New Experiments upon Heat. Phil. Trans. 1786. P. 273. These experiments relate principally to the conducting powers of various mediums for heat; but the results are unavoidably complicated with the effects of radiation, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VACUUM">vacuum</a> is supposed to possess a conducting power more than half as great as that of common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. 4. Experiments on the Production of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPHLOGISTICATED">Dephlogisticated</a> Air from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">Water</a> with various Substances. Phil. Trans. 1787. P. 84. These experiments tend to show that the air obtained, by Priestley and Ingenhousz, from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> under water, was derived rather from the water itself than from the substances immersed in it. 5. Experiments made to determine the Positive and Relative Quantities of Moisture absorbed from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">Atmosphere</a> by Various Substances. P. 240. He finds that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> is more absorbent of moisture than any other substance compared with it; and hence explains the supposed advantage of woollen worn next the skin. 6. Experiments on Heat. Phil. Trans. 1792. P. 48. The author attributes the effect of loose substances in obstructing the passage of heat to their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTRACTION">attraction</a> for air, and to their impeding its circulation; and he supposes this to be the only manner in which <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a> communicate heat. 7. Account of a Method of Measuring the Comparative Intensity of Light emitted by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUMINOUS">Luminous</a> Bodies. Phil. Trans. 1794. P. 67. Placing them at such distances, that the shadows <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> by each may appear equally dark. 8. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">Letter</a> announcing a Donation for a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIZE">Prize</a> Medal. Phil. Trans. 1797. P. 215. 9. Experiments to determine the Force of Fired Gunpowder. P. 272. This force he supposes to amount to between 20,000 and 50,000 atmospheres, instead of 10,000, as Bernoulli computed it; but he makes a great mistake in supposing that the whole of the water which can possibly be contained in the gunpowder would be sufficient to furnish as much <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEAM">steam</a> as would be required, since steam, under a pressure of 20,000 atmospheres, must be considerably more dense than water itself. (See Steam Engine, in this Supplement.) 10. Inquiry concerning the Source of the Heat excited by Friction. Phil. Trans. 1798. P. 80. The capacity of the chips of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> afforded by friction in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BORING">boring</a> a cannon, was found not to differ from that of the iron in its original state: hence it is inferred, that the heat could not have been furnished by them, and that it must probably have been <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a>. Mr Thompson Haldalt afterwards repeated the experiment under circumstances still more decisive; and Sir Humphry Davy showed that two pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a> rubbed together, in a room below the freezing temperature, would melt each other. 11. Inquiry concerning the Chemical Properties that have been attributed to Light. P. 449. He attributes these properties to the effect of an intense heat confined to a small space; but the later experiments on the chemical effects of the spectrum are sufficient to supersede this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>. 13. An Account of a Curious Phenomenon observed on the Glaciers of Chamouny, with some Observations on the Propagation of Heat in Fluids. Phil. Trans. 1804. P. 25. An effect depending on the expansion of water in cooling near the freezing point. 14. Concerning the Nature of Heat, and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">Mode</a> of its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">Communication</a>. P. 77. He conjectures that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> is a positive <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, capable of being propagated by radiation. Several of these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> were reprinted under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Philosophical Papers. Vol. I. S. Lond. 1802. 15. The Essays constitute 4 volumes Svo. Lond. 1795 . . 1800. Reprinted 1800. In French, 2 v. S. Genev. 1799. Recueil de Rapports . . sur les soupes. Par. 1801. They are 18 in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. i. Account of an Establishment for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">Poor</a> at Munich. In Ital. S. Venice, 1798. ii. On Establishments for the Poor in general. iii. Of Food, and of Feeding the Poor. iv. Of Chimney Fireplaces. v. Account of several Public Institutions formed in Bavaria. vi. On the Management of Fire, and the Economy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">Fuel</a>. vii. On the Propagation of Heat in Fluids, extending to Liquids the doctrine which he had before advanced respecting Elastic Fluids. viii. On the Propagation of Heat in Various Substances. Phil. Trans. ix. Experimental Inquiry concerning the Source of Heat excited by Friction. x. On <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KITCHEN">Kitchen</a> Fireplaces and Kitchen Utensils. xi. On Chimney Fireplaces. xii. On the Salubrity of Warm Rooms in Cold <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">Weather</a>. xiii. On the Salubrity of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATHING">Bathing</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">Construction</a> of Warm <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">Baths</a>. xiv. Supplementary Observations on the Management of Fires. xv. On the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">Use</a> of Steam for Transporting Heat. xvi. On the Management of Light in Illumination, with an Account of a New Portable <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-LAMP">Lamp</a>. xvii. On the Source of the Light manifested in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMBUSTION">Combustion</a> of Inflammable Bodies. xviii. On the Excellent Qualities of Coffee, and the Art of Making it in Perfection. 16. There are several little papers on Steam Kitchens, on the Strength of Soft Materials, and on some other similar subjects, in the first numbers of the Journals of the Royal Institution. S. Lond. 1800. 17. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of investigations relating to Heat and Light, which Count Rumford began to communicate to the Royal Society, were continued, and rather more fully detailed, in several of the volumes of the Memoirs of the Institute, Mathematical Class; into which they were, of course, admitted as the productions of a Foreign Associate. The first of these is in the sixth volume. 4. Par. 1806. P. 71, containing a Description of a New <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">Instrument</a>; a thermoscope, or a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENTIAL">differential</a> thermometer, resembling that of Leslie. Further Experiments, in the effect of blackening the surface. (20.) iv. P. 97. Researches Continued; on the different properties of bodies with respect to radiation, and to conducting power. (21.) v. P. 106. Further Researches; some good experiments on the passage of heat through solids. (22.) vi. P. 123. Experiments on the Heat of the Solar Rays; which was found not to be affected by their convergence or divergence, or by their having met in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FOCUS">focus</a> and crossed each other. (23.) vii. Vol. VII. i. 1806. P. 78. Remarks on the Temperature of Water at the Maximum of Density; making it 41° of Fahrenheit, or 5° centigrade. Phil. Trans. 1804. (24.) viii. Vol. VIII. i. 1807. P. 223. On the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISPERSION">Dispersion</a> of the Light of Lamps by Screens of Ground Glass, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">Silk</a>, and so forth; with a Description of a New Lamp. (25.) ix. P. 249. On the Cooling of Li- guids in Vases of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORCELAIN">Porcelain</a>, gill and not gilt; showing the utility of gilding them externally, with some good reasoning on the nature of heat. 26. He was latterly engaged in composing a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> on The Nature and Effects of Order, which he never completed, although no person was better qualified to write on the subject. Count Rumford certainly possessed considerable facility of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>, and there was a very laudable spirit of originality in his views and modes of reasoning, although he had never leisure to acquire profound learning in any department of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>. "In person he was above the middle size, with a dignified and pleasing <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of countenance, and a mildness in his manner and his tone of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>. He was ambitious of fame and distinction, and had too great a propensity to dictate," without sufficiently regarding the opinions of others who were of equal authority with himself. His mode of life was abstemious, and his health was even supposed to have suffered from too great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTINENCE">abstinence</a>, though his regimen was much more the result of medical opinions respecting his health, than of his own peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a>. [Pictet, Bibliothèque Britannique, and Baldwin's Literary Journal. Gent. Mag. Vol. LXXXIV. Aikin's General Biography, X. 4. Lond. 1805. Chalmers' Biographical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>, XXIX. 8. Lond. 1816.]

TIDES

Pages 718-726

The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> of the phenomena of the tides has been justly considered as uniting some of the greatest difficulties that occur in the various departments of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>. It implies, first, a knowledge of the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVITATION">gravitation</a>, concerned in the determination of the forces immediately acting on the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and of the periods and distances of the celestial bodies, which modify the magnitudes and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a> of these forces; and secondly, of the hydraulic theories of the resistances of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>, and of the motions of waves and undulations of all kinds, and of the theoretical determination of the form and density of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, as well as of the geographical observation of the breadth and depth of the seas and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, which occupy a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of its surface; so that the whole subject affords abundant scope for the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of mathematical skill, and still more for the employment of that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> and contrivance, which enables its possessor to supersede the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of prolix computations, wherever they can be avoided. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of the tides is naturally divided into several periods in which its different departments have been progressively cultivated. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, from the times of Posidonius and Pytheas, and the moderns before Newton, were contented with observing the general dependence of the tides on the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, as following her transit at an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> of about two hours, and their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> increase and decrease not only every fortnight, but also in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of about eight years; the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> step consisted in the determination of the magnitude and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the solar and lunar forces, by which the general effects of the tides were shown, in the Principia, to be the necessary consequences of these forces; the third <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> point was the demonstration of Maclaurin, that the form of an elliptic spheroid affords an equilibrium under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the disturbing forces concerned; while the further <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> illustrations of the subject by Euler and Bernoulli, though they afforded some useful details, involved no new principle that can be put in competition with Maclaurin's demonstration: the fourth important step was made by Laplace, who separated the consideration of the form, affording <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> equilibrium, from that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> occasioned by the continual change of that form, while former theorists had taken it for granted, that the surface of the sea very speedily assumed the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of a fluid acted by similar forces, but remaining perfectly at rest, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> assuming instantly the form in question. Laplace's computation is however limited to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of an imaginary ocean, of a certain variable depth, assumed for the convenience of calculation, rather than for any other reason. Dr Thomas Young has extended Laplace's <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of considering the phenomena to the more general case of an ocean covering a part only of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-EARTH_S">earth's</a> surface, and more or less <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> in its form; he has also attempted to comprehend in his calculations the precise effects of hydraulic friction on the times and magnitudes of the tides. As far as the resistance may be supposed to vary in the simple ratio of the velocity, Dr Young's theory is sufficiently complete, and explains several of the peculiarities which are otherwise paradoxical in their appearance; but there still remains a difficulty to be combated with respect to the effects of a resistance <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> of the velocity, and this, it is hoped, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be in great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> removed in the present article, which, however, from the space that is allotted to it, must be considered rather as a supplementary fragment than as a complete treatise. It will be divided into four sections: The first relating to the contemporaneous progress of the tides through the different seas and oceans, as collected from observation only; the second to the magnitude of the disturbing forces tending to change the form of the surface of the earth and sea: the third to the theory of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> vibrations with resistance; and the fourth to the application of this theory to the progress and successive magnitudes of the tides, as observable at any one port. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">Sect</a>. I.—Of the Progress of Contemporary Tides, as inferred from the times of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">High</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">Water</a> in Different Ports. The least theoretical consideration, relating to the tides, is that of their progress through the different parts of the ocean, and of its dependent seas. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a> of these ought to be very completely attainable from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> observation, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of high water had been accurately observed at a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of ports throughout the world; and, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, if the earth were covered in all parts with a fluid of great and nearly uniform depth, the tides of this fluid would be so regular, that a very few observations would be sufficient to enable us to deduce the whole of the phenomena from theory, and to trace the great waves, which would follow the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and moon round the globe, so as to make its circuit in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, without any material deviation from uniformity of motion and succession. Having collected, for the actual state of the sea and continents, an abundant store of accurate observations of the precise time of high water with regard to the sun and moon, for every part of the surface, and having arranged them in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> according to the order of their occurrence, as expressed in the time of any one meridian, we might then suppose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> to be drawn on a terrestrial globe, through all the places of observation, in the same order; and these lines would indicate, supposing the places to be sufficiently numerous, so as to furnish a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of tides very nearly contemporary, the directions of the great waves, to which that of the progress of the tides in succession must be perpendicular. If, however, we actually make such an attempt, we shall soon find how utterly inadequate the observations that have been recorded are, for the purpose of tracing the forms of the lines of contemporary high water with accuracy or with certainty, although they are abundantly sufficient to show the impossibility of deducing the time of high water at any given <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> from the Newtonian <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>, or even from that of Laplace, without some direct observation. It might at least be supposed very easy to enumerate the existing observations, scanty as they may be, in a correct order; but there are a number of instances in which it is wholly uncertain whether the time observed at a given port relates to the tide of the same morning in the open ocean, or to that of the preceding evening; this inconvenience may, however, in some measure be remedied, by inserting such places in two different parts of the table, at the distance of 12½ hours from each other. The following Table is the result of the best approximation that could be obtained in this manner, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> lines having been partially traced on a map of the world, in order to afford some little direction to the correct insertion of the times of high water without the material <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a> of half a day. The three great natural divisions of the Atlantic, the Pacific, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> Oceans, are distinguished into different columns, and some of the places, which seem to form separate systems of tides, are still further subdivided in a similar manner; but this arrangement may easily be neglected by those who are inclined to question its propriety. The principal authorities are the Requisite Tables; Lalande's Treatise, in the fourth volume of his Astronomy; a manuscript Hydrographical Memoir by Mr Henry Foster, Lieut. R. N. of his Majesty's ship Conway, Capt. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">Hall</a>; and A Series of Observations made at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">Island</a> of Ascension in 1820, by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Campbell, R. N., obligingly communicated by Captain Hall to the author of this Article. Secondly, That the southern extremity of the line advances as it passes the Cape of Good Hope, so that it turns up towards the Atlantic, which it enters obliquely, so as to arrive, nearly at the same moment, at the Island of Ascension, and at the Island of Martin Vaz, or of the Trinity. Thirdly, After several irregularities about the Cape Verd <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">Islands</a>, and in the West Indies, the line appears to run nearly east and west from St Domingo to Cape Blanco, the tides proceeding due northwards; and then, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> still more to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, the line seems to run N. W. and S. E., till at last the tide runs almost due east up the British Channel, and round the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Scotland into the Northern Ocean, sending off a branch <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the North Sea to meet the succeeding tide at the mouth of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>. Fourthly, Towards Cape <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">Horn</a> again there is a good deal of irregularity; the hour lines are much compressed between South Georgia and Terra del <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FUEGO">Fuego</a>, perhaps on account of the shallower water about the <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol9.html#article-FALKLAND_ISLANDS"><a class="xref" </a>href="vol8.html#article-FALKLAND">Falkland</a> Islands and South Shetland. In the fifth place, At the entrance of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PACIFIC_OCEAN">Pacific Ocean</a>, the tides seem to advance very rapidly to New Zealand and Easter Island; but here it appears to be uncertain whether the line of contemporary tide should be drawn nearly N. and S. from the Gallapagos to Terra del Fuego, or N. E. and S. W. from Easter Island to New Zealand; or whether both these partial directions are correct: but on each side of this line there are great irregularities, and many more observations are wanting before the progress of the tide can be traced with any tolerable accuracy, among the multitudinous islands of the Pacific Ocean, where it might have been hoped that the phenomena would have been observed in their greatest simplicity, and in their most genuine form. Lastly, Of the Indian Ocean the northern parts exhibit great irregularities, and among the rest they afford the singular phenomenon observed by Halley in the Port of Tonkin, and explained by Newton in the Principia: the southern parts are only remarkable for having the hour lines of contemporary tides considerably crowded between <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-NEW_HOLLAND">New <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> and the Cape of Good Hope, as if the seas of these parts were shallower than elsewhere. These inferences respecting the progress of the tides are not advanced as the result of any particular theory, nor even as the only ones that might possibly be deduced from the table: thus the supposition that the direction in which the tides advance must be perpendicular to the hour lines of contemporary tides, is not by any means absolutely without exception, since a quadrangular lake, with steep shores in the direction of the meridian, would have the times of high water the same for every point of its eastern or western halves respectively, and there could be no correctly defined direction of the hour lines in such a case. But if any portion of the sea could be considered as constituting such a lake, its properties would be detected by a sufficient number of observations of high water, and the existing table does not appear to indicate any such <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> that require to be otherwise distinguished than as partial irregularities. There may also be some doubt respecting the propriety of the addition of 12½ hours that has been made to the time of high water in the north eastern parts of the Atlantic: but it seems extremely improbable that the same tide should travel north easterly into the English Channel and into the Northern Ocean, and at the same time westerly across the Atlantic, as it must be supposed to do, if it were considered as primarily originating in the neighbourhood of the Bay of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISCAY">Biscay</a>; on the other hand, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> of the great wave round the continents of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> seems to be very like the sort of refraction which takes place on every shelving <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> with respect to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> waves, which, whatever may have been their primitive origin, acquire always, as they spread, a direction more and more nearly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to that of the coast which they are approaching: and the suppositions which have been here advanced respecting the succession of the tides in different ports, allowing for the effect of a multitude of irregularities proceeding from partial causes, appear to be by far the most probable that can be immediately inferred from the table, at least in its present state of imperfection. Sect. II.—Of the Disturbing Forces that occasion the Tides. Since the phenomena of the tides, with regard to their progress through the different oceans and seas, as they exist in the actual state of the earth's surface, appear to be too complicated to allow us to hope to reduce them to computation by means of any general theory, we must, in the next place, confine our <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the order in which the successive changes occur in any single port, and having determined the exact magnitude of the forces, that tend to change the form of the surface of the ocean at different periods, and having also examined the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the vibratory motions, of which the sea, or any given portion of it, would be susceptible, in the simplest cases, after the cessation of the disturbing forces; we must afterwards endeavour to combine these causes, so as to adapt the result to the successive phenomena, which are observed at different times in any one port. Theorem A. ("E."—Nich. Journ. Jul. 1813.)
