The disturbing force of a distant attractive body, urging a particle of a fluid in the direction of the surface of a sphere, varies as the sine of twice the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ALTITUDE">altitude</a> of the body. The <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTRACTION">attraction</a>, exerted by the sun and moon on all the separate particles composing the earth, is exactly compensated by the centrifugal force derived from the earth's annual revolution round the sun, and from its monthly revolution round the common centre of gravity of the earth and moon: but the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of the attractions, exerted at different <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of the earth, must necessarily produce a disturbing force, depending on the angular position of the point with regard to the sun or moon, since the centrifugal force is the same for them all; the disturbing force being constantly variable for any one point, and depending partly on the difference of the distance of the point from the mean distance, and partly on the difference of the direction of the luminary, from its direction with respect to the centre, or, in other words, on its <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARALLAX">parallax</a>. It will be most convenient for computation to consider both these forces, for a sphere covered with a fluid, as referred to the direction of the circumference of the sphere, which will differ but little from that of the fluid; and it will appear that both of them, when reduced to this direction, will vary as the product of the sine and cosine of the distance from the diameter pointing to the luminary, that is as half the sine of twice the altitude: for the difference of gravitation, which depends on the difference of the distance, will always vary as the sine of the distance from the bisecting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> perpendicular to that diameter, and will be reduced to the direction of the surface, by diminishing it in the ratio of the cosine to the radius: and the effect of the difference of direction will be originally proportional to the sine of the distance from the diameter, and will in like manner be expressed, when reduced, by the product of the sine and cosine; and each force, thus reduced, will be equal, where it is greatest, to half of its primitive magnitude, since $\sin \cos 45^\circ = \frac{1}{2}$. "Thus, the gravitation towards the moon at the earth's surface, is to the gravitation towards the earth as 1 to 70 times the square of 60, or to 256 217: and the former disturbing force is to the whole of this as 2 to 60 at the point nearest the moon, and the second as 1 to 60 at the equatorial plane; and the sum of both, reduced to the direction of the circumference, where greatest, as 3 to 121; that is, to the whole force of the earth's gravitation, as 1 to 10 334 000; and in a similar manner we find, that the whole disturbing force of the sun is to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of the particles as 1 to 25 736 000." Or, if we call the moon's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> parallax $p$, and substitute $\frac{1}{p}$ for the distance, the whole of the lunar disturbing force in the direction of the surface will be $\frac{3}{2} \cdot \frac{F^2}{70} = \frac{3}{140} F^2$; or, if $z$ be the moon's zenith distance from any point of the surface, $f = \frac{3}{70} F^2 \sin \cos z$. Theorem B. [F]. The inclination of the surface of an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> spheroid, slightly elliptical, to that of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> sphere, varies as the sine of twice the distance from the circle of contact; and a particle resting on any part of it, without friction, may be held in equilibrium by the attraction of a distant body, [situated in the direction of the axis.] If a sphere be inscribed in an oblong spheroid, the elevation of the spheroid above the sphere must obviously be proportional, when measured in a direction parallel to the axis of the spheroid, to the ordinate of the sphere, that is, to the sine of the distance from its equator, and when reduced to a direction perpendicular to the surface of the sphere, it must be proportional to the square of that sine; and the tangent of the inclination to the surface of the sphere, which is equal to the fluxion of the elevation divided by that of the circumference, must be expressed by twice the continual product of the sine, the cosine, and the ellipticity, or rather the greater elevation, $e$, the radius being considered as unity: so that the elevation $e$ will also express the tangent of the inclination where it is greatest, since $2 \sin \cos 45^\circ = 1$; and the inclination will be everywhere as the product of the sine and cosine. If, therefore, the density of the elevated parts be considered as evanescent, and their attraction be neglected, there will be an equilibrium, when the ellipticity is to the radius as the disturbing force to the whole force of gravitation: for each particle, situated on the surface, will be actuated by a disturbing force tending towards the pole of the spheroid, precisely equal and contrary to that portion of the force of gravitation which urges it in the opposite direction down the inclined surface. Hence, if the density of the sea were supposed inconsiderable, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> with that of the earth, the radius being 20 839 000 feet, the greatest height of a lunar tide in equilibrium would be 2.0166 feet, and that of a solar tide .8097: that is, supposing the moon's horizontal parallax about 57', and her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> $\frac{1}{12}$ of that of the earth. Theorem C. [G]. The disturbing attraction of the thin shell, contained between a spheroidal surface and its inscribed sphere, varies in the same proportion as the inclination of the surface, and is to the relative force of gravity depending on that inclination, as three times the density of the shell, to five times that of the sphere. We may imagine the surface of the sphere to be divided by an infinite number of parallel and equidistant circles, beginning from any point at which a gravitating particle is situated, and we may suppose all these circles to be divided by a plane perpendicular to the meridian of the point, and consequently bisecting the equatorial plane of the spheroid: it is obvious, that, if the elevations on the opposite sides of the plane be equal at the corresponding points of each circle, no lateral force will be produced; but when they are unequal, the excess of the elevated <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> on one side above that of the other side will produce a disturbing or lateral force. Now, the elevation being everywhere as the square of the distance \( x \) from the equatorial plane, we may call it \( e^2x^2 \), and the difference, corresponding to any point of that <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEMICIRCLE">semicircle</a>, which is the nearer to the pole of the spheroid, will be \( e(x-x') = e(x+x')(x-x') \). But \( x+x' \) is always twice the distance of the centre of the supposed circle from the equatorial plane; and the distance of this centre from that of the sphere will be \( c \cos \psi \), if \( \psi \) be the angular distance of the circle from its pole; and calling \( \phi \) the distance of this pole, from the equatorial plane of the spheroid, the distance in question will be \( \cos \psi \sin \phi \), and \( x+x'=2\cos \psi \sin \phi \); and the difference \( x-x' \) is twice the actual sine of the arc \( \psi \) in the supposed circle, that is, twice the natural sine, reduced in the ratio of unit to the radius of this circle, which is \( \sin \psi \), reduced again to a direction perpendicular to the equatorial plane; whence \( x-x'=2\sin \psi \cos \psi \cos \phi \): and \( x^2-x'^2=4\sin \psi \cos \psi \sin \phi \cos \phi \). Hence it follows, that in different positions of the gravitating particle, the effective elevation at each point of the surface, similarly situated with respect to it, is as the product of the sine and cosine of its angular distance \( \phi \) from the equatorial plane, the other quantities concerned remaining the same in all positions. But the inclination of the surface of the spheroid, as well as the original disturbing force, varies in the same proportion of the product of the sine and cosine of the distance \( \phi \): consequently, the sum of this disturbing attraction and the original force will also vary as the inclination of the surface, and may be in equilibrium with the tendency to descend towards the centre, provided that the ellipticity be duly commensurate to the density of the elevated parts. Now, in order to find the actual magnitude of the disturbing attraction for a shell of given density, we must compute the fluent of \( \frac{4}{3}e \sin \psi d\psi \sin \cos \psi \sin \phi \), reduced first according to the distance and direction of each particle from the given gravitating particle; and we must compare the fluent with \( \frac{4}{3}\pi \), the attraction of the whole sphere at the distance of the radius or unity. But for the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> \( \psi \), the portion of the force acting in the common direction of \( \sin \psi \) is to the whole attraction at the same distance as \( \sin \psi \) to 1, so that the attractive force of any point of the semicircle will be \( 4e \sin \psi \cos \psi \sin \phi \), and its fluxion will be as \( \sin \psi \cos \phi \), of which the fluent is \( \frac{4}{3}e \sin \psi \cos \phi \), or when \( \psi=180^\circ \), \( \frac{4}{3}\pi \), and \( \frac{4}{3}\pi \sin \psi \) will express the effect of the disturbing attraction of the semicircles, of which \( \sin \psi \) is the radius, reduced to the direction of the middle point, of which the distance is \( 2\sin \psi \): the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> for this distance is as its square to 1; and for the direction, as the distance to \( \sin \psi \), together making the ratio of \( \frac{\sin \psi}{8\sin \psi} \), and the ultimate fluxion of the force will be \( 2e\pi \sin \psi \cos \phi \sin \cos \phi \) \[ \frac{\sin \psi}{8\sin \psi} \cdot d\psi = 2e\pi \frac{\sin \psi \cos \phi}{8\sin \psi} \sin \cos \phi \] but \( \sin \psi = 2\sin \cos \phi \), and the fraction becomes \[ \frac{8\sin \psi \cos \phi}{8\sin \psi} \cdot \cos \phi = \cos \phi \cdot \cos \phi = \cos \phi \cdot \cos \phi \cdot (\cos^2 \phi - \sin^2 \phi) = \cos^2 \phi - \cos^2 \phi = 2\cos^2 \phi \] Now, taking the fluent from \( \psi=0 \) to \( \psi=180^\circ \), we have \( 2f \cos \phi \cdot 2d\psi = \frac{8}{3} \cdot \frac{4}{5} \) and \( f \cos \phi \cdot 2d\psi = \frac{4}{3} \cdot \frac{4}{5} \) (Art. Fluents, n. 361, 359): the difference being \( \frac{3}{5} \cdot \frac{4}{5} = \frac{4}{5} \), whence the fluent of the force is found \( 2e\pi \sin \cos \phi \times \frac{4}{5} \times \frac{1}{n} \), calling the density of the fluid \( \frac{1}{n} \); or, where it is greatest, \( \sin \cos \phi \) being \( \frac{4}{5} \cdot \frac{4}{5} \), while the attraction of the sphere itself is \( \frac{4}{3}\pi \), which is to \( \frac{4}{5}\pi \) as 1 to \( \frac{3}{5}\pi \); and since the elevation \( e \) expresses also the maximum of the relative force of gravity depending on the tangent of the inclination (Theorem B), it is obvious that the disturbing attraction \( \frac{3}{5}e \) must be to the relative force \( e \), as \( \frac{3}{5} \) to 5. Corollary 1. If \( n=1 \), as in a homogeneous fluid sphere or spheroid, the disturbing attraction becomes \( \frac{3}{5}e \), and this attraction, together with the primitive force \( f \), must express the actual elevation \( e \), or \( \frac{3}{5}e + f = e \), whence \( f = \frac{2}{5}e \), and \( e = \frac{5}{2}f \), giving 2.024 and 5.042 for the magnitude of the solar and lunar tides, when \( f=.8097 \) and 2.0166 respectively. But this is obviously far from the actual state of the problem. Corollary 2. Supposing \( n = 5.4 \) (See Journ. R. I. Apr. 1820), we have \( \frac{3e}{27} + f = e \), and \( c = \frac{27}{24}f = \frac{9}{8}f \); so that the height of the primitive tides of an ocean of water, covering the whole surface of the earth, such as it actually is, ought to be .911 for the solar, and 2.27 for the lunar disturbing force; that is, supposing the sea to be without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INERTIA">inertia</a>, so as to accommodate itself at once to the form of equilibrium. But, in the actual state of the irregularities of the seas and continents, it is impossible to pay any regard to this secondary force, since the phenomena do not justify us in supposing the general form of the surface of the ocean such as to give rise to it. Theorem D. [H]. When the horizontal surface of a liquid is elevated or depressed a little at a given point, the effect will be propagated in the manner of a wave, with a velocity equal to that of a heavy body which has fallen through a space equal to half the depth of the fluid, the form of the wave remaining similar to that of the original elevation or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEPRESSION">depression</a>. Illustr. Celest. Mech. 378. p. 318. <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCHOLIUM">Scholium</a>. The demonstration of this theorem implies that water is incompressible, and that the pressure of each particle placed on the surface is instantaneously communicated through the whole depth of the fluid to the bottom. These suppositions are not indeed strictly accurate in any case, but they introduce no sensible error when the surface of the wave similarly affected is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> in comparison with the depth of the fluid. A <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> author, of celebrity, seems to have taken it for granted, that the pressure is propagated with the same velocity downwards and laterally; at least, if such is not his meaning, he has been somewhat unfortunate in the choice of his expressions; but there seems no reason whatever, why water should communicate force more slowly when it is perfectly confined, than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a> would do; and the divergence of the pressure of a certain portion of the surface of water, elevated a little, for example, above the rest, may be compared to the divergence of a sound entering into a detached chamber by an aperture of the same size with the given surface, which is probably small in comparison with its direct motion, but equally rapid, and in both cases depending on the modulus of the elasticity of the medium. Theorem E. [I]. A wave of a symmetrical form, with a depression equal and similar to its elevation, striking against a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> vertical obstacle, will be reflected, so as to cause a part of the surface, at the distance of one fourth of its whole breadth, to remain at rest; and if there be another opposite obstacle at twice that distance, there may be a perpetual vibration between the surfaces, the middle point having no vertical motion. Nat. Phil. I. p. 289. 777. Scholium 1. The elevation and depression of a spheroid, compared with the surface of the sphere of equal magnitude, exhibits a symmetrical wave in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of the proposition: and it is not necessary, that the shores should be very rocky or perpendicular, in order to produce a strong reflection; for, even the vibration of the water in the bottom of a common hemispherical basin is considerably permanent. Corollary 2. The vibrations of the water supposed to be contained in a canal, following the direction of the equator, and 90° in length, would be synchronous with the passage of a wave 180° in breadth, over any point of a canal of the same depth, and surrounding the whole globe. Scholium 2. It has been usual to consider the elevation of the tides, as identical with that of an oblong spheroid, measured at its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERTEX">vertex</a>, and therefore as amounting to twice as much as the depression of the same spheroid at the equator, considered in relation to the mean height belonging to a sphere of the same magnitude: but, the supposition is by no means applicable to the case of a globe, covered partially and irregularly with water, so that in almost all cases of actual tides, the elevation must be considered as little if at all greater than the depression, as far as this cause only is concerned; there are, however, some other reasons to expect, that the elevation of the great wave might often arrive at a distant port in somewhat greater force than the depression. Theorem F. [K]. The oscillations of the sea and of lakes, constituting the tides, are subject to laws exactly similar to those of pendulums capable of performing vibrations in the same time, and suspended from points which are subjected to compound regular vibrations, of which the constituent periods are completed in half a lunar, and half a solar day [or in some particular cases a whole day]. Supposing the surface of the sea to remain at rest, each point of it would become alternately elevated and depressed, in comparison with the situation in which it might remain in equilibrium; its distance from this situation varying according to the regular <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENDULUM">pendulum</a> (see Theorem B); and like all minute vibrations, it will be actuated by forces indirectly dependent on, and proportional to, this distance; so that it may be compared to a pendulous body remaining at rest in the vertical line, about which its point of suspension vibrates, and will consequently follow the motion of the temporary horizon, in the same manner as the pendulum follows the vibration of its point of suspension, either with a direct or a retrograde motion, according to circumstances, which will be hereafter explained: the operation of the forces concerned being perfectly analogous, whether we consider the simple hydrostatic pressure depending on the elevation, or the horizontal pressure, derived from the inclination of the surface, or the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENTIAL">differential</a> force immediately producing elevation and depression, depending on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> of the horizontal pressure, and proportional to the curvature of the surface. It becomes therefore necessary for the theory of the tides, to investigate minutely the laws of these compound and compulsory vibrations; which, together with the resistances affecting them, will be the subject of the next <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECTION">section</a>. Sect. III.—Of the Effects of Resistance in Vibrating Motions, whether Simple or Compound. Theorem G. If \( dw + Ads + Bsds + Dwds = 0 \); we have \( e^{\left(\frac{B}{D} + \frac{<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AD">AD</a> - B}{DD}\right)} = c \); ble being = 1. Scholium. For the better understanding of the mode of investigation which will be employed in these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a>, it will be proper to premise some remarks on the investigation of fluxional equations, by means of multipliers. A person, unacquainted with the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of modern mathematicians, would naturally understand, by a "criterion of integrability," some mode of distinguishing an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> that would be integrated, from one that was untractable; while, in fact, this celebrated criterion relates only to the accidental form in which the expression occurs, and not to its essential nature. If we take, for instance, the well known case of the fluxion of \( \frac{h}{y} \) \( \frac{dx}{dy} = y \frac{dx}{xy} - x \frac{dy}{xy} \), and making this \( = 0 \), we have also \( y \frac{dx}{xy} - x \frac{dy}{xy} = 0 \); and this expression no longer fulfils the conditions of integrability, until we multiply it again by \( \frac{1}{xy} \), and restore it to its perfect form. The direct investigation of such a multiplier is generally attended by insuperable difficulties; and the best expedient, in practical cases, is to examine the results of the employment of such multipliers, as are most likely to be concerned in the problem, with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDETERMINATE">indeterminate</a> coefficients, and to compare them with the equations proposed. In common cases, the finding of fluents, when only one variable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> is concerned, requires little more than the employment of a Table such as that of Meier Hirsch, or that which constitutes the Article Fluents in this Supplement; and the demonstration of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of the solution is in general furnished at once, for each case, by taking the fluxion of the quantity inserted in the Table as the fluent: but for the separation of different variable quantities, where they are involved with each other, the employment of proper multipliers is one of the most effectual expedients; and it is still more essential to the solution of equations between <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUXIONS">fluxions</a> of different orders, or their coefficients. Such equations require in general to be compared with some multiple of the exponential quantity \( e^{mt} \), which affords fluxions of successive orders, that have simple relations to each other, especially when \( dt \) is considered as constant. The multiples of \( \sin Ct \) and \( \cos Ct \), are also very useful in such investigations, and for a similar reason; but the solutions that they afford are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> less comprehensive than the former; though they are often simpler, and more easily obtained. It is not, however, necessary that the exponent of the multiplier should flow uniformly, as will appear from the first example of a problem which has been solved by Euler in his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">Mechanics</a>: the subsequent examples will possess somewhat more of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a>. Demonstration. The fluxion of \( e^{nt} (w + ps + q) \) is \( e^{nt} (dw + pds + (nw + nps + ng) ds) = e^{nt} dw + (p + ng) ds + ndsds + nds \); and comparing with this \( e^{nt} (dw + Ads + Bds + Dws) \), we have \( w = D \), \( np = B \), and \[ p = \frac{B}{n} = \frac{B}{D}; \text{ and, lastly, } p + nq = A, q = \frac{A - p}{n} = \frac{AD - B}{DD}; \] consequently the fluxion of \( e^{Ds} \left( w + \frac{B}{D} \right) + \frac{AD - B}{DD} \) is equal to nothing, and that quantity is constant, or equal to \( c \). Example. Let the given equation be that of a cycloidal pendulum, moving with a resistance proportional to the square of the velocity, or \( \frac{d^2 s}{dt^2} + Bs - D \frac{ds^2}{dt^2} = 0 \). Scholium 2. The space \( s \) being supposed to begin at the lowest point of the curve, the fluxion \( ds \) is <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a> during the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> on the positive side, and the force \( dds \) is consequently negative, and equal, when there is no resistance, to \( Bs \), \( B \) being a positive coefficient, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a>, in the case of gravitation, to \( \frac{2g}{l} \) or \( \frac{32}{l} \), \( l \) being the length of the pendulum, and \( g \) the descent of a falling body in the first second. The coefficient \( -D \) is negative, because the resistance acts in a contrary direction to that of the force \( Bs \), as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> as \( s \) remains positive, and coincides with it on the negative side. But in the return of the pendulum the signs are changed; so that the equation can only be applied to a single vibration: since the two forces in question oppose each other in the same points of the curve in which they before agreed, while the square \( \frac{ds^2}{dt^2} \) must always remain positive. Solution. If we multiply the given equation by \( ds \), and make the square of the velocity, or \( v = w = \frac{d^2 s}{dt^2} \), we have \( ds \frac{dds}{dt^2} + Bsds - D \frac{ds^2}{dt^2} ds = 0 = \frac{1}{2} dw + Bsds - Dwds \), and \( dw + 2Bsds - 2Dwds = 0 \); which, compared with the theorem, gives us \( 0 \) for \( A \), \( 2B \) for \( B \), and \( -2D \) for \( D \); and the solution becomes \[ e^{-2Ds} \left( w + \frac{B}{D} - \frac{B}{2DD} \right) = c, \text{ or } w = \frac{B}{D} + \frac{B}{2DD} + \frac{2Ds}{ce} \text{; and if } w = 0 \text{ when } s = \lambda, \text{ we have } \frac{B}{D} + \frac{B}{2DD} + \frac{2Ds}{ce} = 0, \text{ or, putting } \frac{B}{D} + \frac{B}{2DD} = \beta, \beta + ce^{2Ds} = 0, \] and \( c = -\beta e^{-2Ds} \); \( \beta \) being also \( \frac{B}{2DD} \) if \( \gamma = 1 + 2D \). We may also substitute \( \sigma \) for \( \lambda - s \), and \( ce^{2Ds} = -\beta e^{2D(\sigma - \lambda)} \), will become \( -\beta e^{-2Ds} \), and \[ w = \frac{B}{D} + \frac{B}{2DD} - \beta e^{-2Ds} = \frac{B}{2DD} (1 - \gamma e^{-2Ds}) + 2Ds). \] Now \( e^{-2Ds} = 1 - 2Ds + 2D^2s^2 - \frac{1}{2}D^3s^3 + \ldots \). \[ \frac{3}{2}D^4\sigma^4 - \ldots; \quad \text{and } (1 + 2D\lambda)e^{-2D\sigma} = 1 + 2D\lambda - 2D\sigma - 4D^2\sigma^2 + 2D^3\sigma^3 - D^4\sigma^4 - \ldots; \] whence \(w = \frac{B}{2DD}(2D\sigma - 2D(\lambda - \sigma) + 4D^2\sigma - 2D^3\sigma^3 - \ldots)\) \[= B(2\sigma - \gamma\sigma^2 + \frac{2}{3}D^2\sigma^3 - \frac{1}{3}D^3\sigma^4 + \ldots).\] Corollary 1. From this solution we obtain the point at which the velocity is greatest; and, by reversing the equation, we may also find the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of the vibration. For when \(w = 0\), we have \(B\sigma = D\sigma\), and \(B = D\sigma\), which is the obvious expression of the equality of the resistance to the propelling force. Putting the greatest value of \(w = x\), and the corresponding value of \(s = s\), we have \(x = \frac{B}{D^2} + \frac{B}{2DD} + \frac{2D\sigma}{D^5}\), since \(B = D\sigma\), and \(\frac{B}{2DD} = -ce = \frac{B\gamma}{2DD}e^{2D(\sigma - \lambda)}\); whence \(\frac{1}{\gamma} = e^{2D(\sigma - \lambda)}\), and \(\gamma = e^{2D(\lambda - \sigma)}\); consequently \(hl\gamma = 2D(\lambda - \sigma) = hl(1 + 2D\lambda)\), and \(2D\sigma = 2D\lambda - hl(1 + 2D\lambda)\), and \(s = \frac{1}{2D}\left(2D^2\sigma^3 - \frac{8}{3}D^3\sigma^4 + \ldots\right) = D^2\sigma^3 - \frac{4}{3}D^3\sigma^4 + \ldots\) And since \(x = \frac{B}{D^2}\), we have \(x = \frac{B}{2DD}(2D\lambda - hl[1 + 2D\lambda])\). Lemma. For the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVERSION">reversion</a> of a series, or of a finite equation, if \(z = ax + bx^2 + cx^3 + \ldots\) we have \(z = \frac{1}{a}z - \frac{b}{a^2}z^2 + \frac{c}{a^3}z^3 + \ldots\)

TOOKE

Pages 736-743

an ingenious grammarian and an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> politician, born in Westminster, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1736, was the son of Mr John Horne, a tradesman living in Newport Market. He was the third of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> children; but his father, having acquired considerable affluence, sent him first for a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to Westminster School, and then to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ETON">Eton</a>, where he remained five <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> six years without particularly distinguishing himself, and was removed sooner than had been intended on account of the accidental loss of an eye. He went, in 1755, to St John's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, and took a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of Bachelor of Arts there. He then became an usher in a school at Blackheath, kept by Mr Jennings; but he was soon after induced by his father to take deacon's orders, and obtained a curacy in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>. His own preference, however, was so much in favour of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, that in 1756 he entered as a student of the Middle Temple; but in 1760 he was persuaded to return to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and to receive ordination as a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>; and he officiated for three years in the chapelry of New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRENTFORD">Brentford</a>, which his father had purchased for him; performing his duties with decency, and taking some pains to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> the elements of medicine for the sake of the poorer members of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a>. He then went as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> to France with the son of Mr Elwes, a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERKSHIRE">Berkshire</a>, well known for his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> and his economy. In 1765, he commenced his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CAREER">career</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> an anonymous pamphlet in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of Wilkes and his party. He returned to the continent, and made the tour of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> with a Mr Taylor; and at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> he formed an intimacy with Wilkes himself, who then found it convenient to reside there. He had altogether laid aside his clerical character in these excursions, but he resumed it for a short time after his return: soon, however, he relap- sed into his political amusements; exerting himself, with some success, in various elections, as a partisan of his friend Wilkes, and taking up the cause of a Mrs Bigby, in the pursuit of an "<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> of blood," against the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDERERS">murderers</a> of her husband, who were supposed to have obtained a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> through corrupt <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>; though the widow at last disappointed him by accepting a pecuniary compensation for her <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of appeal. He was, however, successful, on his own behalf, in repelling a prosecution for a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBEL">libel</a> on Mr Onslow; and he gained some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> with a party in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> by suggesting to Beckford, then <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Mayor of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, the reply which he made to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a>'s answer to their remonstrance, and which may still be seen, engraved on the pedestal of Beckford's statue in Guildhall. He was soon after very active in establishing the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> for supporting the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">Bill</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">Rights</a>, and in obtaining the liberation of Bingley, the printer, who had been somewhat hastily committed to prison by Lord <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANSFIELD">Mansfield</a>. He had reason to be dissatisfied, in the year 1770, with the conduct of Wilkes, in some pecuniary transactions relating to the Society for the Bill of Rights: both parties appeared to the public in a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> somewhat ridiculous on the occasion, and neither of them gained in respectability, though the Society did not appear to value Wilkes the less for the exposures that took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; it was, however, shortly after dissolved, and most of its members, except the particular friends of Wilkes, were incorporated into the Constitutional Society. The next year, Mr Tooke completed his academical course at Cambridge, by taking the degree of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">Master</a> of Arts, though not without some opposition. He exerted himself greatly about this time, in procuring the publication of the debates of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">House</a> of Commons in the daily papers, notwithstanding the well-known standing Orders of the House; and so far as he was instrumental in carrying this point, he appears to have rendered at least one very essential <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; but Wilkes, and especially Almon, the bookseller, are said to have a still stronger claim to the merit of this transaction, whatever may have been its character. He had also a sharp contest with the anonymous "Junius," against whose hasty attack he defended himself with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> spirit and energy, and with unexampled success. In 1773, he made a formal resignation of his living, and meant at the same time completely to lay aside his clerical character, though no person seems to have felt himself authorised to accept this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his resignation; and he began to study the law very diligently, intending to make it the occupation of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. He adopted soon after a singular method of forcing himself upon the notice of the public, and of the House of Commons in particular: an inclosure bill being about to be hurried, as was reported, a little too rapidly through the House, he wrote some paragraphs in a newspaper, which reflected very severely on the conduct of the Speaker, on purpose that he might be summoned to appear before the House; and being placed at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, he gave such reasons for his conduct as produced some animated discussions, and in the end was supposed, though probably without foundation, to have caused the bill to be modified in some oppressive clauses. By these means he obtained the favour of Mr Tooke of Purley, who thought himself aggrieved by the bill in its original state, and received from him such assurances of testamentary favours as induced his nephew, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> Harwood, to agree upon a partition of their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> interest in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVERSION">reversion</a> of his estate; though Mr Horne never received, first and last, more than L.8000 from the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, notwithstanding the subsequent change of his name about the year 1782, in acknowledgment of his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>'s kindness, and his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> intimacy and frequent residence at Purley; the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> legatee, after all, being a Mr Beaseley. Mr Horne Tooke was, of course, a strenuous opposer of the American <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>; and in 1777, he published a very offensive advertisement, in which the sufferers in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Lexington were described as having been murdered by the King's troops. For this attack on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">Government</a>, he was tried at Guildhall, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1777; he conducted his own defence, but he was found guilty of the libel, and sentenced to a year's imprisonment in the King's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENCH">Bench</a>, and a fine of L.200. It was on this occasion that he first appeared before the public as a grammarian, in the criticisms which constitute his celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">Letter</a> to Mr Dunning. The next year he suffered a still severer <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>, in the refusal of the society of the Inner Temple to admit him to the bar, on account of his having taken orders; so that his prospects of professional advancement were utterly annihilated. This occurrence made him still more bitter against the existing Government, and in 1780 he printed some severe remarks upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> of Lord <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a>. He attempted to establish himself as a practical <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a> in Huntingdonshire; but he caught an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGUE">ague</a>, and soon became disgusted with an agricultural life; he returned to London, and occupied for some years a house near Soho <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">Square</a>. His <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of Parliamentary <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REFORM">reform</a>, contained in a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> letter addressed to Mr Dunning, were by no means extravagant, and he continued to adhere, in this respect, rather to the party of Mr Pitt than to that of Mr Fox. The publication of his grammatical dissertations, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the Diversions of Purley, afforded but a slight and imperfect intermission of his political pursuits, for his etymological works are as replete with the politics of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> as his speeches and his pamphlets; another of which appeared in 1788, under the title of Two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">Pair</a> of Portraits, being intended to serve the cause of Pitt's party in their elections. But in 1790 he became himself a candidate for the representation of Westminster, in opposition to Mr Fox and to Lord Hood; and he distinguished himself sufficiently as a popular orator, though he was not successful in the contest. He was tried, in 1794, for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">High</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">Treason</a>, together with several other members of the Corresponding <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">Societies</a>, who had been active in attempting to introduce some imitations of the French Revolution in the plans of reform which they brought forward. He exhibited on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> somewhat more of firmness than of good <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>: one of his associates had before been acquitted, and the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JURY">jury</a> speedily returned a similar verdict with respect to himself. He after- Tooke. wards dedicated the second volume of his *Diversions of Purley* to his counsel, Gibbs and Erskine, and to the jury who tried him. In 1796, he again became a candidate for the representation of Westminster; but again without success: and, notwithstanding his strong opinions respecting a reform in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">Parliament</a>, he afterwards condescended to accept from Lord Camelford, in 1801, a seat for the nominal burgh of Old Sarum. It was then to be determined <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a clergyman could sit in the House of Commons; but the ministry, instead of contesting the point with respect to his particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, brought in a bill to decide the question in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a> for the future, and he remained in the House till the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of the Parliament in the next year, but without particularly distinguishing himself in its proceedings. His last public effort, as a party <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, was made in espousing for a short time the cause of Mr Paull, as candidate for Westminster; but, he abandoned this gentleman in a subsequent contest. The later years of his life were chiefly passed in the society of a select circle of friends, who frequently partook of his hospitality at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WIMBLEDON">Wimbledon</a>. He died in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1822, leaving his property to some <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> daughters; for he had never been married. He was buried in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EALING">Ealing</a> church, and not in his garden, as he had directed; his executors thinking themselves the less bound by these instructions, as a literal compliance with them might have been unfavourable to the "<a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>" of the property. 1. His earliest publication was a pamphlet entitled *The Petition of an Englishman*, 1765. It consisted principally of apologies, for the private conduct and immoral writings of Wilken. 2. He also published *A Sermon* while he continued in the church, that is, before the year 1773: but it attracted little notice. 3. *A Letter to Mr Dunning*, 1778. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of his grammatical system, arising out of remarks on the particles employed by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTORNEY_GENERAL">Attorney-General</a> in his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDICTMENT">indictment</a>, and by the judges in his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>: it was afterwards incorporated into the *Diversions of Purley*. 4. *Facts*, 1780: consisting of remarks on the administration of Lord North; with some additions relating to finance, by Dr Price. 5. *A Letter on Parliamentary Reform*, 1782: addressed to Mr Dunning, afterwards Lord Ashburton. 6. *Epea Pteroenta, or Diversions of Purley*, 8. 1786. Ed. 2. 4. Part I. 1798. Part II. 1802. His great and celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>: rich indeed in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ETYMOLOGY">etymology</a> and in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, but meagre in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> and in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METAPHYSICS">metaphysics</a>. 7. *A Letter to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>*, 1787: relating to the supposed <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> with a Catholic. 8. *Two Pair of Portraits*, 8. 1788. The two Pitts contrasted, in opposite columns, with the two Foxes, in colours by no means favourable to the latter. 9. Many of his *Letters* have been printed in Stephens's *Life of Tooke*, 2 v. 8. Lond. 1813. It is from the last mentioned publication, that this historical sketch of Mr Tooke's life has principally been extracted: it now becomes necessary to add some remarks on his literary and moral qualifications; and in both these <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of view, the subject has been treated in so masterly a manner by the author of an article in the Quarterly Review, who is supposed to be a near relation of Tooke's most intimate friend, the late Colonel Bosville, that it would be presumption in any man to go over the same ground, without adopting very nearly the eloquent and energetic expressions, which that noble and learned person has employed. "Mr Tooke," says the accomplished Reviewer of the *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of his Life* (Q.R. Vol. VII. No. xiv. p. 325), "was possessed of considerable learning, as indeed his writings sufficiently show. To other more casual acquirements, he united a very extensive acquaintance with the Gothic dialects, of which he has so copiously and so judiciously availed himself in his etymological researches." But it must be remarked, that a person more intimately acquainted with the "Gothic dialects" as living languages <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> easily discover, that his knowledge of them was in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> but superficial, or that he was indebted for it more to grammars and dictionaries, than to any extensive study of the authors who had written in those languages, or to any <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of speaking them; and such a person will easily find a variety of instances, in which a very different etymon to that which he has assigned, will naturally suggest itself as the true origin of the word in question. (P. 320.) "Though Mr Tooke's philosophical works are the results of no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> and industry, yet they are neither written in a truly philosophical spirit, nor do they display traces of a mind, which, even if it had been wholly dedicated to the study of metaphysics, would have much enlarged the bounds of our knowledge in that nice and intricate branch of science. His object seems to have been rather to retard, than to advance the progress of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, by recalling us from those <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> conclusions as to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and operations of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> mind, which are built upon observation and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, to vague speculations, drawn from the imperfect <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> existing between the moral and the physical world. There can be no doubt, that the proposition, which he has succeeded in establishing, is highly interesting and important; and that, in the illustration of it, he has shown great learning, ingenuity, and research. But then, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, he has so monstrously exaggerated its importance, and so widely mistaken its tendency, and has attempted to raise so vast a superstructure upon such a narrow, slippery, and inadequate foundation, that we are quite lost in amazement, when we recollect how completely the sagacity, which guided him so well in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> of his principal fact, appears to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> him, when he comes to apply that fact to the purposes of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a>. The distance between what he has proved, and what he wishes us to believe that he has proved, is enormous. What he has proved is, that all words, even those that are expressive of the nicest operations of our minds, were originally borrowed from the objects of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> perception; a circumstance highly curious in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, consequently in the history of the human mind itself, and the complete demonstration of which, of course, reflects great credit upon its author. What he thinks he has proved is, that this etymological history of words is our true guide, both as to the present import of the words themselves, and as to the nature of those things, which they are intended to signify: a proposition so monstrous, that he has nowhere ventured to enunciate it in its general form, but has rather left it to be collected from the tenor of his remarks upon particular instances. In truth, the inferences at which Mr Tooke arrived, far from being warranted by his facts, are directly the contrary of those to which he ought naturally to have been led by the result of his own studies, when they were most successful. In tracing upwards, through all the mazes of etymology, the origin of words, he ought to have seen more clearly, if possible, than any body else, that their real present <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> is not to be sought for in their primitive signification, or in the elements of which they were originally composed, but that, on the contrary, their actual import, with which alone in reasoning we have to do, hardly ever corresponds with their etymological meaning, although the one always bears to the other a certain resemblance, more or less accurate, according to the greater or less effect of time and accident. One could without difficulty understand, how a person, unaccustomed to such considerations, and misled by a few instances partially chosen, should adopt a theory like that which Mr Tooke was desirous to establish; but how a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, minutely acquainted with the whole subject, and proceeding upon a most copious induction of particulars, should not have perceived that, in ninety-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> instances out of a hundred, such a doctrine would <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> absurdity, is, to us at least, inconceivable." The Reviewer then follows Mr Dugald Stewart in some very <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> criticisms, which this acute metaphysician had already made on several of Mr Tooke's examples, fully proving the complete fallacy of the system which so completely confounds the definition of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> with its etymology. Mr Tooke has, indeed, the merit of having demonstrated pretty clearly that all the parts of speech, including those which grammarians had often considered as expletives and unmeaning particles, may be resolved more or less completely into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOUNS">nouns</a> and verbs: but on the one hand it has been observed, that the very same doctrine may be clearly traced back to the works of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>; and on the other, it may be asserted with equal truth, if we wish to carry the theory to its utmost <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, that language consists only of nouns and one verb; since all verbs may in fact be resolved into participles, or <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-ADJECTIVES">adjectives</a>, compounded with auxiliary verbs, as well as those which exhibit this complication in their exterior form. "In the ordinary intercourse of life," Mr Tooke "was kind, friendly, and hospitable."—(P. 325.) "We doubt whether his temper was naturally good; but if it was not, he had a merit the more; for he had so completely subdued it by care and self-control, as never to betray, under any provocation, the slightest mark of that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRRITABILITY">irritability</a> which often accompanies talent, and which gains so rapidly upon those who know not how to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> against its approaches. Indeed, the aspect under which he appeared in private was by no means such as the stern cynicism and ferocious turbulence of his public conduct would have led one to expect; and those, whose <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of him has been formed exclusively upon his political character and his writings, will have some difficulty in believing that the curate of Brentford was one of the best bred gentlemen of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>. In this respect he was a sort of phenomenon. He was born in a low station: at no <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> did he appear to have possessed any remarkable advantages for the study of good breeding; on the contrary, the greater part of his life was spent in constant intercourse with coarse, vulgar, and uneducated men; yet his natural taste was so good, and he had profited so judiciously by whatever opportunities he enjoyed, that courts and high stations have seldom produced a better example of polite and elegant behaviour, than was exhibited by the associate of Messrs Hardy and Thelwall. Indeed, his manner had almost every excellence that manner can display: <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>, vivacity, frankness, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>. Perhaps, indeed, in its outward forms, and in that which is purely conventional, his courtesy wore the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of the 'vieille cour,' and was rather more elaborate, than is consistent with the practice of this lounging unceremonious age; but it was never forced or constrained, and it sat not ungracefully upon an old man." It may, however, deserve to be remarked, in contemplating this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARADOX">paradox</a>, though rather as a collateral coincidence than as a satisfactory explanation, that even from his infancy Tooke had actually seen something of the very highest society, having been admitted once or twice a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEICESTER">Leicester</a> House as a play-fellow to the late King: and though he may have learned but little from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the manners of the young Prince, yet the early habit of self-restraint, imposed by such a presence, may easily have imprinted some courtly traces on his character, which were not easily effaced, and which an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a> with the heirs of the first families of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, throughout his boyhood, at Westminster and at Eton, must naturally have made still more distinct and permanent. "He never appeared to greater advantage than in conversation." "He possessed an inexhaustible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUND">fund</a> of anecdotes, which he introduced with great skill, and related with neatness, grace, rapidity, and pleasantry: he had a quick sense of the ridiculous, and was a great master of the whole art of raillery, a dangerous talent, though the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of it in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> was always tempered by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a> and good humour." "In spite of labour and dissipation (p. 328), his life was protracted to a period which indicated an originally sound and vigorous frame. For the last twenty years, however, he was subject to several severe, distressing, and incurable infirmities. These he bore with a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a> and firmness which it was impossible not to admire: to the very last he never suffered himself to be beaten <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by them, nor ever for one moment indulged in complaint, or gave way to despondency. In the intervals of pain, nay, even when actually suffering under it, he preserved a self-command, which enabled him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a>, not only with spirit and vigour, but with all his accustomed cheerfulness and pleasantry, never making any demand upon the sympathy of his friends, or mentioning his own situation at all, except when occasionally, and by a very pardonable exercise of his sophistry, he amused himself in exalting its comforts, and explaining away its disadvantages; displaying, in this respect, a manly spirit and a practical philosophy, which, if they had been brought to bear upon his moral, as well as upon his physical condition, if they had been employed with as much effect in reconciling him to his political <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCLUSION">exclusion</a> as to his bodily sufferings, might have produced, not the very imperfect character we have been attempting to delineate, in which the unfavourable traits bear so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> a proportion to those of a nobler and more benign <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a>, but the venerable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a> of a truly wise and virtuous man." Reid's Memoirs, 8. Lond. 1812; Quarterly Review, June 1812; A. Stephens's Life of Tooke, 2 v. S. Lond. 1813; British Critic, N. S. Vol. I. p. 79, 193; (Aikin's General Biography, IX. 4. Lond. 1814; Chalmers's Biographical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>, XXIX. 8. Lond. 1816.) (A. L.) TURKISH EMPIRE. Although this empire has undergone but slight alterations since the account of it contained in the Encyclopaedia was written, yet, as its <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STATISTICS">statistics</a> have had some new light thrown on them by recent publications, we shall give a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> sketch of its present state. The extent of this empire has been variously estimated by different writers; and, after consulting them, we rather concur in the calculations made by Hassel, the latest of them, founded on the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHARTS">charts</a> of Reichart and Niedls, because they are corroborated by the last map constructed by Arrowsmith, and by that of Lapless. In this account of the extent of the empire we have included all those countries over which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> claims the sovereignty, although in many of them that sovereignty is either not acknowledged or very feebly exercised. | Square Miles | |--------------| | Turkey in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> contains | 180,074 | | Turkey in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> on the Continent | 436,629 | | <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">Islands</a> of Turkey in Asia | 11,050 | | The African Dominions | 276,480 | | **Total** | **904,233** | In countries where no censuses have been taken in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times, in which no registers of births or deaths are preserved, where no general conscription has been introduced, and where even the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of houses is not known, the accounts of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> must be <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> estimates or rather conjectures; and, therefore, it is not extraordinary that different writers should have presented results so distant from each other as those we have examined. Two censuses have, indeed, been instituted; one in the middle of the sixteenth, and the other at the beginning of the seventeenth century. Their results are not, however, now known; and if they were, they would scarcely be tolerable guides at this day, when the whole state of affairs has undergone such great alterations. Hassel, in 1816, calculated the whole number of Turkish subjects at 24,070,000; and, in 1819, Lichtenstern estimated them at 24,880,000, whilst Gräberreck reckoned them to be in round numbers 23,000,000. Though these industrious writers thus approached nearly to each other in their totals, they differ most widely in the component parts. Thus, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR">Asia <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>, they disagree to the extent of five or six millions; and in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> and its dependencies to the extent of three or four. The financial affairs of the Turkish empire are involved in still greater obscurity than the state of the population. From the system, which uniformly prevails, by which every governor of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> collects imposts, and expends them on the local objects under his management—that which is received into the general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a> bears no proportion to that which is extracted from the subject. Many of the provinces are compelled to deliver contributions in their productions, which productions are appropriated to some specific public department. Thus Egypt was required to deliver to the arsenal 1000 quintals of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, 200 jars of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, 2000 pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, and 140 quintals of linen yarn; and to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERAGLIO">Seraglio</a> 36,000 measures of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, 45,000 okas of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, 2000 measures of pease, besides stipulated quantities of ginger, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CINNAMON">cinnamon</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>, and other smaller <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. The other provinces are required in a similar manner to contribute to the demands of the Imperial Government. The annual sum which flows into the treasury has been estimated, by Contemir and Thornton, at about L3,000,000 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">Sterling</a>, and by Eton at near L4,000,000. Whatever may be the amount of the public income, it is distinct from the revenues which accrue to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">Emperor</a> personally, of which no account can be obtained; but it is imagined that they amount to much more than the expenditure of the imperial establishment, and that vast sums have been accumulated in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> treasury. These personal revenues arise from domains, from confiscations, from presents, and from the sale of governments and other offices. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Marcellus, in a work published at the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a> in 1732 (Stato Militare de Imperio Ottomanno), asserts, that, at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Ibrahim in 1639, his successor, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONRAD">Conrad</a> IV., found L33,000,000 Sterling in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>; and that, as, by a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> law, every Emperor is bound to increase this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>, during his reign, it had been vastly augmented at the time he wrote. This accumulation of private treasure is deemed an indispensable part of the state policy of Turkey, where, as in every despotic government, the individual filling the throne is exposed to sudden insurrections and interior revolutions. Meusel thinks that this treasure was much reduced by the war with Russia, which terminated in 1812, when the private hoods were compelled to come forth in aid of the national treasury to a very great, but unknown, extent; as the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> was then paid with coins of very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> dates. The expenses of the government are involved in as much obscurity as the income from which they are defrayed. The greater part of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> costs but little in time of peace; being fur- nished with necessaries by the several provinces in which they are quartered, and which are collected from their feudatories by the governors of them. The debt of the state, which, in 1803, amounted to only L.3,500,000 Sterling, has been increased by the various unfortunate events that have occurred since that period to upwards of L.70,000,000; and, in spite of forced loans, to which the government has had recourse, and of large contributions from the religious establishments, the state-obligations pay an interest at the rate of 12 per cent. Under a government, where all <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> is held on the condition of military service, the number of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> must be great in proportion to the population; but in Turkey the numbers have been kept down by the want of means to provide the necessary arms and equipments. According to the most recent accounts, the regular army amounts to 125,000 infantry, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>, artificers, sappers, miners, and armourers, included; and 12,500 cavalry; but to the latter may be added 100,000 feudal horsemen, who may be made available for internal defence. The Janisaries make 80,000 of the infantry; and these are rather garrison <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a>, for the most part, than regular troops. The best corps consist of those called the new regulars, amounting to 24,000 men, who, as well as the artillery, are armed and disciplined after European models. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a> of Turkey has of late declined. It now consists of 15 ships of the line, the same number of frigates, and about 30 smaller vessels. Very few of these ships are fit for service; and the naval arsenal is so destitute of stores that fewer still can be equipped. At all times the best seamen in their fleet consisted of Greeks; and, since the insurrection of that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, greater difficulties than before have been found in working and fighting their ships. This accounts for the different disasters which the Turkish navy has experienced during the course of the existing contests with their Greek subjects. As the greater part of the inhabitants of the Turkish dominions are collected in and around the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> for security, the intervals of land between these towns are almost wholly uncultivated. Where any cultivation is practised, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is highly grateful, and produces abundant returns for the labour bestowed on it in corn, wine, oil, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, hemp, cotton, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, madder, and other <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a> materials. The woods afford excellent <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> in abundance. Horses, cows, sheep, goats, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAME">game</a>, are plentifully reared. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">fisheries</a>, both in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> and seas, are much neglected, except by the Greeks, who have occasion for them from the numerous fasts prescribed by their religious tenets. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">Honey</a> and wax are liberally supplied; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> is collected in all the provinces south of the Danube. The mineral products are now almost wholly confined to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, though <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver were formerly worked in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Bosnia, and those of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOLDAVIA">Moldavia</a> and Wallachia are rich in minerals. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> in Turkey are neither numerous nor abundant. The best of them is <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> of various colours and qualities. Dyes of several kinds, but especially that made from madder, and universally known through Europe by the name of Turkey-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, are supplied. Cottons are made in several places, as are coarse woollen cloths and carpets. Silks and silk gaizes, of a very delicate texture, are made at Constantinople, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SALONICA">Salonica</a>, and at Scio. Iron, and especially <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> wares, are furnished from several parts of the empire. Besides these, the smaller articles, snuff, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>, sail-cloth, glass <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARE">ware</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a>, are produced, but not in quantities equal to the demand. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of Turkey is almost exclusively in commerce. The hands of the Greek and Armenian subjects, or of Europeans established in the commercial cities, who are collectively distinguished by the name of Franks. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> exports consist of cotton wool, silk, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, oil, currants, rosin, wine, horses, cows, skins and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HIDES">hides</a>, leather, linseed, corn, cheese, Turkish yarn, and carpets. The chief imports are—cloths of wool, silk, and cotton, colonial wares, glass, watches, hardware, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, paints, cabinet ware, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUREMBERG">Nuremberg</a> wares, precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, jewellery, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> slaves from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, from <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEORGIA">Georgia</a>, and the Caucasian territory. The greatest traffic is with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, partly by land. The next in amount is with England, and then follows that with France, Italy, and Russia. The internal trade of Turkey is extensive, chiefly in the hands of Armenians, who <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> the productions of Europe for those of Asia, including <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIA">India</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>. Nearly the whole mercantile shipping belongs to the Greek subjects of the empire, whose resistance to its authority has an injurious effect on its general commerce. The chief trading cities in European Turkey are Constantinople, Salonica, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALLIPOLI">Gallipoli</a>, and Galatz. The Turkish divisions of the empire are purely military, founded on feudal principles, and even retaining the military names. The whole dominion is divided into twenty-five districts, which are subdivided into sandshaks (Standards); each sandshak contains a number of tracts, called tiamars or siamets (Sabres). Besides these, there are other divisions, used purely for the civil and financial purposes of the government. The European part of Turkey comprehends the four provinces of Roumelia, Bosnia, the Islands, and the principalities of Moldavia and Wallachia. Roumelia is subdivided into sandshaks or standards, and contains about 6,000,000 inhabitants. The most populous cities, and their estimated inhabitants, as calculated by Andreossy in the year 1815, according to the consumption of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, were the following: - Constantinople, 597,000; <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ADRIANOPLE">Adrianople</a>, 100,000; - Salonica, 60,000; Sofia, 46,000; Ruschak, 30,000; - Philopopolis, 30,000; Ionina, 30,000; <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LARISSA">Larissa</a>, 25,000; - Sistove, 21,000; Varma, 16,000; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MISITRA">Misitra</a>, 16,000; - Scutori, 16,000; Tripoliza, 12,000; Sillistra, 10,000; - and Baba, Nicopoli, Stovi, or Uskub, and Pristina, from 9000 to 10,000 each. Bosnia contains about 850,000 inhabitants. The cities are Bosna-Serai, with 65,000; Banjaluka, with 15,000; Zwornick, with 14,000; and Trebon, with 10,000 souls. The Ejalet Dschesair, or Province of the Islands, according to Lichtenstern, contained in 1819 about Turkish Empire. 525,000 inhabitants, chiefly Greeks, and the following cities: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALIPOLI">Galipoli</a>, with 17,000; Castorea, with 18,000; Betagela, with 15,000; <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HYDRA">Hydra</a>, with 40,000; Candia, with 15,000; Negroponte, with 16,000; Canes, with 12,000; and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> and Levadia, with 10,000 inhabitants each. Wallachia and Moldavia are rather under the nominal than the real government of Turkey, though the Waiwode is nominated by the Porte. He is always appointed from some of the noble Greek families, generally for a short period, and uniformly by means of bribery. Wallachia contains about 1,000,000 inhabitants, chiefly of the Greek church, and they are governed by ancient feudal laws, which are corruptly administered by magistrates who owe their authority to barefaced corruption. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUCHAREST">Bucharest</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, contains from 50,000 to 60,000 inhabitants. Moldavia has been contracted by cessions to Russia, and now contains about 500,000 inhabitants, who are of the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and under a government similar to that of Wallachia. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JASSY">Jassy</a>, the capital, contains 27,500 inhabitants. Galatz, a trading city on the Danube, has about 8000 regular inhabitants, and a vast number of strangers, who <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> to it for commercial purposes. Turkish Asia comprehends the following countries: 1st, The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> of Asia Minor, with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Cyprus, and some smaller islands in the Egean and the Mediterranean seas, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> of Marmora. 2d, That part of Georgia which has remained to Turkey since the last peace with Russia. 3d, A portion of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a>. 4th, The whole country of Mesopotamia, that of the Curdo, and a part of Irack. 5th, The whole of Soristan or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, with which the Turks include the district of Yemen in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, over which they have no actual power, and the cities of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECCA">Mecca</a>, Medina, and Jeddo, which have been lately again taken by them from the Wahabees, but which properly form a part of Arabia. These natural or ancient divisions are now scarcely regarded by the Turks. The whole dominion is, for purposes of administration, divided into twenty-one governments, viz. 1st, Anatolia, including that portion of Asia Minor which comprehends the provinces of Bithynia, Paphlagonia, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALATIA">Galatia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSIA">Mysia</a>, Lydia, Lycia, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARIA">Caria</a>, and Pisidia. The chief cities are, Kukatia, or Cotyaum, with, according to Malte-Brun, 50,000 inhabitants; Brussa, with, according to Kinneir, 50,000; <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERGAMO">Bergamo</a>, the ancient Pergamos, Anatolia, with, according to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAUFORT">Beaufort</a>, 8000; Kara-hissa, with 60,000; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGORA">Angora</a>, with 20,000; Kastimuni, with 13,000; Sinope, with 10,000; <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMYRNA">Smyrna</a>, with 100,000; Scalamuwo, with, according to Galt, 20,000; Scio, in the island of that name, with 25,000, according to Galt, 20,000; to Wittman, 25,000; and to Olivier, 30,000; almost wholly Greeks, and lately destroyed. 2d, Kibris, or the island of Cyprus, with about 120,000 inhabitants, of whom 16,000 are in the city of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NICOSIA">Nicosia</a>. 3d, Itschill, a part of Asia Minor, comprehend- ing the ancient <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CILICIA">Cilicia</a>, Isauria, and Pamphylia. Its chief cities are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADANA">Adana</a>, with 30,000 inhabitants; and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TARSUS">Tarsus</a>, with 30,000. 4th, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARAMANIA">Caramania</a>, comprehending a portion of Asia Minor, which was formerly Cappadocia, and parts of Galatia, and Phrygia <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a>. Its chief cities are, Konia, or Iconium, with 30,000 inhabitants; La-renda, or Caraman, with, according to Kinneir, 15,000; and Aschier, or Antioch, with 60,000. 5th, Merash, extending over part of Cappadocia, of Armenia Minor, and of Cilicia Campestris.
