Mr Bigge remarks, that "though the free settlers have not, as a body, been the most successful improvers, either of their own condition or that of the colony, yet the best cultivated estates, and the greatest quantity of cattle, belong to them, though they have not lately engaged in mercantile operations." The large grants that have been recently made have rendered the quantity of land, held by classes of individuals, a less accurate criterion of property than it was before those grants were made. In the year 1810, the land cleared was to the land granted as 1½ to 4; but in the year 1820, when the land granted was 389,000 acres, the portions returned as cleared were 54,898 acres, or as 1½ to 7. Of the cleared land, in 1820, 16,706 acres were cultivated to yield wheat, 11,270 maize, 1230 barley, 379 rye and oats, 213 peas, and beans, 504 potatoes, and 1994 in orchards and garden ground. The future progress of this colony must depend mainly on the productions raised from the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, and hence the condition of its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, including the breeding of cattle, becomes a most interesting subject. The first land settled near <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-SYDNEY">Sydney</a>, though then moderately fertile, has been exhausted by over-cropping, so that a considerable expenditure in manure, or in labour for fallowing, or in both, is indispensable to renew its productive powers. It has hence become necessary to pay attention to the production and proper application of manure, as well as to the cultivation of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> food for the cattle. Lucerne, sanfoin, and burnet, as well as rye-grass and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEADOW">meadow</a> fescue, have been introduced and gradually assimilated to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>. It has been remarked of the grass seeds imported from Europe, that their first and second flowering is in conformity with the season in Europe; but that the next time they flower according to the season of New South Wales. The cost of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECLAIMING">reclaiming</a> an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACRE">acre</a> of forest land, of converting it into tillage, and of sowing it with wheat, is calculated to amount to L.6, 10s. The cost of the same operation to fit it for maize would be L.5, 8s. 6d. Mr Cox, the surveyor, has estimated, that on a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">farm</a> of 50 acres, when the government supplied subsistence for six months, the expense would exceed the produce L.5, 19s. the first year; that in the second year the produce would exceed the expenditure L.49, 10s., and in the third year L.36, 10s.; after which, recourse must be had to the renovating power of manure. Maize and wheat are grown on the same land in one year; the former when hoed well, and twice hilled up, being found a good <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> for the latter. Wheat is sowed in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> or April, and harvested in November. Maize is sowed in November and gathered in April. The produce of wheat on the Hawkesbury settlement, from 1804 to 1814, was from 21 to 25 bushels to the acre, and since the last of those periods from 15 to 20 bushels. The land on the rising ground is inferior to that on the borders of the river, but the wheat grown on it, though yielding less in quantity, is of a superior <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>. Mr Oxley, the Surveyor-General, thinks the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> produce of wheat on the colony does not exceed 10 bushels to the acre; whilst, on land of similar quality, the produce of maize is from 30 to 60 bushels. The price of wheat has been from 11s. to 12s. 6d.; of maize from 3s. to 7s. per bushel. Besides the grains, attempts have been directed to several articles whose cultivation appears suitable to the climate. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">Flax</a> has been grown with success, but has not been extended from the very limited demand for it in the settlement. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">Tobacco</a> has been well produced, but from want of sufficient practice in curing the leaves, the tobacco of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">Brazil</a> has been so generally preferred, as to leave but little inducement to grow it in the colony; though of late, some improvements in drying offer a prospect of more success. Vines have not yet been prosperous, owing to blights which probably have arisen from improper exposure to prevailing winds. As this is an object of great importance, Mr J. Macarthur has paid much attention to rectify any errors, and hopes are entertained of more favourable results in future, than have hitherto been produced. The same <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, one of the earliest settlers, with his characteristic spirit, has been at pains to introduce the olive, and as far as can be judged from the trees, which are yet but in their infancy, with the greatest <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> of success. All the finer <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of Europe are most profusely brought forth, and in some gardens, the choicer kinds of the tropics are successfully cultivated. The breeding of cattle must, however, be the most sure <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> to the prosperity of the colony for some years to come. The numbers of horned cattle have quintupled between the years 1810 and 1820. In the latter year they amounted to 54,103; besides those tame cattle, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> have grown up wild in the woods, derived from some stock which early strayed from the settlement, and which were supposed to have perished, till their offspring were discovered in large herds in the interior. The sheep have been tripled in ten years. In 1820, they amounted to 99,487. Mr Macarthur has a flock of 6800, of which about 300 are pure Merinos, and yield <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> of excellent fineness. As the duty on wool from New South Wales has been reduced to 8d. per lb. in Great Britain, eager hopes are entertained of success, which will naturally tend to increase the numbers, and to improve the quality of the wool. The average <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of the fleeces of the New South Wales Merinos is about 2 lb. 7 oz. Some few bales of that wool have been sold in England at 5s. 6d. per lb.; and one at 10s. 4d.; but the far greater part have hitherto sold at about 2s. The importation into Great Britain has been, in 1819, 71,299 lbs.; 1820, 112,616 lbs.; 1821, 175,433 lbs. The increase of horses has been in nearly the same ratio as the sheep. In 1810, they were 1114; and in 1820, 3659. They are generally of the European breed, with a mixture of the Arabian brought from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIA">India</a>. Pigs and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a> have increased in nearly the same proportion as other stock. The mineral productions of this settlement are yet but slightly ascertained. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">Iron</a> has been found about eight miles from Port-Dalrymple, which is said to be equal in quality to that of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a> have not yet been worked. There is abundance of coal at Hunter's River, about 50 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PORT_JACKSON">Port-Jackson</a>. The vein is three feet thick, was worked by a passage from the river, but is now by a shaft 112 feet deep, and the labour of twenty-seven men can extract twenty tons per day. In this labour, the criminals from Sydney are destined to be employed. Lime, for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, has hitherto been burnt from oyster-shells, as no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a> has been discovered near the settled ports. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">Common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> has been extracted from <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, but from the bitter not being accurately separated, the culinary salt of England, notwithstanding its price, is generally preferred. The circumstances of the colony are not favourable to manufactories; but some <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a>, blankets, wool, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TARES">tares</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> stockings, and coarse cloths, have been made from the native wool. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-POTTERY">Pottery</a> wares, of different kinds, have also been made, but they have not yet acquired the art of glazing them. The most advantageous operation of manufacture is <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TANNING">tanning</a>; but, from want of sufficient practical knowledge, it has been hitherto badly performed. The bark of the mimosa, a tree that abounds in the interior, is found to contain the requisite properties for tanning <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HIDES">hides</a>. With a little more <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, and with some regulations to prevent damage to the hides on flaying them, the colony might supply itself with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> from the cattle bred and slaughtered at home. The foreign trade of the colony consists of the importations of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, spirits, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>, and cotton goods, from <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>; of tea, sugar-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CANDY">candy</a>, silks, and some clothing, made of English cloth, from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>; of iron and hardware, cottons, millinery, wines, porter, cheese, and salted <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, from England; and of sugar, tobacco, and spirits, from Brazil. The exportations have hitherto been but trifling. Wool has been already noticed; <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> skins and fish <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> might have formed returns but for their being <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with higher duty in England, if taken by a colonial than by a British vessel. Exportations to China have been made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDAL">sandal</a>-wood, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEARL">pearl</a> shells, previously collected at the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">Islands</a>. Some attempts have been made to export flour to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> of Good Hope, and horses to Batavia; some coals have also been shipped for Bengal and for Batavia. The shipping of the colony consists of twenty-seven vessels, from 15 to 184 tons burden. This branch of industry is much retarded in its growth by the restrictions which are found necessary to prevent the escape of convicts by sea. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> trade has been assisted by the establishment of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a>; but the institution has been injured by having suffered its cashier to defraud it of nearly L. 10,000, being half the capital. The principal circulating medium is the bills of the Government, or receipts for stores received by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMISSARY">Commissary</a>, which amount to about L. 40,000. The smaller operations are performed by means of the notes of the bank; which are issued for 2s., 6d., 5s., 10s., 20s., and five pounds. The legal <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> in the colony was 8%, and is now raised to 10 per cent. By the accounts of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> for seven years, ending September 1821, it appears that the taxes collected in that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> amounted to L. 174,310, 10s. and the expenditure to L. 163,790, 8s. The income is derived chiefly from port dues, import duties, licences, and tolls. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> expenditure has been on the establishments for <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> and female orphans, and for public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>—for public buildings and works—for salaries to officers—and for public and judicial charges. In all the grants, reservations of land have been made for the support of the clergy, and for the maintenance of schools. The clergy are under the inspection of one of their number, denominated senior chaplain. Some Roman Catholic chapels are building, and one for the Wesleyan <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METHODISTS">Methodists</a>. The public services of religion are reported to be attentively observed. The administration of justice is executed in a court established by special <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of Parliament, in which the Chief is an English Barrister; and recently an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTORNEY_GENERAL">Attorney-General</a> has been appointed, who is to be the general prosecutor of all offenses. See Wentworth's New South Wales; Parliamentary Papers ordered, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">House</a>, to be printed at the following dates—19th <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1822, 19th April 1821, 13th March 1823, 9th March 1821. (w. w.)

WATT

Pages 842-848

a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, mechanician, and civil engineer, whose inventive talents, extensive knowledge of the sciences and arts, and practical application of them to the purposes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> him in the foremost <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of those illustrious men, whose discoveries have influenced the state of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, and conferred distinction upon their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>-grandfather farmed his own small estate in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Aberdeen, but engaging in the civil wars, was killed in one of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MONTROSE">Montrose</a>'s battles, and his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> lost to his family. His son, Thomas Watt, left an infant, was brought up by relations, and hav- ing a turn for the mathematical sciences, made such proficiency by his own exertions, under very unto- <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARD">ward</a> circumstances, occasioned by the persecutions of the times, as to enable him at a later and quieter <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> to establish himself at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GREENOCK">Greenock</a>, as a teacher of these sciences, and of the dependent arts of survey- ing and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>. There he acquired reputation, and dying in 1794, at the advanced age of 91, left a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> record of his partiality to his profession in the inscription upon his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> in the West <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a>- yard.* He had two sons, John and James; the former brought up as a mathematician, settled first at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AYR">Ayr</a>, and afterwards at Glasgow, where he was much em- ployed in surveying and directing the improvement of estates; was an able <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and drew neatly and accurately, which was not very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in those days. He died in 1737, at an early age, leaving a Survey of the River <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLYDE">Clyde</a>, from Glasgow to the Point of Toward, which was published by his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> several years afterwards. James, his younger brother, of an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>, ingenious, and enterprising mind, became a merchant in Greenock, and was for upwards of twenty years a member of the Town-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">Council</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>, and a zealous promoter of the improvements of the town. By his wife, Agnes Muirheid, he had two sons, James, the subject of the present article, and John, a youth of promising abilities, who was lost at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> soon after he became of age. Misfortunes in trade, and the decay of the faculties of his mind, oc- casioned his retirement from business some years be- fore his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened in 1782, in his eighty- fourth year. James Watt, his eldest son, and only surviving child, was born at Greenock, the 19th <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1736. He received the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> in the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> of his native town; but from the ex- treme delicacy of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, was with difficulty enabled to attend the classes, and owed much of his acquirements to his studious habits at home. Little more is known of his early years, than that, from the first, he manifested a partiality for <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> con- trivances and operations, and frequently employed himself in that way. The desire of improvement in an art then little practised in Scotland, induced him to go to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in his eighteenth year, and there to place himself under the tuition of a mathematical in- strument-maker; but he remained little more than a twelvemonth, the infirm state of his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> com- pelling his return to the paternal <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a>. In that short period, he appears to have made great proficiency, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>, after his return to Scotland, to perfect himself in this art, both at home and on his visits to his mother's relations at Glasgow, where it was his wish to establish himself. But some opposi- tion being made by the corporations, who considered him as an intruder upon their privileges, the Professors of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a> took him under their protection, and accommodated him with an apartment and premises for carrying on his business within their precincts, with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> and office of Mathematical <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">Instrument</a>- maker to the University. This took place in 1757, when he was twenty-one years of age, and it must be inferred, that he had already given satisfactory proofs of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> to the eminent men who then adorn- ed that seat of learning; of whom it is sufficient to mention the names of Robert Simpson, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a> Smith, Dr <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a>, and of Dr Dick, the Professor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>. There Mr Watt applied sedu- lously to business, and in the few intervals which its concerns, and ill-healthallowed, cultivated those various talents which distinguished him in after life; and there a lasting friendship was formed with the kindred minds of Dr Black, and of Mr, afterwards Dr John, Robison; then a student at the University, and nearly of his own age. He remained in the College until some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in the year 1763, when he removed into the town previous to his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a>, Miss Miller, which took place in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> of the following year. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEAM_ENGINE"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol19.html#article-STEAM">Steam</a>-Engine had been a frequent subject of conversation between Mr Robison and himself, and * He is there styled, Professor of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">Mathematics</a>. the former had suggested the possibility of its application to the moving of wheel <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>. About the year 1761 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 1762, Mr Watt had tried some experiments on the force of steam in a Papin's digester, and had constructed and worked with strong steam a small <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a>, consisting of an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a> syringe; the bottom of the rod of which was loaded with a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, alternately admitting the steam below the piston, and letting it off to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>. Observing the imperfections of this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>, he soon abandoned it; but the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> necessary to be bestowed upon his business prevented his reconsidering it, until the winter of 1763-4, when he was employed by the Professor of Natural Philosophy to put in order a working model of a steam-engine upon Newcomen's construction. When he had repaired it and set it to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, he found that the boiler, though <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> in proportion to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a>, was barely able to supply it with steam for a few strokes per minute, and that a great <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INJECTION">injection</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> was required, though it was but lightly loaded by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PUMP">pump</a> attached to it. It soon occurred, that the cause lay in the little cylinder (two inches diameter, six inches stroke), <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> a greater surface to condense the steam than the cylinders of larger engines did, in proportion to their respective contents. By shortening the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> of water in the pump, less steam and less injection water were required, and the model worked at a proper speed. Thus the purpose for which it was put into his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> was accomplished; and with this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of accounting for the defect and this result, most artists would have been satisfied. Not so Mr Watt. He had now become aware of a great consumption of steam, and his curiosity was excited to a more accurate <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> of the causes, in which he proceeded in a truly philosophical manner. The cylinder of his small model being of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, he conceived that less steam would be condensed by substituting cylinders of some material which would transmit <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> more slowly. He made a larger model with a cylinder (six inches diameter, and one foot stroke) of wood, soaked in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and baked to dryness. He ascertained, from experiments made with boilers of various constructions, that the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> water is neither in proportion to the evaporating surface, nor to the quantity of water, as had been supposed, but to the heat that enters it; and that the latter depended chiefly on the quantity of surface exposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the fire. He likewise determined the weight of coal required for the evaporation of any given quantity of water. Being convinced that there existed a great <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a> in the statement which had been previously given of the bulk of water when converted into steam, he proceeded to examine that point by experiment; and discovered, that water, converted into steam of the heat of boiling water, was expanded to 1800 times its bulk: or, as a rule for ready calculation, that a cubic inch of water produced a cubic foot of steam. He constructed a boiler to be applied to his model, which should show, by inspection, the quantity of water evaporated, and consequently, would enable him to calculate the quantity of steam used in every stroke of the engine. This he now proved to be several times the full of the cylinder. He also observed, that all attempts to improve the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VACUUM">vacuum</a>, by throwing in more injection water, caused a disproportionate waste of steam: and it occurred to him, that the cause of this was the boiling of water in vacuo at very low heats (recently determined, by Dr <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CULLEN">Cullen</a>, to be under 100°); consequently, at greater heats, the injection water was converted into steam in the cylinder, and resisted the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> of the piston. He now perceived clearly, that the great waste of steam proceeded from its being chilled, and condensed by the coldness of the cylinder before it was sufficiently heated to retain it in an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> state; and that, to derive the greatest advantage, the cylinder should always be kept as hot as the steam that entered it, and that, when the steam was condensed, it should be cooled <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to 100°, or lower, in order to make the vacuum complete. Early in 1765, the fortunate thought occurred to him of accomplishing this, by condensing the steam in a separate vessel, exhausted of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and kept cool by injection, between which and the cylinder a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> was to be opened every time steam was to be condensed, while the cylinder itself was to be kept constantly hot. No sooner had this occurred to him, than the means of effecting it presented themselves in rapid succession. These have been in a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> already described in the Encyclopaedia. A model was constructed, and the experiments made with it, placed the correctness of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a>, and the advantages of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>, beyond the reach of doubt. In the course of these trials, he was much struck by the great heat communicated to the injection water by a small quantity of steam, and proceeded by a very simple experiment to satisfy himself upon that subject, when he discovered that water converted into steam <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> heat about six times its own weight of water at 47° or 48° to 212°. He mentioned this extraordinary fact to Dr Black, who then explained to him his doctrine of latent heat, to the support of which, Mr Watt had afterwards the satisfaction of contributing his experiments. From some of these he was led to suppose the latent heat of steam to be above 100°, but he afterwards considered 960° a more accurate determination. From others, he deduced the important conclusion, that the sum of the latent and sensible heat of steam, at different temperatures, is a constant quantity, the latent heat increasing as the sensible heat diminishes; or, in other words, that a given weight of water in the state of steam contains nearly the same quantity of heat, whatever may be the bulk or density of the steam. He also, at this time, made experiments upon the capacities of different bodies for heat, and upon the heats at which water boils under various pressures; from which he ascertained, that where the heats proceeded in an arithmetical, the elasticities proceeded in a geometrical ratio, the curve of which he laid down. These he repeated some years after with more accuracy. We have been thus minute in our details of the successive steps by which Mr Watt proceeded to his great improvement upon the principle of the steam-engine, in order to convey some idea of the sagacity, ingenuity, and science, with which he conducted the investigation. Our limits will oblige us to be more brief in our narrative of his subsequent improvements. From this period (the early <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of 1765), his mind became very much engaged in contriving the machinery for executing his improvement upon a large <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>; but the want of funds prevented his attempting it, until he was induced to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> himself to Dr Roebeck, who had a short time before completed his establishment of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARRON">Carron</a> Ironworks, and who, in addition to his known qualities of ingenuity and enterprise, was considered to be possessed of ample means of introducing the invention to the public. He agreed to enter into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, upon having the proceeds of two-thirds of the invention assigned to him; and an engine upon a large scale was then constructed by Mr Watt, at Kinnel, near <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BORROWSTOUNNESS">Borrowstounness</a>, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a> then resided; the trials made with which gave satisfaction. But the introduction of the invention to the public was retarded, on the one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, by the pecuniary difficulties in which the Doctor became involved, by the failure of several of his multifarious undertakings; and on the other, by the employment, which the rising reputation of Mr Watt, for knowledge and skill in the line of a civil engineer, procured him. He was employed, in 1767, to make a survey for a canal of junction between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Forth and Clyde, by what was called the Lomond passage, and attended <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">Parliament</a> on the part of the subscribers, where the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">bill</a> was lost. An offer was then made to him of undertaking the survey and estimate of an intended canal from the Monkland <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COLLIERIES">Collieries</a> to Glasgow; and these proving satisfactory, the superintendence of the execution was confided to him. This was quickly followed by his being employed by the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TRUSTEES">Trustees</a> for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">Fisheries</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">Manufactures</a> in Scotland, to make a survey of a canal from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PERTH">Perth</a> to Forfar, through Strathmore; and soon afterwards, by the Commissioners of the Annexed Estates, to furnish a report and estimate of the relative advantages of opening a communication between the Firth of Clyde and the Western Ocean, by means of a navigable canal across the isthmus of Crinan,* or that of Tarbert. Business of this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> now crowded upon him; and surveys, plans, and estimates, were successively undertaken by him for the harbours of Ayr, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PORT_GLASGOW">Port-Glasgow</a>, and Greenock; the deepening of the river Clyde; the rendering navigable the rivers Forth and Devon, and the water of Leven; the making of a canal from Machrihanish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> to Campbeltown, and of another between the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> Canal and the harbour of Borrowstounness; the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of bridges at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMILTON">Hamilton</a> and at Rutherglen, &c. &c. In these surveys he made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of a new micrometer, and a machine for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">perspective</a>, which he had invented to facilitate his operations. Our limits do not allow us to go into the details of his Reports, which are remarkable for their perspicuity and accuracy, although the work of a self-taught engineer. The last and greatest work upon which he was employed was the survey and estimate of the line of a canal between Fort-William and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERNESS">Inverness</a>, since executed by Mr Telford, upon a larger scale than was at that time proposed, under the name of the Caledonian Canal. Whilst engaged upon this survey, in the latter part of the year 1773, Mr Watt received the account of the death of his affectionate wife, leaving him a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> and a son. He appears soon after to have made up his mind to adopt the advice of his friend Dr Small of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRMINGHAM">Birmingham</a>, and the invitation of Mr Boulton, to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> in England. He had secured his title to his Improvements for saving Steam and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">Fuel</a> in Fire Engines, by patent, in the year 1769; but all hopes of carrying them into effect, by the assistance of Dr Roebeck, being at an end, he had induced that <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> to agree, for certain considerations, to transfer his share of the patent to Mr Boulton of Soho, near Birmingham—a gentleman equally distinguished by his knowledge of the arts, and his enterprising spirit, who had some years before established his manufactory upon a scale as unrivalled for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> and elegance, as for the variety and perfection of the processes carried on. In conjunction with him an application was made to Parliament for an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> of the patent, and an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> prolonging it for twenty-five years was obtained in the year 1775, when the business of making steam-engines was commenced by the firm of Boulton and Watt. Mr Watt now married for his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> wife Miss Macgrigor, the daughter of an old friend, at Glasgow, and devoted himself to the improvement of the details of the engine with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of application and exertion not to be expected from his delicate and infirm state of health; and he found in his partner a zealous and able coadjutor. Some engines for pumping water were soon made upon a large scale, and the savings in fuel were demonstrated by repeated comparative trials to amount to three-fourths of the quantity consumed by those of the best construction before in use. A <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPUTATION">deputation</a> from the mining <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of Cornwall was sent to ascertain the fact, and their report led to the introduction of the improved engines into that county, to which they have proved of such vast utility. The immediate application of the powers of steam to giving a rotary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a> had formed an early object of Mr Watt's attention, and he had deeply considered the various means of effecting this. One method of producing a continued movement in one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> was by a steam wheel, described in his patent of 1769. Various others of a similar kind suggested themselves to him, of some of which drawings and models were made; but the difficulty of rendering them steam and air-tight, and the loss of power by friction, induced him to turn his thoughts to the adaptation of the reciprocating motion to the production of a continued regular rotary one. This he accomplished by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of improvements, the exclusive property of which he secured by successive patents in the years 1781, 1782, 1784, and 1785; including, among other inventions, the rotary motion of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and planet <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a>,† the expansive principle, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> engine, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> motion, and the --- * The Crinan Canal was executed several years afterwards, under the direction of his friend Mr Rennie, with some variations. † Mr Watt had originally intended to derive the rotary motion from the working beam by means of a connecting rod and crank; but the workman employed to make the model communicated it to a neighbour. smokeless <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a>. The application of the centrifugal regulating force of the governor gave the finishing stroke to the machine. The invention of the separate condenser, and the contrivances necessary to give it full effect, would alone have established the fame of Mr Watt; but when to these are added the various inventions called forth to perfect his rotative engines, we are impressed by a union of philosophical research, of physical skill, and of mechanical ingenuity, which has, we believe, no parallel in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times. The perfection thus given to the rotative engine soon led to its general application for imparting motion to almost every <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of mill-work and machinery; and gave an impulse, unexampled in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of inventions, to the extension of our manufactures, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a>, and wealth. Nor were Mr Watt's inventive powers confined to the steam-engine. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of preserving accurate copies of his various drawings and of his letters, containing <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and important calculations; and the desire of avoiding that labour himself, which he did not think it <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to entrust to others, led him, in the year 1780, to contrive a copying <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a>, the exclusive property in which he secured by Letters Patent, and commenced the manufactory of them in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARTNERSHIP">partnership</a> with Mr Boulton, and his friend, Mr Keir, under the firm of James Watt and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a>—a contrivance of great simplicity, and of which he reaped an ample benefit in the time, labour, and expense it saved to himself, to say nothing of its advantages to the public. In the winter of 1784-5, he put up an apparatus for heating the room in which he drew and wrote by means of steam. The possibility of doing this we find suggested by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> Cooke in the Philosophical Transactions for 1745; but we know not whether this was known to Mr Watt when he made this first practical attempt, from which he deduced proportions of surface, &c., which afterwards served to guide his firm in the introduction of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> in larger buildings. Chemical studies engaged much of his attention during his busiest time, and at the very period when he was most engaged in perfecting his rotative engines, and in managing a business become considerable, and, from its <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a>, requiring <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> attention, he entered deeply into the investigations then in progress relative to the constitution and properties of the different gases. Early in 1783, he was led, by the experiments of his friend and neighbour, Dr Priestley, to the important conclusion, that water is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPHLOGISTICATED">dephlogisticated</a> and inflammable <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-AIRS">airs</a> (as they were then called) deprived of their latent or elementary heat, and he was the first to make known this theory. This was done in a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to Dr Priestley, dated the 28th April 1783, in which he states the Doctor's experiments to have come in aid of some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> notions of his own, and supports his conclusions by original experiments. That letter Dr Priestley received in London; and, after showing it to several members of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Society, he delivered it to Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Banks, with a request that it might be read at some of the public meetings of the Society; but before that could be complied with, Mr Watt, having heard of some new experiments made by Dr Priestley, begged that the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> might be delayed. Those new experiments soon afterwards proved to have been delusive, and Mr Watt sent a revised edition of his letter to Mr De Luc on the 26th November of the same year, which was not read to the Society until the 29th April 1784, and appears in the Philosophical Transactions for that year, under the title of Thoughts on the Constituent Parts of Water and of Dephlogisticated Air, with an Account of some Experiments upon that Subject. In the interim, on the 15th January 1784, a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> by Mr Cavendish had been read, containing his Experiments on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMBUSTION">Combustion</a> of the Dephlogisticated and Inflammable Airs, and drawing the same inference as Mr Watt; with this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> only, that he did not admit elementary heat into his explanation. He refers in it to his knowledge of Mr Watt's paper, and states his own experiments to have been made in 1781, and mentioned to Dr Priestley; but he does not say at what period he formed his conclusions; he only mentions that a friend of his had given some account of his experiments in the summer of 1783 to Mr Lavoisier, as well as of the conclusion drawn from them. It is quite certain, that Mr Watt had never heard of them; and Dr Blagden has stated, that he mentioned at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> the opinions of both the English philosophers, which were not admitted without hesitation, nor until the French chemists had satisfied themselves by experiments of their own.* Mr Watt also has the merit of being the first person to introduce into this country, and to carry into effect, on a practical scale, in any country, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLEACHING">bleaching</a> of linens and cottons by oxymuriatic acid, the invention of his friend, Mr Berthollet. That gentleman had communicated his invention to Mr Watt at Paris in the winter of 1786-7, whither he had proceeded with Mr Boulton at the instance of the French <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, to suggest improvements in the mode of raising water at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARLY">Marly</a>, and his mind was instantly alive to the extensive application of which it admitted. He advised Mr Berthollet to secure the property by an English patent; but that he declined, and left his friend to make such use of it * There is a confusion of dates in the accounts of this affair. Mr Watt's letter to Mr De Luc in the Philosophical Transactions appears dated 26th November 1784, which is evidently an error of the press. Mr Cavendish, in his letter, read 15th January 1784, speaks of Mr Watt's paper "as lately read before the Society," whereas the paper itself purports to have been read on the 29th April 1784. This we cannot explain. as he thought proper. He, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, communicated it to his father-in-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, Mr Macgrigor, and gave directions for the construction of the proper vessels and machinery; and soon after himself superintended the first trials at his bleachfield near Glasgow, which proved eminently successful. Some years after this, Mr Watt was led, by the illness of the daughter, and some apprehensions entertained for the son, who were the issue of his second marriage, to consider the subject of the medical application of the factitious airs, and to contrive various apparatuses for that purpose, which were described by himself, in his friend Dr Beddoes's publications on Pneumatic Medicine. We have not space to particularize other improvements introduced by Mr Watt, or at his suggestion, into various arts; for there were few arts with the details of which he was not intimately acquainted, and to the practical professors of which he was not able and willing to impart information. We shall only mention, that, before he left Glasgow to settle in England, he had assisted some of his friends in the establishment of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-POTTERY">pottery</a> there, to the success of which his experiments and advice had greatly contributed, and in which he afterwards continued a partner. At a later period, he occupied himself much upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, having the transparency, and nearly the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> of marble, from which he made many casts. This promoted, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it did not create a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a> and statuary, and led to his employing himself, during the last years of his life, in the contrivance of a machine for multiplying busts and other carved work, which he left in a very forward state. Mr Watt did not escape the common <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> of eminent men, that of meeting with pirates of his inventions, and detractors from his merit. The latter, indeed, were but few, and their efforts transitory; but the former were numerous, and in proportion to the benefits expected to arise from an evasion of the patent dues claimed by Boulton and Watt; though these were established upon the liberal footing of receiving only one-third of the savings of fuel compared with the best steam-engines previously in use. In consequence, the attention both of Mr Watt and of Mr Boulton was greatly occupied, from the year 1792 to the year 1799, in defending their patent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> against numerous invaders, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of whom were supported by a portion of the mining interest of Cornwall, although the respectable part of it refused to concur in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>. The admission of their respective sons into the partnership, in 1794, infused vigour into their proceedings; and, after repeated verdicts, establishing the novelty and utility of Mr Watt's inventions, the validity of his claim was finally confirmed in the year 1799 by the unanimous decision of all the Judges of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">Court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENCH">Bench</a>. In 1800, upon the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of the act of Parliament passed in his favour, he withdrew from business, resigning his shares to his two sons; of whom the youngest, Mr Gregory Watt, died soon after, having given splendid proofs of literary and philosophical talents, and left a durable record of the latter, in his paper On Basalt in the Philosophical Transactions. Mr Watt continued to the close of life to interest himself in the pursuits of his former associates, and to maintain an uninterrupted friendship with Mr Boulton, whom he survived several years. On two occasions afterwards, in 1811 and 1812, he gave proofs of the undiminished powers of his mind in his former profession. In the one instance, he was induced, by his grateful recollections of his residence in Glasgow, to assist the proprietors of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER_WORKS">water-works</a> there with a plan for supplying the town with better water, by means of a suction pipe, with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a>, laid across the bottom of the Clyde, accompanied with instructions for insuring the supply of water on the opposite side; a plan which answered completely, and for which the proprietors presented him with a handsome memorial of their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a>. In the other instance, he was prevailed upon by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> solicitation of the Lords Commissioners of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">Admiralty</a>, to attend a deputation of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">Navy</a> Board, and to give with his friend, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Huddart, and Mr J. Jessop, an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> upon the works then carrying on at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHEERNESS">Sheerness</a> Dockyard, and the farther ones projected by Messrs Rennie and Whidby; on which occasion, he no less gratified the gentlemen associated with him, by the clearness of his general views, than by his knowledge of the details, and received the thanks of the Admiralty. Mr Watt, also, at a still later period, in 1814, yielded to the wishes of his friends in undertaking a revision of Professor Robison's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> on Steam and Steam-Engines in the Encyclopaedia Britannica; and enriched them with valuable notes, containing his own experiments upon steam, and a short history of his principal improvements upon the engine itself. His originally infirm health had been subjected to severe trials by the great exertions of his mind, during the period of carrying into execution his improvements on the steam-engine, and had with difficulty resisted the cares and anxieties attending upon business, and those created by the subtleties of the law, during the protracted proceedings of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> long years. There appears to have been an organic defect in his digestion, and its effects were intensely severe sick headaches; but, by continual <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a> and good management of his constitution, which he treated with much medical skill, it improved as he advanced in years; and with faculties little impaired he reached his 84th year, when, after a short illness, rather of debility than of pain, he expired in the bosom of his family at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> at Heathfield, in the county of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFFORD">Stafford</a>, on the 25th August 1819. His remains are deposited in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCEL">chancel</a> of the adjoining parochial church of Handsworth, near those of Mr Boulton. An excellent bust had been made of him, some years before his death, by Mr Chantry, and a statue is now nearly finished by the same great <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>; intended by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FILIAL">filial</a> piety to be placed upon his tomb, and to convey to distant ages a faithful representation of those features in which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of intense thought were blended with the mild <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of benevolence. Mr Watt was elected a member of the Royal Society of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> in 1784; of the Royal Society of London in 1785; and a corresponding member of the Batavian Society in 1787. In 1806, the hono- rary degree of Doctor of Laws was conferred upon him by the spontaneous and unanimous vote of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">Senate</a> of the University of Glasgow; and in 1808, he was elected first a corresponding, and afterwards a foreign member of the Institute of France. In this brief narrative of his long, busy, and useful life, we have endeavoured to confine ourselves to a statement of the principal facts, and shall now add the Character drawn up, soon after his death, by a distinguished writer, who knew him well, and enjoyed a large portion of his esteem. "It is with pain that we find ourselves called upon, so soon after the loss of Mr Playfair, to record the decease of another of our illustrious countrymen, and one to whom mankind has been still more largely indebted—Mr James Watt, the great improver of the steam-engine. "This name fortunately needs no commemoration of ours; for he that bore it survived to see it crowned with undisputed and unenvied honours; and many generations will probably <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> away before it shall have 'gathered all its fame.' We have said that Mr Watt was the great improver of the steam-engine; but, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, as to all that is admirable in its structure, or vast in its utility, he should rather be described as its inventor. It was by his inventions that its action was so regulated as to make it capable of being applied to the finest and most delicate manufactures, and its power so increased as to set weight and solidity at defiance. By his admirable contrivances, it has become a thing stupendous alike for its force and its flexibility,—for the prodigious power which it can exert, and the ease, and precision, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCTILITY">ductility</a>, with which it can be varied, distributed, and applied. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> of an elephant that can pick up a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PIN">pin</a> or rend an oak is as nothing to it. It can engrave a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>, and crush masses of obdurate metal like wax before it,—draw out, without breaking, a thread as fine as gossamer, and lift a ship of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> like a bauble in the air. It can embroider muslin and forge anchors,—cut <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> into ribbands, and impel loaded vessels against the fury of the winds and waves. "It would be difficult to estimate the value of the benefits which these inventions have conferred upon the country. There is no branch of industry that has not been indebted to them; and in all the most material, they have not only widened most magnificently the field of its exertions, but multiplied a thousandfold the amount of its productions. It is our improved steam-engine that has fought the battles of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and exalted and sustained, through the late tremendous contest, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> greatness of our <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>. It is the same great power which now enables us to pay the interest of our debt, and to maintain the arduous struggle in which we are still engaged, with the skill and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of countries less oppressed with <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-TAXATION">taxation</a>. But these are <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and narrow views of its importance. It has increased indefinitely the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> comforts and enjoyments, and rendered cheap and accessible all over the world the materials of wealth and prosperity. It has armed the feeble hand of man, in short, with a power to which no limits can be assigned, completed the dominion of mind over the most refractory qualities of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, and laid a sure foundation for all those future <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a> of mechanic power which are to aid and reward the labours of after generations. It is to the genius of one man, too, that all this is mainly owing; and certainly no man ever before bestowed such a gift on his kind. The blessing is not only universal, but unbounded; and the fabled inventors of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a> and the loom, who were deified by the erring gratitude of their rude contemporaries, conferred less important benefits on mankind than the inventor of our present steam-engine. "This will be the fame of Watt with future generations; and it is sufficient for his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> and his country. But to those to whom he more immediately belonged, who lived in his society, and enjoyed his conversation, it is not perhaps the character in which he will be most frequently recalled—most deeply lamented—or even most highly admired. Independently of his great attainments in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>, Mr Watt was an extraordinary, and in many respects a wonderful man. Perhaps no individual in his age possessed so much and such varied and exact information,—had read so much, or remembered what he had read so accurately and well. He had infinite quickness of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a>, a prodigious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, and a certain rectifying and methodising power of understanding, which extracted something precious out of all that was presented to it. His stores of miscellaneous knowledge were immense,—and yet less astonishing than the command he had at all times over them. It seemed as if every subject that was casually started in conversation with him, had been that which he had been last occupied in studying and exhausting;—such was the copiousness, the precision, and the admirable clearness of the information which he poured out upon it without effort or hesitation. Nor was this promptitude and compass of knowledge confined in any degree to the studies connected with his ordinary pursuits. That he should have been minutely and extensively skilled in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a> and the arts, and in most of the branches of physical science, might perhaps have been conjectured; but it could not have been inferred from his usual occupations, and probably is not generally known, that he was curiously learned in many branches of antiquity, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METAPHYSICS">metaphysics</a>, medicine, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ETYMOLOGY">etymology</a>, and perfectly at home in all the details of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, music, and law. He was well acquainted, too, with most of the modern languages—and familiar with their most recent literature. Nor was it at all extraordinary to hear the great mechanician and engineer detailing and expounding, for hours together, the metaphysical theories of the German logicians, or criticising the measures or the matter of the German <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. "His astonishing memory was aided, no doubt, in a great measure, by a still higher and rarer <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a>—by his power of digesting and arranging in its proper place all the information he received, and of casting aside and rejecting, as it were instinctively, whatever was worthless or immaterial. Every <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a> that was suggested to his mind seemed instantly to take its place among its other rich furniture, and to be condensed into the smallest and most convenient form. He never appeared, therefore, to be at all encumbered or perplexed with the verbiage of the dull books he perused, or the idle talk to which he listened; but to have at once extracted, by a kind of intellectual <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALCHEMY">alchemy</a>, all that was worthy of attention, and to have reduced it for his own use, to its true value and to its simplest form. And thus it often happened that a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> more was learned from his brief and vigorous account of the theories and arguments of tedious writers, than an ordinary student could ever have derived from the most faithful <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the originals,—and that errors and absurdities became manifest from the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> clearness and plainness of his statement of them, which might have deluded and perplexed most of his hearers without that invaluable assistance. "It is needless to say, that, with those vast resources, his conversation was at all times rich and instructive in no ordinary degree; but it was, if possible, still more pleasing than wise, and had all the charms of familiarity, with all the substantial treasures of knowledge. No man could be more social in his spirit, less assuming or fastidious in his manners, or more kind and indulgent towards all who approached him. He rather liked to talk,—at least in his later years; but though he took a considerable share of the conversation, he rarely suggested the topics on which it was to turn, but readily and quietly took up whatever was presented by those around him, and astonished the idle and barren propounders of an ordinary theme, by the treasures which he drew from the mine they had unconsciously opened. He generally seemed, indeed, to have no choice or predilection for one subject of discourse rather than another; but allowed his mind, like a great cyclopedia, to be opened at any letter his associates might choose to turn up, and only endeavoured to select from his inexhaustible stores what might be best adapted to the taste of his present hearers. As to their capacity he gave himself no trouble; and, indeed, such was his singular talent for making all things plain, clear, and intelligible, that scarcely any one could be aware of such a deficiency in his presence. His talk, too, though overflowing with information, had no resemblance to lecturing or solemn discoursing, but, on the contrary, was full of colloquial spirit and pleasantry. He had a certain quiet and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> humour, which ran through most of his conversation, and a vein of temperate jocularity, which gave infinite zest and effect to the condensed and inexhaustible information, which formed its main staple and characteristic. There was a little air of affected testiness, and a tone of pretended rebuke and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a>, with which he used to address his younger friends, that was always felt by them as an endearing mark of his kindness and familiarity,—and prized accordingly, far beyond all the solemn compliments that ever proceeded from the lips of authority. His <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> was deep and powerful,—though he <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> spoke in a low and somewhat monotonous tone, which harmonised admirably with the weight and brevity of his observations, and set off to the greatest advantage the pleasant anecdotes which he delivered with the same grave brow and the same calm smile playing soberly on his lips. There was nothing of effort, indeed, or impatience, any more than of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> or levity, in his demeanour; and there was a finer expression of reposing strength, and mild self-possession in his manner, than we ever recollect to have met with in any other person. He had in his character the utmost abhorrence for all sorts of forwardness, parade, and pretension; and, indeed, never failed to put all such impostors out of countenance, by the manly plainness and honest intrepidity of his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> and deportment. "In his temper and dispositions he was not only kind and affectionate, but generous, and considerate of the feelings of all around him, and gave the most liberal assistance and encouragement to all young persons who showed any indications of talent, or applied to him for <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> or advice. His health, which was delicate from his youth upwards, seemed to become firmer as he advanced in years; and he preserved, up almost to the last moment of his existence, not only the full command of his extraordinary intellect, but all the alacrity of spirit, and the social gaiety which had illuminated his happiest days. His friends in this part of the country never <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> him more full of intellectual vigour and colloquial <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANIMATION">animation</a>,—never more delightful or more instructive than in his last visit to Scotland in autumn 1817. Indeed, it was after that time that he applied himself, with all the ardour of early life, to the invention of a machine for mechanically copying all sorts of sculpture and statuary,—and distributed among his friends some of its earliest performances, as the productions of a young artist <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> entering on his 83d year. "This happy and useful life came at last to a gentle close. He had suffered some inconvenience through the summer; but was not seriously indisposed till within a few weeks from his death. He then became perfectly aware of the event which was approaching; and with his usual tranquillity and benevolence of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, seemed only anxious to point out to the friends around him the many sources of consolation which were afforded by the circumstances under which it was about to take place. He expressed his sincere gratitude to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> for the length of days with which he had been blessed, and his exemption from most of the infirmities of age, as well as for the calm and cheerful evening of life that he had been permitted to enjoy, after the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> labours of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> had been concluded. And thus, full of years and honours, in all calmness and tranquillity, he yielded up his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, without pang or struggle,—and passed from the bosom of his family to that of his God! "He was twice married, but has left no issue but one son, long associated with him in his business and studies, and two grandchildren by a daughter who predeceased him. He was a Fellow of the Royal <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">Societies</a> both of London and Edinburgh, and one of the few Englishmen who were elected members of the National Institute of France. All men of learning and science were his cordial friends; and such was the influence of his mild character and perfect fairness and liberality, even upon the pretenders to

WEIGHTS AND MEASURES

Pages 848-861

The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">bill</a> for ascertaining and establishing Uniformity of Weights and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">Measures</a>, which passed the Imperial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">House</a> of Commons in the Session of 1823, not having been carried through the House of Lords, the subject has less immediate <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> at the present moment than there has been every reason to suppose, for a few years past, that it would by this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> have acquired. But there is little doubt that the discussion <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be revived either in the Upper <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the Lower House of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">Parliament</a> before many more months have elapsed; and it seems to be highly improbable that any insuperable difficulties should stand in the way of its ultimate success. This presumption is founded on no hasty view of the subject in question, but upon a laborious and somewhat painful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of the historical progress of the measures which have been taken respecting it, and especially of the laws of England respecting uniformity of practice in different parts of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; a uniformity which, though generally esteemed by all governments a thing to be encouraged and enforced, has often proved to be no more subjected to the control of legislative enactment, than the introduction of a uniformity of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> and a grammatical accuracy of speech would be found in every <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of an extensive empire. Augustus is said to have endeavoured in vain to force a new Latin word into the language of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Rome; the French, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, after all their labours to recommend a uniform system of measures, have ended in such a complication, that for the most simple purposes of practical <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a> and civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, it is become usual to carry in the pocket a little ruler, in the form of a triangular prism, one of the sides containing the old established <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> and inches of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> foot, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> the millimetres, centimetres, and decimetres of the revolutionary school, and the third the new ultraroyal <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of the Jacobin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, with the royal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>, the inches consisting each of the 36th part of a metre, or the four millionth of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of the meridian of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> such occurrences as these be calmly considered, they will make us more disposed to diminish than to increase the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of penal statutes intended to compel the inhabitants of the different parts of a country to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> their own convenience conjointly with that of their neighbours, and to spare themselves the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of a few arithmetical operations in the course of every market <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; and we shall feel that it is more incumbent on a wise <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> to endeavour to facilitate both the attainment of correct and uniform standards of legal existing measures of all kinds, and the ready understanding of all the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> and local terms applied to measures, either regular or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>, by the multiplication of glossaries and tables for the correct <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of such terms. Measures have apparently always been derived, in the first instance, from some part of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> person; a foot, a pace, a fathom, the orgyia or stretch of the arms, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUBIT">cubit</a>, a palm, and a finger; these have probably all been used in the earlier states of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> by each individual from the magnitude of his own person; and afterwards a standard measure has been established by authority from the real or supposed magnitude of the person of some <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a>, in order for the attainment of more perfect uniformity in practice; though it is said, that in some parts of the East the Arabs still measure the cubits of their cloth by the fore arm, with the addition of the breadth of the other hand, which serves to mark the end of the measure, as the thumb which was formerly added at the end of the yard by the English clothiers. It ought not, however, to be forgotten, that any one of these terms possesses an advantage, for popular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> and for the convenience of future ages and of remote countries, which would be lost by the introduction of any more arbitrary measurement; thus a hand's breadth, or a foot, is always sufficiently understood, without any definition, to enable us to form to ourselves a tolerable accurate <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of the magnitude intended to be described; and there is scarcely an instance of the caprice of denomination having ever extended so far as to make the measure called a foot in any country so small as half a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> foot, or so <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> as two feet of an ordinary person, and certainly not of its amounting to three ordinary feet; while a metre, even to those who know that the word implies a measure, might as well have meant a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a>, or an inch, or a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-QUART">quart</a>, as a length somewhat greater than a yard. The idea of accurately verifying the standard of a country by any other means, than that of a comparison with some actually existing original, can scarcely have occurred, except in a very advanced <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of the progress of civilisation. It was indeed enacted, in the time of our Henry the Third, that an ounce should be the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of 640 dry grains of wheat taken from the middle of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a>, that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> should be twelve ounces, a gallon of wine eight pounds, and eight gallons of wine a bushel of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; but this seems rather a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> for making a single standard than a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> intended for the continual verification of the standard in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of any minute uncertainty.
